questions.stem: Which action BEST meets minimum patient identification practice before starting EEG?
options: Confirm identity by face and the room number only
Match name and date of birth to the written order
Ask the caregiver to state the name, then proceed
Confirm identity once the electrodes are applied
questions.explanation: Matching two identifiers (for example full name and date of birth) to the order before starting reduces wrong-patient procedures. Face recognition and room number are not reliable identifiers, a caregiver statement alone is a single unverified identifier, and confirming identity after hookup is too late.

questions.stem: An EEG order is missing the clinical indication. The MOST appropriate technologist action is:
options: Proceed, since the indication is not needed
Enter an indication based on your impression
Clarify the indication with the ordering provider
Postpone the study until a new order is issued
questions.explanation: The clinical indication guides recording strategy, so the technologist should clarify it with the ordering provider and record the clarification. Proceeding ignores information that shapes the study, inventing an indication is fabrication, and postponing for a new order delays care when a simple clarification suffices.

questions.stem: The order reads 'routine EEG' but the patient is actively convulsing in the ED. The technologist should:
options: Record it as a routine EEG exactly as ordered
Begin with photic stimulation to capture events
Wait until it stops, then begin a routine hookup
Get urgent medical help and follow emergency steps
questions.explanation: An actively convulsing patient is a medical emergency: the technologist should obtain immediate physician evaluation and follow the lab's urgent/emergency protocol. Running a routine study ignores the emergency, photic stimulation is inappropriate during a convulsion, and waiting without escalation delays treatment of possible status epilepticus.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST documentation when patient identity was initially mismatched but corrected before recording?
options: Record the mismatch and how it was resolved
Leave it out, since it was fixed before recording
Replace the order and leave no explanation
Mention it verbally to the reader afterward
questions.explanation: Documenting the discrepancy, how it was resolved and that correct identifiers were confirmed supports safety, auditability and continuity of care. Omitting it hides a safety event, replacing the order without explanation breaks the audit trail, and a verbal mention leaves no permanent record.

questions.stem: Which element MOST directly supports legal defensibility of the EEG record?
options: A longer recording regardless of quality
Accurate identifiers and time-stamped entries
A notch filter applied to every recording
One standard montage used for the whole study
questions.explanation: Accurate patient identifiers and time-stamped documentation of key actions are the core of a medicolegally defensible record. Recording length does not compensate for poor quality, routine notch use is a technical choice that can mask problems, and montage choice does not affect legal defensibility.

questions.stem: Which environment factor MOST commonly contributes to non-cerebral electrical artifact during EEG?
options: Dim lighting kept on during the recording
A soft pillow placed under the patient's knees
Nearby powered equipment and poor grounding
A cotton blanket placed over the patient
questions.explanation: Nearby powered devices and poor grounding are the most common environmental sources of non-cerebral electrical artifact such as line noise. Dim lighting, a knee pillow and a cotton blanket do not introduce electrical interference; comfort measures usually reduce movement artifact.

questions.stem: Before taking the EEG cart into an isolation room, the FIRST priority is to:
options: Check that the montage settings are loaded
Confirm that the photic stimulator works
Turn the notch filter on before entering
Prepare PPE and follow isolation precautions
questions.explanation: Infection-control compliance comes first when entering an isolation room: prepare the correct PPE and follow the isolation requirements for the cart and supplies. Loading montages, testing the photic stimulator and setting filters are technical steps that do not protect the patient, staff or equipment from transmission.

questions.stem: A new 50/60 Hz artifact appears after plugging the cart into a different outlet. BEST next step:
options: Check ground, outlet, and nearby devices first
Turn on the notch filter as the first step
Raise the low-frequency filter setting
Lower sensitivity until the noise is gone
questions.explanation: New line-frequency artifact after changing outlets points to a grounding or environmental source, so check ground integrity, the outlet, nearby devices and leads first. The notch filter only attenuates the symptom and can distort EEG, the low-frequency filter acts on slow activity, and lowering sensitivity hides cerebral activity as well as the noise.

questions.stem: Which practice MOST helps prevent 'electrode pop' artifact?
options: Display the study at a faster sweep speed
Good skin prep and securely anchored leads
Set the high-frequency filter to 15 Hz
Use an average reference montage only
questions.explanation: Electrode pop comes from unstable electrode-skin contact, so careful skin prep, secure attachment and stable, anchored leads prevent it. Sweep speed, a lower HFF and montage choice only change how the recording is displayed; they do not prevent the sudden contact changes that cause pops.

questions.stem: Which item is MOST essential to confirm before starting recording?
options: That the patient is likely to fall asleep
That the room has a window for daylight
Adequate storage space on the EEG system
That the video camera is set to color
questions.explanation: Insufficient storage can stop or corrupt the recording and compromise the whole study, so it must be confirmed before starting. Sleep is helpful but not guaranteed or essential, daylight is irrelevant, and color video is a preference rather than an essential pre-recording check.

questions.stem: Effective patient rapport MOST directly reduces which recording problem?
options: ECG artifact from the heartbeat
Line noise from nearby equipment
Slowed posterior dominant rhythm
Movement artifact from anxiety
questions.explanation: Good rapport calms the patient, reducing behavioral and movement artifact and improving tolerance of activation procedures. ECG artifact is cardiac in origin, line noise is environmental, and the PDR frequency is a cerebral feature that rapport does not change.

questions.stem: A patient is fearful that electrodes 'shock'. BEST response:
options: Explain that electrodes only record brain signals
Explain that the current is too small to be felt
Reassure them that the EEG result will be normal
Proceed, as the worry usually passes once started
questions.explanation: EEG electrodes only record the brain's electrical activity and deliver no current, so explaining this and answering questions reduces anxiety and artifact. Saying the current is too small to feel wrongly implies current is delivered, promising a normal result is inappropriate, and proceeding without addressing the concern ignores the patient.

questions.stem: For a child with ASD who resists touch, the BEST approach is to:
options: Apply electrodes quickly while staff hold the child
Stepwise desensitization with caregiver help and breaks
Request sedation before any attempt at hookup
Apply only a few electrodes to shorten the hookup
questions.explanation: Stepwise desensitization, caregiver involvement and planned breaks improve success and reduce distress in children with ASD while keeping the child safe. Restraint increases distress and movement, sedation is not the first approach before accommodations are tried, and a reduced electrode set compromises the study.

questions.stem: Which is MOST appropriate documentation of patient cooperation?
options: "Patient was difficult and uncooperative throughout study"
"Uncooperative patient; overall study quality likely poor"
"Limited cooperation; HV not completed; frequent movement"
"Behavior noted as typical for this type of patient here"
questions.explanation: Objective, specific descriptions of cooperation (what was or was not completed and what behaviors occurred) support interpretation and professionalism. The other notes are subjective or judgmental and do not tell the reader what actually happened or how it affected the recording.

questions.stem: The technologist should encourage patient questions primarily to:
options: Replace the need for obtaining formal consent
Reduce the time needed for taking a history
Lengthen the recording for better sampling
Improve understanding, comfort, and cooperation
questions.explanation: Encouraging questions improves the patient's understanding and comfort, which improves cooperation and safety. Questions do not replace formal consent, do not shorten history-taking, and are not a method of extending recording time.

questions.stem: Which instruction MOST improves yield for a sleep-deprived EEG?
options: Use hair oil before the test
Avoid sleep prior to the study as directed
Stop all medications without advice
Skip meals before the test
questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation increases likelihood of sleep during recording.

questions.stem: A patient asks whether to stop antiseizure medication before EEG. BEST response:
options: Follow the ordering provider's instructions
Stop it 24 hours before to improve the yield
Skip the morning dose only on the test day
Take a double dose the night before the test
questions.explanation: Medication changes are directed by the ordering provider; usual antiseizure medication is generally continued unless the provider directs otherwise. Stopping it or skipping a dose on the technologist's advice risks seizures, and doubling a dose risks toxicity; none is the technologist's decision.

questions.stem: Which is MOST important to include when explaining photic stimulation?
options: It commonly triggers a seizure in most people
Flashing light is used, and they may ask to stop
It stimulates the brain with a mild current
Their eyes must stay open for the whole test
questions.explanation: Patients should know photic stimulation uses flashing light to assess the brain's response, may rarely provoke abnormalities, and can be stopped at their request. It does not trigger seizures in most people, no current is applied, and flashes are delivered with eyes open and closed at different stages.

questions.stem: Which consent-related statement is MOST accurate?
options: Consent is implied once a doctor orders the EEG
Refusal can be overridden if the patient is anxious
Patients may refuse, and refusal must be respected
A family member may override an adult's refusal
questions.explanation: Competent patients have the right to refuse, and the refusal must be respected and documented per policy. A physician order does not replace consent, anxiety is not grounds for overriding refusal, and a family member cannot override a competent adult's decision.

questions.stem: Pre-test hair preparation is important primarily because:
options: It changes seizure frequency
It reduces impedance and improves signal quality
It makes photic stimulation stronger
It increases PDR frequency
questions.explanation: Clean scalp/hair improves electrode contact and signal quality.

questions.stem: Which history element is MOST important to document for event correlation?
options: Family history of seizures in relatives
Date of the patient's first diagnosis
Dates of the patient's prior EEG studies
Time and description of the last event
questions.explanation: The timing and semiology of the most recent event guide event correlation and recording strategy. Family history, date of first diagnosis and prior EEG dates are useful background but do not help correlate current events with the recording.

questions.stem: Medication documentation is MOST complete when it includes:
options: Name only
Dose and time of last dose
Color of tablet
Cost and manufacturer
questions.explanation: Dose/timing affect EEG background and yield.

questions.stem: Which history item MOST helps assess HV safety?
options: Cardiopulmonary disease or a recent stroke
Handedness and language dominance history
Time of the last meal before the test
Family history of photosensitive epilepsy
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation screening looks for contraindications such as significant cardiopulmonary disease, recent stroke or sickle cell disease, applied per lab policy. Handedness is relevant to lateralization, meal timing affects the HV response (hypoglycemia) rather than safety, and photosensitivity relates to photic stimulation.

questions.stem: A patient had a seizure 'sometime last week' with unclear details. BEST documentation approach:
options: Enter an exact date that seems most likely
Note it as uncertain with the best description
Leave the last-event field blank until later
Record a definite seizure type for clarity
questions.explanation: Accurate records include uncertainty: note that the timing is uncertain and obtain the best available description from the patient, caregiver or records. Entering a guessed date or a definite seizure type is fabrication, and leaving the field blank loses information that is available.

questions.stem: Documenting skull defects is important because it can:
options: Increase PDR frequency
Alter amplitude/field and affect localization
Eliminate artifact
Guarantee epileptiform discharges
questions.explanation: Skull defects can change recorded amplitude and field distribution.

questions.stem: Which statement is MOST accurate about electrode placement?
options: If impedance is low, placement accuracy is guaranteed
10–20 measurement accuracy is required for reliable localization
Placement can be estimated if the patient is asleep
Electrode location does not affect interpretation
questions.explanation: Localization depends on accurate 10–20 placement.

questions.stem: Persistently similar waveforms across adjacent channels with unusually low impedances MOST suggests:
options: Mu rhythm
Electrode bridging
Photoparoxysmal response
Hyperventilation effect
questions.explanation: Bridging electrically connects electrodes and distorts localization.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST practice for managing electrode impedances during a routine EEG?
options: Check them once at hookup, then rely on the tracing afterwards
Bring all sites to acceptable values and recheck after movement
Accept higher values when the notch filter clears the line noise
Recheck them only at the end, just before the electrodes come off
questions.explanation: Impedances should be brought to acceptable, balanced values and rechecked whenever the patient moves or artifact appears, because contact changes during a study. A single check at hookup misses later deterioration; using the notch filter masks a contact problem instead of fixing it; checking only at the end is too late to improve the recording.

questions.stem: A reference electrode becomes intermittently loose. The MOST likely effect is:
options: Artifact confined to the single channel nearest that electrode
No visible change, since common-mode rejection cancels it out
Artifact limited to the bipolar channels on the same side
Artifact in all referential channels, possibly false asymmetry
questions.explanation: In a referential montage every channel uses the reference as its second input, so an unstable reference contaminates all of those channels at once and can create false asymmetries. It is not confined to one channel; common-mode rejection does not cancel a fault in one input; and bipolar channels do not use the reference, so they would be the ones unaffected.

questions.stem: Which documentation is MOST helpful if a non-standard electrode position was used?
options: An annotation on the recording and a note of the new position
A verbal note to the reader at handoff, with no written record
Renaming the electrode to the nearest standard 10-20 label
A note on the requisition form, kept apart from the recording
questions.explanation: Any deviation from standard placement should be annotated on the recording and described in the technical notes so the reader localizes correctly. Verbal handoff is lost; relabeling to a standard name hides the deviation and causes mislocalization; a note kept apart from the recording may never reach the interpreter.

questions.stem: Which change MOST likely attenuates slow waves and masks diffuse slowing?
options: Lowering the high-frequency filter too far
Turning on the 60 Hz notch filter throughout
Switching to a faster display sweep speed
Raising the low-frequency filter too high
questions.explanation: Raising the low-frequency (high-pass) filter attenuates delta and theta, so diffuse slowing can look less prominent. Lowering the HFF attenuates fast activity, not slow waves; the notch acts on a narrow band around line frequency; a faster sweep speed spreads waves horizontally but does not reduce their amplitude.

questions.stem: Which change can make the EEG APPEAR to have higher-frequency activity without changing true cerebral frequency?
options: Slowing the paper (sweep) speed
Lowering the low-frequency filter
Turning the notch filter off
Reducing the sensitivity slightly
questions.explanation: Slowing the paper speed (e.g. 30 to 15 mm/s, or more seconds per screen) compresses each wave horizontally, so activity looks faster although the true frequency is unchanged. Lowering the LFF lets more slow activity through rather than making waves look faster; turning the notch off only lets line-frequency noise back in; changing sensitivity alters amplitude, not apparent frequency.

questions.stem: The notch filter is BEST used when:
options: When line noise persists after the source has been addressed
Routinely at the start of each recording to prevent noise
When spikes need to look sharper for easier identification
When slow activity must be reduced for a steadier baseline
questions.explanation: The notch filter attenuates a narrow band at line frequency but can distort sharp components, so it is a fallback after correcting the noise source. Routine use hides contact problems; it does not sharpen spikes (it can blunt them); and it does not act on slow activity, which is the domain of the low-frequency filter.

questions.stem: Reducing sensitivity (higher µV/mm) MOST likely causes:
options: Spikes to look taller and sharper relative to the background
Line-frequency noise to become more prominent in all channels
Low-amplitude activity to look smaller and be under-recognized
Slow waves to appear faster across the whole page of EEG
questions.explanation: A higher µV/mm value means each millimeter represents more voltage, so everything is drawn smaller and low-amplitude activity can be missed. Spikes are drawn shorter, not taller; noise is scaled down with the signal rather than increased; and sensitivity changes the vertical scale only, not frequency.

questions.stem: Which setting change MOST risks distorting spike morphology?
options: A slightly faster paper speed
An excessively low high-frequency filter
A slightly higher sensitivity
A slightly higher low-frequency filter
questions.explanation: An overly low HFF (aggressive low-pass filtering) attenuates the fast components of sharp transients, so spikes look blunted and rounded and may be mistaken for sharp waves or slow activity. A faster paper speed spreads waves out without changing their shape in the signal; a small sensitivity change alters amplitude only; a modestly higher LFF mainly attenuates slow activity, not the sharp rising edge of a spike.

questions.stem: Why are montage changes important during routine EEG?
options: They help clarify localization and confirm suspected discharges
They improve the signal-to-noise ratio of each recorded channel
They lower electrode impedance by re-routing the amplifier inputs
They replace the need for hyperventilation and photic stimulation
questions.explanation: Viewing the same data in several montages shows the field and phase relationships of a discharge, which helps localize it and separate true discharges from artifact. Montage choice does not change the recorded signal-to-noise ratio or electrode impedance (those depend on contact and amplifiers), and it does not substitute for activation procedures.

questions.stem: Phase reversal in a bipolar montage is MOST useful for:
options: Confirming impedances
Identifying the site of maximal negativity
Eliminating artifacts automatically
Diagnosing epilepsy subtype
questions.explanation: Phase reversal helps localize maximal negativity.

questions.stem: A sharp transient appears in only one channel of a referential montage. BEST next step:
options: Mark it as epileptiform, since referential views localize well
Turn on the notch filter and reassess the channel morphology
Review other montages for a field and look for artifact sources
Repeat hyperventilation to see if the transient recurs
questions.explanation: A transient confined to one electrode with no field is suspicious for artifact (for example electrode pop), so the next step is to check other montages for a physiologic field and phase reversal and to inspect that electrode. Calling it epileptiform is premature; the notch filter only addresses line noise; repeating HV does not answer whether this event was artifact.

questions.stem: Which montage often helps detect lateralized slowing most clearly?
options: A Cz reference montage that refers every electrode to vertex
A single-hemisphere montage showing only the affected side
A bipolar longitudinal montage that pairs homologous chains
A montage with every electrode referred to the left ear
questions.explanation: Longitudinal bipolar chains laid out left and right in parallel allow direct comparison of homologous regions, which shows lateralized slowing well. A Cz reference can be contaminated by central activity; a one-sided montage gives nothing to compare against; a single-ear reference contaminates the ipsilateral side and creates false asymmetries.

questions.stem: Recording strategy should be modified primarily based on:
options: Technologist preference and habit
The time of day the study is booked
Patient age, condition, and indication
Which activation equipment is free
questions.explanation: Recording strategy (montages, activation, duration, sleep) is tailored to the patient's age and clinical condition and to the question asked by the referral. Personal preference, the time the study is booked, or which equipment happens to be free are logistical factors that should not drive the strategy.

questions.stem: Hyperventilation was omitted due to poor cooperation. What should be done?
options: Leave HV out of the notes, since no HV data exist
Substitute a longer photic run labeled as activation
Note in the record that HV was omitted and why
Have the patient do HV later while drowsy or asleep
questions.explanation: When an activation procedure is not performed, the technical record should state that it was omitted and the reason (here, poor cooperation) so the reader does not assume a normal HV response. Leaving it out invites a wrong assumption; photic stimulation is a different activation and cannot be relabeled as HV; HV cannot be performed meaningfully in drowsiness or sleep.

questions.stem: Which response during photic stimulation is MOST expected in normal subjects?
options: Photoparoxysmal response
Photic driving at some frequencies
Generalized 3 Hz spike-wave
Continuous rhythmic delta activity
questions.explanation: Photic driving is a normal physiologic response.

questions.stem: During HV a patient becomes very dizzy, unsteady, and says they feel faint. BEST action:
options: Reassure the patient and continue HV to the full 3 minutes
Pause HV for 30 seconds, then resume until 3 minutes are done
Stop HV, attend to the patient, and note symptoms and duration
Stop HV, then restart it later to achieve the full 3 minutes
questions.explanation: Marked dizziness with near-syncope is a reason to end HV: stop, attend to the patient, and record the symptoms and how long HV was performed. Mild lightheadedness is common, but continuing or resuming after near-faint symptoms puts the patient at risk; restarting later to complete 3 minutes repeats the provocation without clinical need.

questions.stem: Sleep was ordered but not achieved. BEST technical note is:
options: Sleep attempted but not achieved, with the reason stated
No comment on sleep, since none was actually recorded
Sleep recorded, as the patient appeared drowsy at times
Brief sleep obtained, based on eye closure and stillness
questions.explanation: The record must reflect the true state: sleep was attempted, not achieved, and why, so the reader knows sleep-activated findings could not be assessed. Omitting it lets the reader assume sleep was not requested; drowsiness is not sleep; eye closure and stillness without EEG sleep features do not establish sleep.

questions.stem: Eye opening/closure is performed primarily to assess:
options: Cardiac rhythm
Background reactivity
HV contraindications
Electrode impedance
questions.explanation: Eye opening and closure test background reactivity: the posterior dominant rhythm should attenuate with eye opening and return on closure, which also helps identify it. ECG shows cardiac rhythm, contraindications to HV come from the history, and impedance is measured with the impedance meter.

questions.stem: High-frequency 'fuzzy' activity that increases with jaw clenching MOST suggests:
options: Cerebral beta
Muscle artifact (EMG)
PDR
Delta slowing
questions.explanation: EMG increases with muscle tension.

questions.stem: A rhythmic waveform time-locked to the QRS complex most likely represents:
options: Seizure activity
ECG artifact
Mu rhythm
Photic driving
questions.explanation: ECG artifact can contaminate EEG channels.

questions.stem: Which is the BEST practice for 60 Hz line noise?
options: Keep the notch on for every study so the tracing stays clean
Raise the low-frequency filter until the 60 Hz noise is reduced
Correct the source first; use the notch only if still needed
Lower the high-frequency filter to 15 Hz before checking leads
questions.explanation: Line noise usually reflects a technical problem (poor contact, high or unbalanced impedance, a bad ground, nearby equipment), so the source should be corrected first and the notch used only if noise persists, since the notch can distort sharp activity. Routine notch use hides contact problems; the LFF acts on slow frequencies, not 60 Hz; dropping the HFF to 15 Hz attenuates spikes and skips troubleshooting.

questions.stem: Sweat artifact typically appears as:
options: Slow baseline drift that eases with cooling and drying
Fast, low-voltage spikes over both temporal regions
Sharp, regular transients time-locked to the heartbeat
Abrupt, steep deflections confined to one electrode
questions.explanation: Sweat changes the electrode-skin interface and produces very slow, swaying baseline shifts, often across several electrodes, which improve when the patient is cooled and the scalp dried. Fast temporal spikes suggest muscle, heartbeat-locked transients are ECG artifact, and abrupt steep deflections at one electrode are electrode pops.

questions.stem: A single channel shows intermittent high-amplitude sharp transients with no field and coinciding with head movement. MOST likely:
options: Focal epileptiform discharges
Electrode pop/movement artifact
Hypsarrhythmia
PDR breakthrough
questions.explanation: Electrode movement causes pops without physiologic field.

questions.stem: K-complexes are MOST associated with:
options: Wakefulness
N2 sleep
REM sleep
Seizure activity
questions.explanation: K-complexes are characteristic of N2.

questions.stem: Mu rhythm is MOST often seen over which region?
options: Occipital
Central
Frontal pole
Temporal
questions.explanation: Mu is central and may block with movement.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST supports that a temporal 'wicket' pattern is a benign variant?
options: Arciform waves in brief trains without background disruption
A clear after-going slow wave following each sharp component
Reliable activation by intermittent photic stimulation
Isolated, high-amplitude spikes appearing during wakefulness
questions.explanation: Wickets are arciform (mu-like) waves in brief trains over the temporal regions, typically in drowsiness in older adults, without disturbing the background and without an epileptiform field. An after-going slow wave is a feature of epileptiform discharges; wickets are not a photic-driven phenomenon; isolated high-amplitude spikes in wakefulness point toward epileptiform activity rather than a benign variant.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes focal slowing from generalized slowing?
options: Focal slowing appears only in sleep; generalized slowing appears in wakefulness
Focal slowing is faster than 4 Hz; generalized slowing is slower than 4 Hz
Focal slowing is unreactive to eye opening; generalized slowing is reactive
Focal slowing is regional and persists across montages; generalized is diffuse
questions.explanation: The distinction is topographic: focal slowing is confined to a region and is seen consistently across montages, while generalized slowing involves most channels diffusely. Either type can occur in wakefulness and sleep; frequency (theta vs delta) does not define focal vs generalized; reactivity can vary in both and does not separate them.

questions.stem: A well-formed posterior dominant rhythm in an awake adolescent is MOST typically:
options: 1–2 Hz
4–5 Hz
questions.explanation: Adolescent PDR is generally in alpha range.

questions.stem: During a suspected seizure event, which annotation is MOST useful?
options: The clock time of onset and the montage being viewed
The impedance values and filter settings at onset
The suspected seizure type and the likely diagnosis
Behaviors, responsiveness, and the onset and offset times
questions.explanation: The reader needs to correlate the EEG with what the patient did: observed behaviors, tested responsiveness, and onset/offset timing. Clock time and montage alone give no clinical correlation; impedances and filters are technical data, not event description; naming the seizure type or diagnosis is the interpreter's role, not an annotation.

questions.stem: A prolonged convulsive seizure occurs during EEG. The technologist should FIRST:
options: Keep recording and note the onset time for the interpreter
Protect the patient from injury and summon help right away
Reattach loose electrodes to preserve the ictal recording
Test responsiveness first, then decide whether help is needed
questions.explanation: With a prolonged convulsive seizure the first priority is the patient: protect from injury and call for help per the emergency plan, while the recording continues. Noting onset time and reattaching electrodes come after patient care; delaying the call for help to test responsiveness wastes time in a possible emergency.

questions.stem: Documenting responsiveness during an event helps differentiate:
options: The posterior rhythm from the mu rhythm
Seizures from non-seizure behavioral events
Cardiac ECG artifact from scalp muscle artifact
Photic driving from the hyperventilation response
questions.explanation: Testing responsiveness during an event shows whether awareness was impaired, which helps the reader separate seizures from non-seizure events and correlate with any EEG change (or with artifact). PDR versus mu is separated by location and reactivity to eye opening versus movement; ECG versus muscle artifact by morphology and timing; photic versus HV responses by which procedure was running.

questions.stem: What is the BEST way to confirm whether rhythmic activity during an event is artifact?
options: Correlate with behavior, check ECG, and review the field
Raise the notch filter and re-review the same montage
Lower the display sensitivity and recheck one channel
Label it ictal if it is rhythmic and sustained over time
questions.explanation: Artifact is confirmed by correlating the activity with what the patient is doing at the bedside, checking the ECG channel for pulse or cardiac artifact, and reviewing several montages for a plausible cerebral field. A notch filter only attenuates line-frequency noise, changing sensitivity alters display size but not the source, and rhythmicity alone does not make activity ictal.

questions.stem: The EEG shows a brief burst of generalized spike-wave. The patient shows no visible change and answers a test question normally. Which annotation is MOST appropriate?
options: 'Absence seizure occurred; patient unaware of event'
'Generalized epilepsy confirmed during this recording'
'Brief movement artifact burst; no clinical change seen'
'Generalized spike-wave burst; no clinical change; responsive'
questions.explanation: The annotation should be objective: what the EEG showed and what was observed clinically, including tested responsiveness, without a diagnosis. Calling it an absence seizure or confirmed epilepsy is an interpretation reserved for the physician, and labeling a true spike-wave burst as movement artifact is inaccurate.

questions.stem: Which approach is MOST appropriate for neonatal EEG?
options: Apply the full adult 10-20 array without any modification
Adapt the montage and strategy to neonatal age and context
Record wakefulness only, as neonatal sleep is uninformative
Raise the low-frequency filter to reduce slow neonatal waves
questions.explanation: Neonatal EEG needs a reduced, adapted montage, polygraphic channels and a strategy that reflects conceptional age and clinical context. Small heads do not accommodate the full adult array; sleep states are central to neonatal interpretation; raising the LFF attenuates the slow activity that is normal and important in neonates.

questions.stem: In ICU EEG, the BEST approach to high artifact burden is to:
options: Use narrow filter settings throughout so the tracing looks clean
Fix electrodes and grounding, annotate artifact, keep filters standard
Keep the notch on and rely on it for all electrical interference
Raise the µV/mm value so that artifact looks less prominent
questions.explanation: ICU artifact is best handled at the source (electrodes, grounding, equipment) and by annotating what cannot be fixed, while keeping filters near standard so cerebral activity is not distorted. Narrow filters attenuate real slowing and spikes; the notch addresses only line frequency; lowering the display sensitivity shrinks cerebral activity along with artifact.

questions.stem: Which statement is MOST accurate about electrocerebral inactivity (ECI) EEG studies?
options: A standard 20-minute study at routine settings is sufficient
Recording at 7 μV/mm is preferred so noise is not over-amplified
The technologist may declare ECI when no activity is visible
Defined technical standards apply, e.g., 2 μV/mm and 30+ minutes
questions.explanation: ECI recordings follow specific technical standards (for example sensitivity of 2 µV/mm for at least 30 minutes of recording with appropriate calibrations, adequate interelectrode distances, stimulation and documentation of all steps). A routine study at routine settings does not meet them; 7 µV/mm is too insensitive to exclude low-voltage activity; ECI is an interpretation made by the physician, not the technologist.

questions.stem: A key risk of overly aggressive filtering during suspected ECI evaluation is:
options: Increasing electrode impedance at each site
Amplifying ECG artifact in all channels
Raising the noise floor of the recording
Masking low-amplitude cerebral activity
questions.explanation: Aggressive filtering attenuates low-amplitude cerebral activity along with noise, which can create a false impression of electrocerebral inactivity, so ECI recordings use standard filter settings. Filters do not change electrode impedance, they do not amplify ECG artifact, and they lower rather than raise the displayed noise.

questions.stem: Special EEG protocols are MOST important because they:
options: Match strategy to the population and clinical question
Shorten the exam by skipping activation procedures
Standardize every study to one fixed montage set
Let the study be read without the patient history
questions.explanation: Special protocols (neonatal, ICU, ECI, sleep-deprived and others) tailor electrodes, settings, activation, and safety measures to the population and clinical question, improving safety and diagnostic yield. They are not mainly for shortening the study, they do not lock every study into one montage set, and they do not remove the need for clinical history.

questions.stem: After electrode removal, the technologist should:
options: Give the patient a brief summary of the EEG findings
Leave paste to dry so it flakes off more easily at home
Clean the scalp and confirm the patient is comfortable
Discard all cup electrodes, including the reusable ones
questions.explanation: Aftercare means removing paste from the scalp per policy and making sure the patient is comfortable and stable before leaving. Technologists do not give results; paste left on the scalp irritates skin; reusable electrodes are cleaned and disinfected rather than discarded.

questions.stem: A patient reports dizziness after standing post-EEG. What is the BEST next step?
options: Walk the patient briskly to the exit to restore circulation
Offer water and discharge once the dizziness eases
Have the patient stand still for a minute, then discharge
Have the patient sit or lie down and call for assistance
questions.explanation: Dizziness on standing risks a fall, so the patient should be seated or laid down and help summoned per policy, with the event documented. Walking the patient out or keeping them standing invites a fall, and discharging after symptoms ease skips assessment and escalation.

questions.stem: Skin breakdown at electrode sites is MOST likely reduced by:
options: Gentle prep with limited abrasion, checking fragile skin
Vigorous abrasion to get impedances as low as possible
Using collodion at all sites for every routine study
Using extra-firm cap straps to keep electrodes from moving
questions.explanation: Skin breakdown is reduced by gentle, adequate prep without excessive abrasion and by monitoring vulnerable patients (neonates, elderly, long-term studies). Aggressive abrasion damages skin; routine collodion adds chemical and removal irritation; tight straps create pressure injury.

questions.stem: Which aftercare statement is MOST appropriate when asked 'Was it normal?'
options: Say it looked normal to you, pending the formal reading
Explain that the interpreting clinician reviews the results
Describe the main waveforms you saw in plain language
Say you cannot discuss anything about the test at all
questions.explanation: Results are interpreted by the qualified clinician, so the technologist explains that the study will be reviewed and can describe the process and expected timeline. Giving a provisional "normal" or describing waveforms is informal interpretation; refusing to discuss anything is unhelpful when the process can be explained.

questions.stem: Post-study patient status should be documented especially when:
options: Photic stimulation produced a driving response
The recording was entirely within normal limits
An event occurred or the patient's condition changed
The study ran longer than its scheduled time slot
questions.explanation: Post-study status must be recorded when a clinical event occurred, the patient needed assistance, or the condition changed, because these affect safety and interpretation. A photic driving response is a normal finding, a normal recording does not by itself trigger status notes, and run time is not a status change.

questions.stem: Which practice BEST matches infection-control standards?
options: Reuse single-use electrodes if they look visibly clean
Rinse reusable electrodes with tap water between patients
Skip disinfection when the study lasted under an hour
Disinfect reusable electrodes per manufacturer guidance
questions.explanation: Reusable electrodes are cleaned and disinfected according to protocol and the manufacturer's instructions after each patient. Single-use items are not reused even if they look clean; water rinsing is not disinfection; short study duration does not reduce contamination risk.

questions.stem: Hand hygiene is MOST critical:
options: Before and after patient contact and after removing gloves
After patient contact only, since gloves protect beforehand
Only when hands are visibly soiled or after the study
Before donning gloves, but not after removing them
questions.explanation: Standard precautions call for hand hygiene before and after patient contact and after glove removal, since gloves can have micro-tears and hands are contaminated on removal. Gloves do not replace pre-contact hygiene; visible soiling is not the only trigger; skipping hygiene after glove removal is a classic error.

questions.stem: Which is BEST for cleaning an EEG headbox/cables after a contact precaution case?
options: Any hospital disinfectant at hand, wiped off immediately
An approved, compatible disinfectant with correct dwell time
Soaking the headbox and cables in disinfectant solution
Hand sanitizer gel from the dispenser, left to air dry
questions.explanation: Equipment is cleaned with an approved disinfectant compatible with the device, left wet for the labelled dwell time, following manufacturer instructions. Wiping off immediately defeats the dwell time and an unapproved agent may damage equipment; soaking electronics damages them; hand gel is not an equipment disinfectant.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a cracked electrode cup. BEST action:
options: Use it if its impedance measures acceptably low
Seal the crack with tape and continue the setup
Take it out of service and use a new electrode
Disinfect it for a longer cycle, then reuse it
questions.explanation: A cracked cup can harbor pathogens and give unstable recordings, so it is removed from service and replaced, with the defect reported per policy. Low impedance does not make it safe; tape does not seal it reliably; longer disinfection cannot reach organisms in the crack.

questions.stem: PPE selection should be based on:
options: Technologist preference and comfort during setup
Whether hyperventilation or photic is planned
The patient's age and the expected study length
Isolation status, task exposure risk, and policy
questions.explanation: PPE is chosen by institutional policy, the patient's isolation status and the exposure risk of the task. Personal preference is not a basis; activation procedures and patient age or study length do not determine transmission risk.

questions.stem: Which statement belongs in a technologist technical description?
options: Findings support frontal lobe epilepsy; consider MRI
HV not done due to poor cooperation; photic unremarkable
Recommend starting valproate given these discharges
Generalized epilepsy; follow-up EEG in six months
questions.explanation: Technical descriptions record conditions and observations, such as an omitted activation and its reason. Diagnoses, imaging suggestions and medication or follow-up recommendations belong to the interpreting clinician.

questions.stem: Which is MOST appropriate language for a behavioral event with no EEG correlate?
options: Psychogenic non-epileptic event, confirmed on EEG
Non-epileptic event; no seizure activity occurred
Clinical event seen; no clear EEG change during it
Behavioral event, likely voluntary; EEG normal
questions.explanation: The technologist describes what was observed clinically and whether an EEG change accompanied it. Labelling the event psychogenic, non-epileptic or voluntary is a diagnosis; scalp EEG can miss some seizures, so no correlate does not prove a non-epileptic event.

questions.stem: A key goal of the technologist report is to:
options: Offer a preliminary diagnosis to guide the reader
Record impedance values as the main quality measure
Summarize the clinical history to justify the study
Provide objective context that supports interpretation
questions.explanation: The technologist report gives objective technical and clinical context (state, events, settings, artifacts) that helps the reader interpret accurately. Diagnosis is outside scope; impedances are only one element; justifying the study is not its purpose.

questions.stem: If the system does not auto-document settings, the technologist should record at minimum:
options: Any filter, sensitivity and montage changes made
Photic frequencies used and total HV duration
The final impedance values and the electrode type
Start and end times plus the patient's sleep state
questions.explanation: If settings are not auto-logged, the technologist records filter, sensitivity and montage changes and other adjustments that alter what the reader sees. Activation details, impedances and timing are useful but do not tell the reader how displayed waveforms were altered.

questions.stem: When an activation is omitted, the report should:
options: State only that it was omitted, no reason
State that it was omitted and the reason
Leave it out, as no data were recorded
List it as performed, with no response seen
questions.explanation: An omitted activation is recorded with the reason (e.g., refusal, contraindication), because the reader needs both. Noting the omission without the reason is incomplete; leaving it out leaves the reader guessing; listing it as performed falsifies the record.

questions.stem: Which is BEST practice for EEG data management?
options: Save copies to an encrypted personal USB drive
Keep files on the acquisition PC indefinitely
Archive in the secure institutional system
Delete local files once the reading is final
questions.explanation: EEG data are archived per institutional policy on secure, access-controlled systems that meet retention rules. Personal devices breach confidentiality even if encrypted; local storage is not a managed archive; deleting files violates retention requirements.

questions.stem: A technologist wants to show an interesting EEG to a friend outside the care team. BEST action:
options: Share it once the name is removed from the screen
Share it in a private, password-protected group chat
Show a screen photo with the identifiers covered
Do not share it outside approved educational channels
questions.explanation: Recordings are confidential; use outside the care team requires approved, de-identified educational processes per policy. Removing a name or covering identifiers may leave other identifiers (face, dates); a private chat is still an unauthorized disclosure.

questions.stem: Spike-detection software is BEST described as:
options: A replacement for interpretation
An assistive tool that requires expert review
A guarantee of epilepsy
Unrelated to EEG quality
questions.explanation: Software assists; expert review is required.

questions.stem: Which situation MOST requires extra care with data handling?
options: Video-EEG showing the patient's face and name
A de-identified teaching file with no video
A blank form template saved on a shared drive
An anonymized research dataset with coded IDs
questions.explanation: Video-EEG with a visible face and embedded identifiers carries direct identifiers and needs the most protection. De-identified teaching files, blank templates and coded research data carry little or no identifiable information.

questions.stem: Retention and archiving rules are MOST determined by:
options: Technologist preference and storage space
Whether the EEG was read as normal or not
The referring clinician's personal request
Institutional policy and applicable laws
questions.explanation: Retention and archiving periods are set by institutional policy and applicable regulations. Storage space, the result of the study and an individual's request do not override those requirements.

questions.stem: A patient requests to stop the EEG. The MOST appropriate action is to:
options: Continue, because the study was ordered by a doctor
Stop the recording and escalate the refusal to the team
Reassure the patient and finish the remaining steps
Finish the current activation before stopping
questions.explanation: Patients may withdraw consent at any time, so the recording is stopped, the refusal is escalated to the appropriate staff or ordering provider according to policy, and it is documented. A doctor’s order does not override refusal, and reassuring the patient into finishing or completing an activation first both ignore the request.

questions.stem: Which setting is MOST appropriate for discussing patient information?
options: Elevator with coworkers
Public hallway with family present
Private setting with authorized team members
Social media without names
questions.explanation: Confidential information only with authorized staff in appropriate settings.

questions.stem: Which statement about patient consent is MOST accurate?
options: Patients can withdraw consent at any time
Consent is implied once the patient arrives
Consent given by signing cannot be revoked
Consent is needed only for photic stimulation
questions.explanation: Consent is ongoing: a patient may withdraw it at any point, and the technologist then stops and follows policy. Arriving for the test does not make consent implied for everything, a signed form does not remove the right to withdraw, and consent covers the whole procedure, not only photic stimulation.

questions.stem: A family member demands the EEG conclusion immediately. BEST response:
options: Share your impression but say it is preliminary
Tell them it looks normal so they stay calm
Explain that the interpreting clinician gives results
Show them the tracing and point out findings
questions.explanation: Interpretation is outside the technologist’s scope, so the family is told that results come from the interpreting clinician; the technologist can still explain the process and expected timeline. Sharing a preliminary impression, offering false reassurance, or pointing out findings on the tracing are all forms of interpreting the study.

questions.stem: Confidentiality includes protecting:
options: Only the patient’s name and medical record number
Only the diagnosis and the test results
Only data stored in the electronic record
Any information that could identify the patient
questions.explanation: Confidentiality covers any information that can identify a patient directly or indirectly, such as name, dates, images, or details that together point to one person, in any format. Limiting it to names and record numbers, to diagnoses and results, or to electronic data leaves other identifiers unprotected.

questions.stem: Which action BEST demonstrates working within scope of practice?
options: Explaining the likely diagnosis to the family
Suggesting antiseizure dose changes to the team
Noting technical findings and escalating concerns
Telling the patient what the EEG prognosis is
questions.explanation: Technologists document technical observations and pass concerns through proper channels. Giving a diagnosis, recommending medication changes, and predicting prognosis are physician tasks outside technologist scope.

questions.stem: Objective documentation is BEST characterized by:
options: Summary labels such as “uncooperative patient”
The technologist’s impression of the diagnosis
Brief notes listing only abnormal waveforms
Neutral descriptions of observed behaviors
questions.explanation: Objective notes describe what was seen (behaviors, state, conditions affecting the recording) in neutral terms. Judgmental labels are subjective, diagnostic impressions are outside scope, and listing only abnormal waveforms omits the context needed for interpretation.

questions.stem: Effective team communication during EEG is BEST described as:
options: Casual shorthand to save time on busy shifts
Accurate terminology with clear, timely updates
Sharing personal impressions of the diagnosis
Waiting to raise concerns until the study ends
questions.explanation: Good team communication uses accurate medical terminology and is clear and timely. Casual shorthand invites misunderstanding, personal diagnostic impressions are outside scope, and delaying concerns until the end of the study can delay care.

questions.stem: A technologist observes a pattern concerning for nonconvulsive seizures on ICU EEG (per lab role). BEST action:
options: Escalate promptly via the lab’s alert pathway
Note it for review at the end of the shift
Tell the family that the patient is seizing
Adjust the filters to clarify the pattern first
questions.explanation: Possible nonconvulsive seizures need prompt escalation through the lab’s pathway to the responsible clinician, with the notification documented. Waiting until shift end delays treatment, telling the family is a diagnosis outside scope, and adjusting filters does not address the clinical concern.

questions.stem: Constructive feedback to colleagues should be:
options: Given in front of the team so all can learn
Saved for the annual performance review
Private, specific, and focused on care quality
General, so no one feels singled out
questions.explanation: Constructive feedback is private, specific, and aimed at improving quality and patient safety. Public feedback can embarrass, waiting for an annual review delays correction, and vague general comments do not help the person improve.

questions.stem: Which practice BEST supports electrical safety during EEG?
options: Use a frayed cable if the tracing looks clean
Rely on the notch filter to manage all noise
Use an ungrounded extension cord when needed
Inspect equipment and keep connections sound
questions.explanation: Electrical safety depends on intact, inspected equipment and proper connections and grounding. A frayed cable is a shock hazard even if the tracing looks clean, the notch filter only attenuates 60 Hz interference and does nothing for safety, and ungrounded extension cords defeat equipment grounding.

questions.stem: SDS/MSDS information is MOST relevant when:
options: Choosing montages for a pediatric study
Handling cleaning or disinfection chemicals
Selecting photic stimulation frequencies
Setting electrode impedance thresholds
questions.explanation: Safety Data Sheets describe chemical hazards, handling, and PPE, so they matter when using cleaning and disinfection chemicals. Montage choice, photic frequencies, and impedance thresholds are recording parameters unrelated to chemical safety.

questions.stem: Which is an appropriate seizure-safety precaution in the lab?
options: A lowered bed with rails up and a call bell in reach
A padded tongue blade at the bedside for seizures
Wrist restraints applied before the recording
Leaving the patient alone during sleep recording
questions.explanation: Seizure precautions aim to reduce fall and injury risk and allow rapid help: a low bed, raised or padded rails, and a call system in reach. Objects are not placed in the mouth, restraints can cause injury, and patients at seizure risk are not left unattended.

questions.stem: Infection control protocols are MOST commonly guided by:
options: Each technologist’s own preferred practices
The EEG system manufacturer’s user manual
Institutional policy and public health guidance
Whether the patient appears visibly unwell
questions.explanation: Infection control follows institutional policy built on public health guidance such as CDC standard and transmission-based precautions. Personal preference is inconsistent, the EEG manual covers cleaning of that device only, and patients who look well can still transmit infection.

questions.stem: Which action is MOST appropriate if you suspect a chemical exposure from disinfectant?
options: Finish the study, then rinse at the end of shift
Apply a neutralizing chemical to the area
Wait to see whether symptoms develop
Follow the exposure plan and seek prompt care
questions.explanation: A suspected chemical exposure is managed with the institution’s exposure plan: first aid such as flushing per the SDS, prompt medical evaluation, and reporting. Delaying until shift end or waiting for symptoms risks injury, and applying another chemical can worsen it.

questions.stem: A patient becomes unresponsive with no apparent breathing. The technologist should FIRST:
options: Complete the montage change before reassessing
Keep recording quietly to capture the event
Page the EEG reader and await instructions
Call a code and start CPR if trained to do so
questions.explanation: An unresponsive patient who is not breathing needs immediate activation of emergency response and BLS/CPR by trained staff. Finishing a montage change, recording the event, or waiting for the reader all delay resuscitation.

questions.stem: During a convulsive seizure, the technologist's priority is to:
options: Restrain the limbs to limit jerking
Protect from injury and time the event
Place a bite block to protect the tongue
Stop recording to focus on the patient
questions.explanation: The priority during a convulsive seizure is preventing injury, timing the event, and following emergency protocol while the recording continues. Restraint can cause injury, nothing goes in the mouth, and stopping the recording loses ictal data without improving care.

questions.stem: Which documentation is MOST essential during an emergency event?
options: Event timing, behaviors, responsiveness, and actions
The montage, filter, and sensitivity settings in use
Electrode impedances checked right after the event
The patient’s diagnosis and current medication list
questions.explanation: The essential record of an emergency is a timeline: onset and end times, observed behaviors, responsiveness testing, interventions, and notifications made. Settings and impedances are routine technical data, and the diagnosis and medication list are already in the chart.

questions.stem: Oxygen equipment is present in the lab. The technologist should:
options: Adjust oxygen flow for any patient who asks for it
Start oxygen for any patient who appears anxious
Use oxygen only within training, scope, and policy
Use oxygen to reduce photoparoxysmal responses
questions.explanation: Oxygen is used only as allowed by the technologist’s training, scope, and institutional policy, calling for help when needed. Adjusting flow on request or for anxiety is unauthorized treatment, and oxygen is not a treatment for photoparoxysmal responses.

questions.stem: If a seizure lasts longer than expected and status epilepticus is suspected, the BEST action is to:
options: Wait for it to end, then call the reading team
Shut off the EEG system to focus on the patient
Leave to find the EEG reader in person
Call for emergency help and stay with the patient
questions.explanation: Suspected status epilepticus requires immediate emergency response according to institutional protocol while the technologist keeps the patient safe. Waiting for it to end delays treatment, shutting off the EEG loses data, and leaving the patient unattended is unsafe.

questions.stem: An EEG shows diffuse theta-delta slowing. After raising the low-frequency filter from 0.5 Hz to 5 Hz, the slowing appears reduced. The technologist should:
options: Conclude that the encephalopathy improved during the study
Recognize a filter effect and review at standard settings
Keep the 5 Hz setting, since it gives a cleaner baseline
Decrease the display gain to judge the remaining slowing
questions.explanation: A higher LFF attenuates delta and theta, so the apparent reduction is a technical effect, not clinical improvement; the record should be reviewed at standard settings (the standard LFF is 0.5-1 Hz). Concluding improvement misreads a filter change; keeping 5 Hz keeps the slowing understated; reducing gain makes the slowing look smaller still.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient shows brief, arch-shaped transients in the temporal region during drowsiness. They occur in trains, do not disrupt background, and lack aftergoing slow waves. The technologist's BEST interpretation is:
options: Interictal spikes from a temporal focus
Muscle artifact from the temporalis
Wicket spikes, a benign temporal variant
Benign small sharp spikes of sleep
questions.explanation: Wicket spikes are benign arch-shaped (mu-like) temporal transients that occur in trains during drowsiness in adults, do not disrupt the background and lack an aftergoing slow wave; they should be noted but not overinterpreted. Interictal spikes are usually isolated, disrupt the background and have an aftergoing slow wave; temporalis muscle artifact is very fast and spiky, not arch-shaped; small sharp spikes are tiny, single, very brief transients rather than arciform trains.

questions.stem: A sharp wave appears maximal at C3 in a referential montage but shows phase reversal at C3-Cz in a bipolar montage. The MOST accurate localization is:
options: The abnormality is at the reference electrode
The abnormality is at C3, confirmed by phase reversal in bipolar montage
The abnormality is at Cz, since that's where the phase reverses
Phase reversal is meaningless and should be ignored
questions.explanation: Phase reversal in bipolar montage localizes the abnormality to the electrode between the two channels showing the reversal. C3-Cz reversal indicates C3 is the source.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child's EEG shows an 8.5 Hz posterior rhythm that attenuates with eye opening. The technologist should:
options: Recognize it as a normal posterior dominant rhythm for age
Recognize it as posterior slowing, since adults run near 10 Hz
Recognize it as a rhythmic posterior epileptiform discharge
Raise the high-frequency filter to look for hidden fast activity
questions.explanation: The posterior dominant rhythm (PDR) speeds up with maturation, reaching about 8 Hz by age 3 and adult values (about 9-11 Hz) in adolescence, so 8.5 Hz at age 6 is normal; attenuation with eye opening confirms it is a true PDR. Judging it against the adult 10 Hz value misreads it as slowing; a reactive, well-formed rhythm is not an epileptiform discharge; changing the HFF does not reveal a hidden faster rhythm.

questions.stem: All electrodes show impedance values of 3-5 kΩ, but Fp1 shows 8 kΩ. The EEG has excessive noise. The technologist should:
options: Proceed, since every value is still below the 10 kΩ limit
Lower the sensitivity so the noise is less visible on screen
Switch to a montage that leaves out the Fp1 electrode
Re-prep Fp1 so its impedance matches the other electrodes
questions.explanation: Fp1 is both above the usual 5 kΩ target and mismatched with its neighbors; impedance imbalance degrades common-mode rejection and lets noise through, so re-prepping Fp1 is the fix. Passing a loose 10 kΩ limit ignores the imbalance; lowering sensitivity only shrinks the display of noise and signal alike; dropping Fp1 loses frontal coverage instead of fixing contact.

questions.stem: A central rhythm at 10 Hz appears arch-shaped and attenuates when the patient moves their right hand. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: Mu rhythm, a normal central rhythm
Central epileptiform discharges
Muscle artifact from hand movement
Posterior alpha spreading centrally
questions.explanation: Mu rhythm is a normal arch-shaped 7-11 Hz central rhythm that attenuates with movement, or intention to move, of the contralateral limb, here the right hand blocking the left central (C3) mu. Epileptiform discharges are not blocked by hand movement, muscle artifact is fast and spiky rather than a 10 Hz arciform rhythm, and posterior alpha blocks with eye opening rather than hand movement.

questions.stem: A technologist increases sensitivity from 7 μV/mm to 3.5 μV/mm to 'see more detail.' The waveforms appear larger. The technologist should understand that:
options: Only the display scale changed; brain voltage is unchanged
The amplifier is now recording a higher true scalp voltage
The signal-to-noise ratio of the recording has improved
Hidden epileptiform activity will now become visible
questions.explanation: Sensitivity (µV/mm) sets how many microvolts each millimeter of deflection represents; going from 7 to 3.5 µV/mm doubles the displayed height but does not change the voltage the brain produces. The true scalp voltage is the same; noise is scaled up along with signal, so the signal-to-noise ratio is unchanged; a display change does not create discharges that were not present.

questions.stem: During N2 sleep, a technologist observes 12-14 Hz spindles maximal centrally and K-complexes. The patient then shows low-amplitude, desynchronized activity with conjugate saccadic eye movements, while chin EMG drops to its lowest level. This transition is BEST recognized as:
options: Arousal into wakefulness
Transition into REM sleep
An electrodecremental seizure
A return to N1 drowsiness
questions.explanation: REM sleep shows a low-amplitude desynchronized background, rapid eye movements, loss of spindles and K-complexes, and the lowest chin EMG (atonia). Arousal to wakefulness brings increased muscle tone and often alpha; an electrodecremental seizure lacks this sleep context and atonia; N1 has slow rolling eye movements and vertex waves.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old patient with known sickle cell disease is scheduled for EEG. The technologist should:
options: Perform HV as for any 12-year-old
Perform HV for 1 minute at lower depth
Omit HV because of the risk of sickling
Omit photic stimulation but perform HV
questions.explanation: Hypocapnia and hypoxia from HV can provoke a sickling crisis, so HV is omitted in sickle cell disease and the reason documented, consulting the ordering physician if unsure. Standard or shortened HV still carries the risk, and omitting photic stimulation addresses the wrong procedure.

questions.stem: An EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave complexes that are perfectly synchronous across all channels, maximal frontally, and occur in bursts. The technologist should classify this as:
options: Focal epileptiform activity requiring localization
Generalized spike-and-wave, typical of absence epilepsy
Artifact from muscle activity
Normal variant requiring no action
questions.explanation: Generalized spike-and-wave is characterized by bilateral synchrony, symmetric distribution, and frontal maximum. This pattern is typical of generalized absence epilepsy, not focal.

questions.stem: A regular, 1 Hz sharp transient appears in all channels, time-locked across montages, and correlates with the patient's pulse. The technologist should identify this as:
options: Electrode pop artifact
Muscle (EMG) artifact
Generalized spike activity
ECG (cardiac) artifact
questions.explanation: Regular sharp transients at about 1 Hz, seen in many channels and time-locked to the pulse, are ECG artifact; an ECG channel or palpating the pulse confirms the correlation. Electrode pops are irregular and confined to one electrode; muscle artifact is fast and irregular; generalized discharges are not locked to the heartbeat.

questions.stem: An awake adult's EEG shows a 9 Hz posterior rhythm that does NOT attenuate with eye opening. The technologist should:
options: Document it as a normal, reactive posterior rhythm
Document poor reactivity and the patient's state
Document it as rhythmic epileptiform activity
Document it as an alpha coma pattern
questions.explanation: A normal posterior dominant rhythm attenuates with eye opening, so poor reactivity should be documented together with the patient's state, since drowsiness, medication or encephalopathy can explain it. It is not a normal reactive rhythm, a 9 Hz posterior rhythm is not epileptiform, and alpha coma applies to unresponsive comatose patients, not an awake adult.

questions.stem: An EEG system samples at 200 Hz. The highest frequency that can theoretically be represented without aliasing is:
options: 200 Hz
400 Hz
100 Hz
50 Hz
questions.explanation: By the Nyquist theorem the highest representable frequency is half the sampling rate: 200 Hz / 2 = 100 Hz. Frequencies above this alias into lower frequencies. 200 Hz equals the sampling rate itself, 400 Hz is double it, and 50 Hz is one quarter of it. In practice a sampling rate of at least 3-4 times the highest frequency of interest is preferred.

questions.stem: An EEG shows diffuse theta-delta slowing with preserved PDR reactivity. The technologist should recognize that:
options: This indicates severe encephalopathy requiring immediate intervention
This suggests mild-moderate encephalopathy; preserved reactivity is a favorable sign
This is normal for all age groups
This indicates focal pathology
questions.explanation: Diffuse slowing indicates encephalopathy, but preserved PDR reactivity suggests the encephalopathy is not severe. Reactivity is a key prognostic indicator.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation at 15 Hz, the EEG shows a 15 Hz response over the occipital region that is time-locked to the flash rate. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: A photoparoxysmal response
Occipital epileptiform activity
Photic stimulator artifact
Normal photic driving
questions.explanation: Occipital activity at the flash rate, time-locked to the flashes, is photic driving, a normal response. A photoparoxysmal response contains spikes or spike-and-wave; occipital epileptiform activity would show spikes rather than smooth rhythmic waves; a stimulator (photoelectric) artifact is a sharp deflection at the electrodes near the lamp, not cerebral rhythmic activity.

questions.stem: An EEG shows a brief, isolated sharp wave in the left temporal region with no evolution, no clinical change, and a normal background. The technologist should classify it as:
options: An interictal epileptiform discharge
An electrographic seizure onset
A periodic lateralized discharge
A postictal sharp transient after a seizure
questions.explanation: An isolated sharp wave without evolution, clinical change, or background disruption is an interictal epileptiform discharge. A seizure onset requires rhythmic, evolving activity; periodic lateralized discharges recur at regular intervals rather than appearing once; and a postictal transient requires a preceding seizure, which did not occur.

questions.stem: A technologist uses subdermal needle electrodes for a patient with thick, matted hair. The technologist should be aware that:
options: They give better signal quality than cups in most patients
They make impedance checks unnecessary after insertion
They carry infection risk, so prepared cups are preferable
They have lower impedance than well-prepared cup electrodes
questions.explanation: Subdermal needles break the skin, require sterile single-use technique and carry infection and needlestick risk, so well-prepared cup electrodes are preferred whenever scalp access allows. Needles do not give better signal quality; their impedance still must be checked; and they typically have higher, not lower, impedance than well-prepared cups.

questions.stem: An EEG shows slowing maximal at T5 and T6. The technologist should understand that this localizes to:
options: Bilateral hippocampi and amygdalae
Bilateral occipital calcarine cortex
Bilateral posterior temporal cortex
Brainstem reticular formation
questions.explanation: T5 and T6 (P7/P8 in the modified system) overlie the left and right posterior temporal cortex, and scalp EEG mainly reflects activity of the cortical surface near the electrodes. Deep structures such as the hippocampus and amygdala are poorly represented on scalp EEG; occipital calcarine cortex lies under O1/O2; brainstem dysfunction produces diffuse or bilateral changes rather than a posterior temporal maximum.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old performs hyperventilation for 3 minutes. 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave complexes appear during HV and resolve when HV stops. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: Normal HV buildup that resolves after overbreathing ends
HV-activated 3 Hz spike-wave typical of absence epilepsy
Breathing-related movement artifact during the HV period
Hypoglycemia-related slowing enhanced by hyperventilation
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation-activated 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave in a child is the classic finding of childhood absence epilepsy and is a significant activation. Normal HV buildup is rhythmic slowing without spikes, breathing artifact does not produce generalized spike-wave complexes, and hypoglycemia enhances slowing during HV but does not create spike-wave discharges.

questions.stem: Regular, high-amplitude deflections appear in Fp1 and Fp2, symmetric and in phase, time-locked to visible eye blinks. The technologist should identify this as:
options: Frontal sharp waves
Lateral eye movement artifact
Glossokinetic artifact
Eye blink artifact
questions.explanation: Blinks produce symmetric, in-phase deflections maximal at Fp1 and Fp2, and correlation with visible blinks confirms artifact. Frontal sharp waves would not be time-locked to blinks; lateral eye movements give opposite-polarity deflections at F7 and F8; glossokinetic artifact follows tongue movement.

questions.stem: A technologist understands that EEG measures:
options: Current flowing through the brain tissue
Magnetic fields from cortical neurons
Regional changes in cerebral blood flow
Voltage differences between electrodes
questions.explanation: EEG records potential (voltage) differences between pairs of electrodes. It does not measure current flow directly; magnetic fields are recorded by magnetoencephalography (MEG), and blood-flow changes are measured by techniques such as fMRI or SPECT.

questions.stem: Isolated, brief, low-amplitude sharp transients under 50 ms appear in the temporal regions during drowsiness and light sleep, with little or no aftergoing slow wave. The technologist should recognize these as:
options: Interictal temporal lobe spikes
Muscle artifact from the temporalis
Rhythmic midtemporal theta of drowsiness
Benign epileptiform transients of sleep
questions.explanation: BETS (small sharp spikes) are isolated, low-amplitude (under about 50 µV), very brief (under 50 ms) mono- or diphasic transients in drowsiness and light sleep with little or no aftergoing slow wave and no background disruption; they are a normal variant. Interictal spikes are usually higher amplitude with an aftergoing slow wave and background disruption, temporalis artifact is fast, repetitive and persists into wakefulness with jaw tension, and rhythmic midtemporal theta is a run of notched 5-7 Hz waves rather than isolated sharp transients.

questions.stem: A technologist switches from bipolar to average reference montage. A focal sharp wave that was subtle in bipolar becomes more prominent. The technologist should understand that:
options: The display changed with the montage; the discharge did not
The discharge has grown in amplitude since the switch
The average reference has introduced a new artifact source
A faulty electrode in the bipolar chain was hiding it
questions.explanation: Montages differ in which electrodes are subtracted. In a bipolar chain, neighbors with similar potentials partly cancel, so a broad discharge can look subtle; against an average reference it can appear more prominent. This is a montage effect, not a clinical change. Nothing suggests the discharge grew, the change is explained without new artifact, and a faulty electrode would produce its own artifact rather than selective cancellation.

questions.stem: A 2-week-old neonate's EEG shows periods of high-amplitude activity alternating with periods of relative suppression. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: Abnormal burst suppression requiring intervention
Trace alternant, a normal discontinuous pattern in neonates
Seizure activity
Artifact from movement
questions.explanation: Trace alternant is a normal discontinuous pattern in neonates (up to ~44 weeks post-conceptual age). It shows alternating high-amplitude bursts and suppression, distinct from abnormal burst suppression.

questions.stem: A technologist lowers the high-frequency filter from 70 Hz to 15 Hz to 'reduce muscle artifact.' Small sharp transients become less visible. The technologist should understand that:
options: The transients were muscle artifact that is now correctly hidden
The epileptiform activity has resolved since the filter change
Low HFF can attenuate spikes and sharp waves, masking findings
A 15 Hz HFF is the recommended setting for routine recordings
questions.explanation: Spikes and sharp waves contain fast components, so an HFF of 15 Hz attenuates them and can mask epileptiform activity; standard HFF is about 70 Hz. Muscle can be reduced at 15 Hz, but so can real sharp transients, so their loss is not proof they were artifact; a filter change cannot make discharges resolve; and 15 Hz is not a routine setting.

questions.stem: A technologist observes a sharp transient with duration of 80 ms and pointed morphology. The technologist should classify this as:
options: A spike (20-70 ms duration)
A sharp wave (70-200 ms duration)
A slow wave (>200 ms)
Normal background activity
questions.explanation: Sharp waves are defined as 70-200 ms duration. Spikes are 20-70 ms. An 80 ms transient is a sharp wave, not a spike.

questions.stem: An EEG shows 60 Hz artifact in all channels. The technologist checks and finds the ground electrode impedance is 50 kΩ. The technologist should:
options: Re-prep or replace the ground electrode before anything else
Turn on the 60 Hz notch filter and continue the recording
Lower the high-frequency filter to 35 Hz to reduce the noise
Raise the µV/mm setting so the 60 Hz noise is less prominent
questions.explanation: A 50 kΩ ground explains line noise in every channel, so the ground should be fixed first. The notch should be a fallback once the source cannot be corrected; lowering the HFF to 35 Hz attenuates 60 Hz only partly and also attenuates fast activity; reducing display sensitivity shrinks noise and EEG together without correcting anything.

questions.stem: During N2 sleep, a technologist observes a high-amplitude, sharp transient maximal at Cz that is not part of a K-complex. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: An epileptiform spike at Cz
An electrode pop at Cz
A vertex sharp transient
A central sleep spindle burst
questions.explanation: Vertex waves are normal sharp, high-amplitude transients maximal at Cz in N1 and N2 sleep. They are not epileptiform; an electrode pop is confined to one electrode with an abrupt vertical rise and no field; spindles are rhythmic 12-14 Hz bursts rather than a single transient.

questions.stem: An EEG shows prominent, symmetric beta activity (18-25 Hz) over the frontal regions. The patient is on benzodiazepines. The technologist should:
options: Treat it as abnormal fast activity that needs intervention
Classify it as a run of epileptiform fast spike discharges
Recognize it as a benzodiazepine-induced beta effect
Lower the high-frequency filter to suppress the beta
questions.explanation: Prominent frontal beta (18-25 Hz) is a common, expected effect of benzodiazepines and other sedative drugs; it should be noted but not overinterpreted. It is not abnormal fast activity needing intervention, symmetric beta is not epileptiform, and lowering the HFF would attenuate genuine cerebral activity rather than address its cause.
