questions.stem: During photic stimulation, the EEG shows spike-and-wave complexes that are NOT time-locked to the flash rate and persist after stimulation stops. This is BEST classified as:
options: A photoparoxysmal (abnormal) response
Normal photic driving at the flash rate
Photomyogenic (muscle) artifact
Normal posterior background activity
questions.explanation: Spike-and-wave that is not time-locked to the flashes and outlasts the stimulation is a photoparoxysmal response, which is abnormal and must be reported. Photic driving is time-locked rhythmic activity without spikes; photomyogenic artifact is frontal muscle activity that stops with the flashes; spike-and-wave is not normal background.

questions.stem: An EEG shows periodic, high-amplitude triphasic waves with frontal maximum in a patient with hepatic encephalopathy. The technologist should recognize that:
options: Triphasic waves typical of a metabolic encephalopathy
Lateralized periodic discharges from a focal lesion
Generalized spike-wave complexes of absence epilepsy
Vertex sharp transients seen in normal light sleep
questions.explanation: Periodic, frontally predominant triphasic waves in a patient with hepatic failure are the classic pattern of metabolic (toxic-metabolic) encephalopathy and are not usually treated as seizures. They are generalized rather than lateralized, they lack the spike-wave morphology of absence epilepsy, and vertex waves are normal sleep transients, not periodic waking discharges.

questions.stem: A patient arrives for EEG and reports taking 'seizure medication' but cannot recall the name. The technologist should:
options: Document no medications, since the name cannot be confirmed
Document a likely drug name based on the stated diagnosis
Postpone the study until the drug name can be documented
Document 'seizure medication, name unknown' and seek the list
questions.explanation: Documenting what is known (an unnamed seizure medication) and trying to obtain the full list gives the reader accurate context, since medications such as benzodiazepines and antiseizure drugs affect the background and discharge frequency. Recording no medications is inaccurate; guessing a drug name records false information; postponing is unnecessary because incomplete information can be noted.

questions.stem: An EEG shows a persistent 30% amplitude asymmetry with lower amplitude over the right hemisphere. The PDR is 9 Hz bilaterally. How should the technologist regard this finding?
options: A definite focal abnormality over the right side
Electrode artifact that needs no further mention
Evidence of a right hemisphere seizure focus
Possibly a normal variant; correlate clinically
questions.explanation: An amplitude asymmetry under about 50% with a symmetric PDR frequency can be a normal variant, but it may also reflect pathology, so it should be documented accurately for the interpreter to correlate clinically. It is not a definite abnormality at this degree, a persistent asymmetry should not be dismissed as artifact without checking electrodes and montages, and asymmetry alone does not indicate a seizure focus.

questions.stem: A single channel (C3) shows brief, high-amplitude, sharp deflections that occur randomly, are not time-locked to any visible movement, and appear only in that channel. The technologist should identify this as:
options: Focal epileptiform activity at C3
Electrode pop artifact at C3
Muscle artifact over C3
Mu rhythm fragments at C3
questions.explanation: Brief, random, high-amplitude deflections confined to one electrode with no field are electrode pop from intermittent poor contact at C3. Epileptiform discharges have a field over neighbouring electrodes; muscle artifact is sustained fast activity; mu rhythm is arciform 8-13 Hz activity.

questions.stem: A technologist understands that epileptiform discharges result from:
options: Excessive, hypersynchronous neuronal firing
Increased cerebral blood flow to the cortex
A diffuse reduction in neuronal activity
Poor electrode contact over the region
questions.explanation: Epileptiform discharges arise from hyperexcitability with excessive firing and abnormal synchronization of neuronal populations. Increased blood flow is a consequence of activity, not its cause; reduced neuronal activity produces slowing or attenuation rather than discharges; and poor electrode contact produces artifact, not true epileptiform activity.

questions.stem: During a clinical seizure, the EEG shows sudden, marked attenuation of background activity (electrodecremental pattern) followed by rhythmic fast activity. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: A movement artifact
An arousal from sleep
Amplifier saturation
An ictal onset pattern
questions.explanation: A sudden electrodecremental attenuation of the background followed by rhythmic fast activity during a clinical seizure is a classic ictal onset pattern. Movement artifact is high-amplitude and irregular rather than an attenuation followed by evolving fast rhythm; an arousal can attenuate the background but is not followed by evolving rhythmic fast activity; amplifier saturation produces flat-topped clipping, not a physiologic evolution.

questions.stem: A technologist understands that 'time constant' is directly related to:
options: The high-frequency filter setting
The sampling rate of the system
The low-frequency filter setting
The electrode impedance at each site
questions.explanation: Time constant describes the low-frequency (high-pass) filter: TC = 1 / (2π × LFF cutoff), so a shorter time constant corresponds to a higher LFF and more attenuation of slow activity. The HFF is described by its cutoff frequency, the sampling rate determines the Nyquist limit, and impedance concerns electrode contact; none of these is the time constant.

questions.stem: During drowsiness, a technologist observes 14 Hz positive spikes over the posterior temporal regions in an adolescent. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: Interictal posterior temporal spikes
Muscle artifact from the neck
Benign 14 and 6 Hz positive bursts
Rhythmic midtemporal theta of drowsiness
questions.explanation: 14 and 6 Hz positive bursts are benign comb-shaped positive spikes, maximal over the posterior temporal regions, seen in drowsiness and light sleep in children and adolescents; they are not epileptiform. Interictal spikes are surface-negative, neck muscle artifact is not rhythmic at 14 Hz with positive polarity, and rhythmic midtemporal theta is a notched 5-7 Hz drowsiness variant, not 14 Hz positive spikes.

questions.stem: In a bipolar montage, a sharp wave shows phase reversal between F3-Fz and Fz-F4. The technologist should localize this to:
options: At the F3 electrode
At the F4 electrode
At the Cz electrode
At the Fz electrode
questions.explanation: In a bipolar chain, a phase reversal localizes to the electrode shared by the two channels that point toward each other. Fz is common to F3-Fz and Fz-F4, so the discharge is maximal at Fz. F3 and F4 are each in only one of the reversing channels, and Cz is not part of either derivation.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old child's EEG shows a 6 Hz posterior rhythm that is reactive to eye opening. The technologist should:
options: Recognize it as abnormal posterior slowing for this age
Recognize it as an age-appropriate posterior dominant rhythm
Recognize it as a rhythmic epileptiform pattern in the occiput
Raise the filters to check whether faster activity is hidden
questions.explanation: The posterior dominant rhythm is about 5-6 Hz around the first year and rises to about 8 Hz by age 3, so a reactive 6 Hz rhythm at 18 months is normal for age. Calling it slowing applies older-child or adult norms; a reactive, sinusoidal background rhythm is not epileptiform; changing filters does not uncover a hidden faster rhythm.

questions.stem: A patient with recent stroke and hemiparesis is scheduled for EEG. The technologist should:
options: Perform HV as usual, since the physician ordered it
Ask the ordering physician whether HV is appropriate
Omit all activation and tell the physician afterward
Do photic only and have the physician add HV later
questions.explanation: Recent stroke is a relative contraindication to HV because hypocapnic vasoconstriction may worsen cerebral perfusion, so the technologist checks with the ordering physician before HV. Performing HV routinely ignores the risk; omitting all activation (including photic, which is not contraindicated) is unnecessary; deferring HV to a later decision avoids the needed discussion now.

questions.stem: An EEG shows 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave complexes that occur in bursts, are perfectly synchronous, and are activated by hyperventilation. The technologist should recognize this pattern as:
options: Childhood absence epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
Frontal lobe epilepsy
questions.explanation: Bursts of perfectly synchronous 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave activated by hyperventilation are the classic pattern of childhood absence epilepsy (formerly petit mal). JME typically shows faster 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave, LGS shows slow 1.5-2.5 Hz spike-and-wave on an abnormal background, and frontal lobe epilepsy produces focal discharges that may spread but are not regular 3 Hz generalized bursts.

questions.stem: All electrodes show impedance of 2 kΩ except Fp1 at 15 kΩ. The EEG shows excessive noise. The technologist should:
options: Proceed, since Fp1 is still under the 20 kΩ limit
Turn on the notch filter to reduce the visible noise
Re-prep Fp1 to bring it in line with the other electrodes
Raise the µV/mm setting to make the noise less visible
questions.explanation: Fp1 is far above the usual 5 kΩ target and badly mismatched with the 2 kΩ electrodes; the imbalance reduces common-mode rejection and causes noise, so re-prepping Fp1 is the fix. A 20 kΩ limit is not an accepted standard; the notch would mask a contact problem; reducing display sensitivity shrinks noise and signal alike.

questions.stem: An EEG shows low-amplitude, desynchronized background with bursts of conjugate eye movements and no spindles or K-complexes. Muscle tone is low. The technologist should identify this as:
options: N1 sleep
Relaxed wakefulness
N2 sleep
REM sleep
questions.explanation: REM sleep shows a desynchronized low-amplitude background, rapid eye movements, absent spindles/K-complexes and low muscle tone. N1 has slow rolling eye movements and vertex waves; wakefulness has higher muscle tone and posterior alpha; N2 has spindles and K-complexes.

questions.stem: An awake adult's EEG shows prominent 5-7 Hz theta activity diffusely. The technologist should:
options: Accept it as a normal finding in any awake adult
Label it as an interictal epileptiform pattern
Treat it as eye-movement artifact and disregard it
Note the patient's state, as drowsiness can explain it
questions.explanation: Diffuse theta in adults is state-dependent: normal in drowsiness but abnormal in a fully alert adult, so the technologist should establish and note the patient's state. It is not normal in every awake adult, diffuse theta is not an epileptiform pattern, and dismissing it as eye-movement artifact ignores a possible abnormality.

questions.stem: An EEG recorded in a warm room shows very slow, irregular baseline drift affecting multiple channels. The technologist should identify this as:
options: Diffuse slowing from encephalopathy
Muscle artifact
Sweat artifact
Respiration artifact
questions.explanation: Very slow, irregular drift over several channels in a warm room is sweat artifact, caused by sweat altering skin potentials and electrode contact. Diffuse slowing is cerebral delta/theta without the very slow drifting baseline; muscle artifact is fast; respiration artifact is rhythmic and follows breathing.

questions.stem: An EEG shows polymorphic delta slowing (1-3 Hz) confined to the right temporal region, persisting across montages. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: Benign temporal slowing of the elderly patient
Focal slowing suggesting an underlying lesion
Generalized slowing from encephalopathy
Eye movement artifact in temporal leads
questions.explanation: Persistent focal polymorphic delta confined to one region suggests an underlying structural or functional abnormality there, and persistence across montages argues against artifact. Benign temporal slowing of the elderly is intermittent, sparse theta/delta, usually left-sided; generalized slowing would not be confined to one region; eye movement artifact is frontopolar and time-locked to eye movements.

questions.stem: A technologist changes sweep speed from 30 mm/s to 10 mm/s. The technologist should understand that:
options: The displayed brain frequencies have slowed by a factor of three
The sampling rate dropped, so fast activity is less accurate
Only the horizontal display changed; waves look compressed
Waveforms now spread out, making spikes easier to identify
questions.explanation: Sweep speed (time base) only changes how much time fits on a page: at 10 mm/s waveforms are compressed, which suits surveying slow waves and background, while 30 mm/s spreads them out for spike review. The brain frequencies are unchanged, the sampling rate is independent of display speed, and slowing the sweep compresses rather than spreads waveforms.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected epilepsy has a normal routine EEG. The technologist should understand that:
options: It rules out epilepsy if the study included sleep
It rules out epilepsy when HV and photic were done
It excludes epilepsy if the last seizure was recent
It does not exclude epilepsy; more recording may help
questions.explanation: A normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy because interictal discharges are intermittent; a sleep-deprived study or prolonged monitoring increases the chance of capturing them. Including sleep, HV, or photic stimulation raises yield but still cannot rule epilepsy out, and a recent seizure does not make a normal study conclusive.

questions.stem: A technologist measures and marks electrode positions using the 10-20 system. The technologist should understand that:
options: Accurate measurement supports localization and serial comparison
Approximate placement is acceptable if left-right symmetry is kept
Measuring matters mainly for frontal sites; others can be estimated
Software corrects placement errors when montages are reformatted
questions.explanation: Electrode positions define where activity is localized and allow comparison between studies, so 10-20 measurements must be accurate at every site. Symmetric but inaccurate placement still mislocalizes; all regions need measuring, not only frontal; and digital remontaging re-references the recorded channels but cannot move electrodes that were misplaced.

questions.stem: During wakefulness with eyes open, a technologist observes sharp, positive transients over the occipital region that occur with saccadic eye movements. The technologist should recognize these as:
options: Occipital interictal epileptiform spikes
Lambda waves from visual scanning
Positive occipital transients of sleep
A photic driving response
questions.explanation: Lambda waves are normal, surface-positive, sharply contoured occipital transients that occur during wakefulness with eyes open while the patient scans a visual scene (saccades). Interictal spikes are surface-negative and unrelated to eye movements, POSTS have a similar shape but occur in sleep, and photic driving requires a flashing stimulus.

questions.stem: A technologist uses a 60 Hz notch filter to reduce line noise. The technologist should be aware that the notch filter:
options: Can distort spikes; fix the noise source first
Affects only activity at exactly 60 Hz
Is preferred to rechecking ground and leads
Sharpens fast activity such as spikes
questions.explanation: A notch filter attenuates a narrow band around 60 Hz and can distort the sharp components of spikes and sharp waves. Best practice is to correct the noise source (ground, impedances, nearby equipment) and use the notch only if that fails. It affects nearby frequencies, not just exactly 60 Hz; it is not a substitute for troubleshooting; and it does not sharpen spikes.

questions.stem: An EEG shows slowing maximal at T5. The technologist should understand that this localizes to the:
options: Left posterior temporal cortex
Left hippocampus and amygdala
Left inferior frontal cortex
Left parietal-occipital cortex
questions.explanation: T5 (P7 in the modified system) overlies the left posterior temporal cortex, and scalp EEG primarily reflects superficial cortical activity under the electrode. Deep mesial structures such as the hippocampus and amygdala are poorly represented on scalp EEG; the inferior frontal region lies under F7; the parietal-occipital region lies under P3/O1.

questions.stem: A technologist observes a sharp wave followed by a slow wave. The technologist should understand that:
options: It must be present before any discharge is called epileptiform
It follows spikes but does not follow sharp waves
It indicates that the transient is an electrode artifact
It is common but not required to call a discharge epileptiform
questions.explanation: An aftergoing slow wave is common in epileptiform discharges and supports the call, but it is not required; morphology, a physiologic field and context matter more. It is therefore not mandatory, it follows both spikes and sharp waves, and its presence argues for a cerebral discharge rather than an electrode artifact.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation at 20 Hz, the EEG shows generalized spike-and-wave complexes that are NOT time-locked to the flash and continue for 2 seconds after stimulation stops. This finding is:
options: Normal photic driving at 20 Hz
Photomyogenic muscle artifact
An abnormal photoparoxysmal response
A normal harmonic driving response
questions.explanation: Generalized spike-and-wave not time-locked to the flashes and outlasting the stimulus is a photoparoxysmal response, which is abnormal. Normal driving and harmonic responses are rhythmic posterior waves without spikes; photomyogenic artifact is frontal muscle activity that stops when the flashes stop.

questions.stem: A 35-week post-conceptual age neonate's EEG shows periods of high-amplitude activity alternating with periods of relative suppression. The technologist should:
options: Recognize a normal discontinuous pattern for this age
Recognize abnormal burst suppression for this age
Recognize an electrographic seizure with postictal suppression
Recognize a severe encephalopathic pattern for this age
questions.explanation: At 35 weeks post-conceptual age a discontinuous record with high-amplitude bursts alternating with lower-amplitude periods is normal (trace discontinu evolving into trace alternant, which persists to about 44 weeks). Burst suppression is invariant and unreactive with a near-flat interburst background; a seizure shows evolving rhythmic activity; normal maturational discontinuity does not indicate encephalopathy.

questions.stem: A technologist understands that differential amplifiers work by:
options: Amplifying each input separately and adding them
Amplifying only the signal at the active input
Amplifying signals common to both inputs
Amplifying the difference between the two inputs
questions.explanation: A differential amplifier amplifies the voltage difference between its two inputs (active and reference) and rejects signals common to both, measured by the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR). It does not add the inputs, does not amplify one input alone, and suppresses rather than amplifies common-mode signals.

questions.stem: A technologist observes 12-14 Hz rhythmic activity maximal centrally, waxing and waning in 0.5-1 s bursts during sleep. The technologist should identify this as:
options: Sleep spindles
Mu rhythm
Sedative-induced beta
Rhythmic midtemporal theta
questions.explanation: Sleep spindles are 12-14 Hz waxing-waning bursts maximal centrally and characteristic of N2. Mu rhythm is a waking 7-11 Hz central rhythm; sedative beta is faster and more continuous, often frontal; rhythmic midtemporal theta is a drowsy temporal 5-7 Hz variant.

questions.stem: In an average reference montage, a focal sharp wave appears prominent. The technologist switches to a linked-ear reference. The sharp wave becomes less visible. The technologist should understand that:
options: The discharge has resolved since the reference was changed
Its visibility depends on the reference and field, not a change
The average reference created the discharge as an artifact
The linked-ear view is the accurate picture of the field
questions.explanation: How prominent a discharge looks depends on the reference: if the ear electrodes pick up part of the field (common with temporal discharges), a linked-ear reference subtracts some of it and the discharge looks smaller. The discharge has not resolved; the average reference did not create it, as it was seen with a defined field; and no single reference is the true picture, since each can be contaminated.

questions.stem: After a clinical seizure, the EEG shows diffuse suppression followed by gradual return of background. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: Ongoing electrographic seizure
Postictal background suppression
Electrode detachment artifact
A burst-suppression pattern
questions.explanation: Diffuse suppression after a seizure, followed by gradual return of the background, is postictal suppression, an expected finding after seizure termination that supports a true ictal event. Ongoing seizure activity would be rhythmic and evolving, electrode detachment affects individual channels rather than producing a diffuse gradual recovery, and burst suppression alternates bursts with suppression rather than recovering steadily.

questions.stem: Which filter change can mask or distort important EEG findings?
options: Lowering the LFF too far, masking slowing
Raising the LFF too high, masking slowing
Raising the HFF too high, masking slowing
Lowering the LFF too far, blunting spikes
questions.explanation: A high LFF (high-pass) attenuates delta and theta, so diffuse slowing can look less prominent. Lowering the HFF too far is the other common error, as it attenuates spikes. Lowering the LFF preserves slow activity, and raising the HFF preserves fast activity, so those changes do not mask these findings.

questions.stem: Which characteristic of benign EEG variants helps distinguish them from epileptiform activity?
options: A prominent aftergoing slow wave
Evolution in frequency over seconds
No disruption of the background rhythm
A pointed morphology with a wide field
questions.explanation: Benign variants such as wicket spikes, BETS and mu rhythm typically do not disrupt the background and usually lack an aftergoing slow wave. A prominent aftergoing slow wave, a pointed transient with a broad physiologic field, and evolution over seconds are features of epileptiform or ictal activity, not benign variants.

questions.stem: Which factor MOST contributes to excessive EEG noise and artifact?
options: Large impedance differences between electrodes
Using a bipolar instead of a referential montage
Recording with a slower display sweep speed
Uniformly low impedances at all electrodes
questions.explanation: Large impedance differences between electrodes degrade common-mode rejection and are a major source of noise; poor grounding is another. Montage choice and sweep speed change only how data are displayed, and uniformly low impedances reduce noise rather than cause it.

questions.stem: Which characteristic helps identify a transient as an epileptiform discharge?
options: Confinement to a single electrode channel
A physiologic field across neighboring electrodes
A smooth, rounded, sinusoidal morphology
Appearance only with eye blinks or with chewing
questions.explanation: Epileptiform discharges have a physiologic field, appearing with graded amplitude across neighboring electrodes; they also have a pointed, sharp morphology that stands out from the background. Confinement to one channel suggests electrode artifact, a smooth sinusoidal shape is typical of background rhythms rather than spikes, and time-locking to blinks or chewing indicates eye-movement or muscle artifact.

questions.stem: Which statement about age-related EEG development is true?
options: The posterior rhythm reaches adult frequency by age one
Posterior rhythm frequency rises with maturation
Awake theta is abnormal at any age, including childhood
Background amplitude is higher in adults than in children
questions.explanation: The posterior dominant rhythm speeds up with age, from a few Hz in infancy to about 8 Hz by age 3 and adult values in adolescence. Theta and some delta are normal in awake children but abnormal in a fully awake adult. Adult frequency is not reached by age one; awake theta is expected in children; background amplitude is generally higher in children than in adults.

questions.stem: Which condition is a recognized contraindication to hyperventilation?
options: Absence epilepsy
Febrile seizures
Benign rolandic spikes
Sickle cell disease
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is a contraindication because HV-induced hypocapnia and hypoxia can trigger a sickling crisis; recent stroke and raised intracranial pressure are also contraindications. Absence epilepsy is a key indication for HV, and a history of febrile seizures or benign rolandic spikes is not a reason to avoid it.

questions.stem: Which pair of graphoelements is characteristic of N2 sleep?
options: Vertex waves and slow eye rolling
Sawtooth waves and rapid eye movements
Sleep spindles and K-complexes
High-voltage delta over 20%
questions.explanation: N2 is characterized by sleep spindles (12-14 Hz, central) and K-complexes. Either one is sufficient to score N2 under AASM; both need not be present. Vertex waves with slow rolling eye movements mark N1; sawtooth waves and rapid eye movements mark REM; high-voltage delta over 20% of the epoch defines N3.

questions.stem: Which statement about montages is correct?
options: Referential montages localize mainly by phase reversal
Bipolar montages help localize through phase reversal
Bipolar montages show the true amplitude at each site
Average reference suits generalized spikes best
questions.explanation: Bipolar montages localize activity by phase reversal at the electrode common to adjacent channels. Referential montages (especially average reference) can also enhance focal abnormalities, but they localize mainly by amplitude, not phase reversal. Bipolar channels show differences between neighbours rather than true amplitude, and generalized spikes contaminate an average reference.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST reliably distinguishes ictal from interictal EEG activity?
options: Evolution in frequency, amplitude, or field
Higher amplitude of the individual spikes
Presence of an aftergoing slow wave
Sharper, more pointed spike morphology
questions.explanation: Ictal activity evolves in frequency, amplitude, or spatial distribution over time, often with clinical correlation; isolated discharges without evolution are interictal. Spike amplitude, an aftergoing slow wave and pointed morphology are features of individual epileptiform discharges and do not separate ictal from interictal activity.

questions.stem: Which pairing of artifact and identifying feature is correct?
options: Eye blink: frontal maximum, time-locked to blinks
Muscle: slow, smooth waves, maximal at the vertex
Sweat: fast spiky activity over the temporalis
Electrode pop: field spread over many channels
questions.explanation: Eye blinks are frontally maximal (Fp1/Fp2) and time-locked to visible blinks. ECG artifact is also recognisable (regular, about 1 Hz, time-locked to the QRS, often temporal/ear leads). Muscle artifact is fast, not slow; sweat is very slow drift; electrode pop is confined to one electrode.

questions.stem: Which is a characteristic of a normal adult posterior dominant rhythm?
options: Attenuates when the eyes open
Increases when the eyes open
Is maximal over frontal leads
Has a frequency of 4 to 7 Hz
questions.explanation: A normal adult PDR is 8-13 Hz, maximal posteriorly, and attenuates with eye opening. It does not increase with eye opening, it is not frontally maximal, and 4-7 Hz is the theta range, which would be slow for an awake adult. The PDR may be poorly formed or absent in some normal patients.

questions.stem: A technologist should understand that sensitivity settings affect:
options: The actual voltage the brain generates
The horizontal time scale of the page
The vertical display scale of waveforms
The frequency content of the signal
questions.explanation: Sensitivity (μV/mm) sets how tall a given voltage is drawn on the display; it does not change the voltage the brain produces. The horizontal time scale is set by the sweep (timebase), and frequency content is shaped by the filters, not by sensitivity.

questions.stem: Along with reactivity, which background feature best grades the severity of a diffuse encephalopathy?
options: Amplitude of the photic driving response
Amount of frontal beta activity present
Degree of slowing, theta versus delta
Patient's age at the time of the study
questions.explanation: Severity of diffuse encephalopathy is graded mainly by the degree of background slowing (delta is worse than theta) and by reactivity (preserved reactivity is favorable). Photic driving amplitude is not a severity measure, frontal beta mostly reflects medication, and age provides context but does not grade severity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes photic driving from a photoparoxysmal response?
options: Driving is time-locked; a PPR can outlast the flashes
Driving is generalized; a PPR is confined to occipital
Driving outlasts the flashes; a PPR stops with them
Driving occurs only below 5 Hz; a PPR only above 30 Hz
questions.explanation: Photic driving is occipital activity time-locked to the flash rate and is normal, whereas a photoparoxysmal response (PPR) is epileptiform, often generalized, and may persist after stimulation. The other statements reverse the distribution or persistence of the two phenomena or give frequency limits that do not exist.

questions.stem: Which statement about EEG localization is MOST accurate?
options: Scalp EEG localizes activity to a region, not an exact point
Scalp EEG pinpoints subcortical lesions within a few millimeters
Each electrode records only the cortex directly beneath its cup
Deep and superficial generators appear with similar amplitude
questions.explanation: Scalp EEG mainly reflects superficial cortical activity and gives regional localization rather than exact anatomical pinpointing. It cannot precisely localize subcortical lesions; volume conduction means each electrode samples a broad area of cortex, not just the tissue under its cup; and deep generators are attenuated by distance, so they appear much smaller than superficial ones.

questions.stem: Which feature characterizes generalized spike-and-wave complexes?
options: Bilateral synchrony and symmetric distribution
Consistent onset in one temporal lobe
Phase reversal at a single electrode
Maximum amplitude over the occipital poles
questions.explanation: Generalized spike-and-wave complexes are bilaterally synchronous and symmetric, and are commonly frontally maximal. A consistent temporal onset or a phase reversal at a single electrode indicates a focal discharge, and an occipital maximum is not the typical distribution of generalized spike-and-wave.

questions.stem: Which pairing of sweep speed and purpose is correct?
options: 30 mm/s, to spread waveforms out for spike review
10 mm/s, to spread waveforms out for spike review
30 mm/s, to compress the page for slow-wave review
60 mm/s, to compress the page for slow-wave review
questions.explanation: A faster sweep (30 mm/s) gives more millimeters per second, spreading waveforms out so spike morphology is easier to see; a slower sweep (10 mm/s) compresses the page, which helps survey slow waves and background. 10 mm/s compresses rather than spreads; 30 mm/s and 60 mm/s spread rather than compress the page.

questions.stem: Which is a characteristic of mu rhythm?
options: Attenuation with contralateral movement
Blocking with eye opening, like alpha
Maximal amplitude over the occiput
Activation by hyperventilation
questions.explanation: Mu rhythm is an arch-shaped central (C3/C4) rhythm that attenuates with movement, or the intention to move, of the contralateral limb; it is a normal variant. Unlike alpha it does not block with eye opening, it is central rather than occipital, and it is not activated by hyperventilation.

questions.stem: Which practice MOST improves electrode contact and signal quality?
options: Spreading paste across neighboring sites for contact
Moisturizing the scalp with lotion before applying cups
Using larger cups so the skin needs no preparation
Cleaning and gently abrading the scalp at each site
questions.explanation: Cleaning away oil and debris and gently abrading the outer skin layer lowers impedance and stabilizes contact, followed by an adequate amount of conductive paste at each site. Paste spreading between sites creates a salt bridge that shorts electrodes together; lotion leaves an insulating film; a larger cup does not replace skin preparation.

questions.stem: Which activation procedure is MOST likely to provoke generalized spike-wave in a child with suspected absence epilepsy?
options: Sleep deprivation
Photic stimulation
Hyperventilation
Prolonged eye closure
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation is the most effective activator of the 3 Hz spike-wave of childhood absence epilepsy, often provoking a typical absence. Sleep deprivation also improves yield in epilepsy evaluation but is less specific for absences, photic stimulation mainly activates photosensitive generalized epilepsies, and eye closure is a weaker trigger.

questions.stem: Which is a common cause of 60 Hz line noise in EEG?
options: Sweating under the scalp electrodes
Poor contact at the ground electrode
Patient chewing during the recording
Eye blinks during photic stimulation
questions.explanation: 60 Hz artifact commonly results from poor ground electrode contact or high impedance, or from nearby electrical equipment; fix the source before using a notch filter. Sweating produces slow baseline sway, chewing produces muscle artifact, and eye blinks produce frontal slow deflections.

questions.stem: Which statement about EEG signal measurement is correct?
options: Displayed polarity depends on the montage and input order
Each channel records absolute voltage at one scalp site
Each channel measures current flowing between two inputs
An upward pen deflection means input 1 is relatively positive
questions.explanation: Polarity in EEG is relative: what a deflection means depends on which electrodes are in inputs 1 and 2 of the montage. Each channel records a voltage difference between two inputs, not an absolute voltage at one site and not current; by convention an upward deflection means input 1 is negative relative to input 2.

questions.stem: Which criterion is used to classify an epileptiform transient as a spike rather than a sharp wave?
options: Its duration: under 70 ms versus 70-200 ms
Its amplitude: above or below 100 µV
Its polarity: surface-negative or positive
Its location: temporal versus frontal
questions.explanation: Spikes and sharp waves are separated by duration: spikes last 20-70 ms and sharp waves 70-200 ms. Both share a pointed morphology distinct from the background. Amplitude does not distinguish them, most epileptiform discharges of either type are surface-negative, and both can occur in any region.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST helps identify muscle (EMG) artifact?
options: Maximal at the vertex, increasing during drowsiness
Maximal occipitally, attenuating with eye opening
Maximal in one electrode, unrelated to any movement
Maximal temporally/frontally, increasing with tension
questions.explanation: EMG is maximal over the temporalis and frontalis and increases with muscle tension or movement; it is also high frequency (about 20-300 Hz). Vertex activity in drowsiness describes vertex waves; occipital activity attenuating with eye opening is the alpha rhythm; a single electrode unrelated to movement suggests electrode pop.

questions.stem: Which statement about prominent frontal beta activity is MOST accurate?
options: It is a typical sign of ongoing seizure activity
It is a common benzodiazepine or barbiturate effect
It is the expected finding in slow-wave sleep
It is a characteristic sign of phenytoin toxicity
questions.explanation: Prominent frontal beta is a common medication effect of benzodiazepines and barbiturates and is not in itself abnormal brain activity. It does not indicate ongoing seizures, slow-wave sleep is dominated by delta activity, and phenytoin toxicity is associated with slowing rather than prominent beta.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly pairs graphoelements with NREM sleep stages?
options: Vertex waves in N2 only; spindles and K-complexes in N1
Vertex waves in REM; spindles and K-complexes in N1-N2
Vertex waves in N1-N2; spindles and K-complexes in REM
Vertex waves in N1-N2; spindles and K-complexes in N2
questions.explanation: Vertex waves appear in N1 and persist in N2 (maximal at Cz), while spindles and K-complexes define N2. Vertex waves are not limited to N2 or a REM feature, and spindles and K-complexes are not N1 or REM findings; REM features rapid eye movements.

questions.stem: Which statement about montage selection is correct?
options: Referential aids localization; bipolar aids field assessment
Bipolar shows true amplitude; referential shows phase reversal
One well-chosen montage is enough for full interpretation
Bipolar aids localization; referential aids field assessment
questions.explanation: Bipolar montages localize through phase reversal, while referential montages show amplitude and the extent of the field. Multiple montages of both types are used for comprehensive interpretation. The reversed pairing is wrong, bipolar channels do not show true amplitude, and a single montage leaves blind spots.

questions.stem: Which change indicates ictal evolution?
options: A fixed rhythm repeating without change
Isolated spikes at a steady interval
Brief bursts identical from start to end
Progressive change in frequency and field
questions.explanation: Ictal evolution means progressive change over time in frequency (for example fast to slower), amplitude, or spatial spread. A fixed unchanging rhythm, isolated spikes at a steady interval, and stereotyped bursts that do not change all lack evolution and are more consistent with interictal or periodic patterns.

questions.stem: Which statement about neonatal EEG patterns is true?
options: A normal neonatal EEG is continuous from 28 weeks onward
Normal neonatal patterns change little with conceptual age
Discontinuity such as trace alternant is normal in neonates
Trace alternant is normal only in infants under 32 weeks
questions.explanation: Discontinuous patterns, including trace alternant in quiet sleep, are normal in neonates up to about 44 weeks post-conceptual age, and normal patterns change markedly with post-conceptual age. Preterm records at 28 weeks are largely discontinuous; neonatal patterns are highly age-dependent; trace alternant is a term-age pattern, not limited to very preterm infants.

questions.stem: Which statement is true regarding notch filter use?
options: Leave it on routinely for every recording
Use it mainly to reduce slow sweat artifact
Use it in place of rechecking impedances
Use it only if the 60 Hz source cannot be fixed
questions.explanation: The notch filter is a last resort after the source of line noise (ground, impedances, equipment) has been addressed, because it can distort spikes and other activity near 60 Hz. It should not be left on routinely or substituted for troubleshooting, and it acts on line frequency, not on slow sweat artifact.

questions.stem: Which factor helps determine whether an amplitude asymmetry is significant?
options: Its presence in a single referential montage
The patient's handedness alone
Any measurable difference between sides
Its consistency across montages and findings
questions.explanation: Significance depends on the degree of asymmetry (under about 50% may be a normal variant), its consistency across montages, and correlation with other findings such as focal slowing or epileptiform activity. A finding seen in only one referential montage may reflect reference contamination, handedness alone does not explain asymmetry, and not every measurable difference is abnormal.

questions.stem: Which medication class is classically associated with prominent frontocentral beta activity on EEG?
options: Beta-blockers
Benzodiazepines
Opioid analgesics
Lithium carbonate
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines (like barbiturates) characteristically increase frontocentral beta activity, so medication history matters when beta is prominent. Beta-blockers do not produce excess beta despite the name; opioids tend to produce slowing; lithium is associated with slowing and sometimes sharp activity rather than prominent beta.

questions.stem: Which feature characterizes the classic 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave of absence epilepsy?
options: A consistent onset in one temporal lobe
A 4-6 Hz rhythm with polyspike components
A slow 1.5-2.5 Hz spike-and-wave rhythm
Bilaterally synchronous, symmetric bursts
questions.explanation: Classic absence spike-and-wave is bilaterally synchronous and symmetric, usually frontally maximal, and is readily activated by hyperventilation in children. A consistent temporal onset indicates a focal process, 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave is typical of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and 1.5-2.5 Hz slow spike-and-wave is typical of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST helps identify electrode pop artifact?
options: Sharp wave with a field across adjacent channels
Steep deflection confined to a single channel
Rhythmic deflection recurring at the heart rate
Slow deflection synchronous with every eye blink
questions.explanation: Electrode pop is a brief, steep, high-amplitude deflection confined to one electrode and occurring randomly rather than with movement. A field across adjacent channels suggests cerebral activity; heart-rate deflections are ECG artifact; blink-synchronous deflections are eye artifact.

questions.stem: In adults, diffuse theta activity is BEST described as:
options: Abnormal in any state, including drowsiness
Typical of the alert, eyes-closed adult state
Normal in drowsiness, abnormal when fully alert
An epileptiform sign whenever it is recorded
questions.explanation: Theta in adults is state-dependent: normal during drowsiness and light sleep but abnormal when the patient is fully awake and alert, so patient state must be noted. It is not abnormal in drowsiness, the alert eyes-closed state is characterized by alpha rather than theta, and theta is not epileptiform in itself.

questions.stem: Which statement about sampling rate and frequency representation is correct?
options: The Nyquist frequency is twice the sampling rate in use
Frequencies above half the sampling rate alias as lower ones
Frequencies above the sampling rate alias; lower ones do not
Sampling rate affects amplitude scaling but not frequency
questions.explanation: The Nyquist frequency equals half the sampling rate, and any signal component above it aliases, appearing as a false lower frequency. The Nyquist frequency is not twice the sampling rate, aliasing begins above half the sampling rate rather than above the full rate, and sampling rate does determine which frequencies can be represented.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes 14 and 6 Hz positive spikes?
options: Negative-polarity spikes, maximal frontally in deep sleep
Benign positive bursts, posterior temporal, drowsy/light sleep
Epileptiform discharges, maximal midline central when awake
Benign positive bursts, occipital, awake with eyes open
questions.explanation: 14 and 6 Hz positive spikes are a benign variant of children and adolescents, seen in drowsiness and light sleep with a posterior temporal maximum. They are positive (not negative) and not frontal or deep-sleep findings; they are not epileptiform; occipital positive transients with eyes open describe lambda waves.

questions.stem: Which statement about phase reversal in bipolar montages is correct?
options: It localizes to the electrode common to both channels
It localizes to the electrode at the end of the chain
It indicates reversed polarity of the amplifier inputs
It requires the activity to appear in only one channel
questions.explanation: A phase reversal localizes the maximum to the electrode shared by the two adjacent channels, and the activity must be present in both channels for the reversal to occur. An end-of-chain maximum produces no reversal, reversal is a property of the field rather than an input wiring fault, and activity in only one channel cannot reverse.

questions.stem: Which feature BEST distinguishes REM sleep from NREM sleep on EEG?
options: High-voltage delta with slow rolling eye movements
Posterior alpha rhythm that blocks with eye opening
Low-voltage mixed activity with rapid eye movements
Synchronized spindles with high chin muscle tone
questions.explanation: REM shows a desynchronized, low-voltage mixed-frequency background with rapid eye movements and low muscle tone, whereas NREM shows synchronized activity (spindles/K-complexes in N2, slow waves in N3). High-voltage delta is N3 and slow rolling eye movements are N1; reactive posterior alpha is wakefulness; spindles are NREM.

questions.stem: Which statement about electrode impedance is MOST accurate?
options: Only absolute values matter, not their balance
Any value under 10 kΩ prevents contact artifact
Imbalance between electrodes can cause artifact
Higher impedance improves common-mode rejection
questions.explanation: Impedance balance is critical: differences between electrodes (for example more than about 5 kΩ) can cause artifact even when each value is individually acceptable. Absolute values alone do not tell the whole story, being under 10 kΩ does not guarantee artifact-free recording, and higher impedance worsens common-mode rejection.

questions.stem: Which statement about posterior dominant rhythm (PDR) frequency and age is true?
options: A PDR below 9 Hz is abnormal at any age after infancy
PDR frequency peaks in infancy and then falls with age
PDR frequency stays the same after the first birthday
A slower PDR in young children is normal for their age
questions.explanation: PDR frequency increases with brain maturation, so a slower rhythm in a young child is age-appropriate (about 8 Hz is reached by age 3). An 8 Hz PDR is normal in many children and adults, so a 9 Hz cut-off is wrong; frequency rises rather than falls with age; it keeps increasing well beyond the first year.

questions.stem: Which pattern is characteristic of ictal onset?
options: A single spike with a slow wave
Brief, non-evolving sharp transients
Rhythmic fast activity that evolves
Wicket spikes in temporal regions
questions.explanation: Ictal onset commonly shows rhythmic activity (fast, theta, or delta) that evolves, and may begin with an electrodecremental attenuation of the background. A single spike-and-slow-wave and brief non-evolving sharp transients are interictal, and wicket spikes are a benign drowsiness variant.

questions.stem: A technologist raises LFF from 0.1 Hz to 1.0 Hz and observes that diffuse slowing appears reduced. The technologist should understand that:
options: This is a filter effect, not a real change
The encephalopathy has actually improved
The slowing was artifact from the start
The patient has moved into deeper sleep
questions.explanation: Raising the LFF attenuates slow activity, so slowing looks less prominent even though the brain activity is unchanged; the recording should be interpreted at standard settings (LFF about 0.1-1 Hz). The change does not reflect clinical improvement, does not show that the original slowing was artifact, and is unrelated to sleep stage.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes lambda waves?
options: Positive occipital sharp transients of light NREM sleep
Negative occipital spikes evoked by flashing light stimulation
Positive occipital sharp transients during visual scanning
Arch-shaped central waves blocked by moving the opposite hand
questions.explanation: Lambda waves are surface-positive occipital sharp transients time-locked to saccadic eye movements while the awake patient scans a scene with eyes open. Similar positive occipital transients in light sleep are POSTS; spikes evoked by flashes describe a photoparoxysmal response; arch-shaped central waves blocked by hand movement are mu rhythm. Lambda waves are normal.

questions.stem: Which history MOST calls for caution with, or omission of, hyperventilation?
options: A remote history of childhood febrile seizures
Recent stroke or raised intracranial pressure
A new diagnosis of absence epilepsy
A family history of photosensitivity
questions.explanation: Recent stroke and raised intracranial pressure call for caution or omission of HV because hypocapnic vasoconstriction can reduce cerebral perfusion; sickle cell disease and severe cardiorespiratory disease are other contraindications. Febrile seizures and a family history of photosensitivity are not contraindications, and absence epilepsy is a main indication for HV.

questions.stem: Which statement about the limits of scalp EEG is MOST accurate?
options: Thalamic activity is recorded about as well as convexity cortex
Activity from deep structures such as hippocampus is poorly seen
Scalp EEG records mainly from the subcortical white matter tracts
The skull and scalp have little effect on the recorded amplitude
questions.explanation: Scalp EEG primarily reflects superficial cortical activity, so deep structures such as the hippocampus and thalamus are poorly represented. Thalamic activity is not recorded as well as convexity cortex; white matter tracts do not generate the summated postsynaptic potentials EEG records; and the skull and scalp markedly attenuate and spread the signal.

questions.stem: Which EEG finding is the MOST favorable prognostic sign in a patient with diffuse encephalopathy?
options: A background that stays reactive to stimulation
Continuous delta that does not change with stimuli
Burst-suppression with long periods of flat EEG
Diffuse alpha-range activity unreactive to stimuli
questions.explanation: Preserved reactivity (the background changes with eye opening, noxious or auditory stimuli) is a favorable sign in diffuse encephalopathy, as is milder slowing (theta rather than delta). Unreactive continuous delta, burst-suppression and unreactive alpha-frequency (alpha coma) patterns all indicate severe dysfunction and a poorer outlook.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST helps identify sweat artifact?
options: Slow baseline drift across several channels
Fast spiky activity rising with jaw tension
Regular sharp deflections at the heart rate
Abrupt steep deflection in a single channel
questions.explanation: Sweat artifact is a very slow, irregular baseline drift over several channels, worse in warm conditions, caused by sweat altering skin potentials; it can mimic slowing. Fast activity with jaw tension is muscle; heart-rate deflections are ECG; an abrupt single-channel deflection is electrode pop.

questions.stem: Which statement about aftergoing slow waves in epileptiform discharges is true?
options: They are required in every epileptiform discharge
They follow spikes but not sharp waves
They are common but not required for classification
Their presence indicates electrode artifact
questions.explanation: Aftergoing slow waves are common but not required; morphology, a physiologic field and context are more important when classifying a discharge as epileptiform. They are not mandatory, they can follow both spikes and sharp waves, and they support a cerebral origin rather than an artifact.

questions.stem: Which statement about the average reference montage is correct?
options: It best displays high-amplitude generalized discharges
It is immune to contamination by large discharges
It can make focal sharp waves more prominent than bipolar
It localizes chiefly through phase reversal in chains
questions.explanation: Because the average reference subtracts activity common to all electrodes, a focal sharp wave can stand out more than in a bipolar montage, where neighbouring electrodes share and cancel it. High-amplitude generalized discharges contaminate the average, large discharges are exactly what contaminate it, and phase-reversal localization is a feature of bipolar chains.

questions.stem: Which BEST describes normal posterior dominant rhythm reactivity?
options: Increases with eye opening, fades on eye closure
Unaffected by opening or closing the eyes
Attenuates only during mental arithmetic tasks
Attenuates with eye opening, returns on closure
questions.explanation: A normal PDR attenuates with eye opening and returns when the eyes close; poor reactivity may reflect drowsiness, medication or encephalopathy. It does not increase with eye opening, a rhythm unaffected by eye state is abnormal, and although mental effort can attenuate alpha, eye opening is the main reactivity test.

questions.stem: Why does a sleep-deprived EEG increase the likelihood of capturing epileptiform activity?
options: It promotes sleep, which raises interictal discharge rates
It lowers scalp impedance, which improves signal quality
It raises alpha amplitude, unmasking posterior spikes
It lowers amplifier noise, so small spikes stand out
questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation makes sleep more likely during the recording and itself increases cortical excitability, and sleep raises the rate of interictal discharges and activates some seizure types. It does not change electrode impedance, it tends to reduce rather than raise alpha, and it has no effect on amplifier noise; the gain in yield comes from promoting sleep and increasing cortical excitability.

questions.stem: Which statement about differential amplifiers is MOST accurate?
options: They amplify signals common to both inputs
They reject signals that differ between inputs
They add the two inputs together before display
They reject signals that are common to both inputs
questions.explanation: Differential amplifiers amplify the difference between active and reference inputs and reject common-mode signals present at both, quantified by the CMRR. They do not amplify common signals, they amplify rather than reject differences, and they subtract rather than add the inputs.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes sleep spindles?
options: 8-10 Hz occipital bursts characteristic of N1
12-14 Hz central bursts characteristic of N2
12-14 Hz central bursts characteristic of REM
4-6 Hz temporal bursts characteristic of N2
questions.explanation: Sleep spindles are 12-14 Hz rhythmic bursts maximal centrally and characteristic of N2; they are normal. Occipital 8-10 Hz activity is alpha; spindles are absent in REM; 4-6 Hz temporal activity is theta, not spindles.

questions.stem: Which statement is true regarding high-frequency filter (HFF) settings?
options: An HFF below 20 Hz can mask slowing
An HFF below 20 Hz can attenuate spikes
A typical routine HFF is about 1-5 Hz
An HFF of 70 Hz can attenuate spikes
questions.explanation: The HFF (low-pass) attenuates activity above its cutoff, so an excessively low setting (below about 20 Hz) blunts spikes and sharp waves. A standard routine HFF is about 70 Hz (35-70 Hz in older practice), which preserves spike morphology. A low HFF does not affect slowing; 1-5 Hz is in the range of LFF, not HFF, settings.

questions.stem: Which statement about persistent focal polymorphic delta slowing is true?
options: It is a benign variant seen in drowsiness
It should vanish in other montages if real
It suggests a structural or functional lesion
It indicates a generalized encephalopathy
questions.explanation: Persistent focal polymorphic delta is abnormal and suggests an underlying structural or functional lesion in that region; true cerebral slowing persists across montages, which helps distinguish it from artifact. It is not a benign drowsy variant, a real finding should persist rather than vanish when montages change, and focal slowing points to a regional, not generalized, process.

questions.stem: Which statement about EEG as a measurement system is correct?
options: It passively records current flowing through the scalp
It passively records voltage differences at the scalp
It records the absolute voltage at a single scalp site
It records magnetic fields produced by cortical dipoles
questions.explanation: EEG is a passive recording system that measures potential (voltage) differences between electrodes; it does not deliver current to the brain. It does not measure current flow, every channel compares two inputs rather than reading an absolute voltage, and magnetic fields are recorded by MEG.

questions.stem: Which practice is essential for good electrode contact during a routine EEG?
options: Applying extra paste instead of skin prep
Cleaning and lightly abrading each site
Turning on the notch filter for all channels
Raising the gain to offset weak contact
questions.explanation: Cleaning and gently abrading the scalp lowers skin impedance and is the foundation of stable contact; adequate paste and secure attachment are also needed, but they supplement rather than replace prep. Extra paste over unprepared skin leaves impedance high and risks bridging; the notch filter and gain only change how the signal is processed or displayed and do not improve contact.

questions.stem: Which pattern is commonly seen after seizure termination?
options: Immediate return to normal baseline
Postictal delta and theta slowing
Continuous 3 Hz spike-and-wave
Increased posterior alpha amplitude
questions.explanation: After a seizure the EEG commonly shows diffuse suppression and/or delta-theta slowing before the background gradually recovers, which helps confirm a true ictal event. An immediate return to baseline is unusual after a significant seizure, continuous spike-and-wave would suggest ongoing status epilepticus, and the alpha rhythm is typically slowed or attenuated rather than increased.

questions.stem: Which feature indicates a photoparoxysmal response rather than normal photic driving?
options: Occipital waves at the flash rate
Occipital waves at twice the flash rate
Discharges that outlast the flash train
Frontal spikes that stop with the flashes
questions.explanation: Epileptiform discharges that are not time-locked and persist after stimulation stops indicate a photoparoxysmal response. Occipital activity at the flash rate or at a harmonic (twice the rate) is normal driving, and frontal spikes that stop with the flashes are photomyogenic muscle artifact.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes benign epileptiform transients of sleep (BETS)?
options: Small, brief temporal spikes most common in alert wakefulness
Broad temporal sharp waves with a prominent aftergoing slow wave
Arch-shaped temporal waves in trains, mainly in older adults
Small, brief temporal spikes in drowsiness, no slow wave after
questions.explanation: BETS (small sharp spikes) are low-amplitude (<50 µV), very brief (<50 ms) temporal spikes seen in adult drowsiness and light sleep, typically without an aftergoing slow wave or background disruption. They disappear in deeper sleep and are not a waking finding; a broad sharp wave with a slow wave suggests an epileptiform discharge; arch-shaped temporal trains describe wicket spikes.

questions.stem: Which filter setting can lead to misinterpretation of EEG findings?
options: An LFF below 0.5 Hz that masks slowing
An HFF of 70 Hz that attenuates spikes
An HFF below 20 Hz that attenuates spikes
A notch filter that masks diffuse slowing
questions.explanation: A very low HFF attenuates fast components, so spikes and sharp waves can look blunted or be missed. A high LFF (which masks slowing) and a notch filter (which distorts activity near 60 Hz) are other sources of error. An LFF below 0.5 Hz preserves slow activity, 70 Hz is a standard HFF, and the notch acts near line frequency rather than on slowing.

questions.stem: Which statement about neonatal EEG discontinuity is true?
options: Trace alternant is normal until about 44 weeks post-conceptual age
Interburst intervals lengthen as post-conceptual age increases
Any discontinuity at term indicates a severe encephalopathy
Trace alternant first appears after 44 weeks post-conceptual age
questions.explanation: Trace alternant is a normal discontinuous quiet-sleep pattern up to about 44 weeks post-conceptual age; continuity increases with maturation, and discontinuity in older infants is abnormal. Interburst intervals shorten, not lengthen, with age; discontinuity at term can be normal trace alternant; trace alternant is seen at term and disappears by about 44 weeks rather than appearing then.

questions.stem: Which feature helps distinguish a true epileptiform discharge from artifact?
options: Involvement of a single isolated electrode
A field that spreads to adjacent electrodes
Time-locking to eye blinks or chewing
An abrupt, square-shaped waveform
questions.explanation: True epileptiform discharges show a physiologic field, spreading with graded amplitude to adjacent electrodes, and a pointed morphology distinct from the background. Single-electrode involvement suggests an electrode pop or poor contact, time-locking to blinks or chewing suggests eye or muscle artifact, and abrupt square waveforms are typical of instrumental or electrode artifact.

questions.stem: Which statement about using multiple montages is correct?
options: Bipolar and referential views give identical information
A referential view is needed only when bipolar is normal
Bipolar views are needed only when artifact is present
Bipolar and referential views give complementary information
questions.explanation: Bipolar montages aid localization via phase reversal and referential montages aid field assessment, so together they give complementary information; using both confirms findings and improves localization accuracy. The two views are not identical, and neither is reserved for a particular situation; both are standard practice.

questions.stem: Under AASM rules, what is REQUIRED to begin scoring an epoch as N2 (N3 criteria not met)?
options: A spindle and a K-complex must both be present
Vertex waves with slow rolling eye movements
Slow-wave activity in 20% or more of the epoch
Either a non-arousal K-complex or a sleep spindle
questions.explanation: Under AASM rules N2 scoring begins when one or more K-complexes not associated with arousal or one or more sleep spindles occur in the first half of the epoch or last half of the previous epoch, provided N3 criteria are not met. Both are not required. Vertex waves with slow rolling eye movements indicate N1; slow-wave activity in 20% or more of the epoch indicates N3.

questions.stem: 60 Hz artifact appears in all channels. What should be checked FIRST?
options: Ground electrode impedance and contact
Whether the notch filter is switched on
The low-frequency filter setting in use
The patient's position and head support
questions.explanation: 60 Hz in every channel suggests a ground or environmental problem, so check ground electrode contact and impedance first, then the electrical environment and nearby equipment. The notch filter only attenuates the symptom, the low-frequency filter acts on slow activity, and head position causes movement rather than line-frequency artifact.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding prominent frontal beta activity?
options: Commonly medication-induced (benzodiazepines, barbiturates)
Is a medication effect, not necessarily abnormal brain activity
Both A and B are correct
Always indicates seizure focus
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Prominent frontal beta is commonly medication-induced and should be documented but not overinterpreted. It's an effect, not necessarily abnormal brain activity.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes ictal from interictal epileptiform activity?
options: Isolated sharp waves with no change
A higher amplitude of each spike
Evolution in frequency or spread
Presence of an aftergoing slow wave
questions.explanation: Ictal activity shows evolution (changes in frequency, amplitude, or distribution) and often clinical correlation, whereas interictal discharges are brief and non-evolving. Isolated unchanging sharp waves are interictal, and spike amplitude or an aftergoing slow wave does not separate ictal from interictal activity.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST helps identify eye blink artifact?
options: Out-of-phase deflections at F7 and F8 on side gaze
Rhythmic central activity blocked by moving a fist
In-phase deflections at Fp1 and Fp2 with each blink
Sharp positive occipital transients in light sleep
questions.explanation: Blinks produce symmetric, in-phase deflections maximal at Fp1 and Fp2, time-locked to visible blinks. Out-of-phase F7/F8 deflections are lateral eye movements; central activity blocked by movement is mu rhythm; positive occipital sharp transients in light sleep are POSTS.

questions.stem: Which statement about the severity of diffuse background slowing is correct?
options: Predominant theta implies more severe dysfunction than delta
Predominant delta implies more severe dysfunction than theta
Theta and delta slowing imply equal degrees of dysfunction
Slowing frequency is unrelated to the degree of dysfunction
questions.explanation: The degree of slowing tracks encephalopathy severity: predominant delta (below 4 Hz) reflects more severe diffuse dysfunction than predominant theta (4-7 Hz). Reversing that order, treating the two as equivalent, or claiming the frequency carries no severity information are all incorrect.

questions.stem: Which sweep speed is most useful for surveying slow waves and the overall background?
options: 30 mm/s, which spreads waveforms out in time
60 mm/s, which stretches each waveform widely
Any speed, as speed alters only the amplitude
10 mm/s, which compresses more time per screen
questions.explanation: A slower sweep such as 10 mm/s compresses more seconds onto each screen, making slow waves, rhythmicity, and the overall background easier to survey. Faster speeds such as 30 or 60 mm/s spread waveforms out and are better for examining spikes and sharp transients, and sweep speed changes the time axis, not amplitude.

questions.stem: How should the electrode where a discharge is maximal (e.g., T5) be interpreted?
options: It marks the exact millimeter location of the generator
It reflects the deep structure lying directly beneath it
It indicates the underlying cortical region, not a point
It identifies the hemisphere opposite to the true source
questions.explanation: Each electrode corresponds to an underlying cortical region (T5 overlies posterior temporal cortex), but scalp localization is a regional approximation, not exact pinpointing. EEG cannot give millimeter accuracy, the maximum reflects superficial cortex rather than a deep structure, and scalp maxima are not routinely contralateral to the generator.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of generalized spike-and-wave discharges?
options: Onset is fixed in one temporal lobe
A frontal amplitude maximum is common
Amplitude is highest at the occiput
They phase-reverse at one electrode
questions.explanation: Generalized spike-and-wave discharges commonly have a frontal maximum and are bilaterally synchronous and symmetric, which distinguishes them from focal patterns. A fixed temporal onset or a phase reversal at a single electrode indicates a focal discharge, and an occipital maximum is not the usual distribution.

questions.stem: Which statement about hyperventilation activation is MOST accurate?
options: It mainly activates focal temporal spikes in adults
It is more effective in older adults than children
It usually suppresses generalized spike-and-wave
It often provokes 3 Hz spike-and-wave in absence
questions.explanation: HV classically provokes 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave and absence seizures in untreated childhood absence epilepsy, and it is more effective in children than adults. It is a weak activator of focal temporal spikes, it is less effective in older adults, and it activates rather than suppresses generalized discharges.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes wicket spikes?
options: Arch-shaped temporal trains without aftergoing slow wave
Arch-shaped central trains that block with hand movement
Isolated temporal sharp waves with an aftergoing slow wave
Small, single temporal spikes seen only in deep N3 sleep
questions.explanation: Wicket spikes are arch-shaped (mu-like) temporal waves occurring in trains or clusters, usually in adults over 30, in wakefulness and drowsiness or light sleep, with no aftergoing slow wave and no background disruption. Central arch-shaped waves blocked by movement are mu rhythm; isolated sharp waves with a slow wave suggest epileptiform discharges; small single spikes of light sleep are BETS, which are not a deep-sleep finding.

questions.stem: A technologist changes sensitivity from 7 μV/mm to 14 μV/mm. The technologist should understand that:
options: Waveforms will appear larger on the display
The recorded brain voltage will decrease
Waveforms will appear compressed in time
Waveforms will appear smaller on the display
questions.explanation: Going from 7 to 14 μV/mm means each millimetre now represents more microvolts, so the same signal is drawn about half as tall. The actual brain voltage is unchanged; only the display scale changed. The horizontal time scale depends on the sweep speed, not on sensitivity.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child's EEG shows an 8 Hz posterior rhythm that is reactive to eye opening. The technologist should:
options: Recognize it as diffuse slowing that is abnormal for age
Recognize it as a rhythmic epileptiform posterior pattern
Recognize it as an age-appropriate posterior rhythm
Raise the filters to look for hidden faster activity
questions.explanation: The posterior dominant rhythm matures from about 4 Hz in early infancy to about 8 Hz by age 3 and adult values in adolescence, so a reactive 8 Hz rhythm at age 4 is normal. Calling it abnormal slowing applies adult norms; a reactive background rhythm is not epileptiform; adjusting filters does not reveal a hidden faster rhythm.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes vertex waves?
options: Sharp transients maximal at Cz in N1 and N2 sleep
Sharp transients maximal at Oz in N1 and N2 sleep
Sharp transients maximal at Cz during REM sleep
Sharp transients maximal at T3/T4 during wakefulness
questions.explanation: Vertex waves are high-amplitude sharp transients maximal at Cz in N1 and N2 sleep and are normal. Occipital sharp transients in sleep are POSTS; vertex waves are not a REM feature; temporal sharp transients in wakefulness are not vertex waves.

questions.stem: All electrodes show 3-4 kΩ impedance except T3 at 12 kΩ. The EEG shows noise. The technologist should:
options: Proceed, since all values are below 20 kΩ
Re-prep T3 to bring it in line with the others
Turn on the notch filter to clear the noise
Lower the sensitivity to reduce the noise
questions.explanation: T3 at 12 kΩ against 3-4 kΩ elsewhere creates an 8-9 kΩ imbalance that degrades common-mode rejection and causes artifact even if each value seems acceptable; re-prepping T3 fixes the cause. Proceeding ignores the imbalance, the notch filter only attenuates line noise, and lowering sensitivity hides the problem.

questions.stem: A technologist observes a sharp transient with 90 ms duration. The technologist should classify this as:
options: A spike
A slow wave
A sharp wave
A polyspike
questions.explanation: Sharp waves last 70-200 ms, so a 90 ms pointed transient is a sharp wave. Spikes last 20-70 ms, slow waves exceed 200 ms, and a polyspike is a run of several spikes rather than a single 90 ms transient. Duration is the key criterion.

questions.stem: A focal sharp wave is subtle in bipolar montage but prominent in average reference. The technologist should understand that:
options: This is a montage effect, not a change in the abnormality
The discharge has worsened since the bipolar epoch
The average reference is contaminated by eye artifact
The bipolar montage has a reversed amplifier input
questions.explanation: Average reference subtracts common-mode activity, so a focal sharp wave can look more prominent than in bipolar chains, where neighbouring electrodes share and cancel it. This reflects montage choice, not a worsening abnormality; eye artifact would not selectively enhance a focal sharp wave; and a reversed input would invert the waveform rather than shrink it.

questions.stem: An awake adult's posterior rhythm shows poor reactivity to eye opening. Which interpretation is MOST appropriate?
options: It may reflect drowsiness, medication, or encephalopathy
It is an expected normal variant needing no comment
It confirms an occipital seizure focus on that side
It indicates that the reference electrode is faulty
questions.explanation: A normal PDR attenuates with eye opening, so poor reactivity is noteworthy and, depending on context, may reflect drowsiness, medication effects or encephalopathy. It is not an expected normal variant, it does not by itself indicate a seizure focus, and a faulty reference would cause artifact across channels rather than isolated loss of reactivity.

questions.stem: Sleep recording is especially useful for activating which seizure type?
options: Psychogenic nonepileptic events
Reading-induced reflex seizures
Startle-induced reflex seizures
Seizures of frontal lobe onset
questions.explanation: Sleep activates interictal discharges and some seizure types, especially frontal lobe seizures, which often occur predominantly from sleep; sleep deprivation further raises yield. Psychogenic nonepileptic events arise from the waking state, and reading- and startle-induced reflex seizures need their specific triggers rather than sleep.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST helps identify ECG artifact?
options: Isolated to a single channel with poor contact
Irregular, fast, and increased by jaw clenching
Slow, wandering, and worse in a warm room
Regular, about 1 Hz, and time-locked to the QRS
questions.explanation: ECG artifact recurs regularly at the heart rate (about 1 Hz) and is time-locked to the QRS on an ECG channel, often in temporal and ear leads. Isolation to one poorly contacting electrode suggests electrode pop; irregular fast activity with jaw clenching is muscle; slow drift in a warm room is sweat.

questions.stem: Which change indicates ictal evolution during a seizure?
options: Frequency shifting from fast to slower
Unchanging frequency and amplitude
Single spikes repeating unchanged
Isolated sharp waves between events
questions.explanation: Ictal evolution includes changes in frequency (commonly fast to slower, or slow to faster), amplitude, or spatial distribution as the discharge spreads. Unchanging frequency and amplitude, stereotyped repeating spikes, and isolated sharp waves between events all lack evolution and are interictal or periodic rather than ictal.

questions.stem: Which statement about EEG polarity and pen deflections is correct?
options: An upward deflection means input 1 is positive relative to input 2
Deflection direction stays fixed regardless of the montage chosen
An upward deflection means input 1 is negative relative to input 2
Deflection direction shows the absolute polarity at one electrode
questions.explanation: By convention an upward deflection means input 1 is negative relative to input 2, so polarity is relative and depends on the montage. Saying upward means input 1 is positive reverses the convention; deflection direction changes when the montage changes; and a channel shows a difference between two inputs, not absolute polarity at one site.

questions.stem: Which statement is true regarding subdermal needle electrodes?
options: They have lower impedance and are preferred for routine EEG
They can be reused after wiping them with alcohol
They give more stable long-term recordings than cups
They need sterile technique and carry more infection risk
questions.explanation: Needle electrodes break the skin, so they require sterile single-use technique and carry a higher infection and needlestick risk; they are reserved for situations where scalp access or prep is limited. They have relatively high impedance and are not preferred for routine EEG, they are disposable rather than reusable, and they are less stable than cups for long-term recording.

questions.stem: Which factor helps determine whether an amplitude asymmetry is clinically significant?
options: Whether it exceeds a 10% difference
Which hemisphere is language-dominant
Its degree: under 50% may be normal
Whether the patient is right-handed
questions.explanation: The degree of asymmetry matters: differences under about 50% may be a normal variant, especially with a symmetric PDR frequency, and significance also depends on consistency across montages and associated slowing or epileptiform activity. A 10% difference is well within normal variation, and language dominance or handedness do not determine whether an asymmetry is abnormal.

questions.stem: Which finding is characteristic of normal photic driving?
options: Symmetric occipital waves time-locked to the flashes
Spike-and-wave persisting after the flashes end
Frontal muscle spikes that stop with the flashes
Occipital waves on one side only, at the flash rate
questions.explanation: Normal driving is symmetric, maximal occipitally, and time-locked to the flash rate. Spike-and-wave that persists indicates a photoparoxysmal response; frontal spikes that stop with the flashes are photomyogenic artifact; a consistently unilateral response is asymmetric and may suggest a lesion on the side lacking driving.

questions.stem: Which description BEST characterizes triphasic waves?
options: Focal spike-wave discharges typical of temporal lobe epilepsy
Low-amplitude fast waves typical of a sedative medication effect
Periodic three-phase waves typical of metabolic encephalopathy
Sharp negative transients typical of normal adult drowsiness
questions.explanation: Triphasic waves are periodic, relatively high-amplitude, three-phase complexes, often frontally predominant, seen in toxic-metabolic encephalopathies such as hepatic or renal failure. They are not focal epileptiform discharges, not the low-voltage beta of sedatives, and not a normal drowsy transient.

questions.stem: Why should a patient's antiseizure medications be documented before the EEG is interpreted?
options: They raise electrode impedance and increase line noise
They may reduce how often epileptiform discharges appear
They typically speed the posterior rhythm above 13 Hz
They reliably increase photoparoxysmal responses
