questions.explanation: Antiseizure medications can reduce the frequency of interictal epileptiform discharges, so a normal or near-normal study must be read in that context (and some, like benzodiazepines and barbiturates, also add beta). They do not affect electrode impedance or line noise, they tend to slow rather than speed the posterior rhythm, and they usually reduce rather than increase photoparoxysmal responses.

questions.stem: Which features characterize classic 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave of absence epilepsy?
options: Perfect bilateral synchrony, symmetric distribution, frontal maximum
Activated by hyperventilation, especially in children
Both A and B are correct
Always focal in one temporal lobe
questions.explanation: Both are correct: 3 Hz spike-and-wave shows perfect synchrony, symmetry, frontal max, and is classically activated by HV in children with absence epilepsy.

questions.stem: Which feature MOST distinguishes electrode pop from cerebral activity?
options: A sharp contour with a steep rising phase
Confinement to one electrode without any field
Occurrence during drowsiness and light sleep
Amplitude above 100 µV in the involved channel
questions.explanation: Electrode pop is confined to a single electrode with no physiologic field, whereas cerebral discharges spread to neighbouring electrodes. Sharp contour and high amplitude are shared with epileptiform discharges; occurrence in drowsiness does not separate artifact from cerebral activity.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding theta activity in adults?
options: Normal during drowsiness and light sleep
Abnormal in fully awake, alert adults
Both A and B are correct
Always indicates pathology regardless of state
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Theta is state-dependent in adults - normal during drowsiness/sleep but abnormal when fully awake. Patient state must be accurately documented.

questions.stem: An EEG system samples at 500 Hz. Which statement is correct?
options: Activity above 250 Hz will alias as lower frequencies
Activity up to 500 Hz is represented accurately
Activity above 1000 Hz will alias as lower frequencies
Activity above 125 Hz will alias as lower frequencies
questions.explanation: At 500 Hz sampling the Nyquist frequency is 250 Hz, so activity up to 250 Hz is represented and anything above it aliases, folding back as false lower frequencies. Activity up to 500 Hz cannot be represented, 1000 Hz confuses Nyquist with doubling the rate, and 125 Hz is a quarter of the rate.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of 14&6 Hz positive spikes?
options: Benign variant, common in children and adolescents
Maximal over posterior temporal regions during drowsiness
Both A and B are correct
Always indicates temporal lobe epilepsy
questions.explanation: Both are correct: 14&6 Hz positive spikes are benign, seen in children/adolescents during drowsiness, maximal posterior temporally. Should not be confused with epileptiform activity.

questions.stem: In a bipolar montage, phase reversal occurs between F3-Fz and Fz-F4. The technologist should localize the abnormality to:
options: F3
Fz
F4
Cz
questions.explanation: In a bipolar montage, a phase reversal localizes the maximum to the electrode common to both channels. Fz is shared by F3-Fz and Fz-F4, so the abnormality is at Fz. F3 and F4 are the outer electrodes of each channel, and Cz is not part of either channel.

questions.stem: Which features distinguish REM sleep from NREM sleep?
options: REM: Desynchronized low-amplitude background, rapid eye movements, low muscle tone
NREM: Synchronized activity (spindles/K-complexes in N2, slow waves in N3)
Both A and B are correct
They are identical
questions.explanation: Both are correct: REM shows desynchronized background with REMs and low tone; NREM shows synchronized activity (spindles/K-complexes or slow waves). These are distinct sleep stages.

questions.stem: Two electrodes read 2 kΩ and 9 kΩ, both within lab limits. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: No artifact is expected since both are acceptable
Only the 2 kΩ electrode needs to be re-prepped
The 7 kΩ imbalance can still produce artifact
The higher value will improve noise rejection
questions.explanation: Impedance balance is more critical than absolute values: a difference of more than about 5 kΩ can cause artifact even when each electrode is individually acceptable, so the 9 kΩ site should be re-prepped. Acceptable individual values do not prevent imbalance artifact, the 2 kΩ site is not the problem, and higher impedance worsens common-mode rejection.

questions.stem: Which statement about posterior dominant rhythm (PDR) maturation is true?
options: PDR frequency is fastest in infancy and slows with age
PDR frequency increases with brain maturation
PDR frequency reaches 10 Hz by about 12 months of age
PDR frequency is fixed once the rhythm first appears
questions.explanation: The PDR speeds up as the brain matures: about 3-4 Hz at 3-4 months, 5-6 Hz around one year, about 8 Hz by age 3 and adult values in adolescence, so a slower PDR in a child is normal for age. It does not slow with age in childhood, it is far below 10 Hz at one year, and it keeps changing after it first appears.

questions.stem: Which pattern can indicate ictal onset?
options: Isolated sharp waves with no change
A single benign wicket spike train
Alpha blocking on eye opening
Abrupt electrodecremental attenuation
questions.explanation: An abrupt electrodecremental attenuation of the background can mark ictal onset and is often followed by rhythmic fast, theta, or delta activity that evolves. Isolated unchanging sharp waves are interictal, wicket spikes are a benign variant, and alpha blocking with eye opening is a normal reactivity response rather than seizure onset.

questions.stem: A technologist raises LFF from 0.1 Hz to 0.5 Hz and observes that diffuse slowing appears less prominent. The technologist should:
options: Recognize a filter effect; review at standard LFF
Note that the encephalopathy has improved
Lower the sensitivity so slowing looks smaller
Conclude the background has now normalized
questions.explanation: Raising the LFF attenuates slow activity, so the apparent reduction in slowing is a technical effect, not a clinical change; the record should be reviewed with a standard LFF (about 0.1-1 Hz). Concluding improvement or normalization misreads the filter effect, and changing sensitivity further only alters display size.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of lambda waves?
options: Positive occipital transients
Occur with saccadic eye movements during wakefulness with eyes open
Both A and B are correct
Always indicate occipital epilepsy
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Lambda waves are positive occipital transients associated with saccadic eye movements during wakefulness. They are normal, not epileptiform activity.

questions.stem: Which conditions require caution or contraindicate hyperventilation?
options: Recent stroke, increased intracranial pressure, sickle cell disease
Severe respiratory conditions or inability to cooperate
Both A and B are correct
All patients can safely perform HV
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Recent stroke, increased ICP, sickle cell disease, and severe respiratory conditions are contraindications. Safety requires recognizing these and consulting with physician when uncertain.

questions.stem: Why are deep structures such as the hippocampus and thalamus poorly represented on scalp EEG?
options: Their neurons fire too fast for EEG amplifiers to record
Their activity lies mostly below the usual recording band
They generate no electrical activity of their own
Distance and tissue attenuation weaken them at the scalp
questions.explanation: Scalp EEG primarily reflects superficial cortex; signals from deep structures are weakened by distance and by attenuation through brain, CSF, skull and scalp. Their firing rates are not beyond amplifier capability, their activity is not mostly below the recording band, and these structures do generate electrical activity; the main problem is distance and attenuation.

questions.stem: Which factors are favorable prognostic indicators in diffuse encephalopathy?
options: Preserved PDR reactivity to eye opening
Mild-moderate slowing (theta) rather than severe (delta)
Both A and B are correct
Complete absence of all background activity
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Preserved reactivity and milder slowing (theta vs delta) are favorable signs. Complete background suppression is ominous, not favorable. These factors help assess severity.

questions.stem: Which features help identify sweat artifact?
options: Slow, irregular baseline drift
Worse in hairy areas, affects multiple channels due to salt bridging
Both A and B are correct
High-frequency activity like muscle
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Sweat artifact shows slow, irregular drift due to salt bridging between electrodes, worse in hairy areas, affecting multiple channels. This can mimic slowing but is technical artifact.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding aftergoing slow waves in epileptiform discharges?
options: Common but not required for epileptiform classification
Morphology (pointed, sharp), field (physiologic), and context are more important
Both A and B are correct
Always present in all epileptiform discharges
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Aftergoing slow waves are common but not required. Classification depends on morphology, physiologic field, and context. Absence of slow wave doesn't exclude epileptiform activity.

questions.stem: Which statement about average reference montage effects is correct?
options: It enhances generalized activity by summing all electrodes
It shows the true, undistorted amplitude at every site
It can enhance focal activity by subtracting common activity
It cannot be contaminated by a large focal discharge
questions.explanation: Subtracting the activity common to all electrodes lets focal abnormalities stand out, so a focal sharp wave may be more visible than in bipolar montage; this is a technical effect, not a change in the abnormality. Generalized activity is reduced, not enhanced, because it enters the average; amplitudes are relative to the average, not absolute; and a large focal discharge can contaminate the average.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of normal PDR reactivity?
options: Attenuates (decreases) with eye opening
Returns when eyes close
Both A and B are correct
PDR should never change with eye state
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Normal PDR attenuates with eye opening and returns with eye closure. This reactivity is a key feature of normal PDR. Poor reactivity may indicate drowsiness, medication, or encephalopathy.

questions.stem: Which activation procedure increases both sleep and interictal discharges during epilepsy evaluation?
options: Hyperventilation for three minutes
Sleep deprivation the night before
Intermittent photic stimulation
Repeated eye opening and closure
questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation before the study makes sleep more likely during the recording and increases interictal discharges; sleep itself activates some seizure types, especially frontal lobe seizures. Hyperventilation mainly activates absence spike-wave, photic stimulation activates photosensitive responses, and eye opening and closure test reactivity rather than producing sleep.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding differential amplifiers?
options: Amplify voltage difference between active and reference electrodes
Reject common-mode noise (present in both electrodes) through CMRR
Both A and B are correct
Amplify all signals equally without discrimination
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Differential amplifiers amplify differences between electrodes and reject common noise through CMRR (common-mode rejection ratio). This is fundamental to EEG signal quality and noise reduction.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of sleep spindles?
options: 12-14 Hz rhythmic bursts
Maximal centrally (C3-C4), characteristic of N2 sleep
Both A and B are correct
Always indicate pathology
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Sleep spindles are 12-14 Hz, central, and characteristic of N2 sleep. They are normal graphoelements, not pathology. Their presence helps identify N2 sleep stage.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding high-frequency filter (HFF) settings?
options: Excessively low HFF (<20 Hz) can attenuate spikes and sharp waves
Standard HFF is typically 35-70 Hz to preserve spikes while reducing very high-frequency noise
Both A and B are correct
HFF settings don't affect spike visibility
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Low HFF attenuates fast activity including spikes. Standard HFF (35-70 Hz) preserves spikes while reducing noise. Too low HFF masks important epileptiform findings - a common ABRET trap.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding focal polymorphic delta slowing?
options: Suggests underlying structural or functional abnormality in that region
Persists across montages, helping distinguish from artifact
Both A and B are correct
Always indicates normal variant
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Focal polymorphic delta is abnormal and suggests pathology (structural lesion, seizure focus, etc.). Persistence across montages confirms it's not artifact. This is a significant finding requiring documentation.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding EEG as a measurement system?
options: EEG is a passive recording system (measures, doesn't deliver electricity)
Measures voltage differences (potential differences), not electrical current flow
Both A and B are correct
EEG delivers current to the brain
questions.explanation: Both are correct: EEG is passive (records voltage differences, doesn't deliver current). This is a fundamental distinction from stimulation or power delivery systems. Understanding this is important for safety and interpretation.

questions.stem: Besides skin preparation, which practice is essential for good electrode contact and signal quality?
options: Enough paste to join neighboring electrode sites
Raising the gain on channels with weak contact
Adequate paste and secure electrode attachment
Applying the notch filter to every channel
questions.explanation: After proper scalp preparation, an adequate amount of conductive paste and secure attachment keep the electrode-skin interface stable. Paste that joins neighboring sites creates a salt bridge that shorts the electrodes; raising gain and applying the notch filter change only processing or display, not the quality of contact.

questions.stem: Which pattern is commonly seen in the postictal period?
options: Immediate return to baseline
Diffuse postictal suppression
Continuous 3 Hz spike-and-wave
Enhanced posterior alpha rhythm
questions.explanation: The postictal period commonly shows diffuse background suppression followed by delta-theta slowing before gradual recovery, which helps confirm a true ictal event and distinguishes it from artifact. An immediate return to baseline is unusual, continuous spike-and-wave suggests ongoing status epilepticus, and the posterior rhythm is typically slowed or attenuated rather than enhanced.

questions.stem: Which features indicate photosensitivity (IPS) rather than normal photic driving?
options: Spike-and-wave complexes NOT time-locked to flash rate
Epileptiform activity that may persist after stimulation stops
Both A and B are correct
Occipital activity that follows flash rate exactly
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Photosensitivity shows epileptiform activity (spike-and-wave) not time-locked to flash and may persist. Normal driving follows flash rate exactly. These are distinct phenomena with different clinical significance.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of BETS (benign epileptiform transients of sleep)?
options: Brief duration (50-100 ms), low amplitude, temporal location
Occur during drowsiness/sleep, lack aftergoing slow waves
Both A and B are correct
Always indicate temporal lobe epilepsy
questions.explanation: Both are correct: BETS are brief, low-amplitude, temporal, occur during drowsiness/sleep, and lack aftergoing slow waves. They are benign variants, not epileptiform activity.

questions.stem: Which filter settings can lead to misinterpretation of EEG findings?
options: High LFF (>0.5 Hz) masking diffuse slowing
Low HFF (<20 Hz) attenuating spikes, or notch filter distorting activity near 60 Hz
Both A and B are correct
Filter settings never affect interpretation
questions.explanation: Both are correct: High LFF masks slowing; low HFF attenuates spikes; notch distorts activity near 60 Hz. All can cause misinterpretation. Standard settings (LFF 0.1-0.3 Hz, HFF 35-70 Hz) minimize distortion.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding neonatal EEG discontinuity?
options: Trace alternant (discontinuous pattern) is normal up to ~44 weeks post-conceptual age
Discontinuity decreases with increasing post-conceptual age as brain matures
Both A and B are correct
Discontinuity always indicates severe pathology
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Trace alternant is normal in neonates up to ~44 weeks post-conceptual age. Continuity increases with maturation. Discontinuity in older infants/children is abnormal.

questions.stem: Which features help distinguish true epileptiform discharges from artifact?
options: Physiologic field distribution (not confined to single channel, spreads appropriately)
Pointed, sharp morphology distinct from background
Both A and B are correct
Artifact always looks identical to epileptiform activity
questions.explanation: Both are correct: True epileptiform shows physiologic field (spreads appropriately) and pointed morphology. Artifact is often single-channel or non-physiologic. Both features are essential for accurate identification.

questions.stem: Which statement about using multiple montages for interpretation is correct?
options: Comparing montages is needed only for artifact review
A second montage type mainly lowers channel noise
Bipolar and referential views should look identical
Using both types helps confirm findings and localization
questions.explanation: Bipolar montages aid localization via phase reversal and referential montages aid field assessment, so reviewing both confirms findings and improves localization accuracy. Comparison is not limited to artifact review, montage choice does not lower recorded noise, and the two views are expected to look different.

questions.stem: Which graphoelements must be present to identify N2 sleep?
options: Sleep spindles (12-14 Hz central)
K-complexes
Both A and B are correct
Only rapid eye movements
questions.explanation: Both are correct: N2 sleep requires both spindles and K-complexes. REMs occur in REM sleep, not N2. Both elements are necessary for accurate N2 sleep stage identification.

questions.stem: Which steps should be taken when 60 Hz artifact appears in all channels?
options: Check ground electrode impedance and contact first
Check room electrical environment and nearby equipment
Both A and B are correct
Immediately use notch filter without checking source
questions.explanation: Both are correct: 60 Hz affecting all channels suggests ground or environmental issue. Check ground contact/impedance and electrical environment first. Fix source before using notch filter to avoid distortion.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding prominent frontal beta activity?
options: Commonly medication-induced (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, other CNS depressants)
Is a medication effect, not necessarily abnormal brain activity
Both A and B are correct
Always indicates seizure focus
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Prominent frontal beta is commonly medication-induced and should be documented but not overinterpreted. It's an effect of medications, not necessarily abnormal brain activity.

questions.stem: Which features distinguish ictal from interictal epileptiform activity?
options: Ictal shows evolution (frequency/amplitude/distribution changes over time)
Ictal has clinical correlation (seizure occurring)
Both A and B are correct
Isolated sharp waves without evolution are ictal
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Ictal shows evolution and clinical correlation. Isolated sharp waves without evolution are interictal, not ictal. Evolution is the key distinguishing feature.

questions.stem: Which features help identify eye blink artifact?
options: Frontal maximum (Fp1-Fp2), out-of-phase deflections
Time-locked to visible eye blinks
Both A and B are correct
Always appears in all channels equally
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Eye blinks are frontal, out-of-phase, and time-locked to visible blinks. Correlation with visible movement confirms it's artifact, not cerebral activity.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding diffuse slowing severity?
options: Delta slowing (1-3 Hz) indicates more severe encephalopathy than theta (4-7 Hz)
Degree of slowing correlates with encephalopathy severity
Both A and B are correct
Theta and delta slowing indicate equal severity
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Delta slowing is more severe than theta. Degree of slowing (theta vs delta) correlates with encephalopathy severity. This is important for interpretation and prognosis.

questions.stem: Which sweep speed settings are appropriate for different viewing purposes?
options: 30 mm/s: Spreads waveforms for better spike identification
10 mm/s: Compresses for viewing slow waves and overall background
Both A and B are correct
Sweep speed doesn't affect what you can see
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Faster speeds (30 mm/s) spread for spike viewing; slower speeds (10 mm/s) compress for slow wave/background viewing. Both are useful for different purposes in comprehensive interpretation.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding EEG electrode localization?
options: Electrodes correspond to underlying cortical regions (e.g., T5 = posterior temporal cortex)
Localization is regional, not exact anatomical pinpointing
Both A and B are correct
EEG can pinpoint exact submillimeter locations
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Electrodes map to cortical regions, but localization is regional approximation, not exact pinpointing. Understanding this limitation is important for accurate interpretation.

questions.stem: Which features characterize generalized epileptiform patterns?
options: Bilateral synchrony and symmetric distribution
Frontal maximum is common in generalized spike-and-wave
Both A and B are correct
Always focal in one hemisphere
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Generalized patterns show bilateral synchrony, symmetry, and often frontal maximum. This distinguishes them from focal patterns which are asymmetric and localized.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding hyperventilation activation?
options: More effective in children than adults for activating absence seizures
Can activate 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave in absence epilepsy
Both A and B are correct
Never activates any epileptiform activity
questions.explanation: Both are correct: HV is more effective in children and classically activates 3 Hz spike-and-wave in absence epilepsy. This is a well-established, highly effective activation procedure for absence seizures.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of wicket spikes?
options: Arch-shaped, occur in trains, temporal region
No aftergoing slow wave, no background disruption
Both A and B are correct
Always indicate temporal lobe epilepsy
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Wicket spikes are arch-shaped, temporal, occur in trains, lack aftergoing slow waves, and don't disrupt background. They are benign variants, not epileptiform activity.

questions.stem: A technologist changes sensitivity from 7 μV/mm to 14 μV/mm. The technologist should understand that:
options: Waveforms will appear smaller on the display
Actual brain voltage is unchanged; only display scaling changed
Both A and B are correct
The brain activity has actually decreased
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Higher sensitivity value (14 μV/mm) means lower gain (smaller display). Actual brain voltage is unchanged; only the display scale changed. This is a display setting, not a change in brain activity.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child's EEG shows an 8.5 Hz posterior rhythm that is reactive to eye opening. The technologist should:
options: Treat it as posterior slowing that is abnormal at this age
Treat it as an occipital rhythmic epileptiform pattern
Raise the HFF to uncover any hidden faster activity
Accept it as a normal posterior rhythm for a 5-year-old
questions.explanation: Posterior rhythm frequency increases with age, reaching about 8 Hz by age 3 and adult values in adolescence, so a reactive 8.5 Hz rhythm at age 5 is age-appropriate. Treating it as slowing applies adult norms; reactivity and normal morphology argue against an epileptiform pattern; raising the HFF does not create or reveal a faster background rhythm.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of vertex waves?
options: High-amplitude, sharp transients maximal at Cz
Occur during N1 and N2 sleep stages
Both A and B are correct
Always indicate pathology
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Vertex waves are high-amplitude, sharp, maximal at Cz, and occur during N1/N2 sleep. They are normal sleep graphoelements, not pathology. Their presence helps identify sleep stages.

questions.stem: All electrodes show 2-3 kΩ impedance except P3 at 11 kΩ. The EEG shows noise. The technologist should:
options: Proceed, as values under 20 kΩ are acceptable
Apply the notch filter to suppress the noise
Re-prep the ground electrode and leave P3 alone
Re-prep P3 to bring it in line with the others
questions.explanation: P3 at 11 kΩ against 2-3 kΩ elsewhere creates an 8-9 kΩ imbalance that causes artifact even if each value seems acceptable; re-prepping P3 corrects the cause. Proceeding ignores the imbalance, the notch filter only attenuates line noise, and the ground electrode is not the outlier here.

questions.stem: A technologist observes a sharp transient with 75 ms duration. The technologist should classify this as:
options: A sharp wave
A spike
A slow wave
A polyspike
questions.explanation: Sharp waves last 70-200 ms, so a 75 ms pointed transient is (just) a sharp wave. Spikes last 20-70 ms, slow waves exceed 200 ms, and a polyspike is a run of several spikes rather than one transient. Duration is the key criterion for this classification.

questions.stem: A focal sharp wave is subtle in bipolar montage but prominent in average reference. The technologist should understand that:
options: The abnormality has worsened
Average reference enhances focal activity by subtracting common activity; this is a montage effect
The recording is artifact-contaminated
Bipolar is always superior
questions.explanation: Average reference can enhance focal abnormalities by subtracting common-mode activity. This is a technical effect of montage choice, not a change in the actual abnormality. Both montages are valuable.

questions.stem: An awake adult's PDR shows poor reactivity to eye opening. The technologist should consider:
options: Normal PDR should attenuate with eye opening; poor reactivity should be documented
Poor reactivity may indicate drowsiness, medication effects, or encephalopathy depending on context
Poor reactivity is always normal
Both A and B are correct
questions.explanation: Both A and B are correct: Normal PDR should attenuate with eye opening, and poor reactivity should be documented. Poor reactivity may indicate drowsiness, medications, or encephalopathy depending on context - it is NOT always normal (Option C is false). Context (patient state, medications, clinical history) is important for interpretation.

questions.stem: Which activation procedures can improve diagnostic yield in epilepsy evaluation?
options: Sleep-deprived EEG (increases sleep and interictal activity)
Sleep recording (activates some seizure types, especially frontal lobe epilepsy)
Both A and B are correct
Activation procedures never help
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Sleep-deprived EEG increases sleep and interictal discharges. Sleep itself activates some seizure types, especially frontal lobe. Both significantly improve diagnostic yield in epilepsy evaluation.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding differential amplifiers?
options: Amplify voltage difference between active and reference electrodes
Reject common-mode noise (present in both electrodes) through CMRR
Both A and B are correct
Amplify all signals equally without discrimination
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Differential amplifiers amplify differences between electrodes and reject common noise through CMRR (common-mode rejection ratio). This is fundamental to EEG signal quality and noise reduction.

questions.stem: Which are characteristics of sleep spindles?
options: 12-14 Hz rhythmic bursts
Maximal centrally (C3-C4), characteristic of N2 sleep
Both A and B are correct
Always indicate pathology
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Sleep spindles are 12-14 Hz, central, and characteristic of N2 sleep. They are normal graphoelements, not pathology. Their presence helps identify N2 sleep stage.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding high-frequency filter (HFF) settings?
options: Excessively low HFF (<20 Hz) can attenuate spikes and sharp waves
Standard HFF is typically 35-70 Hz to preserve spikes while reducing very high-frequency noise
Both A and B are correct
HFF settings don't affect spike visibility
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Low HFF attenuates fast activity including spikes. Standard HFF (35-70 Hz) preserves spikes while reducing noise. Too low HFF masks important epileptiform findings - a common ABRET trap.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding focal polymorphic delta slowing?
options: Suggests underlying structural or functional abnormality in that region
Persists across montages, helping distinguish from artifact
Both A and B are correct
Always indicates normal variant
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Focal polymorphic delta is abnormal and suggests pathology (structural lesion, seizure focus, etc.). Persistence across montages confirms it's not artifact. This is a significant finding.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding EEG as a measurement system?
options: EEG is a passive recording system (measures, doesn't deliver electricity)
Measures voltage differences (potential differences), not electrical current flow
Both A and B are correct
EEG delivers current to the brain
questions.explanation: Both are correct: EEG is passive (records voltage differences, doesn't deliver current). This is a fundamental distinction from stimulation or power delivery systems. Understanding this is important for safety and interpretation.

questions.stem: Which practices are essential for achieving good electrode contact and signal quality?
options: Proper scalp preparation (abrasion/cleaning to reduce impedance)
Adequate conductive paste/gel and secure electrode attachment
Both A and B are correct
Electrode placement doesn't affect signal quality
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Good scalp prep reduces impedance; adequate conductive medium and secure attachment ensure stable contact. These are fundamental practices for quality recordings.

questions.stem: An EEG shows intermittent, rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta activity maximal over the temporal regions, occurring in brief bursts. The technologist should identify this as:
options: Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta activity
Polymorphic delta activity of temporal origin
Rhythmic mid-temporal theta of drowsiness
Temporal intermittent rhythmic delta activity
questions.explanation: Brief bursts of rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta maximal over the temporal regions define TIRDA, which is associated with temporal lobe dysfunction and epilepsy. FIRDA has a frontal maximum; polymorphic delta is irregular in shape and frequency; rhythmic mid-temporal theta of drowsiness is a benign 5-7 Hz variant.

questions.stem: Intermittent, rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta activity appears maximal over the frontal regions in brief bursts. The technologist should recognize this as:
options: Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta activity
Temporal intermittent rhythmic delta activity
Triphasic waves with a frontal predominance
Eye-movement artifact in brief frontal bursts
questions.explanation: Rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta in brief bursts with a frontal maximum is FIRDA, linked to deep midline or diffuse (often toxic-metabolic) dysfunction. TIRDA has a temporal maximum; triphasic waves are periodic three-phase complexes rather than sinusoidal rhythmic delta; eye-movement artifact is maximal at the frontopolar leads with a steep anterior-to-posterior falloff and does not show a cerebral field.

questions.stem: Brief bursts of intermittent, rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta activity appear maximal over the occipital regions. The technologist should identify this as:
options: Posterior slow waves of youth, a normal variant
Occipital intermittent rhythmic delta activity
A slowed posterior dominant rhythm in drowsiness
Lambda waves evoked by visual scanning of a page
questions.explanation: Rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta in brief occipital bursts is OIRDA, seen mainly in children (classically with absence epilepsy). Posterior slow waves of youth are single slow waves fused with the alpha rhythm; a slowed PDR remains in the theta-alpha range; lambda waves are sharp positive occipital transients during visual scanning.

questions.stem: Intermittent, rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta activity appears diffusely without clear regional maximum. The technologist should classify this as:
options: FIRDA, the default label for diffuse IRDA
OIRDA, the default label in younger patients
Generalized IRDA without a regional label
Continuous diffuse polymorphic delta slowing
questions.explanation: IRDA without a clear regional maximum is described as generalized IRDA; the TIRDA, FIRDA and OIRDA labels require a temporal, frontal or occipital maximum and none is a default for diffuse bursts. Continuous polymorphic delta is irregular and persistent, unlike intermittent rhythmic bursts.

questions.stem: Which statement about TIRDA is correct?
options: It is a benign variant of drowsiness in older adults
It is defined by rhythmic theta at 4-7 Hz
It typically reflects deep midline dysfunction
It is associated with temporal lobe dysfunction
questions.explanation: TIRDA (rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta with a temporal maximum) is associated with temporal lobe dysfunction and correlates strongly with temporal lobe epilepsy. It is not a benign drowsy variant, its frequency is delta not theta, and deep midline dysfunction is the association classically given for FIRDA.

questions.stem: Which statement about FIRDA is correct?
options: It is associated with deep midline or frontal dysfunction
It is a normal frontal pattern of light drowsiness
It is a specific marker of temporal lobe epilepsy
It consists of rhythmic 4-7 Hz theta over the frontal leads
questions.explanation: FIRDA (intermittent rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta with a frontal maximum) is associated with deep midline or frontal dysfunction and frequently with toxic-metabolic encephalopathy. It is abnormal rather than a drowsy pattern, the temporal-epilepsy association belongs to TIRDA, and its frequency is delta, not theta.

questions.stem: Which statement about OIRDA is correct?
options: It is a normal variant of the adult alpha rhythm
It is seen mostly in children rather than adults
It is seen mostly in elderly adults with dementia
It consists of 8-13 Hz bursts over the occipital leads
questions.explanation: OIRDA is intermittent rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta with an occipital maximum, seen mainly in children; it is associated with childhood absence epilepsy and with occipital or metabolic dysfunction. It is not an alpha variant, it is not typical of elderly patients with dementia, and its frequency is delta rather than alpha.

questions.stem: Which feature is MOST important for distinguishing TIRDA, FIRDA, and OIRDA?
options: Frequency of the delta waves
Duration of the individual bursts
Location of the field maximum
Age of the patient at recording
questions.explanation: TIRDA, FIRDA and OIRDA share the same intermittent rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta; they are named by where the field is maximal (temporal, frontal, occipital). Frequency is the same across them, burst duration varies within each type, and age only shifts likelihood (OIRDA in children) without defining the pattern.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of IRDA patterns?
options: Continuous irregular delta of varying shape
Periodic sharp discharges at fixed intervals
Rhythmic theta present throughout the record
Rhythmic delta occurring in intermittent bursts
questions.explanation: IRDA patterns consist of rhythmic, fairly sinusoidal 1-3 Hz delta that comes in brief intermittent bursts. Continuous irregular delta describes polymorphic delta; periodic sharp discharges describe LPDs/GPDs; persistent rhythmic theta is neither delta nor intermittent.

questions.stem: A technologist observes TIRDA in a patient with temporal lobe epilepsy. The technologist should understand that:
options: It is distinct from spikes but can coexist with them
It is the same finding as temporal spike discharges
It rules out an active temporal epileptic focus
It is a benign drowsy variant unrelated to epilepsy
questions.explanation: TIRDA is rhythmic delta, a different waveform from temporal spikes, yet the two often coexist because TIRDA correlates strongly with temporal lobe epilepsy and temporal dysfunction. It is not identical to spikes, it does not exclude an epileptic focus, and it is not a benign drowsy variant.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes FIRDA from other frontal slow patterns?
options: It is a frontal spike-and-wave pattern with sharp peaks
It is intermittent rhythmic delta, not continuous slowing
It is continuous polymorphic delta over one frontal lobe
It consists of 4-7 Hz rhythmic theta during drowsiness
questions.explanation: FIRDA occurs as intermittent bursts of rhythmic, sinusoidal 1-3 Hz delta, unlike continuous frontal slowing; it is associated with deep midline or diffuse dysfunction rather than a superficial focal lesion. It has no spike component, is not continuous polymorphic delta, and is delta rather than theta.

questions.stem: Which feature BEST distinguishes OIRDA from the normal posterior dominant rhythm?
options: Continuous alpha that does not block with eye opening
An occipital maximum rather than a frontal maximum
Intermittent 1-3 Hz delta rather than continuous alpha
A faster frequency and larger amplitude than alpha
questions.explanation: OIRDA is intermittent rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta in bursts, whereas the PDR is a relatively continuous 8-13 Hz alpha rhythm that attenuates with eye opening. Both are occipital, so location does not separate them; OIRDA is slower, not faster, and is not continuous alpha.

questions.stem: Generalized IRDA in an adult inpatient is MOST commonly associated with:
options: Normal drowsiness in healthy adults
Psychogenic nonepileptic events
A benign normal variant of youth
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy
questions.explanation: IRDA without focal features most often reflects diffuse cerebral dysfunction, commonly a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy; regional forms add localizing value (FIRDA deep midline/frontal, TIRDA temporal). IRDA is abnormal, so drowsiness, benign variants of youth and psychogenic events are not the usual explanation.

questions.stem: Which pair of features is required to identify an IRDA pattern?
options: Intermittent occurrence and rhythmic delta frequency
Continuous occurrence and irregular delta morphology
Periodic recurrence and sharply contoured morphology
Intermittent occurrence and rhythmic theta frequency
questions.explanation: IRDA is identified by intermittent bursts of rhythmic 1-3 Hz delta, with the regional maximum then used to subclassify it. Continuous irregular delta is polymorphic delta, periodic sharply contoured complexes suggest periodic discharges, and rhythmic theta is outside the delta range.

questions.stem: A technologist observes intermittent rhythmic delta activity but cannot determine a clear regional maximum. The technologist should classify this as:
options: TIRDA, assuming the usual temporal origin
Generalized IRDA without a regional label
FIRDA, assuming the usual frontal origin
OIRDA, assuming the usual occipital origin
questions.explanation: When no clear regional maximum is evident, the pattern is described as generalized IRDA. TIRDA, FIRDA and OIRDA each require a clear temporal, frontal or occipital maximum, and none should be assumed without one.

questions.stem: Which feature BEST distinguishes IRDA from polymorphic delta slowing?
options: IRDA is irregular; polymorphic delta is rhythmic
IRDA is continuous; polymorphic delta is intermittent
IRDA is rhythmic; polymorphic delta is irregular
IRDA is 4-7 Hz; polymorphic delta is 1-3 Hz
questions.explanation: IRDA consists of regular, sinusoidal delta in intermittent bursts, whereas polymorphic delta is irregular in shape and frequency and is often continuous, typically over a structural lesion. The reversed pairings are wrong, and both patterns are in the delta range.

questions.stem: OIRDA recorded in a child is BEST regarded as:
options: A normal developmental variant of the alpha rhythm
A normal finding of drowsiness in school-age children
A photic response unrelated to brain dysfunction
An abnormal finding linked to an underlying disorder
questions.explanation: Although OIRDA is seen mainly in children, it is abnormal and is associated with childhood absence epilepsy and with occipital or metabolic dysfunction. It is not a developmental alpha variant, not a normal drowsy pattern, and not a photic response.

questions.stem: FIRDA is thought to reflect dysfunction of which structures?
options: Deep midline and diencephalic structures
Superficial frontal convexity cortex alone
Mesial temporal and hippocampal structures
Occipital and parietal association cortex
questions.explanation: FIRDA is thought to reflect dysfunction of deep midline structures (thalamus/diencephalon, upper brainstem) projecting to frontal regions, or diffuse dysfunction, rather than the frontal convexity alone. Mesial temporal dysfunction is linked to TIRDA, and occipital involvement to OIRDA.

questions.stem: A patient's EEG shows both TIRDA and temporal sharp waves. The technologist should:
options: Document only the sharp waves, since TIRDA is a variant
Document both, since they are distinct and can coexist
Document only TIRDA, since it includes the sharp waves
Document them as one pattern of temporal slowing
questions.explanation: TIRDA (rhythmic delta) and temporal sharp waves (epileptiform transients) are distinct findings that often coexist, and both should be described. TIRDA is not a benign variant, it does not contain the sharp waves, and merging them into one slowing pattern loses the epileptiform finding.

questions.stem: Which frequency range characterizes IRDA patterns?
options: 4-7 Hz (theta)
1-3 Hz (delta)
8-13 Hz (alpha)
14-30 Hz (beta)
questions.explanation: IRDA patterns are characterized by 1-3 Hz delta frequency. They are slower than theta (4-7 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), or beta (14-30 Hz). The delta frequency is a key identifying feature.

questions.stem: Which statement about the timing of IRDA is correct?
options: It persists continuously throughout the whole record
It recurs at fixed intervals like periodic discharges
It occurs in brief runs separated by background activity
It appears only during deep N3 sleep, not when awake
questions.explanation: IRDA occurs in brief intermittent runs separated by background activity; this helps distinguish it from continuous polymorphic delta. It does not persist throughout the record, it lacks the fixed inter-discharge interval of periodic patterns, and it is seen mainly in wakefulness and drowsiness, typically attenuating in deeper sleep.

questions.stem: An occipital rhythm at 2 Hz appears intermittently in bursts. The technologist should identify this as:
options: A slowed posterior dominant rhythm
Posterior slow waves of youth
Lambda waves from visual scanning
Occipital rhythmic delta (OIRDA)
questions.explanation: Intermittent bursts of rhythmic 2 Hz delta over the occipital regions fit OIRDA (1-3 Hz). A slowed PDR stays in the theta-alpha range and is continuous; posterior slow waves of youth are isolated slow waves fused with alpha; lambda waves are sharp positive transients during visual scanning.

questions.stem: In an adult with FIRDA and no structural lesion on imaging, the MOST likely associated condition is:
options: A toxic-metabolic encephalopathy
Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
Normal drowsiness in the elderly
Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures
questions.explanation: FIRDA is associated with deep midline lesions or frontal pathology, and when imaging shows no lesion the usual cause is a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy. Mesial temporal epilepsy is linked to TIRDA, FIRDA is not a normal drowsy pattern, and psychogenic events do not produce rhythmic delta.

questions.stem: TIRDA is MOST strongly associated with which condition?
options: Childhood absence epilepsy
Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy
questions.explanation: TIRDA correlates strongly with temporal lobe epilepsy and temporal lobe dysfunction, so it carries localizing epileptogenic significance. Childhood absence epilepsy is linked to OIRDA, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy shows generalized polyspike-wave, and toxic-metabolic states are more often associated with FIRDA or generalized IRDA.

questions.stem: When determining the regional maximum of an IRDA pattern, which principle applies?
options: The maximum is set by whichever montage is displayed
Only an average reference montage can localize it
Its maximum should be consistent across montages
A single bipolar montage is sufficient to localize it
questions.explanation: A true regional maximum should be consistent when checked in both bipolar and referential montages; the maximum then determines the label (TIRDA, FIRDA or OIRDA). The displayed montage changes visibility, not the true maximum, and no single montage type is sufficient by itself.

questions.stem: Which statement about the rhythmicity of IRDA is correct?
options: Its waves vary widely in frequency and shape
Its waves are sharply contoured and spiky
Its waves are rhythmic only in the theta range
Its waves are regular in frequency and shape
questions.explanation: IRDA consists of regular, sinusoidal delta waves of fairly constant frequency and shape, which distinguishes it from irregular polymorphic delta. It is not sharply contoured like epileptiform activity, and its rhythmic waves are in the delta (1-3 Hz) range, not theta.

questions.stem: Which statement about the age distribution of OIRDA is correct?
options: It is most common in children, less so in adults
It is most common in elderly patients with dementia
It is largely confined to the neonatal period
It is equally common in children and adults
questions.explanation: OIRDA is seen mainly in children (classically with absence epilepsy) and can occur in adults, but less often. It is not typical of elderly patients, it is not a neonatal pattern, and its frequency is not equal across ages.

questions.stem: When describing IRDA in the technologist notes, which approach is BEST?
options: Use the generic term IRDA regardless of its maximum
Name the regional maximum when one is clearly present
Label it FIRDA unless it is clearly occipital
Describe it as polymorphic delta to avoid labels
questions.explanation: Specify TIRDA, FIRDA or OIRDA when a clear regional maximum is present, and use generalized IRDA when it is not; accurate labels aid interpretation. A generic term discards localizing information, FIRDA is not a default, and calling rhythmic delta polymorphic misdescribes it.

questions.stem: Which feature BEST distinguishes triphasic waves from IRDA?
options: Rhythmic delta waves in intermittent bursts
A strict unilateral temporal field maximum
Periodic waves with a three-phase morphology
Frequency in the 8-13 Hz alpha range
questions.explanation: Triphasic waves are periodic complexes with a characteristic three-phase morphology, often generalized with a frontal predominance, whereas IRDA is sinusoidal rhythmic delta in intermittent bursts. Rhythmic delta bursts describe IRDA itself; triphasic waves are not unilateral temporal and are not in the alpha range.

questions.stem: Which statement about the clinical significance of IRDA is correct?
options: It is a normal variant requiring no further comment
It is diagnostic of an ongoing electrographic seizure
It is a recording artifact from eye movement
It is abnormal and suggests underlying dysfunction
questions.explanation: IRDA patterns are abnormal and indicate underlying cerebral dysfunction; the regional maximum (temporal, frontal, occipital) helps localize it. They are not normal variants, they are not themselves electrographic seizures, and they are cerebral activity rather than eye-movement artifact.

questions.stem: A patient presents with progressive loss of peripheral vision, night blindness, and eventual tunnel vision. Fundoscopy shows bone-spicule pigmentation. Most likely diagnosis is:
options: Macular degeneration
Retinal artery occlusion
Retinitis pigmentosa
Glaucoma
Optic neuritis
questions.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa: Classic triad includes nyctalopia (night blindness), peripheral field loss, and pigmentary retinal changes. Central vision is preserved until late stages. Macular degeneration affects central vision first.

questions.stem: Which condition primarily affects central vision and interferes with fine detail discrimination?
options: Retinitis pigmentosa
Macular degeneration
Glaucoma
Retinal detachment
Optic atrophy
questions.explanation: Macular degeneration: The macula is responsible for high-acuity central vision. Peripheral vision is usually preserved. Retinitis pigmentosa affects peripheral vision first.

questions.stem: Sudden, painless, severe loss of vision in one eye is MOST characteristic of:
options: Conjunctivitis
Blepharitis
Retinal artery occlusion
Cataract
Macular degeneration
questions.explanation: Retinal artery occlusion: Acute ischemia to the retina often described as a 'curtain coming down.' This is an ophthalmologic emergency. Conjunctivitis and blepharitis cause irritation, not sudden vision loss.

questions.stem: Inflammation limited to the eyelid margins, often associated with crusting and irritation, is termed:
options: Conjunctivitis
Uveitis
Blepharitis
Keratitis
Ptosis
questions.explanation: Blepharitis: Affects eyelid margins specifically. Conjunctivitis affects the conjunctival membrane covering the eye. Ptosis is drooping, not inflammation.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes the terms 'ocular' and 'optic'?
options: Optic refers to the eye; ocular refers to the optic nerve and visual path
Ocular refers to eye movements; optic refers to the eyeball as a whole
Ocular refers to the eye; optic refers to the optic nerve and visual path
Ocular refers to the eyelids; optic refers to the cornea and the lens
questions.explanation: Ocular is a general term meaning related to the eye, whereas optic refers specifically to the optic nerve and visual pathways, so the terms are not interchangeable. The reversed pairing is the common trap; ocular is not limited to eye movements or eyelids, and optic does not mean the eyeball, cornea or lens.

questions.stem: A perception that occurs when there is actually nothing there to cause it, such as hearing noises when there are none, is termed:
options: Delusion
Illusion
Delirium
Hallucination
questions.explanation: A hallucination is a false sensory perception with no external stimulus, such as hearing noises when none are present. A delusion is a fixed false belief, an illusion is a misinterpretation of a real stimulus, and delirium is an acute fluctuating confusional state that may include hallucinations but is not the perception itself.

questions.stem: Which statement about the terms 'acute' and 'chronic' is correct?
options: Acute describes a condition of sudden onset and usually short course
Acute describes a condition that is severe, whatever its duration
Chronic describes a condition that is steadily worsening over time
Chronic describes a condition that recurs as brief, sudden attacks
questions.explanation: Acute means sudden onset and usually short duration; chronic means persisting over a long period. Acute is about timing, not severity; chronic refers to duration, not to steady worsening; recurrent brief attacks describe an episodic or paroxysmal condition rather than the meaning of chronic.

questions.stem: A bluish discoloration of the skin caused by low levels of oxygen in the blood is termed:
options: Pallor
Cyanosis
Jaundice
Erythema
questions.explanation: Cyanosis is a bluish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes from low blood oxygen, which may be seen during a seizure or apnea. Pallor is paleness, jaundice is yellowing from bilirubin, and erythema is redness from increased blood flow.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding hepatitis vs cirrhosis?
options: Hepatitis refers to inflammation of the liver; cirrhosis refers to chronic scarring and architectural distortion
Both can result from viral infection, but cirrhosis represents end-stage changes
Both A and B are correct
Hepatitis and cirrhosis are the same condition
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Hepatitis = inflammation. Cirrhosis = chronic scarring/fibrosis. Cirrhosis can result from chronic hepatitis but represents end-stage architectural changes. They are distinct stages.

questions.stem: Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes due to excess bilirubin in the blood, usually a sign of liver disorder, is termed:
options: Cyanosis
Jaundice
Pallor
Erythema
Ecchymosis
questions.explanation: Jaundice: Yellowing due to excess bilirubin, often indicating liver dysfunction. Cyanosis is bluish (low oxygen). These are distinct clinical signs with different pathophysiologies.

questions.stem: Which form of hepatitis is transmitted through contaminated food or water?
options: Hepatitis B
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis D
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route through contaminated food or water, so hand hygiene matters. Hepatitis B and C are bloodborne (also sexual and perinatal), and hepatitis D is bloodborne and occurs only with hepatitis B.

questions.stem: Which statement about Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease is correct?
options: Alzheimer disease usually starts with tremor; Parkinson with memory loss
Both diseases usually start with memory loss before motor signs appear
Parkinson disease shows early diffuse slowing; Alzheimer a normal EEG
Parkinson disease usually starts with motor signs; Alzheimer with memory loss
questions.explanation: Parkinson disease typically presents first with tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia, while Alzheimer disease presents first with memory loss. The EEG is usually normal early in Parkinson disease, and Alzheimer disease shows progressive diffuse slowing. The swapped pairings reverse these features, and memory loss is not the usual first sign of Parkinson disease.

questions.stem: A young adult (age 35) presents with dementia, chorea (involuntary movements), and psychiatric symptoms. Most likely diagnosis is:
options: Huntington disease
Alzheimer disease
Parkinson disease
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
questions.explanation: Huntington disease classically presents in adults aged about 30-50 with chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms (autosomal dominant). Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases usually begin later and lack chorea; Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is rapidly progressive with myoclonus and periodic sharp wave complexes rather than chorea.

questions.stem: Which statement about vascular dementia and Alzheimer disease is correct?
options: Alzheimer tends to decline stepwise; vascular dementia declines gradually
Vascular dementia tends to decline stepwise; Alzheimer declines gradually
Vascular dementia shows diffuse slowing; Alzheimer shows focal slowing
Both progress over weeks and show periodic sharp wave complexes
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia typically worsens stepwise after successive strokes and may show focal slowing, while Alzheimer disease declines smoothly and gradually with diffuse slowing. The swapped pairings reverse these patterns; progression over weeks with periodic sharp wave complexes describes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

questions.stem: A patient presents with rapidly progressive dementia (weeks to months), myoclonus, and EEG shows periodic sharp wave complexes. Most likely diagnosis is:
options: Alzheimer disease
Vascular dementia
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Huntington disease
questions.explanation: Rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months with myoclonus and periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG is classic for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Alzheimer disease and vascular dementia progress over years with diffuse or focal slowing, and Huntington disease presents with chorea and slower decline.

questions.stem: Which statement about encephalitis and meningitis is correct?
options: Meningitis inflames brain tissue; encephalitis inflames the meninges
Encephalitis inflames the spinal cord; meningitis inflames the brain
Encephalitis inflames the ventricles; meningitis inflames the cortex
Encephalitis inflames brain tissue; meningitis inflames the meninges
questions.explanation: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma and often shows diffuse slowing with or without epileptiform discharges; meningitis is inflammation of the meningeal coverings and may show diffuse slowing. The reversed pairing is the common trap; spinal cord inflammation is myelitis and ventricular inflammation is ventriculitis.

questions.stem: A patient develops rapidly ascending weakness, absent reflexes, and recent flu-like illness. EEG is normal. Most likely diagnosis is:
options: Guillain-Barré syndrome
ALS
Multiple sclerosis
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an immune-mediated peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, often after an infection, with ascending weakness and absent reflexes; the EEG is normal because the brain is not involved. ALS is a progressive motor neuron disease without areflexia early, MS is a central demyelinating disease, and myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness with preserved reflexes.

questions.stem: A child has motor impairment and abnormal posture since infancy. Symptoms do not worsen over time. Most likely diagnosis is:
options: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Cerebral palsy
Hydrocephalus
Guillain-Barré syndrome
questions.explanation: Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive disorder of movement and posture caused by injury to the developing brain. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is progressive, hydrocephalus causes enlarging head size and raised pressure rather than a static motor disorder, and Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute, usually recovering neuropathy.

questions.stem: A possibly life-threatening condition in which breathing stops, for either a short or long period of time, is termed:
options: Dyspnea
Tachypnea
Apnea
Bradypnea
questions.explanation: Apnea is the cessation of breathing, which can be life-threatening and is monitored during sleep and neonatal studies. Dyspnea is difficult or labored breathing, tachypnea is rapid breathing, and bradypnea is abnormally slow breathing.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding asthma vs COPD?
options: Asthma is reversible airway inflammation; COPD is chronic, irreversible airflow obstruction
COPD is a combination of emphysema and chronic bronchitis
Both A and B are correct
They are identical conditions
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Asthma = reversible inflammation. COPD = chronic irreversible obstruction (emphysema + chronic bronchitis). Reversibility is the key discriminator for treatment and prognosis.

questions.stem: Increased blood pressure in the arteries supplying blood to the lungs, caused by increased resistance of blood flow in the lungs, usually the result of lung disease, is termed:
options: Systemic hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary edema
Pneumothorax
Atelectasis
questions.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension: Increased pressure in pulmonary arteries, often due to lung disease. Can lead to right heart strain (cor pulmonale). Distinct from systemic hypertension.

questions.stem: Which statement about the terms 'myositis' and 'myopathy' is correct?
options: Myopathy is muscle inflammation; myositis is any disease of muscle
Myositis is spinal cord inflammation; myopathy is muscle disease
Myositis is a disease of nerve; myopathy is a disease of muscle
Myositis is muscle inflammation; myopathy is any disease of muscle
questions.explanation: The suffix '-itis' means inflammation, so myositis is inflammation of muscle, while myopathy is the broad term for any muscle disease, inflammatory or not. The swapped pairing is the common trap; spinal cord inflammation is myelitis, and nerve disease is neuropathy.

questions.stem: Inflammation of the spinal cord which can cause headaches, fever, muscle stiffness, pain, weakness and eventually paralysis is termed:
options: Myelitis
Myelopathy
Myositis
Multiple sclerosis
questions.explanation: Myelitis is inflammation of the spinal cord ('myel-' spinal cord, '-itis' inflammation). Myelopathy is any spinal cord disorder, inflammatory or not; myositis is inflammation of muscle; multiple sclerosis is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the whole CNS rather than the general term for spinal cord inflammation.

questions.stem: A disease in which the protective coverings of nerve fibers in the brain are gradually destroyed with symptoms of numbness to paralysis and loss of control of bodily function is termed:
options: ALS
Multiple sclerosis
Guillain-Barré syndrome
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is a central nervous system disease in which myelin in the brain and spinal cord is progressively damaged, causing symptoms from numbness to paralysis. ALS is degeneration of motor neurons, Guillain-Barre syndrome is peripheral nerve demyelination, and myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction disorder.

questions.stem: Which statement about the terms 'vertebra' and 'spine' is correct?
options: A vertebra is one disk; the spine is the whole column of bones
The spine is a single bone; the vertebrae are the joints in it
A vertebra is one bone; the spine is the whole column of vertebrae
A vertebra is a nerve root level; the spine is the bony column
questions.explanation: A vertebra is a single bone (there are 33 in the column); the spine is the entire column made up of vertebrae, intervertebral disks and ligaments. Disks lie between vertebrae rather than being vertebrae; the spine is not one bone; nerve root levels are named after vertebrae but are not the bones themselves.

questions.stem: The slipping of a vertebra in the spine over the one below it is termed:
options: Disk prolapse
Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolysis
Laminectomy
Spinal fusion
questions.explanation: Spondylolisthesis: Vertebra slipping forward over the one below. Disk prolapse is herniated disk. Spondylolysis is vertebral defect. Laminectomy and spinal fusion are surgical procedures.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding laminectomy vs spinal fusion?
options: Laminectomy removes part of the vertebra to relieve pressure; spinal fusion joins vertebrae together
Laminectomy is decompressive surgery; spinal fusion is stabilizing surgery
Both A and B are correct
They are the same procedure
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Laminectomy = bone removal (decompressive). Spinal fusion = bone joining (stabilizing). Different surgical goals: decompression vs stabilization.

questions.stem: A condition in which the spine curves to one side producing an S-shaped curve is termed:
options: Scoliosis
Kyphosis
Lordosis
Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolysis
questions.explanation: Scoliosis: Side-to-side curve (S-shaped). Kyphosis is excessive outward thoracic curve (hump). Lordosis is excessive inward lumbar curve. These are distinct spinal deformities.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding kyphosis vs lordosis?
options: Kyphosis is excessive outward curvature of the upper spine (hump); lordosis is excessive inward curvature of the lower spine
Kyphosis affects thoracic region; lordosis affects lumbar region
Both A and B are correct
They are the same condition
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Kyphosis = outward thoracic curve (hump). Lordosis = inward lumbar curve. Direction (outward vs inward) and location (thoracic vs lumbar) are key distinctions.

questions.stem: A procedure in which a needle is inserted into the lower region of the spinal canal to take out a sample of spinal fluid or inject a drug is termed:
options: Cisternal puncture
Laminectomy
Ventricular tap
Lumbar puncture
questions.explanation: A lumbar puncture (also called a spinal tap) inserts a needle into the lumbar subarachnoid space to sample cerebrospinal fluid or inject a drug. A cisternal puncture enters the cisterna magna at the base of the skull, not the lower spinal canal; a laminectomy is surgical removal of part of a vertebra; a ventricular tap removes CSF from a lateral ventricle through the skull, not the lower spinal canal.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding retinitis pigmentosa vs macular degeneration?
options: Retinitis pigmentosa affects peripheral vision first; macular degeneration affects central vision first
Retinitis pigmentosa shows bone-spicule pigmentation; macular degeneration shows drusen deposits
Both A and B are correct
They affect vision identically
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Retinitis pigmentosa = peripheral field loss first, bone-spicule pigmentation. Macular degeneration = central vision loss first, drusen deposits. Field of vision affected is the key discriminator.

questions.stem: Drooping of the upper eyelid is termed:
options: Ptosis
Blepharitis
Conjunctivitis
Keratitis
questions.explanation: Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid, seen for example in third-nerve palsy, Horner syndrome or myasthenia gravis. Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins, conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, and keratitis is inflammation of the cornea.

questions.stem: Persistent, rapid, involuntary movement of the eye is termed:
options: Strabismus
Nystagmus
Diplopia
Amblyopia
questions.explanation: Nystagmus is involuntary rhythmic eye movement, which can produce rhythmic eye-movement artifact in frontal and lateral EEG channels. Strabismus is misalignment of the eyes, diplopia is double vision, and amblyopia is reduced vision in one eye from abnormal visual development.

questions.stem: A term describing a condition that affects both sides of the body or two paired organs, such as deafness in both ears, is:
options: Unilateral
Ipsilateral
Bilateral
Contralateral
questions.explanation: Bilateral means affecting both sides of the body or both of a pair of organs. Unilateral means one side only, ipsilateral means on the same side, and contralateral means on the opposite side; these terms are used constantly when describing EEG findings.

questions.stem: An unaware clenching or grinding of the teeth, usually during sleep, is termed:
options: Trismus
Dyskinesia
Dystonia
Bruxism
questions.explanation: Bruxism is unconscious clenching or grinding of the teeth, often during sleep, and produces bursts of muscle artifact on EEG and polysomnography. Trismus is restricted jaw opening from masticatory muscle spasm, dyskinesia is abnormal involuntary movement, and dystonia is sustained muscle contraction causing abnormal postures.

questions.stem: A slow heart rate, usually below 60 beats per minute in adults, is termed:
options: Bradycardia
Tachycardia
Arrhythmia
Fibrillation
questions.explanation: Bradycardia is a slow heart rate, usually below 60 beats per minute in adults, and can be seen on the ECG channel during an EEG. Tachycardia is a rate above 100 bpm, arrhythmia is any abnormal rhythm, and fibrillation is a chaotic, uncoordinated rhythm rather than a slow rate.

questions.stem: Which statement about hepatitis B and hepatitis C is true?
options: Both spread mainly through contaminated food and water
Both can progress to a chronic, long-term infection
Only hepatitis B can progress to a chronic infection
Only hepatitis C can be prevented with a vaccine
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B and C are both bloodborne (also sexual and perinatal) and both can become chronic infections, which is why standard precautions matter. Fecal-oral spread through food and water describes hepatitis A and E; hepatitis C commonly becomes chronic too; a vaccine exists for hepatitis B but not for hepatitis C.

questions.stem: A form of hepatitis that only causes symptoms when the individual is already infected with Hepatitis B is:
options: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis D
Hepatitis E
Autoimmune hepatitis
questions.explanation: Hepatitis D: Requires co-infection with Hepatitis B (defective virus). Cannot exist independently. This is a critical distinction for understanding hepatitis transmission and treatment.

questions.stem: A cancerous tumor of the liver is termed:
options: Hepatitis
Hepatoma
Cirrhosis
Hepatic adenoma
Liver failure
questions.explanation: Hepatoma: Malignant liver tumor (hepatocellular carcinoma). Hepatitis is inflammation. Cirrhosis is scarring. Hepatic adenoma is benign. These are distinct liver conditions.

questions.stem: Which statement about the pathophysiology of Parkinson disease is true?
options: It involves loss of cholinergic neurons in the hippocampus
It involves loss of GABA neurons in the caudate nucleus
It involves loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra
It involves loss of both upper and lower motor neurons
questions.explanation: Parkinson disease results from degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, giving resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity. Cholinergic and hippocampal loss is associated with Alzheimer disease, caudate GABAergic neuron loss with Huntington disease, and combined upper and lower motor neuron loss with ALS.

questions.stem: Which statement about the pathophysiology of Alzheimer disease is true?
options: It involves dopamine neuron loss in the substantia nigra
It involves demyelination of white matter tracts in the CNS
It involves prion-related spongiform change in the cortex
It involves cortical neuron loss, especially in the hippocampus
questions.explanation: Alzheimer disease involves degeneration of cortical neurons, especially in the hippocampus and temporal lobes, so progressive memory loss is the first and dominant symptom. Substantia nigra dopamine loss is Parkinson disease, CNS demyelination is multiple sclerosis, and prion-related spongiform change is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

questions.stem: Which statement about Huntington disease is correct?
options: It mainly degenerates the substantia nigra
It causes degeneration of the caudate nucleus
It is inherited in autosomal recessive form
It usually begins before the age of ten years
questions.explanation: Huntington disease degenerates the basal ganglia, especially the caudate nucleus, and classically causes chorea, psychiatric symptoms and dementia. Substantia nigra degeneration is the hallmark of Parkinson disease; Huntington is autosomal dominant, not recessive; onset is usually at 30-50 years, and childhood onset is the uncommon juvenile form.

questions.stem: Which statement about vascular dementia is correct?
options: It typically shows smooth, gradual decline
It results mainly from amyloid plaque buildup
It typically worsens in a stepwise pattern
Its EEG shows periodic sharp wave complexes
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia results from multiple strokes or chronic ischemia and typically worsens stepwise, with a drop after each vascular event. Smooth, gradual decline and amyloid plaques describe Alzheimer disease; periodic sharp wave complexes suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, whereas vascular dementia may show focal slowing.

questions.stem: Which statement about Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is correct?
options: EEG typically shows 3 Hz generalized spike-wave
Dementia typically progresses over many years
It is caused by a slowly replicating retrovirus
EEG often shows periodic sharp wave complexes
questions.explanation: CJD is a prion disease with rapidly progressive dementia (weeks to months), and the EEG often shows roughly 1 Hz periodic sharp wave complexes, a fairly specific finding. Generalized 3 Hz spike-wave is typical of absence epilepsy; progression over many years fits Alzheimer disease; the agent is a prion, not a virus.

questions.stem: Which statement about HIV-associated dementia is correct?
options: It is a subcortical dementia with slowed thinking
It is a cortical dementia beginning with aphasia
EEG typically shows periodic sharp wave complexes
It typically presents with early memory loss first
questions.explanation: HIV-associated dementia is a subcortical dementia with slowed thinking, poor concentration and motor slowing; the EEG typically shows diffuse slowing. A cortical dementia with early aphasia or memory loss first fits Alzheimer disease; periodic sharp wave complexes point to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

questions.stem: Which statement about amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is correct?
options: It degenerates only lower motor neurons in the cord
It degenerates both upper and lower motor neurons
It is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction
It usually begins with memory and language loss
questions.explanation: ALS degenerates both upper and lower motor neurons; cognition is usually preserved and the EEG is usually normal. Lower-motor-neuron-only involvement describes conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy; neuromuscular junction disease is myasthenia gravis; early memory and language loss suggests a cortical dementia.

questions.stem: Poisoning from poorly preserved food contaminated with dangerous bacterial toxin that results in paralysis is termed:
options: Tetanus
Guillain-Barré syndrome
Botulism
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Botulism: the Clostridium botulinum toxin, often from poorly preserved food, blocks acetylcholine release and causes descending flaccid paralysis. Tetanus toxin causes spastic paralysis; Guillain-Barré is immune-mediated demyelination; myasthenia gravis is autoimmune and not food-borne.

questions.stem: A genetic disorder in which cells carry one extra chromosome, causing intellectual disability and a characteristic appearance, is:
options: Marfan syndrome
Fragile X syndrome
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Down's syndrome
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is trisomy 21 (an extra chromosome 21) with intellectual disability and characteristic features. Fragile X also causes intellectual disability but results from a gene repeat expansion on the X chromosome, not an extra chromosome; Marfan is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder; Duchenne is X-linked.

questions.stem: A disorder of the inner ear, causing hearing loss, ringing in the ear, and sensation that one's surroundings are spinning, is:
options: Ménière's disease
Bell's palsy
Trigeminal neuralgia
Vestibular neuritis
Acoustic neuroma
questions.explanation: Ménière's disease: Inner ear disorder with classic triad (hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo/spinning). Bell's palsy is facial nerve. Trigeminal neuralgia is facial pain. Inner ear + triad = Ménière's.

questions.stem: The medical term for suffocation that can be caused by choking on an object, lack of oxygen in the air, or chemicals such as carbon monoxide which reduce the amount of oxygen in the blood, is:
options: Asphyxia
Apnea
Hypoxia
Anoxia
questions.explanation: Asphyxia is suffocation from any cause, such as choking, low oxygen in the air or carbon monoxide. Apnea is a pause or cessation of breathing; hypoxia and anoxia describe reduced or absent oxygen in tissues, which can result from asphyxia but do not name the suffocation itself.

questions.stem: The throat, the tube connecting the back of the mouth and nose to the esophagus and windpipe. Inflammation of the throat causing sore throat, fever, earache and swollen glands is:
options: Pharynx / Pharyngitis
Larynx / Laryngitis
Trachea / Tracheitis
Esophagus / Esophagitis
Bronchi / Bronchitis
questions.explanation: Pharynx / Pharyngitis: Throat connecting mouth/nose to esophagus/windpipe. Larynx is voice box. Trachea is windpipe. Esophagus is food tube. Anatomical location is critical.

questions.stem: A usually mild and temporary condition common in children under the age of 4 in which the walls of the airways become inflamed and narrow resulting in wheezing and coughing is:
options: Asthma
Croup
Bronchitis
Pneumonia
Epiglottitis
questions.explanation: Croup: Pediatric condition (<4 years), airway inflammation, wheezing, barking cough. Asthma is chronic/recurrent. Bronchitis is lower airway. Age + acute + wheezing = croup.

questions.stem: Protrusion of the spinal cord and its coverings out from the spine, one of the more severe forms of spina bifida, is termed:
options: Myelocele
Myelomeningocele
Spina bifida occulta
Meningocele
questions.explanation: Myelomeningocele: protrusion of the spinal cord and meninges through a vertebral defect, one of the more severe forms of spina bifida. A meningocele contains meninges only; spina bifida occulta has no protrusion; a myelocele is an open, flat neural plate without a covering sac.

questions.stem: Build up of fibrous connective tissue in the bone marrow affecting the production of blood components is termed:
options: Myelofibrosis
Myelosclerosis
Multiple myeloma
Myelitis
Myelopathy
questions.explanation: Myelofibrosis: Fibrous replacement of bone marrow, affects hematopoiesis. Myelosclerosis is sometimes used but myelofibrosis is preferred. Multiple myeloma is cancer. Myelitis is inflammation.

questions.stem: A nerve that carries messages to a muscle that cause the muscle to move is termed:
options: Sensory nerve
Mixed nerve
Motor nerve
Autonomic nerve
questions.explanation: A motor nerve carries efferent signals to muscles, causing movement. A sensory nerve carries afferent signals toward the CNS; a mixed nerve carries both; autonomic nerves supply smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands rather than skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: A cancer affecting cells in the bone marrow is termed:
options: Myeloma
Myelofibrosis
Myelitis
Myelopathy
Myelosclerosis
questions.explanation: Myeloma: Malignant plasma cell cancer in bone marrow. Myelofibrosis is fibrous replacement. Myelitis is inflammation. Myelopathy is general spinal cord disease. '-oma' suffix indicates tumor.

questions.stem: A disorder in which the lower part of the spine is weakened by an abnormally soft vertebra, often involving a defect or stress fracture in the pars interarticularis, is termed:
options: Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolysis
Spondylitis
Disk prolapse
Spinal stenosis
