questions.explanation: Spondylolysis: Vertebral defect/stress fracture (pars interarticularis). Spondylolisthesis is vertebra slipping. Spondylitis is inflammation. Defect vs slipping is the distinction.

questions.stem: A birth defect in which part of the spine fails to close completely. Its mildest form, in which the vertebral arches fail to close but nothing protrudes, is:
options: Myelomeningocele
Meningocele
Myelocele
Spina bifida occulta
questions.explanation: Spina bifida occulta is the mildest form: the vertebral arches fail to close but nothing protrudes, and it is often asymptomatic. A meningocele protrudes meninges only; a myelomeningocele protrudes cord and meninges; a myelocele is an open neural plate. Severity increases with protrusion.

questions.stem: Inflammation of the joints between the bones of the spine is termed:
options: Spondylitis
Spondylolysis
Spondylolisthesis
Spondylosis
Diskitis
questions.explanation: Spondylitis: Inflammation of spinal joints. Spondylolysis = defect. Spondylolisthesis = slipping. Spondylosis = degenerative. '-itis' suffix indicates inflammation.

questions.stem: Pain along the sciatic nerve which runs down the length of the leg to the foot, usually caused by pressure on the nerve due to disk prolapse, tumor, abscess or blood clot, is termed:
options: Sciatica
Radiculopathy
Neuropathy
Neuralgia
questions.explanation: Sciatica is pain along the sciatic nerve down the leg, usually from compression such as disk prolapse. Radiculopathy is a general term for any nerve-root disorder; neuropathy refers to peripheral nerve disease; neuralgia is nerve pain in general, not specific to the sciatic distribution.

questions.stem: Recurrent episodes of dizziness and weakness caused by insufficient blood flow through the posterior circulation are termed:
options: Internal carotid artery stenosis
Vertebrobasilar insufficiency
Transient global amnesia
Orthostatic hypotension
questions.explanation: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency is reduced flow through the vertebral and basilar arteries (posterior circulation) to the brainstem and cerebellum, causing dizziness and weakness. Internal carotid stenosis affects the anterior circulation; transient global amnesia causes isolated memory loss; orthostatic hypotension is a global drop in blood pressure on standing.

questions.stem: A disorder in which one of the disks located between the vertebrae breaks down and the pulpy interior squeezes out, causing pressure on a nerve, also called a slipped or ruptured disk, is:
options: Disk prolapse
Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolysis
Spinal stenosis
Diskitis
questions.explanation: Disk prolapse: Herniated/ruptured disk with nucleus pulposus extrusion, causing nerve compression. Spondylolisthesis is vertebra slipping. Spondylolysis is vertebral defect. Disk vs bone is the distinction.

questions.stem: The shrinkage or near disappearance of a tissue or organ is termed:
options: Hypertrophy
Hyperplasia
Atrophy
Dysplasia
questions.explanation: Atrophy is shrinkage of a tissue or organ, such as cerebral atrophy. Hypertrophy is enlargement from increased cell size; hyperplasia is enlargement from increased cell number; dysplasia is abnormal cell development.

questions.stem: An accumulation of pus in a body tissue, usually caused by bacterial infection, is termed:
options: Cellulitis
Empyema
Gangrene
Abscess
questions.explanation: An abscess is a localized collection of pus within a tissue, usually from bacterial infection. Cellulitis is diffuse spreading infection without a pus pocket; empyema is pus in a pre-existing body cavity such as the pleural space; gangrene is tissue death.

questions.stem: A hollow flexible tube inserted into the body to put in or take out fluid or to open up or close blood vessels is termed:
options: Catheter
Cannula
Stent
Shunt
Drain
questions.explanation: Catheter: Flexible tube for fluid access/vessel manipulation. Cannula is rigid needle. Stent keeps vessel open. Shunt diverts flow. Drain removes fluid. Flexibility + access = catheter.

questions.stem: A waste product that is filtered from the blood by the kidneys and expelled in urine is:
options: Creatinine
Urea
Uric acid
Bilirubin
Albumin
questions.explanation: Creatinine: Muscle metabolism waste product, filtered by kidneys, excreted in urine. Urea is also kidney waste. Uric acid is purine breakdown. Bilirubin is heme breakdown. Creatinine is muscle-specific.

questions.stem: Term meaning 'in place' that is used to describe a cancer that has not spread is:
options: In situ
Metastatic
Invasive
Malignant
Benign
questions.explanation: In situ: Cancer confined to original location, has not spread (invaded or metastasized). Metastatic = spread. Invasive = penetrated tissue. Malignant = cancerous. In situ = localized.

questions.stem: Another term for fatty tissue that stores energy, insulates and cushions the body is:
options: Adipose tissue
Connective tissue
Epithelial tissue
Muscle tissue
Nervous tissue
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue: Fat tissue with energy storage, insulation, cushioning functions. Connective tissue is broader category. Epithelial is lining. Muscle is contractile. Nervous is neural. Fat-specific = adipose.

questions.stem: Difficulty falling and remaining asleep is termed:
options: Insomnia
Narcolepsy
Hypersomnia
Sleep apnea
questions.explanation: Insomnia is difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep. Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness with sleep-onset REM; hypersomnia is excessive sleep or sleepiness; sleep apnea is repeated breathing pauses during sleep.

questions.stem: Surgical removal of dead, damaged or infected tissue or some foreign material from a wound or burn is termed:
options: Debridement
Excision
Incision
Drainage
Irrigation
questions.explanation: Debridement: Removal of necrotic/infected tissue or foreign material from wounds. Excision is general removal. Incision is cutting. Drainage removes fluid. Irrigation is washing. Wound cleaning = debridement.

questions.stem: Anything that can cause cancer is termed:
options: Carcinogen
Mutagen
Teratogen
Oncogene
Tumor suppressor
questions.explanation: Carcinogen: Cancer-causing agent. Mutagen causes mutations (may or may not cause cancer). Teratogen causes birth defects. Oncogene promotes cancer. Tumor suppressor prevents cancer. Cancer-specific = carcinogen.

questions.stem: Related to fever is termed:
options: Afebrile
Febrile
Hyperthermic
Hypothermic
questions.explanation: Febrile means related to or having a fever, as in febrile seizures. Afebrile means without fever; hyperthermic describes elevated body temperature from any cause, not specifically fever; hypothermic means abnormally low temperature.

questions.stem: An unintended and unwanted side effect of some sort of treatment, usually drug therapy, is termed:
options: Therapeutic effect
Drug interaction
Adverse reaction
Contraindication
questions.explanation: An adverse reaction is an unintended, unwanted effect of a treatment, usually a drug. A therapeutic effect is the intended benefit; a drug interaction is one drug altering another's effect; a contraindication is a reason not to give a treatment.

questions.stem: Which statement about epilepsy is correct?
options: It requires an identifiable structural brain lesion
A single provoked seizure establishes the diagnosis
A normal routine EEG excludes the diagnosis
It is defined by recurrent, unprovoked seizures
questions.explanation: Epilepsy is a brain disorder with an enduring tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures; the EEG supports diagnosis by showing epileptiform discharges. Many epilepsies have no structural lesion; a provoked seizure (e.g., from hypoglycemia) is not epilepsy; a routine interictal EEG is often normal in people with epilepsy. Per ILAE 2014, epilepsy is usually diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 h apart, or after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of 60% or more, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.

questions.stem: Excess cerebrospinal fluid within the brain is termed:
options: Hydrocephalus
Meningitis
Intracranial hypertension
Cerebral edema
questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus is excess cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricles of the brain. Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges; intracranial hypertension is raised pressure that can have many causes; cerebral edema is swelling of the brain tissue itself rather than excess CSF.

questions.stem: Another name for idiopathic facial palsy, the usually one-sided, temporary weakness of the facial muscles caused by an inflamed facial nerve, is:
options: Erb's palsy
Bell's palsy
Hemifacial spasm
Trigeminal neuralgia
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is idiopathic, usually unilateral and temporary facial nerve (CN VII) weakness. Erb's palsy is a brachial plexus birth injury affecting the arm; hemifacial spasm is involuntary facial twitching; trigeminal neuralgia is facial pain from CN V.

questions.stem: A virus that is the cause of mononucleosis and is involved in Burkitt's lymphoma is:
options: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
Herpes simplex virus (HSV)
Varicella-zoster virus (VZV)
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
questions.explanation: Epstein-Barr virus: Causes infectious mononucleosis, associated with Burkitt's lymphoma. CMV causes mononucleosis-like illness. HSV causes cold sores. VZV causes chickenpox. HIV causes AIDS. Mononucleosis + lymphoma = EBV.

questions.stem: A disorder causing thickening and hardening of artery walls is termed:
options: Atherosclerosis
Arterial stenosis
Arteriosclerosis
Aneurysm
questions.explanation: Arteriosclerosis is the general term for thickening and hardening of artery walls. Atherosclerosis is a subtype caused by plaque buildup; arterial stenosis is narrowing of the lumen; an aneurysm is a localized dilation of the artery wall.

questions.stem: A dangerous accumulation of chemicals called ketones in the blood, occurring as a complication of diabetes mellitus, is:
options: Hyperglycemia
Hypoglycemia
Diabetic neuropathy
Ketoacidosis
questions.explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a dangerous buildup of ketones causing metabolic acidosis, and can produce encephalopathy with diffuse slowing. Hyperglycemia is high blood glucose alone; hypoglycemia is low blood glucose; diabetic neuropathy is peripheral nerve damage.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding meningitis?
options: Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges usually caused by infection
Viral forms are milder; bacterial forms are life-threatening
Both A and B are correct
Meningitis always affects brain tissue directly
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Meningitis = meningeal inflammation, usually infectious. Viral = milder. Bacterial = life-threatening. Meningitis affects coverings, NOT brain tissue directly (that's encephalitis).

questions.stem: Rare genetic disorder affecting connective tissue, causing abnormalities of joints, bones, tendons, ligaments, arteries and/or the heart, is:
options: Marfan syndrome
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Down's syndrome
Huntington disease
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome: Connective tissue disorder affecting multiple systems (skeletal, cardiovascular, ocular). Ehlers-Danlos also affects connective tissue but different features. Down's is chromosomal. Huntington is neurodegenerative.

questions.stem: A hereditary disease in which the muscles weaken and waste away, similar to Duchenne muscular dystrophy but starts later in life and advances more slowly, is:
options: Becker muscular dystrophy
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Becker muscular dystrophy is X-linked like Duchenne but begins later and progresses more slowly. Duchenne begins in early childhood and is more severe; ALS is a motor neuron disease; myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder.

questions.stem: A genetic condition, seen mainly in boys and beginning in early childhood, in which muscle fibers degenerate and muscles become progressively weaker is:
options: Becker muscular dystrophy
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Spinal muscular atrophy
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked, affects mainly boys, begins in early childhood and causes progressive muscle fiber degeneration. Becker is milder with later onset; spinal muscular atrophy is degeneration of spinal motor neurons, not muscle; myasthenia gravis is autoimmune.

questions.stem: A disorder in which the body's immune system attacks itself is termed:
options: Autoimmune disease
Immunodeficiency
Allergy
Hypersensitivity
Immunosuppression
questions.explanation: Autoimmune disease: Immune system attacks self-tissues. Immunodeficiency is weakened immunity. Allergy is immune overreaction to external antigen. Hypersensitivity is exaggerated immune response. Immunosuppression is reduced immunity.

questions.stem: A dangerous eating disorder mainly affecting young girls in which the sufferer has an intense fear of looking fat, avoids food and loses weight excessively is:
options: Anorexia nervosa
Bulimia nervosa
Binge eating disorder
Obesity
Cachexia
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder with fear of weight gain, food avoidance, excessive weight loss. Bulimia involves binge-purge cycles. Binge eating is overeating without purging. Obesity is excess weight. Cachexia is wasting from disease.

questions.stem: A method of determining focusing errors of the eye in which light is shined through the pupil and the reflected beam is measured is:
options: Retinoscopy
Ophthalmoscopy
Slit lamp examination
Tonometry
Visual acuity test
questions.explanation: Retinoscopy: Objective refraction test using light reflection through pupil to determine refractive error. Ophthalmoscopy views retina. Slit lamp examines anterior eye. Tonometry measures pressure. Visual acuity tests vision.

questions.stem: A clear dome-shaped front portion of the eye's outer covering is:
options: Sclera
Iris
Cornea
Lens
questions.explanation: The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped front of the eye's outer coat; it is positively charged relative to the retina, the basis of eye-movement artifact. The sclera is the white outer coat; the iris is the colored diaphragm; the lens lies behind the iris.

questions.stem: The colored portion of the eye is:
options: Iris
Cornea
Sclera
Retina
Choroid
questions.explanation: Iris: Colored portion controlling pupil size. Cornea is clear anterior. Sclera is white. Retina is light-sensitive back. Choroid is vascular layer. Colored + pupil control = iris.

questions.stem: A membrane lining the inside of the back of the eye that contains light-sensitive nerve cells that convert focused light into nerve impulses making vision possible is:
options: Choroid
Sclera
Cornea
Retina
questions.explanation: The retina lines the back of the eye and contains photoreceptors (rods and cones) that convert light into nerve impulses; it is the negative pole of the corneoretinal dipole. The choroid is the vascular layer; the sclera is the white outer coat; the cornea is the clear front.

questions.stem: Final state of liver disease, in which liver function becomes so impaired that other areas of the body are affected, most commonly the brain, is:
options: Liver failure
Cirrhosis
Hepatitis
Hepatic steatosis
questions.explanation: Liver failure is end-stage loss of liver function affecting other organs, most commonly the brain (hepatic encephalopathy, often with triphasic waves on EEG). Cirrhosis is scarring that may precede failure; hepatitis is inflammation; hepatic steatosis is fat accumulation.

questions.stem: Which pairing of dementia type and typical EEG finding is correct?
options: Early Alzheimer: frontal triphasic waves
Creutzfeldt-Jakob: periodic sharp waves
Vascular dementia: 3 Hz spike-and-wave
Early Parkinson: marked diffuse slowing
questions.explanation: CJD characteristically shows periodic sharp wave complexes. Alzheimer disease shows diffuse slowing that worsens over time (triphasic waves suggest metabolic encephalopathy); vascular dementia may show focal slowing, not 3 Hz spike-and-wave; the EEG in early Parkinson disease is usually normal.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes Parkinson disease from Alzheimer disease?
options: Parkinson begins with memory loss; Alzheimer with motor signs
Both begin with memory loss, but Parkinson progresses faster
Parkinson begins with motor signs; Alzheimer with memory loss
Parkinson begins with hallucinations; Alzheimer with memory loss
questions.explanation: Parkinson disease presents first with motor signs (rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia), and dementia, if it occurs, comes late; Alzheimer disease presents first with memory loss. The reversed pairing is wrong; Parkinson does not begin with memory loss; early hallucinations suggest dementia with Lewy bodies.

questions.stem: Which features are MOST characteristic of Huntington disease?
options: Young adult onset (30-50 years), chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and dementia
Older adult onset, memory loss first, no movement disorder
Childhood onset, progressive weakness, no cognitive changes
All ages, identical to Alzheimer disease
questions.explanation: Huntington = young adult (30-50), chorea + psychiatric + dementia. Alzheimer = older, memory first. Duchenne = childhood, weakness. Age + movement + dementia = Huntington.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes vascular dementia from Alzheimer disease?
options: Alzheimer worsens stepwise; vascular dementia declines gradually
Both decline gradually, but vascular dementia begins earlier
Both decline stepwise, but Alzheimer progresses more rapidly
Vascular dementia worsens stepwise; Alzheimer declines gradually
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia typically worsens stepwise, with a drop after each stroke, whereas Alzheimer disease declines smoothly and gradually. The reversed pairing is a common mix-up; neither 'both gradual' nor 'both stepwise' captures the key discriminator, which is the pattern of progression.

questions.stem: Which features are MOST characteristic of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)?
options: Slow decline over years with gradual posterior slowing
Stepwise decline with focal deficits and focal slowing
Rapid dementia, myoclonus, periodic sharp wave complexes
Childhood onset, slow decline, periodic complexes every 4-15 s
questions.explanation: CJD causes a rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months with myoclonus, and the EEG typically shows generalized periodic sharp wave complexes at about 1 Hz. Slow decline over years with posterior slowing fits Alzheimer disease; stepwise decline with focal findings fits vascular dementia; long-interval periodic complexes (every 4-15 s) in a child fit SSPE.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes encephalitis from meningitis?
options: Meningitis involves brain parenchyma; encephalitis, the meninges
Encephalitis involves brain parenchyma; meningitis, the meninges
Encephalitis involves the ventricular lining; meningitis, the dura
Encephalitis spares awareness; meningitis alters it early on
questions.explanation: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain tissue itself, so altered mental status, seizures and EEG slowing are common; meningitis is inflammation of the meningeal coverings. The first option reverses the two terms; inflammation of the ventricular lining is ventriculitis; encephalitis typically alters awareness early rather than sparing it.

questions.stem: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome is referred for EEG. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: It is a cortical disorder, so the EEG usually shows diffuse slowing
It is a CNS demyelinating disease, so the EEG shows focal slowing
It is a peripheral disorder, so the EEG is usually normal
It causes descending weakness and periodic discharges on EEG
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy of the peripheral nerves with typically ascending weakness, so the EEG is usually normal; an abnormal EEG would suggest CNS involvement or another process. It is not a cortical disorder, it is not a CNS demyelinating disease like multiple sclerosis, and its weakness classically ascends without periodic discharges.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis)?
options: ALS involves degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons
EEG is usually normal because ALS affects motor neurons, not cortical function
Both A and B are correct
ALS always shows epileptiform discharges on EEG
questions.explanation: Both are correct: ALS = UMN + LMN degeneration, normal EEG (motor neuron disease, not cortical). Epileptiform discharges would indicate cortical dysfunction, not motor neuron disease.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes cerebral palsy from muscular dystrophy?
options: Cerebral palsy is progressive; muscular dystrophy is non-progressive
Both are progressive; cerebral palsy stems from a muscle protein defect
Cerebral palsy is a genetic myopathy; MD follows perinatal brain injury
Cerebral palsy is non-progressive; muscular dystrophy is progressive
questions.explanation: Cerebral palsy results from a static (non-progressive) injury to the developing brain, although its motor signs may change as the child grows; muscular dystrophies are inherited muscle disorders that worsen over time. The first option reverses them; cerebral palsy is not caused by a muscle protein defect, and it is a brain injury, not a genetic myopathy.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding retinitis pigmentosa?
options: Retinitis pigmentosa affects peripheral vision first, eventually causing tunnel vision
Fundoscopy shows bone-spicule pigmentation; central vision is preserved until late
Both A and B are correct
Retinitis pigmentosa affects central vision first like macular degeneration
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Retinitis pigmentosa = peripheral field loss first, bone-spicule pigmentation, central vision preserved until late. Macular degeneration = central vision first. Field affected is key.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding macular degeneration?
options: Macular degeneration affects central vision first, interfering with fine detail discrimination
Peripheral vision is usually preserved; fundoscopy shows drusen deposits
Both A and B are correct
Macular degeneration affects peripheral vision first
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Macular degeneration = central vision loss first, peripheral preserved, drusen deposits. Retinitis pigmentosa = peripheral first. Central vs peripheral is the key distinction.

questions.stem: Sudden, painless, severe loss of vision in one eye is MOST characteristic of:
options: Retinal artery occlusion
Conjunctivitis
Cataract
Macular degeneration
Glaucoma
questions.explanation: Retinal artery occlusion: Acute ischemia, sudden painless vision loss ('curtain coming down'), ophthalmologic emergency. Conjunctivitis causes irritation. Cataract is gradual. Macular degeneration is progressive. Sudden + painless = occlusion.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes blepharitis from conjunctivitis?
options: Blepharitis affects eyelid margins; conjunctivitis affects the conjunctival membrane
They are the same condition
Blepharitis always affects the entire eye
Conjunctivitis only affects the eyelids
questions.explanation: Blepharitis = eyelid margin inflammation (crusting, irritation). Conjunctivitis = conjunctival membrane inflammation (red eye, discharge). Location (eyelid vs membrane) is the key distinction.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes hepatitis from cirrhosis?
options: Hepatitis refers to liver inflammation; cirrhosis refers to chronic scarring and architectural distortion
They are the same condition
Hepatitis always leads to cirrhosis immediately
Cirrhosis is always inflammatory
questions.explanation: Hepatitis = inflammation. Cirrhosis = chronic scarring/fibrosis (end-stage architectural changes). Inflammation vs scarring is the key distinction. Cirrhosis can result from chronic hepatitis but represents different stages.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes Hepatitis A from Hepatitis B?
options: Hepatitis A spreads by blood and body fluids; hepatitis B, fecal-oral
Both spread mainly by respiratory droplets and contaminated fomites
Hepatitis A spreads fecal-oral; hepatitis B, by blood and body fluids
Hepatitis A spreads by blood products; hepatitis B, by airborne droplets
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A is spread by the fecal-oral route (contaminated food or water) and does not become chronic; hepatitis B is a bloodborne pathogen spread by blood, sexual contact and other body fluids, which is why standard precautions and hepatitis B vaccination matter in the EEG lab. The other options reverse the routes or assign respiratory or airborne spread, which applies to neither virus.

questions.stem: Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes due to excess bilirubin in the blood is:
options: Jaundice
Cyanosis
Pallor
Erythema
Ecchymosis
questions.explanation: Jaundice: Yellowing from excess bilirubin (liver dysfunction). Cyanosis = bluish (low oxygen). Pallor = paleness. Erythema = redness. Ecchymosis = bruising. Color + cause = jaundice.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes asthma from COPD?
options: Asthma is reversible airway inflammation; COPD is chronic, irreversible airflow obstruction
They are identical conditions
COPD is always reversible
Asthma is always irreversible
questions.explanation: Asthma = reversible inflammation. COPD = chronic irreversible obstruction (emphysema + chronic bronchitis). Reversibility is the CRITICAL discriminator for treatment and prognosis.

questions.stem: A possibly life-threatening condition in which breathing stops completely is:
options: Dyspnea
Apnea
Bradypnea
Tachypnea
questions.explanation: Apnea is complete cessation of breathing and can be life-threatening; it is also monitored during sleep and EMU recordings. Dyspnea is difficult or labored breathing, bradypnea is abnormally slow breathing, and tachypnea is abnormally rapid breathing, so in each of these breathing continues.

questions.stem: Increased blood pressure in the arteries supplying blood to the lungs, usually the result of lung disease, can lead to:
options: Pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain (cor pulmonale)
Left heart failure only
No cardiac effects
Only affects the lungs
questions.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension: Increased pulmonary artery pressure from lung disease, leads to right heart strain (cor pulmonale). Left heart failure is from systemic hypertension. Right heart = pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes myositis from myopathy?
options: Myopathy is muscle inflammation; myositis is any muscle disease
Myositis is muscle inflammation; myopathy is any muscle disease
Myositis is spinal cord inflammation; myopathy is any muscle disease
Myositis is a muscle tumor; myopathy is muscle inflammation
questions.explanation: The suffix "-itis" means inflammation, so myositis is inflammation of muscle, while myopathy ("-pathy", disease) is the broader term for any muscle disease, inflammatory or not. The first option reverses the terms; spinal cord inflammation is myelitis; a muscle tumor would be a myoma, and myopathy is not limited to inflammation.

questions.stem: Inflammation of the spinal cord causing headaches, fever, muscle stiffness, pain, weakness and eventually paralysis is:
options: Myelopathy
Myositis
Multiple sclerosis
Myelitis
questions.explanation: Myelitis is inflammation of the spinal cord ("myel-" cord, "-itis" inflammation) and can progress to weakness and paralysis. Myelopathy is any spinal cord disease, not specifically inflammatory; myositis is muscle inflammation; multiple sclerosis is a demyelinating disease that can involve the cord but is not the term for cord inflammation itself.

questions.stem: A disease in which the protective coverings of nerve fibers in the brain are gradually destroyed, causing symptoms from numbness to paralysis, is:
options: ALS
Guillain-Barré syndrome
Multiple sclerosis
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is gradual destruction of the myelin covering nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord (CNS demyelination), with symptoms ranging from numbness to paralysis. ALS is degeneration of motor neurons, Guillain-Barré is peripheral nerve demyelination, and myasthenia gravis affects the neuromuscular junction.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes vertebra from spine?
options: Vertebra refers to a single bone (one of 33); spine refers to the entire column of bones and cartilage
They are the same thing
Spine refers to a single bone
Vertebra refers to the entire column
questions.explanation: Vertebra = single bone (one of 33 bones). Spine = entire column (all vertebrae + cartilage). Single vs entire column is the key distinction for accurate medical terminology.

questions.stem: The slipping of a vertebra in the spine over the one below it is:
options: Spondylolisthesis
Disk prolapse
Spondylolysis
Laminectomy
Spinal fusion
questions.explanation: Spondylolisthesis: Vertebra slipping forward. Disk prolapse = herniated disk. Spondylolysis = vertebral defect. Laminectomy and spinal fusion are surgical procedures. Bone slipping vs disk herniation is key.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes laminectomy from spinal fusion?
options: Laminectomy removes bone to relieve pressure (decompressive); spinal fusion joins vertebrae together (stabilizing)
They are the same procedure
Laminectomy always joins bones
Spinal fusion always removes bone
questions.explanation: Laminectomy = bone removal (decompressive surgery). Spinal fusion = bone joining (stabilizing surgery). Different surgical goals: decompression vs stabilization.

questions.stem: A condition in which the spine curves to one side producing an S-shaped curve is:
options: Scoliosis
Kyphosis
Lordosis
Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolysis
questions.explanation: Scoliosis: Side-to-side curve (S-shaped). Kyphosis = excessive outward thoracic curve (hump). Lordosis = excessive inward lumbar curve. Direction of curve is the key distinction.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding kyphosis vs lordosis?
options: Kyphosis is excessive outward curvature of the upper spine (hump); lordosis is excessive inward curvature of the lower spine
Kyphosis affects thoracic region; lordosis affects lumbar region
Both A and B are correct
They curve in the same direction
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Kyphosis = outward thoracic (hump). Lordosis = inward lumbar. Direction (outward vs inward) AND location (thoracic vs lumbar) are both key distinctions.

questions.stem: A procedure in which a needle is inserted into the lower region of the spinal canal to take out a sample of spinal fluid or inject a drug is:
options: Cisternal puncture
Lumbar laminectomy
Lumbar puncture
Ventricular tap
questions.explanation: A lumbar puncture (spinal tap) places a needle into the lower spinal canal to sample CSF or inject a drug. A cisternal puncture also samples CSF but at the cisterna magna below the skull, not the lower spine; a laminectomy is open surgery that removes bone; a ventricular tap enters the brain ventricles.

questions.stem: A disorder in which the lower part of the spine is weakened by a defect or stress fracture in the pars interarticularis is:
options: Spondylolysis
Spondylolisthesis
Spondylitis
Disk prolapse
Spinal stenosis
questions.explanation: Spondylolysis: Vertebral defect/stress fracture (pars interarticularis). Spondylolisthesis = vertebra slipping (can result from spondylolysis). Spondylitis = inflammation. Defect vs slipping is distinction.

questions.stem: Pain along the sciatic nerve running down the leg, usually caused by pressure on the nerve due to disk prolapse, is:
options: Sciatica
Radiculopathy
Neuropathy
Neuralgia
Myalgia
questions.explanation: Sciatica: Sciatic nerve-specific pain (leg distribution). Radiculopathy is general nerve root. Neuropathy is peripheral nerve. Neuralgia is nerve pain. Sciatic nerve specific = sciatica.

questions.stem: A tunnel-like passage in the body is termed:
options: Canal
Duct
Fistula
Sinus
Foramen
questions.explanation: Canal: General tunnel-like passageway. Duct is usually glandular. Fistula is abnormal connection. Sinus is cavity. Foramen is opening. Canal is the general term for passageways.

questions.stem: The tension in the main arteries created by the beating of the heart, resistance to flow, and elasticity of blood vessels is:
options: Cardiac output
Vascular resistance
Stroke volume
Blood pressure
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is the pressure (tension) in the main arteries produced by cardiac contraction, resistance to flow and vessel elasticity. Cardiac output is the volume pumped per minute, vascular resistance is only one contributor to pressure, and stroke volume is the volume ejected per beat.

questions.stem: A clear membrane covering the white of the eye and inside of the eyelid that produces fluid lubricating the cornea and eyelid. Inflammation of this membrane is also called 'Pinkeye':
options: Conjunctiva / Conjunctivitis
Cornea / Keratitis
Sclera / Scleritis
Iris / Iritis
Retina / Retinitis
questions.explanation: Conjunctiva / Conjunctivitis: Membrane covering eye white and eyelid inner surface, produces lubricating fluid. Inflammation = conjunctivitis (pinkeye). Cornea is clear dome. Sclera is white. Iris is colored. Retina is light-sensitive.

questions.stem: Which finding MEETS the classic clinical criterion for a diagnosis of epilepsy?
options: Two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart
A single provoked seizure followed by an abnormal EEG
Two or more seizures, whether provoked or unprovoked
Interictal epileptiform discharges without any seizures
questions.explanation: Epilepsy is classically diagnosed after at least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart (the ILAE also allows one unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk). Provoked seizures, such as from hypoglycemia or alcohol withdrawal, do not establish epilepsy; epileptiform discharges without seizures support but do not make the diagnosis, and the EEG complements a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes hydrocephalus?
options: Excess CSF within the ventricles, raising intracranial pressure
Excess CSF in the subdural space after a closed head injury
Brain swelling from excess water within the brain tissue
Blood collecting within the ventricles after a bleed
questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus is accumulation of excess CSF within the ventricles, which raises intracranial pressure and in infants can enlarge the head and cause a bulging fontanelle; it usually needs treatment such as a shunt. CSF in the subdural space is a subdural hygroma, swelling of brain tissue is cerebral edema, and blood in the ventricles is intraventricular hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes Bell's palsy?
options: Unilateral idiopathic CN VII palsy that is usually temporary
Unilateral idiopathic CN V palsy causing facial numbness
Bilateral idiopathic CN VII palsy that is usually permanent
Unilateral CN VII palsy from a stroke that spares the forehead
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic, usually one-sided paralysis of the facial nerve (CN VII) that typically recovers. CN V is the trigeminal nerve, which carries facial sensation; bilateral involvement is rare and the condition is usually temporary; a stroke causes a central facial palsy that spares the forehead, whereas Bell's palsy is peripheral and involves the forehead.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)?
options: EBV causes infectious mononucleosis
EBV is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma
Both A and B are correct
EBV only causes mononucleosis
questions.explanation: Both are correct: EBV causes infectious mononucleosis AND is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma. EBV has multiple disease associations. Mononucleosis + lymphoma association = EBV.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding arteriosclerosis?
options: Arteriosclerosis is a general term for arterial wall thickening and hardening
Atherosclerosis is a subtype of arteriosclerosis involving plaque buildup
Both A and B are correct
They are completely different conditions
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Arteriosclerosis = general term (arterial hardening). Atherosclerosis = subtype (plaque buildup). Atherosclerosis is a form of arteriosclerosis. General vs specific is the relationship.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding ketoacidosis?
options: Ketoacidosis is dangerous accumulation of ketones in the blood
It occurs as a complication of diabetes mellitus and is a medical emergency
Both A and B are correct
Ketoacidosis is always benign
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Ketoacidosis = dangerous ketone accumulation, diabetic complication, medical emergency. NOT benign - requires immediate treatment. Ketones + diabetes + dangerous = ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: Which statement about meningitis is MOST accurate?
options: Viral forms are emergencies; bacterial forms are usually milder
Fungal forms are the most common and the most severe type
It is inflammation of brain tissue, usually from infection
Bacterial forms are emergencies; viral forms are usually milder
questions.explanation: Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, usually from infection; bacterial meningitis is a life-threatening emergency, while viral meningitis is usually milder and self-limited. The first option reverses severity; fungal meningitis is uncommon and mainly affects immunocompromised patients; inflammation of brain tissue itself is encephalitis.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding Marfan syndrome?
options: Marfan syndrome is a rare genetic disorder affecting connective tissue
It causes abnormalities of joints, bones, tendons, ligaments, arteries, and/or heart
Both A and B are correct
Marfan syndrome only affects one body system
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Marfan = genetic connective tissue disorder affecting MULTIPLE systems (skeletal, cardiovascular, ocular). NOT single-system. Genetic + connective tissue + multisystem = Marfan.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST compares Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy?
options: Becker begins earlier and progresses faster than Duchenne
Both are autosomal recessive and affect boys and girls equally
Duchenne begins earlier and progresses faster than Becker
Duchenne is non-progressive, while Becker worsens over time
questions.explanation: Duchenne and Becker are both X-linked dystrophinopathies that mainly affect boys; Duchenne begins in early childhood and progresses rapidly, while Becker begins later and progresses more slowly. The first option reverses them; they are X-linked, not autosomal recessive; both are progressive muscular dystrophies.

questions.stem: Which group lists neurological disorders considered autoimmune?
options: Multiple sclerosis, ALS, and Huntington disease
Myasthenia gravis, Parkinson disease, and ALS
Guillain-Barré syndrome, Duchenne dystrophy, and Alzheimer disease
Multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: In autoimmune disease the immune system attacks the body's own tissue; multiple sclerosis (CNS myelin), Guillain-Barré syndrome (peripheral myelin) and myasthenia gravis (acetylcholine receptors) are immune-mediated neurological disorders. ALS, Parkinson and Alzheimer disease are neurodegenerative, Huntington disease and Duchenne dystrophy are genetic, so each distractor group contains non-autoimmune conditions.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding anorexia nervosa?
options: Anorexia nervosa is a dangerous eating disorder mainly affecting young girls
It involves intense fear of looking fat, food avoidance, and excessive weight loss
Both A and B are correct
Anorexia nervosa is always benign
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Anorexia nervosa = dangerous eating disorder, young women, fear of weight gain, food avoidance, excessive weight loss. NOT benign - can be life-threatening. Eating disorder + fear + weight loss = anorexia.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding retinoscopy?
options: Retinoscopy is a method of determining focusing errors of the eye
Light is shined through the pupil and the reflected beam is measured
Both A and B are correct
Retinoscopy is a subjective test requiring patient responses
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Retinoscopy = objective refraction test using light reflection through pupil to determine refractive error. NOT subjective - objective measurement. Objective + light reflection = retinoscopy.

questions.stem: Which description BEST fits the cornea?
options: Colored muscular ring that controls the size of the pupil
Clear dome at the front of the eye that refracts light
White fibrous outer coat that protects the eyeball
Flexible structure behind the pupil that fine-tunes focus
questions.explanation: The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped front of the eye's outer coat and the first structure light passes through; it provides most of the eye's refractive power. The colored ring controlling the pupil is the iris, the white fibrous coat is the sclera, and the flexible structure behind the pupil that fine-tunes focus is the lens.

questions.stem: Which description BEST fits the iris?
options: Clear dome at the front of the eye that refracts light
Pigmented layer of blood vessels beneath the retina
Colored muscular ring that controls the size of the pupil
Clear membrane covering the white of the eye and eyelids
questions.explanation: The iris is the colored, muscular ring that changes pupil size and so regulates how much light enters the eye. The clear refracting dome is the cornea, the vascular pigmented layer beneath the retina is the choroid, and the clear membrane over the white of the eye and inner eyelids is the conjunctiva.

questions.stem: Which description BEST fits the retina?
options: Light-sensitive layer of rods and cones lining the back of the eye
Pigmented layer of blood vessels that nourishes the outer eye
Clear gel filling the space between the lens and back of the eye
Clear dome at the front of the eye that first refracts light
questions.explanation: The retina lines the back of the eye and contains the photoreceptors (rods and cones) that convert light into nerve impulses carried by the optic nerve. The vascular pigmented layer is the choroid, the clear gel is the vitreous humor, and the clear refracting dome at the front is the cornea.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding hepatoma?
options: Hepatoma is a cancerous (malignant) tumor of the liver
It is also called hepatocellular carcinoma
Both A and B are correct
Hepatoma is always benign
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Hepatoma = malignant liver tumor (hepatocellular carcinoma). NOT benign - it's cancer. Malignant + liver + tumor = hepatoma.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding Hepatitis D?
options: Hepatitis D only causes symptoms when the individual is already infected with Hepatitis B
Hepatitis D is a defective virus that requires Hepatitis B for replication
Both A and B are correct
Hepatitis D can exist independently
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Hepatitis D = defective virus requiring Hepatitis B co-infection, cannot exist independently. Requires Hep B = key characteristic. Defective + requires Hep B = Hepatitis D.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding croup?
options: Croup is a usually mild and temporary condition common in children under age 4
It involves inflamed and narrowed airways resulting in wheezing and coughing
Both A and B are correct
Croup only affects adults
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Croup = pediatric (<4 years), mild temporary, airway inflammation, wheezing, barking cough. NOT adult condition. Pediatric + airway + wheezing = croup.

questions.stem: Asphyxia is BEST defined as:
options: Difficult or labored breathing with normal oxygen levels
Abnormally rapid, shallow breathing during exertion
Brief pauses in breathing that occur only during sleep
Impaired breathing that deprives the body of oxygen
questions.explanation: Asphyxia is the medical term for suffocation: impaired breathing or oxygen supply that deprives the body of oxygen, for example from choking, low oxygen in the air, or carbon monoxide; it can cause hypoxic brain injury. Labored breathing is dyspnea, rapid shallow breathing is tachypnea, and breathing pauses during sleep are sleep apnea.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding the pharynx?
options: The pharynx is the throat, connecting the back of the mouth and nose to the esophagus and windpipe
Inflammation of the pharynx (pharyngitis) causes sore throat, fever, earache, and swollen glands
Both A and B are correct
The pharynx is only part of the digestive system
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Pharynx = throat connecting mouth/nose to esophagus/windpipe (both digestive and respiratory). Pharyngitis = inflammation with characteristic symptoms. Throat + dual function = pharynx.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes motor nerves?
options: Afferent fibers carrying signals from muscles to the CNS
Efferent fibers carrying signals from the CNS to muscles
Afferent fibers carrying signals from the skin to the CNS
Interneurons relaying signals within the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Motor nerves are efferent: they carry signals away from the central nervous system to skeletal muscles to produce movement. Afferent fibers from muscles or skin are sensory, carrying information toward the CNS, and interneurons connect neurons within the CNS rather than reaching muscles.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding myelofibrosis?
options: Myelofibrosis is buildup of fibrous connective tissue in the bone marrow
It affects the production of blood components (hematopoiesis)
Both A and B are correct
Myelofibrosis only affects the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Myelofibrosis = fibrous replacement of bone marrow, affects hematopoiesis. NOT spinal cord - it's bone marrow. Bone marrow + fibrosis + hematopoiesis = myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding multiple myeloma?
options: Multiple myeloma is a cancer affecting cells in the bone marrow
It involves malignant plasma cells
Both A and B are correct
Multiple myeloma is always benign
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Multiple myeloma = malignant plasma cell cancer in bone marrow. NOT benign - it's cancer. Bone marrow + plasma cells + malignant = multiple myeloma.

questions.stem: Which form of spina bifida is the LEAST severe?
options: Meningocele, a sac of meninges without spinal cord tissue
Myelomeningocele, a sac containing cord and nerve roots
Myeloschisis, an open, flat plate of exposed neural tissue
Occulta, a closed bony defect with no protrusion of contents
questions.explanation: Spina bifida is a birth defect in which part of the spine fails to close completely. Spina bifida occulta is the mildest form: a hidden bony gap with no protrusion, often without symptoms. A meningocele protrudes meninges, a myelomeningocele protrudes cord and nerves and is the most common severe form, and myeloschisis is an open, flat neural plate.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding spondylitis?
options: Spondylitis is inflammation of the joints between the bones of the spine
The '-itis' suffix indicates inflammation
Both A and B are correct
Spondylitis refers to vertebral slipping
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Spondylitis = spinal joint inflammation (suffix '-itis' = inflammation). Spondylolisthesis = vertebra slipping. '-itis' suffix is key indicator of inflammation.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding the lumbar spine?
options: The lumbar spine is the lower part of the spine between the lowest pair of ribs and the pelvis
It is made up of five vertebrae
Both A and B are correct
The lumbar spine has seven vertebrae like the cervical spine
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Lumbar spine = lower back (ribs to pelvis), five vertebrae. Cervical = 7 vertebrae. Thoracic = 12 vertebrae. Sacral = 5 fused. Number varies by region.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding lordosis?
options: Lordosis is the inward curvature of the spine at the lower back
It is normal to a certain degree but abnormal when excessive (due to overweight, muscle problems, etc.)
Both A and B are correct
Lordosis is always abnormal
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Lordosis = inward lumbar curve, normal in degree but abnormal when excessive. Some curvature is normal. Excessive = abnormal. Inward + lumbar + normal vs excessive = lordosis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient presents with resting tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity. Cognition is intact and the EEG is normal. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Alzheimer disease
Huntington disease
Parkinson disease
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
questions.explanation: Resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity with preserved cognition is early Parkinson disease; its pathology is subcortical (substantia nigra), so the EEG is usually normal early. Alzheimer disease begins with memory loss and diffuse slowing; Huntington disease presents in mid-adult life with chorea and psychiatric change; Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease causes rapid dementia, myoclonus and periodic sharp wave complexes.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old patient develops progressive memory loss over several years as the first symptom, followed by language difficulties. EEG shows diffuse slowing. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Alzheimer disease
Frontotemporal dementia
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Parkinson disease
questions.explanation: Alzheimer disease begins with episodic memory loss, later involves language and visuospatial skills, progresses over years, and shows diffuse background slowing as it advances. Frontotemporal dementia usually starts with behavioral or language change and the EEG is often normal; Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease progresses over weeks to months with periodic complexes; Parkinson disease starts with a movement disorder, not memory loss.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old patient presents with involuntary choreiform movements, depression, and progressive dementia. A parent had a similar illness. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Early-onset Alzheimer disease
Huntington disease
Sydenham chorea
Young-onset Parkinson disease
questions.explanation: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant (an affected parent), begins in mid-adult life (about 30-50) and combines chorea, psychiatric symptoms and dementia. Early-onset Alzheimer disease causes memory-led dementia without prominent chorea; Sydenham chorea is a post-streptococcal disorder of childhood without dementia; young-onset Parkinson disease causes tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia rather than chorea.

questions.stem: A patient's cognitive function declines suddenly after a stroke, then plateaus. Six months later, another stroke causes another sudden decline. EEG shows focal slowing. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Dementia with Lewy bodies
Alzheimer disease
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Vascular dementia
questions.explanation: A stepwise decline, with a drop after each stroke followed by a plateau and focal slowing over the infarcted regions, is typical of vascular dementia. Alzheimer disease declines smoothly and gradually; dementia with Lewy bodies fluctuates with hallucinations and parkinsonism; normal pressure hydrocephalus causes gait disturbance, incontinence and dementia without stroke-linked steps.

questions.stem: A patient develops rapidly progressive dementia over 3 months, with myoclonus. EEG shows periodic sharp wave complexes. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Frontotemporal dementia
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Vascular dementia
Alzheimer disease
questions.explanation: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease causes dementia progressing over weeks to months, myoclonus, and periodic sharp wave complexes at about 1 Hz on EEG. Alzheimer disease progresses over years with diffuse slowing; frontotemporal dementia starts with behavior or language change and often has a normal EEG; vascular dementia declines stepwise with focal findings.

questions.stem: A patient presents with fever, headache, and hallucinations. EEG shows diffuse slowing with epileptiform discharges. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Bacterial meningitis
Migraine with aura
Encephalitis
Uremic encephalopathy
questions.explanation: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma, so fever and headache are joined by altered mentation or hallucinations, and the EEG often shows diffuse slowing with or without epileptiform discharges. Meningitis inflames the coverings and less often produces cortical epileptiform activity; migraine with aura lacks fever and a persistently abnormal EEG; uremic encephalopathy causes slowing and triphasic waves without fever and headache as the lead features.

questions.stem: A patient develops rapidly ascending weakness two weeks after a respiratory infection. Reflexes are absent. EEG is normal. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Guillain-Barre syndrome
Myasthenia gravis
Multiple sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barre syndrome is a post-infectious peripheral demyelinating neuropathy with ascending weakness and areflexia; because the cortex is not involved, the EEG is normal. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness with preserved reflexes; multiple sclerosis is a relapsing CNS disorder with brisk reflexes; amyotrophic lateral sclerosis progresses over months with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.

questions.stem: A patient reports progressive loss of peripheral vision and night blindness. Fundoscopy shows bone-spicule pigmentation. Central vision is preserved. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This is consistent with retinitis pigmentosa: peripheral field loss first, night blindness, bone-spicule pigmentation, central vision preserved until late
This is macular degeneration because central vision is always affected first
Peripheral vision loss never occurs in retinal disorders
All retinal disorders affect vision identically
questions.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa: Peripheral field loss FIRST, night blindness (nyctalopia), bone-spicule pigmentation, central vision preserved until late. Macular degeneration = central first. Field affected is key.

questions.stem: A patient reports difficulty reading and recognizing faces, but peripheral vision is intact. Fundoscopy shows drusen deposits. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This is consistent with macular degeneration: central vision loss first, fine detail discrimination affected, drusen deposits, peripheral vision preserved
This is retinitis pigmentosa because peripheral vision is always affected first
Central vision loss never occurs in retinal disorders
All retinal disorders affect the same area of vision
questions.explanation: Macular degeneration: Central vision loss FIRST (reading, faces), drusen deposits, peripheral vision preserved. Retinitis pigmentosa = peripheral first. Central vs peripheral is the key distinction.

questions.stem: A patient reports sudden, painless, severe vision loss in one eye, described as 'a curtain coming down.' Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This is consistent with retinal artery occlusion: acute ischemia, sudden painless vision loss, ophthalmologic emergency
This gradual vision loss is characteristic of cataracts
Sudden vision loss never occurs in retinal disorders
All vision loss is painful
questions.explanation: Retinal artery occlusion: Acute ischemia, sudden painless vision loss ('curtain'), ophthalmologic emergency. Cataracts = gradual. Conjunctivitis = irritation. Sudden + painless = occlusion (emergency).

questions.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis B develops gradual liver function decline over years, with imaging showing architectural distortion and nodular changes. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This progression from hepatitis (inflammation) to cirrhosis (scarring/architectural distortion) is characteristic of chronic liver disease
Hepatitis and cirrhosis are the same condition
Chronic hepatitis never leads to cirrhosis
Liver function always improves with time
questions.explanation: Chronic hepatitis can progress to cirrhosis: inflammation → chronic scarring → architectural distortion. Hepatitis = inflammation. Cirrhosis = end-stage scarring. Progression is possible but they are distinct stages.

questions.stem: A patient with liver disease develops yellowing of the skin and eyes, followed by confusion and altered mental status. Which explanation is MOST likely?
options: Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine loss
Uremic encephalopathy from kidney failure
Hypoglycemic encephalopathy from low glucose
Hepatic encephalopathy from liver failure
questions.explanation: Jaundice reflects bilirubin excess from liver failure, and the confusion that follows is hepatic encephalopathy (toxins such as ammonia that the failing liver cannot clear); EEG may show diffuse slowing and triphasic waves. Wernicke encephalopathy follows thiamine deficiency with ataxia and eye signs; uremic encephalopathy follows kidney failure; hypoglycemia is not explained by the jaundice.

questions.stem: A patient with airway obstruction shows improvement with bronchodilator treatment. Spirometry shows reversible airflow limitation. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This reversible obstruction is characteristic of asthma, where bronchodilators improve airflow
This is COPD because all airway obstruction is irreversible
Reversibility never occurs in airway disease
All airway disorders respond identically to treatment
questions.explanation: Asthma: Reversible airway obstruction, bronchodilators improve airflow. COPD = chronic irreversible obstruction. Reversibility is the CRITICAL discriminator. Reversible = asthma.

questions.stem: A bed partner reports that the patient stops breathing during sleep, sometimes for 30 seconds or longer. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Sleep paralysis
Sleep apnea
Narcolepsy with cataplexy
Sleep-related hypoventilation
questions.explanation: Sleep apnea is cessation of airflow during sleep (at least 10 seconds per event), and long pauses can cause marked desaturation. Sleep-related hypoventilation is reduced, not absent, ventilation with rising CO2; sleep paralysis is inability to move at sleep-wake transitions with normal breathing; narcolepsy with cataplexy causes sleep attacks and emotion-triggered loss of tone.

questions.stem: A patient presents with muscle pain and weakness. Laboratory tests show elevated inflammatory markers. Muscle biopsy shows inflammation. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This is consistent with myositis: muscle inflammation causing pain and weakness, indicated by elevated inflammatory markers and biopsy findings
This is myopathy because all muscle diseases involve inflammation
Muscle inflammation never causes symptoms
All muscle disorders are identical
questions.explanation: Myositis: Muscle inflammation, pain + weakness, elevated inflammatory markers, biopsy shows inflammation. Myopathy = general muscle disease (may or may not be inflammatory). Inflammation + muscle = myositis.

questions.stem: A patient presents with episodes of numbness, vision problems, and weakness that improve and then recur. MRI shows demyelinating lesions in the brain and spinal cord. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Myasthenia gravis
Guillain-Barre syndrome
Multiple sclerosis
Recurrent transient ischemia
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis causes relapsing-remitting episodes from demyelinating lesions in the CNS (brain and spinal cord). Guillain-Barre syndrome is peripheral demyelination with a single ascending course; myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction disorder without MRI lesions; transient ischemic attacks resolve within hours and do not produce demyelinating plaques.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of lower back pain and a vertebral defect (spondylolysis) develops worsening symptoms. Imaging shows a vertebra has slipped forward over the one below. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This progression from spondylolysis (vertebral defect) to spondylolisthesis (vertebra slipping) can occur
Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis are unrelated
Vertebra slipping never occurs
All spinal conditions are identical
questions.explanation: Spondylolisthesis can result from spondylolysis: Vertebral defect (spondylolysis) can progress to vertebra slipping (spondylolisthesis). Defect → slipping is possible progression. Related but distinct conditions.

questions.stem: A patient's spine shows a curve to one side in the thoracic region, with a compensating curve in the opposite direction in the lumbar region, producing an S-shape. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This S-shaped curve with compensation is characteristic of scoliosis
This is kyphosis because all spinal curves are outward
Side-to-side curves never occur
All spinal deformities are identical
questions.explanation: Scoliosis: Side-to-side curve (S-shaped), often with compensating curves. Kyphosis = outward thoracic curve. Lordosis = inward lumbar curve. Direction (side-to-side) is key. S-shape = scoliosis.

questions.stem: A patient requires analysis of cerebrospinal fluid and injection of medication into the spinal canal. A needle is inserted into the lower lumbar region. Which procedure is being performed?
options: Cisternal puncture
Laminectomy
Epidural steroid injection
Lumbar puncture
questions.explanation: A lumbar puncture (spinal tap) places a needle into the lumbar subarachnoid space to sample CSF or give intrathecal medication. A cisternal puncture enters at the suboccipital level, not the lumbar region; a laminectomy is open surgery with bone removal; an epidural steroid injection stays outside the dura and does not obtain CSF.

questions.stem: A patient reports hearing voices when no one is present and seeing objects that others cannot see. Which term BEST describes these experiences?
options: Delusions
Illusions
Hallucinations
Depersonalization
questions.explanation: Hallucinations are sensory perceptions without an external stimulus, and they can involve any modality, such as hearing or vision. Delusions are fixed false beliefs, not perceptions; illusions are misinterpretations of a real stimulus; depersonalization is a sense of detachment from oneself.

questions.stem: A patient develops sudden onset of symptoms that resolve within 2 weeks. Which term BEST describes this course?
options: A chronic condition
A relapsing condition
A progressive condition
An acute condition
questions.explanation: An acute condition has sudden onset and short duration. A chronic condition persists over months to years; a relapsing condition repeatedly returns after remission; a progressive condition worsens steadily rather than resolving.

questions.stem: A patient with respiratory distress shows bluish discoloration of the lips and fingertips. Pulse oximetry shows low oxygen saturation. Which term BEST describes this sign?
options: Cyanosis
Jaundice
Pallor
Erythema
questions.explanation: Cyanosis is bluish discoloration of skin and mucosa from low oxygen saturation, and during a recording it signals the need for immediate attention. Jaundice is yellowing from bilirubin; pallor is paleness from reduced blood flow or anemia; erythema is redness from increased blood flow.

questions.stem: A patient has hearing loss affecting both ears. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This affects both sides, which is described as bilateral
This affects one side, which is described as unilateral
Bilateral means affecting only one side
All conditions affect the same number of sides
questions.explanation: Bilateral: Affecting both sides or paired organs. Unilateral = one side. Ipsilateral = same side. Contralateral = opposite side. Number of sides affected is key. Both sides = bilateral.

questions.stem: A patient with prolonged immobility shows muscle shrinkage and weakness. Imaging confirms decreased muscle mass. Which term BEST describes this change?
options: Muscle hypertrophy
Muscle atrophy
Muscle hyperplasia
Muscle necrosis
questions.explanation: Atrophy is the shrinkage of a tissue or organ, and disuse from immobility is a common cause. Hypertrophy is increase in cell size; hyperplasia is increase in cell number; necrosis is cell death from injury, not the gradual loss of mass seen with disuse.

questions.stem: A patient has a localized collection of pus in soft tissue, surrounded by inflamed tissue. Culture shows bacterial infection. Which term BEST describes this lesion?
options: Cellulitis
Empyema
Granuloma
Abscess
questions.explanation: An abscess is a localized collection of pus within tissue, usually from bacterial infection. Cellulitis is diffuse spreading inflammation without a pus pocket; empyema is pus within a body cavity such as the pleural space; a granuloma is a nodule of chronic inflammatory cells, not pus.

questions.stem: A flexible hollow tube is inserted into a blood vessel to administer medication and monitor pressure. Which device is this?
options: Stent graft
Catheter
Shunt
Surgical drain
questions.explanation: A catheter is a flexible hollow tube inserted into the body to deliver or remove fluid or to measure pressure. A stent graft is left in place to hold a vessel open; a shunt diverts flow from one compartment to another; a surgical drain removes fluid from a wound or cavity, not a vessel.

questions.stem: A patient's blood test shows elevated levels of a waste product from muscle metabolism. This substance is filtered by the kidneys and excreted in urine. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This is creatinine: a waste product filtered from blood by kidneys and expelled in urine
This is bilirubin because all waste products are from the liver
Kidneys never filter waste products
All waste products are identical
questions.explanation: Creatinine: Muscle metabolism waste, filtered by kidneys, excreted in urine. Bilirubin = liver waste. Urea = also kidney waste. Source (muscle) is key. Muscle waste + kidney filtered = creatinine.

questions.stem: A cancer is found confined to its original location with no evidence of spread to other tissues. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This is described as 'in situ': meaning 'in place,' used for cancer that has not spread
This is metastatic because all cancers spread immediately
Localized cancer never occurs
All cancers are identical in staging
questions.explanation: In situ: Cancer confined to original location, has not spread (invaded or metastasized). Metastatic = spread. Invasive = penetrated tissue. Localization is key. Localized + no spread = in situ.

questions.stem: A tissue that stores energy, insulates the body, and provides cushioning is examined. Histology shows fat cells. Which statement is MOST likely true?
options: This is adipose tissue: fatty tissue that stores energy, insulates, and cushions the body
This is muscle tissue because all tissues store energy
Fat tissue never has functions
All tissues are identical
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue: Fat tissue with energy storage, insulation, cushioning functions. Muscle = contractile. Connective = structural. Epithelial = lining. Function is key. Fat + storage/insulation = adipose.

questions.stem: A patient reports persistent difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep, leading to daytime fatigue. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
options: Narcolepsy type 1
Idiopathic hypersomnia
Chronic insomnia
Obstructive sleep apnea
questions.explanation: Insomnia is persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, with daytime consequences. Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness and sleep attacks; idiopathic hypersomnia causes long, unrefreshing sleep rather than difficulty falling asleep; obstructive sleep apnea causes breathing pauses and sleepiness, not primary difficulty initiating sleep.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding tumor vs cancer vs neoplasm?
options: Tumor and neoplasm are terms for an abnormal mass that can be benign or malignant
Cancer refers specifically to malignant tumors that can spread and destroy tissue
Both A and B are correct
Tumor, cancer, and neoplasm all mean exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Tumor/neoplasm = abnormal mass (benign OR malignant). Cancer = malignant only (spreads, destroys). Tumor is broader term. Benign vs malignant is the key distinction.

questions.stem: A tumor that is not cancerous, meaning it does not spread through the body but may grow and become dangerous, is termed:
options: Benign tumor
Malignant tumor
Metastasis
Carcinoma
Sarcoma
questions.explanation: Benign tumor: Non-cancerous, does NOT spread (metastasize), but may grow and cause problems by compression. Malignant = spreads. Metastasis = spread process. Benign = no spread.

questions.stem: The spreading of a cancerous tumor to another part of the body through lymph, blood, or across a cavity is termed:
options: Metastasis
Neoplasm
Benign growth
Primary tumor
Carcinoma in situ
questions.explanation: Metastasis: Spread of cancer to distant sites via lymph, blood, or direct extension. Neoplasm = any tumor. Benign = no spread. Primary = original location. In situ = localized. Spread = metastasis.

questions.stem: A group of bone marrow cancers in which white blood cells divide uncontrollably, affecting the production of normal white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets, is termed:
options: Leukemia
Lymphoma
Sarcoma
Carcinoma
Myeloma
questions.explanation: Leukemia: Bone marrow cancer, uncontrolled white blood cell division, affects all blood cell production. Lymphoma = lymph tissue. Sarcoma = connective tissue. Carcinoma = epithelium. Bone marrow + blood cells = leukemia.

questions.stem: A group of cancers of the lymph nodes and spleen that spread to other parts of the body, causing lymph node enlargement and symptoms like fever, weight loss, and loss of appetite, is termed:
options: Lymphoma (Hodgkin or Non-Hodgkin)
Leukemia
Sarcoma
Carcinoma
Myeloma
questions.explanation: Lymphoma: Cancer of lymphoid tissue (lymph nodes, spleen), spreads to other parts, causes lymph node enlargement, B symptoms (fever, weight loss). Hodgkin vs Non-Hodgkin are subtypes. Lymph tissue = lymphoma.

questions.stem: A cancer in connective tissue, fibrous tissue, or blood vessels is termed:
options: Sarcoma
Carcinoma
Leukemia
Lymphoma
Glioma
questions.explanation: Sarcoma: Cancer of connective tissue, fibrous tissue, or blood vessels. Carcinoma = epithelium. Leukemia = bone marrow. Lymphoma = lymph tissue. Glioma = glial cells. Connective tissue = sarcoma.

questions.stem: A cancer that grows on the surface or lining of an organ is termed:
options: Carcinoma
Sarcoma
Leukemia
Lymphoma
Glioma
questions.explanation: Carcinoma: Cancer of epithelium (surface/lining of organs). Sarcoma = connective tissue. Leukemia = bone marrow. Lymphoma = lymph tissue. Glioma = glial cells. Epithelium/lining = carcinoma.

questions.stem: A brain tumor arising from cells that support nerve cells (glial cells), often fast-growing and cancerous, is termed:
options: Medulloblastoma
Meningioma
Neuroblastoma
Glioma
questions.explanation: Gliomas arise from glial (supporting) cells; the most aggressive form is glioblastoma multiforme, a fast-growing malignant tumor that often produces focal slowing on EEG. Medulloblastoma is a cerebellar tumor of childhood; meningioma arises from the meninges and is usually benign; neuroblastoma arises in the adrenal glands or sympathetic chain.

questions.stem: A type of cancerous tumor occurring in the section of the brain that controls posture and balance (cerebellum), found mainly in children, is termed:
options: Medulloblastoma
Glioma
Meningioma
Ependymoma
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of the cerebellum, the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood. Glioma refers to tumors of glial cells, most aggressive (glioblastoma) in adult cerebral hemispheres; meningioma arises from the meninges and is usually benign in adults; ependymoma arises from ependymal cells lining the ventricles and, although it can occur in the fourth ventricle in children, it is not the classic malignant cerebellar tumor.

questions.stem: A cancerous childhood tumor located in the adrenal glands or the sympathetic nervous system is termed:
options: Neuroblastoma
Medulloblastoma
Retinoblastoma
Glioblastoma
Lymphoma
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma: Childhood cancer, adrenal glands or sympathetic nervous system. Medulloblastoma = cerebellum. Retinoblastoma = retina. Glioblastoma = cerebrum. Lymphoma = lymph tissue. Adrenal/sympathetic + children = neuroblastoma.

questions.stem: A hereditary cancerous tumor of the retina affecting infants and children is termed:
options: Retinoblastoma
Neuroblastoma
Medulloblastoma
Glioblastoma
Melanoma
questions.explanation: Retinoblastoma: Hereditary retinal cancer, infants/children. Neuroblastoma = adrenal. Medulloblastoma = cerebellum. Glioblastoma = cerebrum. Melanoma = skin. Retina + hereditary + children = retinoblastoma.

questions.stem: The most serious type of skin cancer, in which a mole changes shape, darkens, becomes painful and/or bleeds easily, composed of cells called melanocytes, is termed:
options: Malignant Melanoma or Melanoma
Basal cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma
Sarcoma
Carcinoma
questions.explanation: Malignant Melanoma: Most serious skin cancer, from melanocytes, mole changes, can metastasize. Basal cell = less aggressive. Squamous cell = moderate. Melanocytes = melanoma.

questions.stem: A type of cancer caused by exposure to large amounts of sunlight, commonly found on the neck, face, and arms, is:
options: Basal Cell Carcinoma
Malignant Melanoma
Squamous cell carcinoma
Sarcoma
Lymphoma
questions.explanation: Basal Cell Carcinoma: Sun exposure-related skin cancer, common on sun-exposed areas (face, neck, arms), less aggressive than melanoma. Melanoma = more serious. Sun exposure + common locations = basal cell.

questions.stem: A cancerous tumor occurring in the lining of the lungs and chest cavity, often associated with exposure to asbestos dust, is termed:
options: Mesothelioma
Lung carcinoma
Sarcoma
Lymphoma
Pleural effusion
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma: Cancer of lung/chest cavity lining (pleura), asbestos exposure association. Lung carcinoma = lung tissue itself. Sarcoma = connective tissue. Asbestos + lining = mesothelioma.

questions.stem: A cancer of lymph tissue that most frequently occurs in the abdomen, ovaries, and bones of the face, associated with malaria and Epstein-Barr virus, is termed:
options: Burkitt's Lymphoma
Hodgkin's Lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma (general)
Leukemia
Multiple myeloma
questions.explanation: Burkitt's Lymphoma: Lymph tissue cancer, abdomen/ovaries/facial bones, associated with malaria and EBV. Hodgkin = different subtype. Non-Hodgkin = broader category. Malaria + EBV + locations = Burkitt's.

questions.stem: A non-cancerous tumor of the pituitary gland is termed:
options: Pituitary adenoma
Pituitary carcinoma
Glioblastoma
Meningioma
Craniopharyngioma
questions.explanation: Pituitary adenoma: Benign pituitary tumor. Pituitary carcinoma = malignant (rare). Glioblastoma = cerebrum. Meningioma = meninges. Craniopharyngioma = different pituitary region. Pituitary + benign = adenoma.

questions.stem: A condition in which connective tissue tumors occur on nerves in the skin, also called Von Recklinghausen's disease, is termed:
options: Neurofibroma
Tuberous sclerosis
Neurofibromatosis
Neurilemmoma
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease) is a neurocutaneous disorder with multiple neurofibromas on skin nerves and cafe-au-lait spots. A single neurofibroma is one tumor, not the syndrome; tuberous sclerosis is a different neurocutaneous disorder with tubers and epilepsy; a neurilemmoma (schwannoma) is a single nerve-sheath tumor.

questions.stem: A term describing a condition from which cancer is likely to develop is:
options: Pre-cancerous
Benign
Malignant
Metastatic
In situ
questions.explanation: Pre-cancerous: Condition with increased cancer risk (e.g., dysplasia, certain polyps). Benign = non-cancerous. Malignant = cancerous. Metastatic = spread. In situ = localized cancer. Increased risk = pre-cancerous.

questions.stem: A disorder that causes excessive sleepiness during the day and frequent, uncontrollable episodes of falling asleep, with onset of sleep directly into REM sleep, is termed:
options: Insomnia
Narcolepsy
Sleep apnea
Idiopathic hypersomnia
questions.explanation: Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep attacks, and sleep-onset REM periods. Insomnia is difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep; sleep apnea causes sleepiness through breathing pauses without sleep-onset REM; idiopathic hypersomnia causes long, unrefreshing sleep without sleep-onset REM periods.

questions.stem: A disorder caused partly or completely by a defect in the patient's genes which carry hereditary information is termed:
options: Acquired disorder
Genetic disorder
Congenital disorder
Autoimmune disorder
questions.explanation: A genetic disorder is caused partly or completely by a defect in the genes that carry hereditary information. An acquired disorder arises after birth from external causes; a congenital disorder is present at birth but may not be genetic; an autoimmune disorder results from the immune system attacking the body.

questions.stem: A fatal neural tube defect in which the cranial end of the neural tube fails to close, resulting in the absence of a major portion of the skull and brain, is termed:
options: Microcephaly
Hydranencephaly
Anencephaly
Encephalocele
questions.explanation: Anencephaly results from failure of the cranial (rostral) neural tube to close, leaving a major portion of the skull and brain absent; the spinal cord is usually present (failure along the whole neural axis is craniorachischisis). Microcephaly is a small head with a present brain; hydranencephaly has an intact skull with the cerebral hemispheres replaced by CSF; encephalocele is protrusion of brain through a skull defect.

questions.stem: A birth defect in which the patient has a very small head is termed:
options: Anencephaly
Hydrocephalus
Microcephaly
Macrocephaly
questions.explanation: Microcephaly is an abnormally small head (birth defect). Anencephaly is absence of much of the brain and skull vault; hydrocephalus is excess CSF that typically enlarges the head; macrocephaly is an abnormally large head.

questions.stem: General term for problems in the development of the spinal cord and brain in an embryo, such as failure of the spine to enclose the spinal cord (spina bifida) and failure of the brain to develop (anencephaly), is:
options: Chromosomal abnormalities
Neural tube defects
Teratogenic effects
Genetic mutations
questions.explanation: Neural tube defects are embryologic failures of brain/spinal cord development, such as spina bifida and anencephaly.
