Chromosomal abnormalities involve whole-chromosome errors (e.g., trisomy); teratogenic effects are malformations caused by drugs or toxins; genetic mutations are changes in individual genes.

questions.stem: A rare disorder mainly affecting those under age 15, characterized by brain and liver damage following a viral infection such as chickenpox or flu, and may be linked to taking aspirin, is termed:
options: Guillain-Barré syndrome
Encephalitis
Meningitis
Reye's syndrome
questions.explanation: Reye's syndrome affects mainly children under 15, causing brain and liver damage after a viral illness such as chickenpox or influenza, and is linked to aspirin use. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a post-infectious peripheral nerve disorder; encephalitis and meningitis are inflammation of the brain and meninges without the characteristic liver injury or aspirin link.

questions.stem: A severe headache usually accompanied by vision problems and/or nausea and vomiting, typically recurring, is termed:
options: Migraine headache
Tension headache
Cluster headache
Sinus headache
questions.explanation: Migraine is a recurrent severe headache often accompanied by visual aura, nausea, and vomiting. Tension headache is a band-like pressure usually without nausea; cluster headache is brief, severe orbital pain in clusters; sinus headache is facial pressure with sinus congestion.

questions.stem: A temporary paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors after prolonged pressure on a nerve in the upper arm (e.g., an arm draped over a chair during deep sleep) is termed:
options: Tardy ulnar nerve palsy
Saturday night palsy
Erb-Duchenne palsy
Bell's palsy
questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy is compression of the radial nerve, usually at the spiral groove of the humerus, causing temporary wrist drop. Tardy ulnar palsy is a slowly developing ulnar neuropathy at the elbow; Erb-Duchenne palsy is an upper brachial plexus birth injury; Bell's palsy is facial nerve weakness. Axillary compression of the radial nerve is usually called crutch palsy.

questions.stem: A disease of the nerve roots caused by disk prolapse, arthritis, or other problems is termed:
options: Myelopathy
Peripheral neuropathy
Radiculopathy
Myelitis
questions.explanation: Radiculopathy is disease of the nerve roots, commonly from disk prolapse or arthritic spurs. Myelopathy is disease of the spinal cord; peripheral neuropathy involves distal peripheral nerves; myelitis is inflammation of the spinal cord.

questions.stem: A nerve running down the arm to the hand that controls muscle movement in the forearm and hand, also conveying sensation to part of the hand, thumb, and index finger, is:
options: Ulnar nerve
Radial nerve
Musculocutaneous nerve
Median nerve
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies most forearm flexors and thenar muscles and carries sensation from the palmar thumb, index, and middle fingers. The ulnar nerve serves the little and ring fingers; the radial nerve serves the extensors and dorsal hand; the musculocutaneous nerve supplies elbow flexors and lateral forearm skin.

questions.stem: A protrusion of the meninges alone (without neural tissue) through a defect in the skull or spinal column is termed:
options: Meningocele
Myelomeningocele
Encephalocele
Myelocele
questions.explanation: A meningocele is a sac of meninges and CSF protruding through a bony defect without neural tissue. A myelomeningocele also contains spinal cord/roots; an encephalocele contains brain tissue; a myelocele is an open, exposed cord without a meningeal sac. These neural tube defects are multifactorial, not purely genetic.

questions.stem: Surgical removal of just the protruding part of a prolapsed disk is termed:
options: Microdiskectomy or microdiscectomy
Laminectomy
Spinal fusion
Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
Diskectomy
questions.explanation: Microdiskectomy: Removal of only the protruding portion of herniated disk (minimally invasive). Laminectomy = bone removal. Spinal fusion = bone joining. ACDF = cervical procedure. Full diskectomy = entire disk. 'Micro' = partial removal.

questions.stem: A term used to describe a disease, disorder, or medical condition that is the direct result of medical treatment is:
options: Idiopathic
Iatrogenic
Nosocomial
Cryptogenic
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic describes a condition caused by medical treatment or care. Idiopathic means no known cause; nosocomial refers specifically to an infection acquired in a healthcare facility; cryptogenic means a cause is presumed but hidden or not identified.

questions.stem: A term used to describe something that occurs with no known cause is:
options: Iatrogenic
Symptomatic
Idiopathic
Acquired
questions.explanation: Idiopathic means arising with no known cause. Iatrogenic means caused by medical treatment; symptomatic means due to an identified underlying lesion or disease; acquired means developed after birth rather than inherited, which says nothing about whether the cause is known.

questions.stem: An abnormal swelling of the wall of an artery caused by weakening in the vessel wall is termed:
options: Stenosis
Infarction
Embolism
Aneurysm
questions.explanation: An aneurysm is an abnormal bulging of an artery wall caused by weakness in the wall. Stenosis is narrowing of a vessel; infarction is tissue death from lost blood supply; embolism is blockage by material carried in the bloodstream.

questions.stem: A condition in which the fingers and toes become pale when exposed to cold or emotional stress, due to sudden narrowing of the arteries that supply them with blood, is termed:
options: Raynaud's Disease
Pericarditis
Narcolepsy
Radiculopathy
Nephritis
questions.explanation: Raynaud's Disease: Vasospastic disorder, fingers/toes turn pale (white→blue→red) from cold/emotional stress, artery narrowing. Pericarditis = heart sac inflammation. Narcolepsy = sleep disorder. Radiculopathy = nerve root. Nephritis = kidney. Cold + fingers white = Raynaud's.

questions.stem: Determination of the amount of oxygen in the blood by measuring the amount of light transmitted through an area of skin is termed:
options: Pulse oximetry
Capnography
Spirometry
Plethysmography
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry estimates blood oxygen saturation from red/infrared light transmitted through the skin (e.g., a fingertip). Capnography measures exhaled CO2; spirometry measures lung volumes and airflow; plethysmography measures volume changes and does not by itself quantify oxygen content.

questions.stem: Infection by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) which causes weakening of the immune system is termed:
options: Severe combined immunodeficiency
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Chronic fatigue syndrome
questions.explanation: AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) results from HIV infection that progressively weakens the immune system. Severe combined immunodeficiency is an inherited immune defect; lupus is an autoimmune disease; chronic fatigue syndrome is not an immunodeficiency caused by a virus such as HIV.

questions.stem: Nerves involved in smell are:
options: Abducens
Trochlear
Olfactory
Trigeminal
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) carries the sense of smell. The abducens (CN VI) and trochlear (CN IV) nerves move the eye; the trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries general facial sensation, including the nasal lining, but not smell.

questions.stem: The feeling that one or one's surroundings are spinning is termed:
options: Dizziness
Syncope
Ataxia
Vertigo
questions.explanation: Vertigo is the illusion that oneself or the surroundings are spinning, usually from vestibular dysfunction. Dizziness is a broader, nonspecific term; syncope is a transient loss of consciousness; ataxia is loss of coordination.

questions.stem: A life-threatening allergic reaction resulting in difficulty breathing and low blood pressure is termed:
options: Septic shock
Anaphylactic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Hypovolemic shock
questions.explanation: Anaphylactic shock is a life-threatening allergic reaction with airway compromise and low blood pressure. Septic shock follows overwhelming infection; cardiogenic shock results from pump failure; hypovolemic shock results from blood or fluid loss. None of the others is allergic in origin.

questions.stem: Informed consent is an agreement to undergo a medical procedure after the technique, its risks, and its possible complications have been explained. This statement is:
options: True
False
Partially correct
Only applies to surgery
questions.explanation: True: Informed consent requires explanation of procedure, risks, and complications before agreement. This applies to all medical procedures, not just surgery. Procedure + risks explained = informed consent.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding tumor classification by cell of origin?
options: Carcinoma arises from epithelium (surface/lining of organs); sarcoma arises from connective tissue
Leukemia arises from bone marrow; lymphoma arises from lymph tissue
Both A and B are correct
All tumors arise from the same cell type
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Carcinoma = epithelium. Sarcoma = connective tissue. Leukemia = bone marrow. Lymphoma = lymph tissue. Cell of origin determines tumor type. This classification system is critical for understanding tumors.

questions.stem: Which statement about brain tumors is correct?
options: Medulloblastoma is a cerebellar tumor mainly of children; glioblastoma is a cerebral tumor mainly of adults
Medulloblastoma is a cerebral tumor mainly of adults; glioblastoma is a cerebellar tumor mainly of children
Medulloblastoma is a cerebellar tumor mainly of adults; glioblastoma is a cerebral tumor mainly of children
Medulloblastoma is a spinal cord tumor mainly of children; glioblastoma is a meningeal tumor mainly of adults
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a posterior fossa (cerebellar) tumor seen mainly in children; glioblastoma is a high-grade glial tumor of the cerebral hemispheres seen mainly in adults, and can produce focal slowing on EEG. The swapped options reverse the site or age pairing; medulloblastoma is not a spinal cord tumor and glioblastoma arises from glial cells, not the meninges (that is meningioma).

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding benign vs malignant tumors?
options: Benign tumors do not spread (metastasize); malignant tumors can spread and destroy tissue
Benign tumors may still grow and become dangerous by compression; malignant tumors spread and invade
Both A and B are correct
Benign and malignant tumors behave identically
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Benign = no spread, but may compress. Malignant = spreads, invades, destroys. Spread capability is the key distinction. No spread = benign. Spreads = malignant.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding Burkitt's lymphoma?
options: Burkitt's lymphoma is associated with malaria and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
It frequently occurs in abdomen, ovaries, and bones of the face
Both A and B are correct
Burkitt's lymphoma has no known associations
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Burkitt's lymphoma = malaria + EBV association, abdomen/ovaries/facial bones. These associations are HIGH-YIELD exam material. Malaria + EBV + locations = Burkitt's.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding mesothelioma?
options: Mesothelioma is cancer of the lining of the lungs and chest cavity
It is often associated with exposure to asbestos dust
Both A and B are correct
Mesothelioma has no known risk factors
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Mesothelioma = lung/chest cavity lining cancer, asbestos exposure association. This is a HIGH-YIELD occupational exposure association. Asbestos + lining = mesothelioma.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding retinoblastoma?
options: Retinoblastoma is a hereditary cancerous tumor of the retina
It affects infants and children
Both A and B are correct
Retinoblastoma only affects adults
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Retinoblastoma = hereditary retinal cancer, infants/children. NOT adult condition. Hereditary + retina + children = retinoblastoma.

questions.stem: Which statement about neurofibromatosis is correct?
options: It is also known as Sturge-Weber syndrome
It is also known as tuberous sclerosis complex
It is also known as von Hippel-Lindau disease
It is also known as von Recklinghausen's disease
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is also called von Recklinghausen's disease; it causes nerve-sheath tumors (neurofibromas) in the skin and can affect many systems. Sturge-Weber syndrome, tuberous sclerosis complex, and von Hippel-Lindau disease are other neurocutaneous disorders with different lesions.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding Raynaud's disease?
options: Raynaud's disease causes fingers and toes to become pale when exposed to cold or emotional stress
It is due to sudden narrowing of arteries supplying the digits
Both A and B are correct
Raynaud's disease only affects the heart
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Raynaud's = vasospastic disorder, fingers/toes pale from cold/stress, artery narrowing. NOT heart disease - it's peripheral vascular. Cold + digits pale = Raynaud's.

questions.stem: Which statement about vertigo is correct?
options: It is an illusion of spinning, often from an inner ear disorder
It is a brief loss of consciousness from reduced cerebral flow
It is a lightheaded, faint feeling without any sense of motion
It is a loss of coordination caused mainly by cerebellar disease
questions.explanation: Vertigo is the sensation that oneself or the surroundings are spinning, a vestibular symptom often due to inner ear disorders. A brief loss of consciousness is syncope; a lightheaded faint feeling is presyncope (part of the broader term dizziness); incoordination from cerebellar disease is ataxia.

questions.stem: Which statement about migraine is correct?
options: Attacks are brief, orbital, and occur in nightly clusters
Attacks are a band-like pressure without nausea or vision change
Attacks recur and often bring visual symptoms or nausea
Attacks are triggered by chewing and cause electric facial pain
questions.explanation: Migraine is a recurrent severe headache often accompanied by visual aura and/or nausea and vomiting. Brief orbital attacks in clusters describe cluster headache; band-like pressure without nausea describes tension headache; electric facial pain triggered by chewing describes trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.stem: Which statement about Reye's syndrome is correct?
options: It causes ascending paralysis in children after a viral illness
It causes brain and liver damage in children after a viral illness
It causes kidney and brain damage in children after strep infection
It causes brain and liver damage in adults after acetaminophen use
questions.explanation: Reye's syndrome mainly affects those under age 15, causing encephalopathy and liver damage after a viral illness such as chickenpox or influenza; it is linked to aspirin use. Ascending paralysis describes Guillain-Barré syndrome; kidney injury after strep is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; acetaminophen overdose causes liver failure but is not Reye's syndrome.

questions.stem: Which statement about neural tube defects is correct?
options: Down syndrome and fragile X are both examples
Cerebral palsy and hydrocephalus are both examples
Lissencephaly and schizencephaly are both examples
Spina bifida and anencephaly are both examples
questions.explanation: Neural tube defects are failures of embryonic brain and spinal cord development, such as spina bifida (spine fails to enclose the cord) and anencephaly (brain fails to develop). Down syndrome and fragile X are genetic/chromosomal disorders; cerebral palsy is an acquired early brain injury syndrome; lissencephaly and schizencephaly are neuronal migration disorders.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes anencephaly from microcephaly?
options: Anencephaly is a small head; microcephaly lacks most brain and skull
Anencephaly lacks most brain and skull; microcephaly is a small head
Anencephaly has excess CSF in the head; microcephaly is a small head
Anencephaly is survivable; microcephaly is fatal within days of birth
questions.explanation: Anencephaly is absence of much of the brain and skull vault and is fatal; microcephaly is an abnormally small head that may be compatible with life. The swapped option reverses them; excess CSF describes hydrocephalus; anencephaly, not microcephaly, is the fatal condition.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes radiculopathy from myelopathy?
options: Radiculopathy affects the spinal cord; myelopathy affects nerve roots
Radiculopathy affects nerve roots; myelopathy affects muscle fibers
Radiculopathy affects nerve roots; myelopathy affects the spinal cord
Radiculopathy affects distal nerves; myelopathy affects the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Radiculopathy is disease of the nerve roots (often from disk prolapse); myelopathy is disease of the spinal cord. The swapped option reverses them; muscle fiber disease is myopathy; disease of distal nerves is peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: Which statement about the olfactory nerve is correct?
options: It is cranial nerve I and carries the sense of smell
It is cranial nerve II and carries the sense of smell
It is cranial nerve I and carries the sense of taste
It is cranial nerve I and is a mixed motor-sensory nerve
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve is cranial nerve I, a purely special sensory nerve for smell. Cranial nerve II is the optic nerve; taste is carried by CN VII, IX, and X; the olfactory nerve has no motor component.

questions.stem: Which statement about anaphylactic shock is correct?
options: It is an allergic reaction with hypertension and a slow heart rate
It is an allergic reaction with airway compromise and hypotension
It is a delayed skin reaction appearing days after exposure
It is a drop in blood pressure caused by blood or fluid loss
questions.explanation: Anaphylactic shock is a life-threatening allergic reaction causing difficulty breathing and low blood pressure, requiring immediate treatment. It causes hypotension and usually tachycardia, not hypertension; a delayed skin reaction days later is delayed hypersensitivity; blood or fluid loss causes hypovolemic shock.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes iatrogenic from idiopathic?
options: Iatrogenic: no known cause; idiopathic: caused by medical care
Iatrogenic: present at birth; idiopathic: with no known cause
Iatrogenic: caused by medical care; idiopathic: genetic cause
Iatrogenic: caused by medical care; idiopathic: no known cause
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic means caused by medical treatment ('iatro-' = physician); idiopathic means arising with no known cause. The swapped option reverses them; 'present at birth' defines congenital; a genetic cause is a known cause, so it is not idiopathic.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes aneurysm from stenosis?
options: Aneurysm is a bulge of a weak artery wall; stenosis is narrowing
Aneurysm is narrowing of an artery; stenosis is a wall bulge
Aneurysm is a clot blocking an artery; stenosis is narrowing
Aneurysm is a bulge of a weak artery wall; stenosis is a tear
questions.explanation: An aneurysm is a ballooning of an artery wall due to weakness; stenosis is narrowing of the vessel lumen. The swapped option reverses them; a clot blocking an artery is thrombosis; a tear in the vessel wall is a dissection.

questions.stem: Which statement about oximetry is correct?
options: It measures blood oxygen directly from an arterial blood sample
It estimates exhaled carbon dioxide from infrared absorption
It estimates blood oxygen from light passed through the skin
It measures airflow at the nose using a temperature sensor
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry non-invasively estimates blood oxygen saturation from light transmitted through the skin. Direct measurement from an arterial sample is blood gas analysis; exhaled CO2 by infrared absorption is capnography; nasal airflow by temperature change is measured with a thermistor or thermocouple.

questions.stem: Which statement about AIDS is correct?
options: It is an inherited defect that weakens the immune system
It is caused by EBV infection that weakens the immune system
It is caused by the immune system attacking the body's tissues
It is caused by HIV infection that weakens the immune system
questions.explanation: AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is caused by HIV infection, which progressively weakens the immune system. It is acquired, not inherited (inherited defects include SCID); EBV causes mononucleosis, not AIDS; the immune system attacking the body's own tissues describes autoimmune disease.

questions.stem: A group of diseases in which cells grow unrestrained in an organ or tissue, that can spread to tissues around it and destroy them or be transported through blood or lymph pathways to other parts of the body, is termed:
options: Cancer
Benign tumor
Neoplasm
Metastasis
Pre-cancerous condition
questions.explanation: Cancer: Uncontrolled cell growth that can spread (metastasize) and destroy tissue. Benign tumor = no spread. Neoplasm = any tumor. Metastasis = spread process. Pre-cancerous = increased risk. Uncontrolled growth + spread = cancer.

questions.stem: Another term for tumor is:
options: Neoplasm
Cancer
Metastasis
Carcinoma
Malignancy
questions.explanation: Neoplasm: Another term for tumor (abnormal mass, benign or malignant). Cancer = malignant only. Metastasis = spread. Carcinoma = specific type. Malignancy = cancerous. Tumor = neoplasm (synonyms).

questions.stem: A non-cancerous nerve-sheath tumor that is the hallmark lesion of neurofibromatosis type 1 is termed:
options: Neuroblastoma
Schwannoma
Neurofibroma
Meningioma
questions.explanation: A neurofibroma is a benign nerve-sheath tumor and the characteristic lesion of neurofibromatosis type 1. Neuroblastoma is a malignant childhood tumor of sympathetic tissue; a schwannoma (neurilemmoma) is also benign but is the hallmark of NF2; a meningioma arises from the meninges.

questions.stem: Which statement about narcolepsy is correct?
options: Sleep onset may occur directly into REM sleep
Sleep onset is usually delayed by more than an hour
Sleep is broken by repeated apneas with desaturation
Sleep onset is marked by an urge to move the legs
questions.explanation: Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness with uncontrollable sleep episodes, and sleep may begin directly in REM (sleep-onset REM periods). Prolonged sleep latency suggests insomnia or a delayed sleep phase; repeated apneas with desaturation describe obstructive sleep apnea; an urge to move the legs at rest is restless legs syndrome.

questions.stem: Which statement about genetic disorders is correct?
options: They arise only from new mutations, not from parents
They can be inherited or arise from new mutations
They are acquired from infections during pregnancy
They are passed on only through the mother's genes
questions.explanation: Genetic disorders are caused partly or completely by defects in genes; they can be inherited from a parent or arise from a new (de novo) mutation. Many are inherited, so "only new mutations" is wrong; infections during pregnancy cause congenital, not genetic, disorders; most inheritance involves both parents, not only maternal genes.

questions.stem: Which statement about anencephaly is correct?
options: It is a survivable defect with a small but normally formed brain
It is a sac of meninges protruding through a defect in the skull
It is a fatal defect with absence of much of the brain and skull
It is a buildup of CSF that enlarges the head before birth
questions.explanation: Anencephaly is a fatal neural tube defect in which the cranial end of the neural tube fails to close, leaving much of the brain and skull vault absent. A small but formed brain describes microcephaly; a meningeal sac through the skull is a cranial meningocele; CSF buildup enlarging the head is hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: Which statement about microcephaly is correct?
options: It is an abnormally large head, often with developmental delay
It is premature fusion of skull sutures causing an odd shape
It is an absent skull vault and forebrain, fatal soon after birth
It is an abnormally small head, often with developmental delay
questions.explanation: Microcephaly is a birth defect with an abnormally small head; it may be associated with developmental delay but is not necessarily fatal. An abnormally large head is macrocephaly; premature suture fusion is craniosynostosis; an absent skull vault and forebrain describes anencephaly.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding neural tube defects?
options: Neural tube defects are problems in development of spinal cord and brain in an embryo
Examples include spina bifida (spine fails to enclose cord) and anencephaly (brain fails to develop)
Both A and B are correct
Neural tube defects only occur in adults
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Neural tube defects = embryologic CNS development problems, examples include spina bifida and anencephaly. These are BIRTH defects from embryonic development, NOT adult conditions. Embryo + CNS = neural tube defects.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding Reye's syndrome?
options: Reye's syndrome mainly affects those under age 15
It is characterized by brain and liver damage following viral infection, and may be linked to aspirin use
Both A and B are correct
Reye's syndrome is safe to treat with aspirin
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Reye's = childhood (<15 years), brain + liver damage, post-viral, aspirin association (AVOID aspirin in children with viral illness). NOT safe with aspirin - aspirin may contribute. Child + aspirin + virus = Reye's.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding migraine?
options: Migraine is a severe headache usually accompanied by vision problems and/or nausea and vomiting
Migraines typically recur (episodic pattern)
Both A and B are correct
Migraines only occur once in a lifetime
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Migraine = severe headache + visual aura + nausea/vomiting, typically RECURRENT (episodic). NOT single episode - recurrence is characteristic. Recurrent + aura + nausea = migraine.

questions.stem: Which statement about Saturday night palsy is correct?
options: It is a temporary wrist drop from radial nerve compression
It is a temporary facial weakness from facial nerve swelling
It is a temporary hand weakness from ulnar nerve compression
It is a permanent arm weakness from a birth stretch injury
questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy is a temporary paralysis (wrist drop) from prolonged compression of the radial nerve, typically against the humerus in the upper arm. Facial weakness from facial nerve swelling is Bell's palsy; ulnar compression causes weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles; a birth stretch injury of the brachial plexus is Erb's palsy.

questions.stem: Which statement about radiculopathy is correct?
options: It is disease of the spinal cord, often from disk prolapse
It is disease of a nerve root, often from disk prolapse
It is inflammation of the spinal cord, often after infection
It is disease of many distal nerves, often from diabetes
questions.explanation: Radiculopathy is disease of the nerve roots, caused by disk prolapse, arthritis (osteophytes), or other problems. Spinal cord disease is myelopathy; spinal cord inflammation is myelitis; disease of many distal nerves is peripheral polyneuropathy.

questions.stem: Which statement about the median nerve is correct?
options: It gives sensation to the little and ring fingers
It gives sensation to the back of the thumb web
It gives sensation to the thumb and index finger
It gives sensation to the lateral forearm only
questions.explanation: The median nerve runs down the arm to the hand, supplies forearm and thenar muscles, and conveys sensation to the palmar thumb, index finger, and part of the hand. The little and ring fingers are ulnar territory; the dorsal thumb web space is radial territory; the lateral forearm is supplied by the musculocutaneous (lateral antebrachial cutaneous) nerve.

questions.stem: Which statement about meningocele is correct?
options: It is a sac of meninges that also contains the spinal cord
It is a sac containing brain tissue through a skull defect
It is a vertebral defect with no sac, covered by skin
It is a sac of meninges and CSF without neural tissue
questions.explanation: A meningocele is a protrusion of the meninges (with CSF) through a defect in the skull or spinal column, without neural tissue. A sac also containing spinal cord is a myelomeningocele; brain tissue through a skull defect is an encephalocele; a skin-covered vertebral defect without a sac is spina bifida occulta. These defects are multifactorial rather than purely genetic.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding microdiscectomy?
options: Microdiscectomy is surgical removal of just the protruding part of a prolapsed disk
It is a minimally invasive procedure (partial removal)
Both A and B are correct
Microdiscectomy always removes the entire disk
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Microdiscectomy = removal of only protruding portion of herniated disk, minimally invasive. NOT entire disk - 'micro' indicates partial removal. Partial + disk = microdiscectomy.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding metastasis?
options: Metastasis is the spreading of a cancerous tumor to another part of the body
It can occur through lymph, blood, or across a cavity
Both A and B are correct
Metastasis refers to the original tumor location
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Metastasis = cancer spread to distant sites, via lymph/blood/direct extension. NOT original location - that's primary tumor. Spread to distant = metastasis.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding pre-cancerous conditions?
options: Pre-cancerous describes a condition from which cancer is likely to develop
Examples include certain types of dysplasia and polyps
Both A and B are correct
Pre-cancerous conditions always become cancer
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Pre-cancerous = increased cancer risk (e.g., dysplasia, certain polyps). NOT always become cancer - increased risk, not certainty. Increased risk = pre-cancerous.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding leukemia?
options: Leukemia is a group of bone marrow cancers with uncontrolled white blood cell division
It affects production of normal white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets
Both A and B are correct
Leukemia only affects white blood cells, not other blood cells
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Leukemia = bone marrow cancer, uncontrolled WBC division, affects ALL blood cell production (WBC, RBC, platelets). NOT only WBC - affects all blood cell lines. Bone marrow + all blood cells = leukemia.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding lymphoma?
options: Lymphoma is cancer of lymph nodes and spleen that can spread to other parts of the body
It causes lymph node enlargement and symptoms like fever, weight loss, and loss of appetite (B symptoms)
Both A and B are correct
Lymphoma never spreads beyond lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Lymphoma = lymph node/spleen cancer, CAN spread to other parts, causes lymph node enlargement and B symptoms (fever, weight loss, appetite loss). NOT confined - it can spread. Lymph tissue + spread + B symptoms = lymphoma.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding sarcoma?
options: Sarcoma is a cancer in connective tissue, fibrous tissue, or blood vessels
It arises from mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin, not epithelium
Both A and B are correct
Sarcoma arises from epithelial tissue
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Sarcoma = connective/fibrous/blood vessel cancer, mesenchymal origin. NOT epithelium - that's carcinoma. Connective tissue origin = sarcoma.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding carcinoma?
options: Carcinoma is a cancer that grows on the surface or lining of an organ
It arises from epithelial tissue
Both A and B are correct
Carcinoma arises from connective tissue
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Carcinoma = cancer of epithelium (surface/lining of organs). NOT connective tissue - that's sarcoma. Epithelial origin = carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which statement about gliomas, including glioblastoma, is correct?
options: They arise from the glial cells that support neurons
They arise from the meninges that cover the brain
They arise from Schwann cells of the cranial nerves
They arise from neurons of the cerebellar cortex
questions.explanation: Gliomas arise from glial (supporting) cells; glioblastoma is the fast-growing malignant form, usually in the adult cerebral hemispheres. Tumors of the meninges are meningiomas, Schwann cell tumors are schwannomas (e.g., acoustic neuroma), and gliomas are not neuronal tumors nor confined to the cerebellum.

questions.stem: Which statement about medulloblastoma is correct?
options: A benign tumor arising from the meninges
A tumor of the adrenal glands or sympathetic chain
A malignant cerebellar tumor seen mainly in children
A slow-growing glioma of the adult cerebrum
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of the cerebellum (posterior fossa) that occurs mainly in children. A benign tumor of the meninges is a meningioma, a tumor of the adrenal glands or sympathetic chain is a neuroblastoma, and gliomas arise from glial cells rather than being embryonal cerebellar tumors.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding neuroblastoma?
options: Neuroblastoma is a cancerous childhood tumor
It is located in the adrenal glands or the sympathetic nervous system
Both A and B are correct
Neuroblastoma only occurs in adults
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Neuroblastoma = childhood cancer, adrenal glands or sympathetic nervous system. NOT adults - it's pediatric. Adrenal/sympathetic + children = neuroblastoma.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding malignant melanoma?
options: Malignant melanoma is the most serious type of skin cancer
It is composed of cells called melanocytes, and moles may change shape, darken, become painful, or bleed
Both A and B are correct
Melanoma is always benign
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Malignant melanoma = most serious skin cancer, from melanocytes, mole changes (shape, color, pain, bleeding). NOT benign - it's malignant and can metastasize. Melanocytes + serious = melanoma.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding basal cell carcinoma?
options: Basal cell carcinoma is a type of cancer caused by exposure to large amounts of sunlight
It is commonly found on the neck, face, and arms (sun-exposed areas)
Both A and B are correct
Basal cell carcinoma is not related to sun exposure
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Basal cell carcinoma = sun exposure-related skin cancer, common on sun-exposed areas (face, neck, arms). NOT unrelated - sun exposure is a major risk factor. Sun + exposed areas = basal cell.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding pituitary adenoma?
options: Pituitary adenoma is a non-cancerous (benign) tumor of the pituitary gland
It can cause hormonal effects depending on the type
Both A and B are correct
Pituitary adenoma is always malignant
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Pituitary adenoma = benign pituitary tumor, can cause hormonal effects. NOT always malignant - it's benign. Pituitary + benign = adenoma.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly defines the terms iatrogenic and idiopathic?
options: Iatrogenic: cause unknown; idiopathic: caused by treatment
Iatrogenic: caused by treatment; idiopathic: cause unknown
Iatrogenic: caused by treatment; idiopathic: inherited cause
Iatrogenic: inherited cause; idiopathic: cause unknown
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic means caused by medical treatment or intervention; idiopathic means no identifiable cause (e.g., idiopathic intracranial hypertension). Swapping the definitions is wrong, and neither term simply means inherited; a known inherited cause is called genetic or hereditary.

questions.stem: Which description BEST defines a cerebral aneurysm?
options: A focal narrowing of an artery from plaque
An abnormal tangle of arteries and veins
A focal bulge of a weakened arterial wall
A clot carried to the brain from the heart
questions.explanation: An aneurysm is an abnormal outpouching (ballooning) of an artery wall at a point of weakness; rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage. Narrowing from plaque is stenosis, a tangle of arteries and veins without capillaries is an arteriovenous malformation, and a traveling clot is an embolus.

questions.stem: Which statements are true regarding oximetry?
options: Oximetry determines the amount of oxygen in the blood
It measures light transmitted through skin (non-invasive method, pulse oximeter)
Both A and B are correct
Oximetry requires invasive blood sampling
questions.explanation: Both are correct: Oximetry = blood oxygen measurement, uses light through skin (pulse oximeter, NON-INVASIVE). NOT invasive - it's non-invasive. Oxygen + light + non-invasive = oximetry.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a small crack in an electrode cable during setup. The MOST appropriate action is:
options: Replace the cable and remove it from service
Wrap the crack in electrical tape and proceed
Proceed if the impedance on that lead is normal
Proceed but avoid moving that electrode lead
questions.explanation: A cracked cable is an electrical hazard and a source of intermittent artifact, so it is replaced and the damaged cable is taken out of service (and the issue documented for quality assurance). Tape is not an approved repair, normal impedance does not prove the insulation is intact, and keeping the lead still does not remove the hazard.

questions.stem: A patient with known sickle cell disease requests hyperventilation activation. The technologist should:
options: Proceed with full hyperventilation as ordered
Hold HV and clarify the order with the provider
Do HV for 90 seconds instead of 3 minutes
Omit HV and leave it out of the record
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is a contraindication to hyperventilation because hypocapnia and vasoconstriction can precipitate a sickling crisis, so HV is held and the order is clarified with the ordering physician, with the discussion documented. Proceeding as ordered ignores the contraindication, a shorter HV still carries the risk, and omitting it unilaterally without discussion bypasses the ordering provider.

questions.stem: A family member asks the technologist about the EEG results while waiting in the hallway. The MOST appropriate response is:
options: Explain that results come from the ordering doctor, not you
Share only the general findings to reassure the family
Show them the tracing on screen but avoid interpreting it
Say the study looked normal if no spikes were seen today
questions.explanation: Technologists neither interpret nor release results, and HIPAA limits disclosure to authorized people; the family should be directed to the ordering physician. Sharing "general" findings, showing the tracing, or saying it looked normal all disclose PHI and amount to an unauthorized, unqualified interpretation.

questions.stem: In the technical report, a technologist should describe findings as:
options: "Findings are diagnostic of generalized epilepsy"
"Generalized spike-and-wave discharges are present"
"This is consistent with a seizure disorder"
"Generalized epileptic seizures are present"
questions.explanation: Technologists describe observed patterns with standardized terms, such as generalized spike-and-wave discharges. Calling findings diagnostic of epilepsy or a seizure disorder is a diagnosis, and labelling discharges as seizures is a clinical interpretation.

questions.stem: A patient offers the technologist their phone number for personal contact after the study. The MOST appropriate response is:
options: Accept the number to maintain rapport
Politely decline and maintain professional boundaries
Accept but only use for medical questions
Accept if the patient seems nice
questions.explanation: Professional boundaries must be maintained. Accepting personal contact information blurs professional boundaries and is inappropriate. Maintain professional relationship only within the clinical setting.

questions.stem: During routine equipment check, the technologist notices inconsistent calibration signals. The BEST action is:
options: Remove it from service and use backup equipment
Use it and add a comment to the technical notes
Use it but adjust channel gains manually
Use it if the patient tracing looks normal
questions.explanation: Inconsistent calibration means the recorded amplitudes cannot be trusted, so the equipment is taken out of service, the supervisor notified and backup equipment used. Annotating the problem or adjusting gains manually still produces an unreliable recording, and a normal-looking tracing does not prove the amplifiers are accurate.

questions.stem: After completing an EEG on a patient with MRSA, the technologist should:
options: Wipe reusable electrodes with standard alcohol pads after the study
Clean as usual, adding enhanced steps only if the next patient is frail
Reuse the electrodes on the next patient after rinsing
Use dedicated or disposable electrodes, disinfected before leaving the room
questions.explanation: MRSA requires contact precautions: use dedicated or disposable equipment where possible, and clean and disinfect reusable items with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant per facility policy before they leave the room. MRSA is not spore-forming, so a sporicide is not required; the cleaning standard does not depend on who the next patient is. A quick alcohol wipe or a rinse before reuse does not meet contact-precaution disinfection requirements.

questions.stem: A technologist wants to use an EEG tracing for a presentation at an outside conference. To comply with HIPAA, they must:
options: Remove the name and MRN shown in the recording header
Obtain verbal permission from the patient before using it
Remove all 18 identifiers so no re-identification is possible
Show it only at a conference closed to the public
questions.explanation: HIPAA de-identification (safe harbor) means removing all 18 identifier types (name, dates, MRN, etc.) with no actual knowledge that the patient could be re-identified. Removing only name and MRN leaves other identifiers such as dates; verbal permission is not a written authorization; a closed audience does not remove the de-identification requirement for external use.

questions.stem: A technologist observes a pattern that looks concerning. In the technical report, they should write:
options: "Abnormal EEG consistent with a seizure disorder"
"Absence seizures provoked by hyperventilation"
"Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave during hyperventilation"
"Generalized epilepsy activated by hyperventilation"
questions.explanation: An objective description gives the pattern, frequency, distribution (e.g., frontally predominant) and activating condition. "Seizure disorder", "absence seizures" and "generalized epilepsy" are clinical interpretations or diagnoses reserved for the interpreting physician.

questions.stem: During an EEG, a patient has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The technologist's FIRST priority is:
options: Keep recording to capture the full seizure onset
Page the neurologist before doing anything else
Protect from injury and keep the airway clear
Halt the recording and hold the limbs still
questions.explanation: The first priority is the patient: protect the head and body from injury and keep the airway clear, continuing the recording only if it can be done without compromising care. Capturing the seizure is secondary, help is summoned while staying with the patient rather than before acting, and restraining the limbs can cause injury and the recording need not be stopped.

questions.stem: A patient with capacity refuses hyperventilation activation. The technologist should:
options: Proceed with HV, since the physician's order overrides refusal
Omit HV quietly and leave it out of the technical report
Get a family member's consent, then document and perform HV
Honor the refusal, document it, and notify the ordering physician
questions.explanation: A patient with capacity may refuse any part of a procedure; the technologist respects the refusal, documents it, and notifies the ordering physician. An order does not override refusal; silently omitting HV leaves the record inaccurate; family consent cannot replace the decision of a patient who has capacity.

questions.stem: Preventive maintenance for EEG equipment should be performed:
options: Only after the equipment malfunctions
On the manufacturer's recommended schedule
Once a year regardless of model or usage
Only during the first year after purchase
questions.explanation: Preventive maintenance follows the manufacturer's recommended schedule and facility policy, so problems are found before they cause failure or a hazard. Waiting for a malfunction is reactive, a fixed annual interval may not match the manufacturer's requirements, and maintenance continues for the life of the equipment.

questions.stem: A technologist posts a photo of an interesting EEG pattern on social media with no patient identifiers visible. This is:
options: Acceptable as long as no names or dates are shown in it
Potentially a violation if the pattern could identify the patient
Acceptable when the post is clearly for education only
Acceptable once all 18 identifiers are cropped from the image
questions.explanation: Removing visible identifiers is not enough when a distinctive pattern or rare finding could let someone recognize the patient; facility social-media policy may also prohibit such posts. Hiding names and dates, an educational purpose, or cropping listed identifiers does not address re-identification risk from the content itself.

questions.stem: The principle 'If it isn't documented, it didn't happen' means:
options: Only abnormal findings and clinical events need recording
Events must be recorded; routine settings can be omitted
Unrecorded details may be added later from memory
Every observation, event and setting must be recorded
questions.explanation: The principle means observations, events and technical parameters must be recorded accurately and completely; anything unrecorded cannot be shown to have happened. Limiting records to abnormal findings or events, omitting settings, or reconstructing details later from memory all break that principle.

questions.stem: EEG equipment must be properly grounded to:
options: Protect against electrical shock hazards
Raise the amplitude of low-voltage signals
Reduce muscle and movement artifact
Meet accreditation paperwork requirements
questions.explanation: Grounding is primarily an electrical safety measure that provides a low-resistance path for leakage current, protecting the patient and staff from shock; it may also help reduce line-frequency interference. It does not amplify signals, has no effect on muscle or movement artifact, and is a safety requirement rather than a paperwork item.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a patient appears distressed during hyperventilation but the physician ordered it. The technologist should:
options: Stop HV, assess the patient, and notify the physician
Continue HV, since the physician ordered a full 3 minutes
Shorten HV to 1 minute, then notify the physician
Coach the patient through it and notify the physician later
questions.explanation: Patient well-being comes before completing an activation: if the patient is distressed, stop HV, assess them, and notify the physician. An order does not require continuing through distress; shortening or coaching the patient through it still continues a procedure that is causing harm.

questions.stem: Multiple electrodes show high impedance during recording. The technologist should:
options: Keep recording and add a note on the tracing
Raise the amplifier gain to compensate
Pause and re-prep the electrodes, then resume
Continue if the tracing looks acceptable
questions.explanation: High impedance degrades signal quality and invites artifact, so the technologist pauses, cleans the skin and reapplies paste or gel to lower impedance, then resumes. Annotating the problem does not fix it, raising gain amplifies the noise along with the signal, and an acceptable-looking tracing can still hide impedance-related distortion.

questions.stem: The ethical principle of justice requires technologists to:
options: Provide preferential treatment to certain patients
Treat all patients fairly and equitably, regardless of background
Prioritize patients based on insurance status
Provide different care based on age
questions.explanation: Justice requires fair and equitable treatment of all patients, regardless of race, religion, socioeconomic status, insurance, or other factors. All patients deserve the same quality of care and respect.

questions.stem: When documenting EEG findings, technologists should use:
options: Subjective interpretations and clinical impressions
Objective, standardized terminology describing observable patterns
Medical diagnoses and clinical conclusions
Casual language and abbreviations
questions.explanation: Technologists must use objective, standardized terminology to describe observable patterns. Avoid subjective interpretations, medical diagnoses, or clinical conclusions. Stay within scope of practice: observe and document, do not interpret clinically.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of photosensitive seizures requests photic stimulation. The technologist should:
options: Run the standard photic sequence as ordered
Omit photic stimulation without further discussion
Run full photic and stop only if a seizure occurs
Clarify with the ordering provider before proceeding
questions.explanation: A known photosensitive patient needs the photic plan clarified with the physician first (for example, which frequencies, whether to stop at the first photoparoxysmal response) with emergency response ready. Running the standard sequence or waiting for a clinical seizure ignores the known risk, and omitting photic unilaterally skips the discussion that decides whether its diagnostic value outweighs the risk.

questions.stem: The HIPAA 'minimum necessary' rule means:
options: Share full records with any staff on the care team
Share patient information only with licensed clinicians
Share only the minimum patient information the task needs
Withhold all information unless the patient signs a release
questions.explanation: HIPAA's minimum necessary standard limits use and disclosure to the least PHI needed for the task. Being on the care team does not entitle staff to full records; the rule is about need, not licensure; and it does not bar sharing needed information for treatment, payment, or operations without a signed release.

questions.stem: Calibration signals should be checked:
options: Only when the equipment is new
Once a month on a fixed schedule
Only when a problem is suspected
At the start and end of each study
questions.explanation: Calibration is recorded at the beginning (and ideally the end) of every recording, or as facility policy specifies, to confirm amplifier and filter function for that study. New equipment still drifts, a monthly check misses problems on the days in between, and waiting for a suspected problem means faulty data may already have been recorded.

questions.stem: The ethical principle 'do no harm' (nonmaleficence) means technologists should:
options: Avoid all procedures that might cause discomfort
Prevent harm and avoid causing injury or distress
Only perform procedures if they're completely safe
Prioritize diagnostic yield over patient comfort
questions.explanation: Nonmaleficence (do no harm) requires preventing harm and avoiding causing injury or distress. This doesn't mean avoiding all procedures, but rather ensuring procedures are performed safely and stopping if harm occurs. Patient safety is paramount.

questions.stem: Required elements of an EEG technical report include:
options: States recorded, settings, observations and events
Abnormal findings and a provisional diagnosis
Pattern descriptions and the clinical impression
Impedance values and the final interpretation
questions.explanation: A technical report includes patient demographics (as permitted), study date/duration, states recorded, technical parameters, objective observations, events and activations. Diagnoses, clinical impressions and final interpretations are not technologist elements.

questions.stem: Standard precautions for infection control require:
options: Enhanced isolation measures for every patient
Treating every patient as potentially infectious
Precautions only for patients with known infection
Precautions only when a patient appears unwell
questions.explanation: Standard precautions treat every patient as potentially infectious and apply hand hygiene, gloves and other protective measures according to anticipated exposure. Enhanced (transmission-based) isolation is reserved for specific infections, and limiting precautions to known or visibly ill patients misses the many people who carry pathogens without symptoms.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a colleague performing a procedure outside their scope of practice. The technologist should:
options: Report it only if a patient is actually harmed by the practice
Confront the colleague in front of the team, then report it
Report it straight to the licensing board without discussion
Address it privately, then report through channels if unresolved
questions.explanation: The professional approach is a private, constructive conversation first, then reporting through appropriate channels (supervisor, quality) if it continues or safety is at risk. Waiting for harm is too late; public confrontation is unprofessional; going straight to the licensing board skips internal channels.

questions.stem: Equipment maintenance and calibration records should be:
options: Documented for all servicing and retained
Documented when a fault is found
Documented by vendor and kept off site
Documented until the warranty expires
questions.explanation: Maintenance and calibration records are documented for all servicing and retained according to facility policy and regulatory requirements, supporting audits, quality assurance and equipment safety. Recording only faults leaves no evidence of routine service, the facility must hold and be able to produce its own records rather than rely on a vendor, and the obligation does not end with the warranty.

questions.stem: During a seizure, the technologist should NOT:
options: Protect the patient's head from injury
Place objects in the patient's mouth
Time the seizure duration
Maintain patient airway if possible
questions.explanation: NEVER place objects in a patient's mouth during a seizure - this can cause injury (broken teeth, airway obstruction). Protect head, time duration, maintain airway, but do NOT insert anything into the mouth. This is a critical safety rule.

questions.stem: A patient requests a copy of their EEG report. The technologist should:
options: Hand over a printed copy once the patient shows photo ID
Route the request through the facility's medical records process
Decline, since patients cannot obtain their own EEG records
Release it once the interpreting doctor gives verbal approval
questions.explanation: Patients have a HIPAA right to access their records, and requests go through the facility's release-of-information (medical records) process. Technologists should not hand out copies directly even with ID; refusing denies a legal right; informal verbal approval from a doctor is not the release process.

questions.stem: A technologist should avoid using which type of language in technical reports?
options: Objective, standardized terminology
Subjective interpretations and clinical diagnoses
Descriptive pattern terminology
Technical parameter descriptions
questions.explanation: Technologists must avoid subjective interpretations and clinical diagnoses. Use objective, standardized terminology to describe observable patterns. Stay within scope of practice: document observations, not clinical interpretations or diagnoses.

questions.stem: A technologist wants to use an EEG tracing showing a rare pattern (seen in only 2 patients in the facility's history) for a teaching presentation at a regional conference. The tracing has no names or dates. This is:
options: Potentially a violation, as the rare pattern could identify them
Acceptable, because the names and dates have all been removed
Acceptable if attendees are all licensed clinicians
Acceptable once the patient gives verbal permission to use it
questions.explanation: With only two such patients in the facility's history, the pattern itself could allow re-identification, so removing names and dates is not sufficient. Limiting the audience to licensed clinicians does not remove the risk, since attendees may still recognize the case, and verbal permission is not a valid HIPAA authorization.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of recent stroke (2 weeks ago) is scheduled for EEG with hyperventilation. The technologist should:
options: Hold HV and query the ordering provider first
Proceed with full hyperventilation as ordered
Do a gentler HV at half the usual depth
Skip HV and leave it out of the notes
questions.explanation: A recent stroke is a relative contraindication to hyperventilation because hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction that may reduce perfusion to vulnerable tissue, so HV is held while the ordering physician is consulted and the discussion documented. Proceeding as ordered ignores the risk, a gentler HV is a unilateral modification, and skipping it without a record hides an important protocol change.

questions.stem: A technologist documents: 'Generalized spike-and-wave discharges consistent with absence epilepsy.' The MOST appropriate correction is:
options: "EEG shows absence seizures, activated by HV"
"Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave, activated by HV"
"Consistent with childhood absence epilepsy"
"Abnormal EEG, epileptiform, likely absence type"
questions.explanation: The correction describes the pattern objectively: generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave activated by hyperventilation. "Absence seizures", "childhood absence epilepsy" and "likely absence type" are clinical interpretations.

questions.stem: During recording, 3 electrodes show impedance >10 kΩ but the tracing appears acceptable. The technologist should:
options: Continue since the tracing looks acceptable
Stop, re-prep those electrodes, then resume
Increase amplifier gain to compensate
Add a note on the tracing and continue
questions.explanation: Impedance above 10 kΩ (under 5 kΩ preferred) increases susceptibility to artifact and distortion even when the tracing looks acceptable, so the technologist stops, re-prepares the electrodes (clean skin, reapply paste) and resumes. Raising gain amplifies noise as well as signal, and annotating the tracing does not correct the problem.

questions.stem: A patient offers the technologist a gift card after completing the EEG study. The technologist should:
options: Accept it graciously as a sincere gesture of appreciation
Accept it if its value is below a small token amount
Politely decline and explain the facility's policy on gifts
Accept it and share it with the whole department staff
questions.explanation: Gifts such as gift cards can blur professional boundaries and create conflicts of interest, so the technologist politely declines and explains facility policy. Accepting as appreciation, judging by value, or sharing it with the department all still accept a cash-equivalent gift from a patient.

questions.stem: A patient with active tuberculosis (TB) requires EEG. The technologist should:
options: Standard precautions with gloves only
Contact precautions with gown and gloves
Airborne precautions with an N95 respirator
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
questions.explanation: Active TB is spread by airborne droplet nuclei, so airborne precautions are needed: a fit-tested N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room where available, following the facility protocol. Standard or contact precautions do not protect against inhaled organisms, and a surgical mask (droplet precautions) does not filter the small airborne particles.

questions.stem: A billing department employee asks the technologist for detailed clinical information about a patient's EEG findings. The technologist should:
options: Share the full findings, since billing needs detail
Share findings if the employee has system access
Refuse to share any patient information at all
Share only the codes and dates that billing needs
questions.explanation: Under the minimum necessary standard, billing receives what it needs (procedure codes, dates of service), not detailed clinical findings. Billing does not need the full findings; system access is not the same as need; refusing everything blocks a legitimate payment function.

questions.stem: During preventive maintenance, the calibration signals on all channels are consistently 2% off the expected value. The technologist should:
options: Tag the unit out, since any deviation is unacceptable
Adjust each channel's gain by 2% to compensate
Check it against the manufacturer's stated tolerance
Disregard it, as only relative amplitudes matter
questions.explanation: Calibration accuracy is judged against the manufacturer's specified tolerance; a small, uniform deviation within specification is acceptable, while one outside it requires service before use. No equipment is accurate to zero deviation, so tagging out for any deviation is incorrect; manual gain adjustment is not a substitute for proper calibration; and absolute amplitude accuracy does matter for measurement and interpretation.

questions.stem: A patient asks the technologist to interpret their EEG results and recommend treatment. The technologist should:
options: Give a brief impression, then refer them to the physician
Explain this is outside your scope and refer them to the physician
Describe the patterns, leaving treatment to the physician
Offer treatment ideas but have them confirm with the physician
questions.explanation: Interpretation and treatment advice are outside technologist scope, so the patient is directed to the physician. Giving an impression or describing what the patterns mean is still interpretation, and suggesting treatment is not made acceptable by later physician confirmation.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a frayed power cord on the EEG machine but the machine functions normally. The technologist should:
options: Keep using it while it still functions normally
Wrap the frayed section with electrical tape
Use it but route the cord away from the patient
Tag it out of service and switch to backup unit
questions.explanation: A frayed power cord is a shock and fire hazard even when the machine works, so it is tagged out of service, the supervisor is notified and backup equipment is used; repair is left to qualified biomedical staff. Normal function does not mean the insulation is safe, tape is not an approved repair, and rerouting the cord does not remove the hazard.

questions.stem: A technologist completes an EEG but forgets to document the photic stimulation protocol used. The technologist should:
options: Insert it into the original note so it reads complete
Leave it out, as photic details are a minor point
Wait to add it until the reader asks about photic
Add a dated, timed addendum explaining the omission
questions.explanation: A missed element is documented promptly as an addendum with date/time explaining the omission. Silently inserting it into the original alters the record; omitting it leaves the record incomplete; waiting for a request delays required information.

questions.stem: A technologist is assigned two EEG studies: one for a VIP patient and one for a regular patient. The technologist should:
options: Give both patients the same quality of care
Do the VIP study first, then the other one
Assign the most senior technologist to the VIP
Allow the VIP extra time and amenities at setup
questions.explanation: The principle of justice requires equal quality of care regardless of status. Reordering by status, reserving the most senior staff, or giving extra time and amenities are all forms of preferential treatment based on VIP status rather than clinical need.

questions.stem: During recording, the technologist notices 60 Hz artifact in all channels. After checking impedance (all <5 kΩ) and verifying proper grounding, the artifact persists. The technologist should:
options: Turn on the notch filter and continue recording
Re-prep every electrode to lower impedance further
Add a note on the tracing and continue recording
Look for nearby unshielded electrical sources
questions.explanation: 60 Hz artifact in all channels despite low impedance and proper grounding points to external interference, so the technologist looks for unshielded equipment, power cords, lights or other electrical sources and removes or relocates them. A notch filter only attenuates the interference and can mask the problem, impedances are already good, and annotating the tracing leaves the source in place.

questions.stem: A patient's family member requests a copy of the patient's EEG report. The technologist should:
options: Release it once the family member shows photo identification
Release it if the patient agrees verbally at the bedside
Require the patient's written authorization or legal proxy status
Refuse, since family members cannot access records at all
questions.explanation: A family member may receive a copy of the record only with the patient's written authorization or legal authority such as power of attorney or guardianship, handled per facility policy. Photo ID proves identity, not authority; verbal agreement is not a records authorization; refusing outright ignores valid authorizations.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of photosensitive seizures requests photic stimulation. The ordering physician's note says 'proceed with caution.' The technologist should:
options: Run the standard photic sequence unchanged
Clarify the photic plan with the ordering provider
Omit photic since a risk has been noted
Run full photic and stop only if a seizure occurs
questions.explanation: "Proceed with caution" is not a specific plan, so the technologist clarifies it with the physician (for example, reduced exposure, which frequencies to use, stopping at the first photoparoxysmal response, emergency response ready). Running the standard sequence or waiting for a clinical seizure ignores the caution, and omitting photic contradicts an order that asked for it to be done.

questions.stem: A technologist observes a pattern and documents: 'This pattern is highly suggestive of temporal lobe epilepsy.' The MOST appropriate correction is:
options: "EEG shows left temporal lobe seizure activity"
"Consistent with left temporal lobe epilepsy"
"Focal sharp waves, left temporal, maximal T3/T5"
"Abnormal EEG suggesting a left temporal focus"
questions.explanation: The objective correction names the waveform, region and maximum (focal sharp waves, left temporal, maximal T3/T5). Seizure activity, temporal lobe epilepsy and a "temporal focus" are clinical interpretations.

questions.stem: Equipment maintenance records show that preventive maintenance was performed 13 months ago, but manufacturer recommends annual maintenance. The technologist should:
options: Tag it for maintenance and use backup equipment
Keep using it, as it is only a month overdue
Use it today and book the service soon
Use it if it appears to function normally
questions.explanation: Maintenance overdue against the manufacturer's schedule means the equipment may not meet safety and quality standards, so it is tagged for maintenance, the supervisor is notified and backup equipment is used until service is completed. Being only slightly overdue, booking the service later, or normal apparent function does not confirm the equipment is safe.

questions.stem: A technologist notices that a patient appears confused and disoriented during the EEG, but the study was ordered as 'routine.' The technologist should:
options: Continue the routine protocol and document the confusion later
Skip activation and document that the patient seemed tired
Document it only if the patient reports feeling unwell or ill
Assess, document findings, and notify the physician if concerning
questions.explanation: A change in mental status is a patient-safety observation: assess the patient, document it, and notify the physician if it is concerning. Continuing routinely delays recognition; labelling it as tiredness misrepresents the observation; waiting for the patient to complain is inappropriate in someone who may not recognize the change.

questions.stem: After completing an EEG on a patient with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), the technologist should:
options: Disinfect with a bleach-based sporicidal agent
Wipe down with alcohol-based disinfectant wipes
Use the routine quaternary ammonium wipes
Clean as usual unless the next patient is frail
questions.explanation: C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol and many routine disinfectants, so equipment is cleaned with a sporicidal agent such as a bleach-based product per facility protocol. Alcohol wipes and routine quaternary ammonium wipes do not reliably kill spores, and the cleaning standard does not depend on the next patient.

questions.stem: A technologist takes a photo of an interesting EEG pattern (no patient identifiers visible) and posts it on a professional EEG discussion forum. This is:
options: Acceptable since no identifiers are visible in the photograph
Potentially a violation - external sharing may breach policy
Acceptable because it serves a clear and educational purpose
Acceptable if the forum requires a professional member login
questions.explanation: Even apparently de-identified patient data shared on external platforms can violate facility policy and, if re-identification is possible, HIPAA. Absence of visible identifiers, an educational purpose, or a closed forum does not by itself authorize sharing.

questions.stem: A single electrode shows intermittent 'pops' (electrode pop artifact) during recording. After checking impedance (acceptable), the artifact persists. The technologist should:
options: Keep recording and add a note on the tracing
Re-prep and reapply that electrode for contact
Lower the high-frequency filter for that channel
Leave it, since only one channel is affected
questions.explanation: Electrode pop (sudden, high-amplitude deflections at one electrode) reflects unstable electrode-skin contact even when impedance reads acceptable, so the electrode is re-prepared: clean the skin, reapply paste or gel and secure contact. A filter change only attenuates part of the artifact without fixing the cause, and one bad channel still degrades the recording and localization.

questions.stem: A technologist realizes they made an error in the technical report (documented wrong montage). The technologist should:
options: Add a dated addendum stating the error and correction
Edit the original entry so the montage reads correctly
Delete the original entry and rewrite it from scratch
Correct it only if a reviewer notices the mismatch
questions.explanation: Record errors are corrected by a dated, timed addendum that explains the original error and the correction, preserving record integrity. Editing over or deleting the original alters the record; waiting for someone to notice leaves known errors in place.

questions.stem: A patient with mild cognitive impairment (but with capacity) refuses sleep deprivation before the EEG. The technologist should:
options: Respect the refusal, document it, and notify the ordering physician
Insist on sleep deprivation, since the physician ordered it
Obtain family consent and document sleep deprivation as done
Document the impairment as grounds to override the refusal
questions.explanation: A patient with capacity may refuse, even with mild cognitive impairment; the technologist respects the refusal, documents it, and notifies the ordering physician. An order does not override refusal; family consent cannot replace that of a capable patient; mild impairment is not grounds to override a capable decision.

questions.stem: During an EEG, a patient has a seizure that lasts 6 minutes without stopping. The technologist should:
options: Continue recording to capture the full seizure
Ensure patient safety, activate emergency response immediately (status epilepticus), and notify physician
Wait 2 more minutes to see if it stops
Only activate emergency if the patient appears in distress
questions.explanation: Seizure lasting >5 minutes (generalized tonic-clonic) = status epilepticus = medical emergency. Activate emergency response immediately, ensure patient safety, notify physician. Do not wait - status epilepticus requires immediate intervention. Continue recording only if it can be done safely during emergency response.

questions.stem: During calibration check, one channel shows calibration signal amplitude 35 µV instead of the expected 50 µV. All other channels show 50 µV. The technologist should:
options: Accept it, since one channel can vary slightly
Accept it, since only one channel is affected
Check that channel; use backup if it persists
Raise that channel's gain to bring it to 50 µV
questions.explanation: A channel reading 35 µV when all others show the expected 50 µV is clearly abnormal, so that channel is investigated; if the discrepancy persists, the equipment is tagged, the supervisor notified and backup equipment used. A 30% shortfall is far beyond normal channel-to-channel variation, one faulty channel can create false amplitude asymmetry, and manually raising its gain hides a fault rather than correcting it.

questions.stem: A research coordinator requests de-identified EEG data for a study. The technologist should:
options: Release it directly (de-identified data needs no review)
Release it once the coordinator signs a short confidentiality note
Route it through the facility's research policy (IRB/privacy review)
Release it if the principal investigator is on the hospital staff
questions.explanation: Research use of patient data follows facility policy, typically IRB/privacy review and any data-sharing agreement the institution requires, with de-identification confirmed. Truly de-identified data is not PHI, but the facility still governs research release, so being labelled de-identified does not bypass that review; an informal confidentiality note or a staff investigator does not replace IRB review.

questions.stem: A technologist documents: 'The EEG is normal with no evidence of seizure activity.' The MOST appropriate correction is:
options: "Normal EEG; no evidence of any seizure disorder"
"Normal study; seizures have been excluded today"
"Normal background; no epileptiform discharges seen"
"No seizure activity; patient is not epileptic"
questions.explanation: The objective correction describes what was seen: a normal background and no epileptiform discharges. Statements about a seizure disorder, excluding seizures or the patient not being epileptic are clinical interpretations a routine EEG cannot support.

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy (immunocompetent) patient with localized shingles whose lesions can be completely covered requires EEG. The technologist should use:
options: Airborne precautions with an N95 respirator
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
Standard precautions, with the lesions covered
Contact precautions plus negative-pressure room
questions.explanation: Per CDC guidance, localized zoster in an immunocompetent patient whose lesions are contained and covered requires standard precautions. Airborne plus contact precautions (N95, negative-pressure room, gown and gloves) are used for disseminated zoster, or for localized zoster in an immunocompromised patient until dissemination is ruled out, so they are not needed here. Droplet precautions do not match the route of spread.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a colleague documenting clinical interpretations in technical reports. The technologist should:
options: Report it only if a patient is harmed by the wording they used
Correct the colleague's reports yourself without telling them
Confront the colleague at the staff meeting, then report it
Raise it privately, then report through channels if it continues
questions.explanation: Technologists documenting clinical interpretations is a scope issue; address it privately and constructively first, then report through appropriate channels if it continues. Waiting for harm is too late; silently editing a colleague's reports is improper; public confrontation is unprofessional.

questions.stem: Equipment maintenance log shows last calibration was 11 months ago. Manufacturer recommends annual calibration. The technologist should:
options: Keep using it and schedule once it is overdue
Wait for the vendor to send a reminder notice
Take it out of service until it is recalibrated
Schedule calibration now, before the due date
questions.explanation: Preventive maintenance is proactive: calibration is scheduled before it becomes due so the equipment stays within specification and there is no gap in availability. Waiting until it is overdue or for a vendor reminder risks lapsing, while the equipment is still in date, so taking it out of service now is unnecessary.

questions.stem: A technologist needs to use a cleaning solution for EEG equipment. The technologist should:
options: Use whatever solution the lab has on hand
Mix it stronger than labeled for better effect
Use it if it is the one colleagues usually use
Check its SDS for handling, hazards, and PPE
questions.explanation: OSHA requires access to the Safety Data Sheet (SDS, formerly MSDS) for workplace chemicals; it gives proper use, hazards, and PPE requirements. Using whatever is on hand or what colleagues use skips that check, and mixing stronger than labeled increases hazard without approval.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a colleague accessing EEG records for a patient not under their care. The technologist should:
options: Report it only if a patient is harmed by the access
Raise it privately and report it if the access was unauthorized
Confront them publicly, then report to the privacy officer
Notify the patient directly so they can file a complaint
questions.explanation: Accessing records without a work need violates HIPAA; the technologist may raise it with the colleague, but confirmed unauthorized access must be reported to the supervisor or privacy officer. Waiting for harm is wrong; public confrontation is unprofessional; patient notification is handled by the privacy office, not the coworker.

questions.stem: A technologist completes an EEG but realizes they forgot to document the patient's state of consciousness during the study. The technologist should:
options: Add it to the original entry without marking the change
Add a dated, timed addendum describing the patient's state
