Raising the LFF or reducing sensitivity only changes how the artifact looks, and omitting the electrode loses data from that region instead of fixing it.

questions.stem: Photic stimulation is usually performed:
options: Mainly with eyes open, fixating on the lamp center
Mainly with eyes closed, adding eyes open if needed
With eyes closed for low rates, open for high rates
With eyes open, and the lamp held 10 cm away
questions.explanation: Photic stimulation is commonly performed with the eyes closed, and eye-open (or eye-closure) trains may be added as the lab's protocol directs. Recording only with eyes open reduces driving in many subjects; splitting eye state by frequency is not a standard method; and 10 cm is too close, the usual distance being about 30 cm.

questions.stem: For detecting subtle focal slowing, the technologist should:
options: Rely on a longitudinal bipolar montage alone
Compare referential and bipolar montages
Rely on an ipsilateral ear reference alone
Speed up the sweep to spread the slow waves
questions.explanation: Subtle focal slowing is best detected by comparing montages: referential views show amplitude differences and bipolar views confirm localization. A single bipolar montage can cancel slowing shared by neighbouring electrodes; an ipsilateral ear reference may be active; a faster sweep spreads waves but makes slow activity harder, not easier, to recognize.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 0.5 Hz and HFF 70 Hz. This filter combination will:
options: Pass all frequencies without attenuation
Pass roughly 0.5-70 Hz, the standard range
Attenuate nearly all cerebral activity
Change amplitude but not frequency content
questions.explanation: A 0.5 Hz LFF attenuates activity below about 0.5 Hz and a 70 Hz HFF attenuates activity above about 70 Hz, so the 0.5-70 Hz range used for routine EEG is passed. Filters always shape some frequencies, so not all pass unattenuated; this wide band preserves most cerebral activity; and filters change frequency content, not just amplitude.

questions.stem: When annotating a clinical event, the technologist should document:
options: Time of onset and the technologist's diagnosis
Time, observed behavior, duration, and EEG change
EEG change and the suspected seizure type
Time of onset and the medication last given
questions.explanation: A useful event annotation records the time, an objective description of what was observed, the duration, and any EEG change, so clinical and EEG findings can be correlated. The technologist should not record a diagnosis or a suspected seizure type, and medication timing alone does not describe the event.

questions.stem: Wicket spikes are best described as:
options: Epileptiform temporal spikes followed by a slow-wave component
Benign 14 and 6 Hz positive bursts over posterior temporal areas
Benign small sharp spikes seen briefly in light sleep
Benign arciform 6-11 Hz temporal waves seen in drowsiness
questions.explanation: Wicket spikes are a benign variant: arciform, mu-like 6-11 Hz waves over the temporal regions, seen mainly in drowsiness and light sleep in adults, with no after-going slow wave. A spike followed by a slow wave suggests an epileptiform discharge; 14 and 6 Hz positive bursts and benign small sharp spikes are different benign variants.

questions.stem: ECG artifact is best reduced by:
options: Lowering the high-frequency filter to attenuate the spikes
Raising the low-frequency filter for the temporal leads
Decreasing the paper speed to compress the complexes
Changing the reference and adding an ECG monitor channel
questions.explanation: ECG artifact is reduced by avoiding references that pick up the cardiac field (for example, by changing from ear references) and by recording a separate ECG channel so the complexes can be matched to the QRS. Filter changes attenuate cerebral activity as well and do not reliably reduce ECG spikes; a slower display speed only compresses the artifact.

questions.stem: During hyperventilation, normal response in adults is typically:
options: Marked posterior delta, as in young children
Generalized spike-and-wave in most adults
Little change or a mild increase in theta
Complete suppression of the alpha rhythm
questions.explanation: In adults HV usually produces little change or only a mild increase in theta, far less than the build-up seen in children. Marked delta build-up is typical of young children; spike-and-wave is abnormal; HV does not normally abolish the alpha rhythm.

questions.stem: Along the midline in the 10-20 system, the distance from Fpz to Oz is:
options: 50% of the nasion-inion distance
90% of the nasion-inion distance
80% of the nasion-inion distance
100% of the nasion-inion distance
questions.explanation: Fpz is placed 10% above the nasion and Oz 10% above the inion, so Fpz to Oz spans the remaining 80% of the nasion-inion distance (divided into 20% segments by Fz, Cz and Pz). 50% is the nasion-to-Cz distance, 90% would omit only one 10% end segment, and 100% is the full nasion-inion distance.

questions.stem: If one electrode has impedance 2 kΩ and its paired electrode has impedance 10 kΩ, this imbalance can cause:
options: Reduced common-mode rejection and more noise
Improved common-mode rejection and less noise
A change in displayed frequency but not noise
An amplitude change limited to the 10 kΩ site
questions.explanation: A differential amplifier rejects common signals best when both inputs see similar impedances. A 2 kΩ vs 10 kΩ mismatch degrades common-mode rejection, letting line noise and other interference through and potentially distorting the signal. Imbalance does not improve rejection, does not simply shift frequency, and is not a clean amplitude change confined to one electrode.

questions.stem: To measure a 150 µV spike accurately on a standard channel, the technologist should use a sensitivity of:
options: 2 µV/mm, giving a 75 mm deflection
50 µV/mm, giving a 3 mm deflection
100 µV/mm, giving a 1.5 mm deflection
10 µV/mm, giving a 15 mm deflection
questions.explanation: Deflection = amplitude ÷ sensitivity. At 2 µV/mm the 150 µV spike would be 75 mm and clip or overlap neighbouring channels; at 10 µV/mm it is 15 mm, on-screen and measurable; at 50 or 100 µV/mm it is only 3 or 1.5 mm, too small to measure accurately. Sensitivity must suit the signal.

questions.stem: If a digital EEG system samples at 200 Hz, the highest frequency that can be accurately recorded without aliasing is:
options: 200 Hz
400 Hz
50 Hz
100 Hz
questions.explanation: The Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, so a 200 Hz system can represent activity up to 100 Hz; higher frequencies alias. 200 Hz equals the sampling rate itself, 400 Hz confuses Nyquist with doubling, and 50 Hz is a quarter of the rate, which is overly conservative.

questions.stem: Before applying electrodes, skin preparation should include:
options: Apply paste or gel directly without cleaning the skin
Clean, lightly abrade as needed, then apply paste or gel
Clean with water only, then apply the electrode dry
Wipe with alcohol only and skip the conductive medium
questions.explanation: Skin preparation means cleaning the site, gently abrading if needed to remove oils and dead cells, and then applying conductive paste or gel; this lowers and balances impedance. Skipping cleaning leaves oils that raise impedance, and applying electrodes without a conductive medium gives poor, unstable contact.

questions.stem: Beta activity in a normal awake adult is typically:
options: High amplitude and maximal over the occipital regions
Low amplitude, occipital, and blocked by eye opening
Low amplitude, frontally predominant, enhanced by some drugs
Seen mainly in N3 sleep, absent during the waking state
questions.explanation: Normal waking beta is low in amplitude and frontocentral, and it can increase with anxiety or with medications such as benzodiazepines and barbiturates. High-amplitude occipital activity that blocks with eye opening describes the alpha rhythm, and N3 sleep is dominated by delta, not beta.

questions.stem: Electrode pop artifact is typically caused by:
options: An HFF set too high for the recording conditions
Poor contact or a sudden impedance change at one site
Head movement shifting several electrodes together
Line interference from nearby unshielded equipment
questions.explanation: Electrode pop comes from unstable contact: a sudden impedance change at one electrode produces an abrupt, steep deflection limited to that electrode. Filter settings do not create pops; head movement affects several channels together; line interference produces continuous 60 Hz activity rather than isolated deflections.

questions.stem: When comparing bipolar and referential montages for the same activity, differences in appearance are:
options: A sign of abnormal activity that needs urgent review
A sign of electrode artifact in the referential channels
A sign of an amplifier fault in one of the montages
Expected, and comparing them helps confirm localization
questions.explanation: Each montage displays the same activity differently because channels compare different electrode pairs, so differences are expected; comparing them helps confirm localization and reveal reference contamination. Montage differences by themselves do not indicate abnormal activity, artifact, or an equipment fault.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 0.1 Hz and HFF 15 Hz. This will:
options: Pass about 0.1-15 Hz, attenuating delta
Pass all frequencies without attenuation
Pass about 0.1-15 Hz, attenuating beta
Change amplitude but not frequency content
questions.explanation: A 0.1 Hz LFF passes nearly all slow activity, while a 15 Hz HFF attenuates activity above about 15 Hz, so beta (and higher frequencies) is attenuated. Delta is well above 0.1 Hz and preserved; not all frequencies pass; and filters change frequency content, not just amplitude.

questions.stem: During hyperventilation, the patient should breathe:
options: Shallowly and quickly, about 60 per minute
Normally, with a deep breath every minute
Deeply but slowly, about 6 to 8 per minute
Deeply and regularly, about 20 to 30 per minute
questions.explanation: Effective HV needs deep, regular breaths at roughly 20 to 30 per minute to lower PaCO2. Shallow rapid breathing mostly moves dead-space air; normal breathing with occasional deep breaths does not produce hypocapnia; slow deep breathing at 6 to 8 per minute does not raise minute ventilation enough.

questions.stem: Standard neonatal EEG typically uses:
options: The full 21-electrode adult 10-20 array
A high-density array of 64 or more electrodes
A bipolar pair of 2-4 scalp electrodes only
A reduced array of about 9-11 electrodes
questions.explanation: Standard neonatal EEG uses a reduced, modified 10-20 array of about 9-11 scalp electrodes suited to the small head. The full adult array crowds electrodes and risks salt bridges, high-density arrays are not routine, and two to four electrodes are a limited amplitude-integrated setup rather than a standard neonatal EEG.

questions.stem: Lateral eye movement artifact is best identified by:
options: Opposite-polarity deflections at F7 and F8
Brief high-frequency spikes over the temporalis
In-phase deflections at Fp1 and Fp2 together
Rhythmic slow waves over the occipital leads
questions.explanation: Lateral eye movements shift the corneoretinal dipole sideways, so F7 and F8 (and the frontopolar leads to a lesser degree) show deflections of opposite polarity, reversing with gaze direction; the lateral rectus may add a small spike. In-phase Fp1/Fp2 deflections are blinks; temporalis spikes are muscle; occipital slow waves are not an eye artifact.

questions.stem: For localizing temporal lobe activity, using a temporal reference (T3/T4) may:
options: Put the reference in the field, distorting localization
Improve localization by recording close to the source
Have no effect, as the reference is electrically neutral
Change only the amplitude, not the apparent location
questions.explanation: A reference placed in the same region as the activity (here a temporal reference for temporal activity) is itself active, so it is in the field and can cancel, invert, or spread the activity, distorting localization. Proximity to the source does not help a reference; no scalp reference is truly neutral; and contamination alters apparent location and polarity, not just amplitude.

questions.stem: A time constant of 0.3 seconds corresponds to an LFF cutoff of approximately:
options: 0.3 Hz
3 Hz
questions.explanation: LFF = 1 / (2π × TC). For TC = 0.3 s, LFF = 1 / (2π × 0.3) ≈ 0.53 Hz. 0.3 Hz just repeats the TC value; 3 Hz is roughly 1/TC without the 2π factor; 0.16 Hz corresponds to a 1 s time constant.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation, the flash lamp should be positioned:
options: About 30 cm from the eyes, at eye level
About 1 m from the eyes, above eye level
About 5 cm from the eyes, at eye level
About 30 cm from the eyes, at chin level
questions.explanation: The photic lamp is normally placed about 30 cm in front of the eyes, centred at eye level, so stimulation is consistent between studies. At 1 m the stimulus is weak; at 5 cm it is uncomfortably close and nonstandard; aiming at chin level makes the stimulus uneven.

questions.stem: Theta activity (4-7 Hz) in normal awake adults is typically:
options: High amplitude and continuous over the occipital regions
Absent in children and seen only in older adults
Prominent and rhythmic, blocking with eye opening
Sparse and low amplitude, more prominent in children
questions.explanation: In normal awake adults theta is sparse and low in amplitude (a little may be seen temporally, especially in older adults or drowsiness), and it is much more prominent in children. Continuous high-amplitude occipital activity or a rhythm that blocks with eye opening describes alpha, and theta is more, not less, prominent in children.

questions.stem: When 60 Hz artifact is present, the technologist should FIRST:
options: Turn on the notch filter before anything else
Lower the high-frequency filter to about 15 Hz
Check the ground, impedances, and nearby equipment
Decrease the sensitivity until it is less visible
questions.explanation: The troubleshooting hierarchy addresses the source first: check the ground, impedances, and nearby unshielded equipment. The notch filter only attenuates the 60 Hz band and is a last resort; lowering the HFF also attenuates fast cerebral activity; decreasing sensitivity shrinks everything without fixing the cause.

questions.stem: A spike is high in amplitude in the longitudinal bipolar channels but low in amplitude in the transverse channels through the same region. This MOST suggests that the spike's voltage field:
options: Changes more steeply side-to-side than front-to-back
Is generalized and equal in amplitude in all chains
Changes more steeply front-to-back than side-to-side
Is introduced by an active ear reference electrode
questions.explanation: Bipolar channels record the voltage difference between neighbours, so channels running along the steepest gradient show the largest deflections. Large longitudinal and small transverse deflections mean the potential falls off mainly front-to-back. A steeper side-to-side gradient would do the opposite, an equal generalized field gives small differences in every chain, and bipolar chains have no ear reference.

questions.stem: If LFF is set to 5 Hz, delta activity (1-3 Hz) will be:
options: Markedly attenuated
Preserved at full size
Increased in amplitude
Shifted into theta range
questions.explanation: A 5 Hz LFF (high-pass) attenuates activity below about 5 Hz, so delta at 1-3 Hz is strongly reduced in amplitude. It is not preserved or enhanced, and filtering changes amplitude rather than shifting the frequency of the waves into another band.

questions.stem: REM sleep is characterized by:
options: Sleep spindles and K-complexes
Low-voltage mixed frequencies with REMs
High-amplitude delta over 20% of the epoch
Vertex waves with slow rolling eye movements
questions.explanation: REM sleep shows low-voltage, mixed-frequency activity with rapid eye movements and low chin EMG (atonia). Spindles and K-complexes define N2; high-amplitude delta occupying more than 20% of the epoch defines N3 (AASM criterion); vertex waves with slow rolling eye movements are features of N1 drowsiness.

questions.stem: Periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) during ICU monitoring are characterized by:
options: Periodic sharp waves or spikes over one hemisphere
Continuous rhythmic delta over both hemispheres
Periodic sharp waves synchronous over both sides
Irregular focal slow waves with no fixed interval
questions.explanation: PLEDs (now LPDs) are sharp waves or spikes that repeat at fairly regular intervals and are lateralized to one hemisphere, often with an acute structural lesion. Bilateral synchronous periodic discharges are GPDs, continuous rhythmic delta is rhythmic delta activity, and irregular focal slowing has no periodic structure.

questions.stem: Muscle artifact is best reduced by:
options: Raising the high-frequency filter setting to 70 Hz
Raising the low-frequency filter setting to 5 Hz
Switching to a referential montage to the ears
Helping the patient relax the jaw, face, and neck
questions.explanation: Muscle artifact is reduced at the source by helping the patient relax (open the mouth slightly, reposition the head and neck). Raising the HFF lets more muscle activity through; raising the LFF attenuates slow activity, not EMG; changing the montage does not reduce muscle activity and ear references may add more.

questions.stem: For detecting generalized activity, the technologist should:
options: Use a single longitudinal bipolar montage throughout
Use an average reference montage as the sole display
Use transverse bipolar chains only, not referential
Use referential, then confirm with a bipolar montage
questions.explanation: Generalized activity is best assessed in a referential montage, which shows its amplitude distribution, and then confirmed in a bipolar montage to rule out reference contamination. Bipolar montages alone can cancel in-phase widespread activity; an average reference is contaminated by generalized discharges; and transverse chains alone omit the amplitude field.

questions.stem: Gamma activity (30-100 Hz) will be preserved with HFF set to:
options: 30 Hz
100 Hz
35 Hz
70 Hz
questions.explanation: The HFF (low-pass) must be at or above the top of a band to preserve it, so gamma (30-100 Hz) needs an HFF of about 100 Hz or higher. A standard 70 Hz HFF attenuates the upper gamma range, and 30-35 Hz settings attenuate nearly all of it.

questions.stem: During hyperventilation, the build-up of slow activity typically:
options: Appears within the first 5 seconds
Appears only after HV has stopped
Develops gradually over 1 to 3 minutes
Develops after 8 to 10 minutes of HV
questions.explanation: Build-up develops gradually over the first 1 to 3 minutes of HV as PaCO2 falls. It does not appear within seconds, it is seen during rather than only after overbreathing, and it does not need 8 to 10 minutes of HV, which is longer than a standard trial.

questions.stem: Delta activity (1-3 Hz) in normal awake adults is typically:
options: Absent or minimal during the waking record
Generalized and high amplitude during waking
Prominent over the posterior head regions
Normally present over both temporal regions
questions.explanation: In a normal awake adult, delta is absent or minimal; definite waking delta is abnormal and suggests encephalopathy or focal dysfunction. Generalized high-amplitude delta is seen in N3 sleep or severe encephalopathy, and prominent posterior or temporal delta in an awake adult is an abnormal finding rather than a normal one.

questions.stem: Eye blink artifact is best reduced by:
options: Raising the low-frequency filter for frontal leads
Having the patient keep the eyes gently closed
Increasing the sensitivity of the frontal channels
Switching to a montage without frontopolar leads
questions.explanation: Blink artifact is reduced at the source by having the patient keep the eyes gently closed (a light hand or cotton pad over the lids can help). Raising the LFF only attenuates the deflections and distorts frontal slowing; increasing sensitivity enlarges the artifact; dropping frontopolar leads loses frontal coverage.

questions.stem: In a bipolar montage, a sharp phase reversal (clear maximum at one electrode) suggests:
options: Generalized activity of equal amplitude
An active reference in the montage
Artifact from a single loose electrode
Focal activity with a clear maximum
questions.explanation: A sharp phase reversal shows the activity is maximal at the electrode common to the two adjacent channels, indicating focal activity with clear localization. Generalized activity of equal amplitude does not produce a focal reversal, bipolar chains use no common reference, and a loose electrode produces irregular non-physiological deflections rather than a consistent field.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 1 Hz and HFF 35 Hz. This filter combination will:
options: Pass about 1-35 Hz, attenuating alpha
Pass all frequencies without attenuation
Pass about 1-35 Hz, attenuating faster beta
Attenuate theta while sparing gamma
questions.explanation: A 1 Hz LFF attenuates activity below about 1 Hz and a 35 Hz HFF attenuates activity above about 35 Hz, so faster beta and gamma are attenuated while 1-35 Hz passes. Alpha lies well within the band; not all frequencies pass; and a 35 Hz HFF attenuates gamma rather than sparing it.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation, if the patient shows photic driving at 8 Hz but not at 16 Hz, this:
options: Suggests photosensitivity
Suggests a focal lesion
Suggests an occipital artifact
Is a normal finding
questions.explanation: Photic driving is usually best near the alpha range and need not occur at every flash rate, so driving at 8 Hz but not 16 Hz is normal. Photosensitivity requires epileptiform discharges; a focal lesion is suggested by a consistent asymmetry, not by frequency selectivity; artifact would not follow the flash rate in this way.

questions.stem: Cup (disk) electrodes are typically used for:
options: Routine scalp EEG, applied with paste
Intraoperative work, placed subdermally
Intracranial EEG, placed on the cortex
Neonatal EEG only, held on with tape
questions.explanation: Cup (disk) electrodes are the standard for routine scalp EEG and are attached with conductive paste or gel (or collodion for long-term studies). Subdermal placement describes needle electrodes; cortical placement describes grids and strips; cups are used at all ages, not only in neonates.

questions.stem: In the 10-20 system, electrode C3 is located:
options: On the coronal line, 20% of the ear-to-ear distance left of Cz
On the coronal line, 10% of the ear-to-ear distance left of Cz
On the coronal line, 10% above the left preauricular point
On the midline, 20% of the nasion-inion distance behind Fz
questions.explanation: On the coronal (central) line from preauricular point to preauricular point, T3 lies 10% above the left preauricular point, C3 a further 20%, and Cz at 50%; so C3 is 20% of the ear-to-ear distance left of Cz. 10% left of Cz is C1 in the extended 10-10 system, not a 10-20 position, 10% above the preauricular point is T3, and 20% behind Fz on the midline is Cz.

questions.stem: Proper grounding of EEG equipment is essential for:
options: Reducing noise but not protecting from shock
Protecting from shock but not reducing noise
Protecting against shock and reducing noise
Calibrating amplitude and filter accuracy
questions.explanation: Proper grounding serves both electrical safety (a low-resistance path that protects against shock) and signal quality (reducing noise and supporting common-mode rejection). Options limited to one benefit are incomplete, and grounding does not calibrate amplitude or filter accuracy.

questions.stem: Sudden impedance changes during recording can cause:
options: A uniform amplitude reduction across all channels
A shift of the dominant frequency in that channel
Electrode pops and baseline shifts in that channel
Rhythmic sharp waves recurring at the heart rate
questions.explanation: Sudden impedance changes at an electrode produce electrode pops and baseline shifts and distort the signal in the channels using it; stable, low impedance prevents this. Impedance changes do not reduce all channels uniformly, do not change the frequency of cerebral rhythms, and do not produce heart-rate deflections (ECG artifact).

questions.stem: If reference contamination is suspected in a referential montage, the technologist should:
options: Re-review with another reference or a bipolar montage
Lower the sensitivity until the activity is less visible
Raise the low-frequency filter to reduce the activity
Continue in the same montage and note it in the log
questions.explanation: Suspected reference contamination is confirmed by viewing the activity with a different reference (average, Cz) or a bipolar montage, which has no common reference. Sensitivity and filter changes alter the display without identifying the source, and simply noting it leaves the localization question unresolved.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 0.5 Hz and HFF 70 Hz. This is:
options: Too restrictive for routine EEG
Too permissive for routine EEG
Settings meant for artifact review
Standard routine EEG settings
questions.explanation: An LFF of about 0.5 Hz and an HFF of 70 Hz are standard routine settings that pass roughly 0.5-70 Hz, covering delta through beta. They are neither unduly restrictive nor too permissive, and they are not a special artifact-review setting.

questions.stem: During hyperventilation, the technologist should monitor:
options: Both the patient and the EEG
The EEG tracing alone
The breathing rate alone
The EEG, then the patient after
questions.explanation: During HV the technologist watches the patient (breathing effort, color, distress) and the EEG at the same time, ready to stop if needed. Watching only the tracing or only the breathing misses either clinical distress or EEG changes, and checking the patient only afterward is too late to stop HV safely.

questions.stem: Sleep spindles in children are typically:
options: Absent until adolescence, then appear abruptly
Smaller and briefer than those seen in adults
More prominent and longer in duration than in adults
Identical in amplitude and duration to adults
questions.explanation: Spindles appear by about 2-3 months of age and in infants and children are more prominent and longer in duration than in adults, sometimes asynchronous in infancy. They do not wait until adolescence to appear, they are not smaller or briefer than adult spindles, and they are not identical to the adult pattern.

questions.stem: Sweat artifact is best reduced by:
options: Cooling the room and keeping the patient comfortable
Lowering the high-frequency filter for all channels
Increasing the sensitivity to view the drift better
Switching to an average reference for the recording
questions.explanation: Sweat artifact is addressed at the source: cool the room, uncover or fan the patient, and maintain good electrode contact. Lowering the HFF affects fast activity, not slow drift; increasing sensitivity makes the drift larger; an average reference spreads the artifact rather than reducing it.

questions.stem: When activity appears larger in referential montage than bipolar montage, this suggests:
options: A sharply focal discharge at one electrode
A broad field not focused at a single electrode
Reduced amplifier gain in the bipolar channels
A high-impedance electrode in the bipolar chain
questions.explanation: Neighbouring electrodes in a bipolar chain share widespread in-phase activity, so the differences are small, whereas a referential montage shows the full amplitude; a larger referential display therefore suggests a broad field. A sharply focal discharge shows clearly in bipolar chains with a phase reversal; amplifier gain is the same across montages; and a single high-impedance electrode causes artifact, not this pattern.

questions.stem: A time constant of 0.5 seconds corresponds to an LFF cutoff of approximately:
options: 0.5 Hz
2 Hz
questions.explanation: LFF = 1 / (2π × TC). For TC = 0.5 s, LFF = 1 / (2π × 0.5) ≈ 0.32 Hz. 0.5 Hz just repeats the TC value; 2 Hz is 1/TC without the 2π factor; 0.16 Hz corresponds to a 1 s time constant.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation, flash intensity should be:
options: As bright as the unit allows
Standardized and consistent
As dim as still produces driving
Adjusted to each patient's wishes
questions.explanation: Flash intensity should be standardized and kept consistent (usually a moderate setting) so results are reproducible and comparable. Maximum brightness is uncomfortable and not standard; searching for the dimmest effective setting and adjusting to preference both make studies inconsistent.

questions.stem: For neonatal EEG, electrode placement must account for:
options: Identical adult measurements and fixed 5 cm spacing
Larger relative head size, adding extra electrodes
Smaller head size, using modified 10-20 spacing
Scalp thickness rather than head circumference
questions.explanation: Neonatal placement must account for the smaller head, so a modified 10-20 system with proportionally adjusted spacing (and fewer electrodes) is used. Adult measurements or fixed spacing do not fit the neonatal head, the head is not larger, and placement is based on head measurements rather than scalp thickness.

questions.stem: Movement artifact is best reduced by:
options: Lowering the high-frequency filter for all channels
Decreasing the sensitivity so the deflections shrink
Switching to a referential montage for the study
Making the patient comfortable and securing the leads
questions.explanation: Movement artifact is reduced by making the patient comfortable to minimise movement and by securing electrodes and cables. Filtering attenuates cerebral activity as well; decreasing sensitivity shrinks the whole tracing; a referential montage does not stop movement artifact.

questions.stem: For detecting focal slowing, bipolar montages are useful because:
options: They display the true absolute amplitude of the slowing
They filter out fast activity that obscures the slowing
They show phase reversal or asymmetry that localizes it
They show slowing at a larger amplitude than referential
questions.explanation: Bipolar montages localize focal slowing through phase reversal and side-to-side amplitude asymmetry. They show voltage differences rather than absolute amplitude, they do not act as a filter, and they usually display widespread slowing at a lower amplitude than a referential montage because neighbouring electrodes share it.

questions.stem: If HFF is set to 15 Hz, alpha activity (8-13 Hz) will be:
options: Mostly attenuated, with beta preserved
Mostly preserved, with beta attenuated
Mostly attenuated, along with beta
Mostly preserved, with beta preserved too
questions.explanation: A 15 Hz HFF (low-pass) passes activity below its cutoff, so alpha at 8-13 Hz is mostly preserved (its fastest part slightly reduced by roll-off), while beta at 20-30 Hz lies above the cutoff and is attenuated. Alpha is not mainly attenuated, and beta is not preserved at this setting.

questions.stem: Sleep activation is most effective for:
options: Photoparoxysmal responses
Posterior alpha asymmetry
Focal temporal lobe discharges
Absence seizures in older adults
questions.explanation: Sleep markedly increases focal temporal lobe epileptiform discharges, making it especially effective for them. Photoparoxysmal responses are tested with photic stimulation, alpha asymmetry is assessed in wakefulness, and absence seizures are classically provoked by HV.

questions.stem: K-complexes are most prominent during:
options: REM sleep
N2 sleep (stage 2)
Wakefulness
N3 sleep only
questions.explanation: K-complexes are most prominent during N2 sleep (stage 2). Understanding sleep stage characteristics is critical for sleep activation and interpretation.

questions.stem: ECG artifact is most commonly seen in electrodes:
options: Fp1, Fp2, F7, and F8 at the frontal poles
T3, T4, and the ear electrodes A1 and A2
Fz, Cz, and Pz along the scalp midline
O1 and O2 near the occipital arteries
questions.explanation: ECG artifact reflects the heart's electrical field and is most often seen in the ear (A1/A2) and temporal electrodes, particularly with ear references and in short, wide-necked patients. Frontopolar leads mainly show eye artifact; midline electrodes are least affected; electrodes near scalp arteries show pulse artifact, not ECG artifact.

questions.stem: Average reference montage is MOST suitable for displaying:
options: High-amplitude generalized spike-and-wave
Diffuse high-voltage delta in encephalopathy
Bilateral synchronous vertex sharp waves
Focal activity with a restricted field
questions.explanation: The average reference works best for focal activity with a restricted field, because such activity contributes little to the average and stands out against it. High-amplitude generalized discharges, diffuse high-voltage delta and widespread vertex waves all enter the average, contaminating the reference so that the activity is reduced or appears with inverted polarity in uninvolved channels.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 2 Hz and HFF 30 Hz. This will:
options: Pass about 2-30 Hz, attenuating theta
Pass all frequencies without attenuation
Pass about 2-30 Hz, attenuating slow delta
Attenuate alpha while sparing gamma
questions.explanation: A 2 Hz LFF attenuates activity below about 2 Hz (slow delta) and a 30 Hz HFF attenuates activity above about 30 Hz (fast beta and gamma), so roughly 2-30 Hz passes. Theta and alpha lie within the band; not all frequencies pass; and a 30 Hz HFF attenuates gamma rather than sparing it.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes what the hyperventilation response depends on?
options: Mainly age; effort has little effect on it
Mainly effort; age has little effect on it
Mainly the baseline EEG and nothing else
Age, effort, baseline EEG, and the individual
questions.explanation: The HV response varies with age (strongest in children), effort and cooperation, the baseline EEG, and individual variation. Statements naming a single factor are wrong because each of these factors contributes; for example a well-performed HV in an adult still produces less build-up than in a child.

questions.stem: Generalized periodic discharges (GPDs) during ICU monitoring are characterized by:
options: Periodic sharp waves or spikes over one hemisphere
Periodic sharp waves or spikes over both hemispheres
Continuous rhythmic delta with no fixed interval
Irregular bilateral slowing with no fixed interval
questions.explanation: GPDs are sharp waves or spikes that repeat at fairly regular intervals and are generalized, appearing bilaterally and synchronously. Discharges limited to one hemisphere are LPDs (PLEDs), continuous rhythmic delta is rhythmic delta activity rather than periodic discharges, and irregular slowing has no periodic structure.

questions.stem: Cable artifact (movement of electrode cables) is best reduced by:
options: Securing and bundling the cables so they cannot swing
Lowering the high-frequency filter for all channels
Decreasing the sensitivity of the affected channels
Switching to a montage that omits the affected leads
questions.explanation: Cable artifact comes from leads moving or swinging, so cables should be bundled and secured. Lowering the HFF attenuates cerebral fast activity; decreasing sensitivity only shrinks the artifact; omitting leads loses data instead of fixing the source.

questions.stem: For routine EEG recording, the technologist should:
options: Use one longitudinal bipolar montage throughout
Use several bipolar and referential montages
Use one ear-referenced montage throughout
Use one average reference montage throughout
questions.explanation: A routine EEG is recorded and reviewed in several montages, both bipolar and referential, so findings can be compared and confirmed. Any single montage, whether longitudinal bipolar, ear-referenced or average reference, has blind spots such as end-of-chain maxima or reference contamination.

questions.stem: If LFF is set to 10 Hz, theta activity (4-7 Hz) will be:
options: Preserved at full size
Increased in amplitude
Shifted into alpha range
Markedly attenuated
questions.explanation: A 10 Hz LFF (high-pass) attenuates activity below about 10 Hz, so theta at 4-7 Hz is strongly reduced in amplitude. It is not preserved or enhanced, and filtering changes amplitude rather than shifting waves into another frequency band.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation with eyes closed, normal photic driving is:
options: Usually more prominent
Usually absent
Seen only in children
Seen only above 30 Hz
questions.explanation: Photic driving is usually more prominent with the eyes closed, when the posterior alpha-range rhythm is present. It is not normally absent with eyes closed, it occurs in adults as well as children, and it is best near the alpha range rather than above 30 Hz.

questions.stem: Vertex waves are most prominent during:
options: REM sleep
Light sleep (N1/N2)
Deep sleep (N3)
Wakefulness
questions.explanation: Vertex waves are most prominent during light sleep (N1/N2). Understanding sleep stage characteristics is critical for sleep activation and interpretation.

questions.stem: Glossokinetic artifact is best reduced by:
options: Lowering the HFF for the frontal channels
Decreasing the sensitivity of all channels
Asking the patient to keep the tongue still
Switching to a montage without frontal leads
questions.explanation: Glossokinetic artifact is reduced at the source by asking the patient to keep the tongue still (and not talk or swallow during the sample). Lowering the HFF does not affect these slow waves; decreasing sensitivity shrinks everything; dropping frontal leads loses coverage without stopping the artifact.

questions.stem: When comparing bipolar and referential montages, if activity appears focal in bipolar but widespread in referential, this suggests:
options: A wider field than bipolar shows, or an active reference
Electrode bridging between two adjacent scalp sites
A high-frequency filter set too low in bipolar channels
Amplifier saturation in the referential channels
questions.explanation: Bipolar chains cancel activity shared by neighbouring electrodes, so the field can be wider than the bipolar view suggests; alternatively, an active reference spreads the activity across referential channels. Bridging makes adjacent channels flat or identical, a low HFF setting attenuates fast activity in every montage, and saturation produces clipped, flat-topped waves.

questions.stem: In the 10-20 system, the distance between Fp1 and F3 is:
options: 10% of the nasion-inion distance
20% of the nasion-inion distance
50% of the nasion-inion distance
100% of the nasion-inion distance
questions.explanation: Fp1 to F3 is 20% of the nasion-inion distance. The 10-20 system uses 10% and 20% increments. Understanding 10-20 system measurements is foundational for electrode placement.

questions.stem: After skin preparation, if impedance remains high (>10 kΩ), the technologist should:
options: Increase the gain on that channel
Re-prepare the site and reapply paste
Apply the notch filter to that channel
Accept it if the tracing looks clean
questions.explanation: Persistently high impedance should be fixed at the source: clean and abrade the site more thoroughly and reapply paste or gel. Raising gain or applying the notch filter only changes the display or processing and leaves the poor contact (and its susceptibility to artifact) in place; a clean-looking trace can deteriorate later.

questions.stem: If sensitivity is set to 5 μV/mm, a 50 μV signal will display as:
options: 1 mm deflection
5 mm deflection
10 mm deflection
250 mm deflection
questions.explanation: Deflection = signal amplitude / sensitivity, so 50 μV / 5 μV/mm = 10 mm. 1 mm and 5 mm result from misapplying the ratio, and 250 mm comes from multiplying amplitude by sensitivity instead of dividing.

questions.stem: To accurately record activity up to 50 Hz without aliasing, the minimum sampling rate should be:
options: 100 Hz
50 Hz
25 Hz
200 Hz
questions.explanation: By the Nyquist theorem the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency of interest, so 50 Hz activity needs at least 100 Hz sampling (in practice systems sample well above this). 50 Hz and 25 Hz are too low and would alias, and 200 Hz is adequate but is not the minimum.

questions.stem: Before starting recording, the technologist should:
options: Check a few representative electrodes, then start
Start recording and check impedances at the end
Check that impedances are below 50 kΩ at each site
Check all impedances are balanced and below 5 kΩ
questions.explanation: Before recording, every electrode impedance should be checked and be balanced and below about 5 kΩ for good common-mode rejection and signal quality. Sampling only some electrodes misses bad contacts, checking at the end is too late to fix problems, and 50 kΩ is far too high.

questions.stem: Posterior dominant rhythm (alpha) in normal awake adults should:
options: Attenuate when the eyes open
Increase when the eyes open
Persist unchanged when eyes open
Appear only when the eyes open
questions.explanation: A normal posterior dominant rhythm is reactive: it attenuates (blocks) with eye opening and returns with eye closure. It does not increase or persist unchanged with eyes open, and it is best seen with the eyes closed rather than open; poor reactivity can be a significant finding.

questions.stem: If an electrode shows intermittent artifacts despite acceptable initial impedance, the technologist should:
options: Continue recording, since the initial impedance was acceptable
Lower the high-frequency filter setting for that one channel
Drop that channel from the montage for the rest of the study
Recheck impedance, re-prep, and replace the lead if it persists
questions.explanation: Contact can deteriorate during a study, so intermittent artifact calls for rechecking impedance, re-preparing the electrode, and replacing the electrode or cable if the problem persists. An acceptable initial value does not guarantee later contact; filtering hides rather than fixes the problem; dropping the channel loses data.

questions.stem: A spike phase-reverses at T3 in the left temporal chain (F7-T3, T3-T5) but shows no phase reversal in the transverse chain T3-C3-Cz-C4-T4, where it is largest in T3-C3. This MOST likely indicates:
options: A midline vertex focus at Cz, the center of the transverse chain
Generalized activity of equal amplitude in every chain on the head
A left mid-temporal maximum at T3, the end of the transverse chain
Contamination from an active ear reference near the left temporal lobe
questions.explanation: The longitudinal temporal chain reverses at T3, placing the maximum at T3 front-to-back. T3 is the first electrode of the transverse chain, so there is no lateral neighbour to reverse against; the maximum shows as the largest deflection in the end channel (end-of-chain effect). The spike is lateralized to the left by the chain in which it reverses. A Cz focus would reverse at Cz, generalized activity would not reverse focally, and bipolar chains use no ear reference.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 0.3 Hz and HFF 50 Hz. This will:
options: Pass about 0.3-50 Hz, attenuating gamma
Pass about 0.3-50 Hz, attenuating delta
Pass all frequencies without attenuation
Attenuate beta while sparing gamma
questions.explanation: A 0.3 Hz LFF attenuates only very slow activity below about 0.3 Hz and a 50 Hz HFF attenuates activity above about 50 Hz, so gamma is attenuated while delta through beta passes. Delta is well above 0.3 Hz; not all frequencies pass; and a 50 Hz HFF preserves beta while attenuating gamma.

questions.stem: If a patient cannot maintain adequate hyperventilation technique, the technologist should:
options: Continue and accept the weak effort
Coach and demonstrate the technique
Skip HV and move on to photic
Stop and reschedule the full study
questions.explanation: Coaching and demonstrating the breathing usually improves effort; if the patient still cannot cooperate, an alternative activation may be used and the attempt and its limits documented. Accepting a weak effort lowers yield, skipping HV without trying to help loses the activation, and rescheduling the whole study is unnecessary.

questions.stem: In neonatal EEG, the background pattern changes with:
options: Birth weight and gestational age
Behavioral state alone, not age
Chronological age since birth only
Conceptional age and behavioral state
questions.explanation: The neonatal background matures with conceptional (postmenstrual) age, which is gestational age plus postnatal age, and it also differs by behavioral state (wakefulness, active sleep, quiet sleep). Gestational age or chronological age alone misses part of the maturity estimate, state alone ignores maturation, and birth weight is not the determinant.

questions.stem: Eye movement artifacts are caused by:
options: Contraction of the extraocular muscles
The corneoretinal potential of the eye
Frontal lobe activity during eye movement
Electrode motion from eyelid movement
questions.explanation: The eye is a dipole with the cornea positive relative to the retina; when the eye moves, this corneoretinal potential changes at nearby electrodes. Extraocular muscles contribute only small spikes; the deflections are not cerebral; eyelid movement modifies but does not generate the main potential.

questions.stem: For localizing occipital activity, using an occipital reference (O1/O2) may:
options: Improve localization by recording close to the source
Have no effect, since the reference is electrically neutral
Change only the amplitude and not the apparent location
Place the reference in the field and distort localization
questions.explanation: An occipital reference used for occipital activity is itself active, so it lies in the field and can cancel, invert, or spread the activity, distorting localization. Being close to the source does not help a reference; no scalp reference is truly neutral; and contamination changes apparent location and polarity, not just amplitude.

questions.stem: A time constant of 0.16 seconds corresponds to an LFF cutoff of approximately:
options: 1.0 Hz
1.6 Hz
6 Hz
questions.explanation: LFF = 1 / (2π × TC). For TC = 0.16 s, LFF = 1 / (2π × 0.16) ≈ 1.0 Hz. 0.16 Hz just repeats the TC value; 1.6 Hz corresponds to a 0.1 s time constant; 6 Hz is roughly 1/TC without the 2π factor.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation, if photic driving occurs at multiple frequencies (e.g., 8, 10, 12 Hz), this is:
options: A photoparoxysmal response
A sign of encephalopathy
A normal response
Photomyogenic artifact
questions.explanation: Driving at several flash rates in and near the alpha range (e.g. 8, 10, 12 Hz) is normal. A photoparoxysmal response requires epileptiform discharges; encephalopathy is shown by background slowing; photomyogenic artifact is frontal muscle activity, not occipital rhythmic driving.

questions.stem: N3 sleep (deep sleep, slow-wave sleep) is characterized by:
options: Low-voltage mixed-frequency activity with sawtooth waves
Sleep spindles and K-complexes on a theta background
Diffuse alpha that attenuates with eye opening
High-amplitude delta in more than 20% of the epoch
questions.explanation: N3 (slow-wave sleep) is scored when high-amplitude (over 75 µV) slow waves of 0.5-2 Hz occupy more than 20% of the epoch. Low-voltage mixed activity with sawtooth waves is REM, spindles and K-complexes on a theta background define N2, and reactive alpha is the waking posterior rhythm.

questions.stem: If electrode cables are moving during recording, this can cause:
options: A uniform drop in amplitude in all channels
A shift in the dominant posterior frequency
Movement artifact and an unstable baseline
Rhythmic activity at the heart rate in ear leads
questions.explanation: Swinging or moving cables create movement artifact and baseline instability and distort the signal, so cables should be secured. They do not uniformly reduce amplitude or change the posterior dominant rhythm, and heart-rate activity in the ear leads is ECG artifact.

questions.stem: For detecting subtle amplitude asymmetries, the technologist should:
options: Use referential, then confirm with bipolar
Rely on a transverse bipolar montage alone
Rely on an average reference montage alone
Rely on a longitudinal bipolar montage alone
questions.explanation: Referential montages show amplitude differences between homologous regions most directly, so they are used to detect subtle asymmetries, which are then confirmed in bipolar montages. Bipolar montages alone show differences between neighbours and can mask amplitude asymmetry, and an average reference alone can be distorted by large activity entering the average.

questions.stem: If LFF is set to 1 Hz and HFF is set to 15 Hz, alpha activity (8-13 Hz) will be:
options: Markedly attenuated
Increased in amplitude
Largely preserved
Shifted into beta
questions.explanation: With LFF 1 Hz and HFF 15 Hz the passband is roughly 1-15 Hz, so alpha at 8-13 Hz is largely preserved (its fastest part slightly reduced by roll-off near 15 Hz). It is not markedly attenuated or enhanced, and filters do not shift waves into another frequency band.

questions.stem: After stopping hyperventilation, the build-up of slow activity typically:
options: Stops within 1 or 2 seconds
Lasts for 10 or more minutes
Peaks 1 to 2 minutes after HV
Fades over about 1 to 2 minutes
questions.explanation: After HV ends, the slowing fades gradually over roughly 1 to 2 minutes as PaCO2 returns to normal. It does not stop instantly, slowing persisting much longer is unexpected and may be abnormal (e.g. hypoglycemia, moyamoya), and build-up peaks during HV, not afterward.

questions.stem: During ICU continuous EEG, rhythmic delta activity (RDA) is best described as:
options: Rhythmic delta, generalized or lateralized, ictal or interictal
Irregular polymorphic delta with no repetitive rhythmic form
A benign drowsiness rhythm with no clinical significance
Periodic sharp waves separated by relatively flat intervals
questions.explanation: RDA is repetitive delta of uniform morphology with no interval between waves; per ACNS 2021 it may be generalized (GRDA) or lateralized (LRDA) and, depending on context and evolution, may be ictal or interictal. Irregular delta is polymorphic slowing, RDA in the ICU is not a benign drowsy rhythm, and periodic sharp waves with intervals are periodic discharges.

questions.stem: Muscle artifact in temporal regions is often caused by:
options: Jaw clenching or temporalis muscle tension
Lateral eye movements toward that side
Arterial pulsation of the temporal artery
Tongue movement during speech or swallowing
questions.explanation: Temporal muscle artifact is usually from jaw clenching, teeth grinding, or temporalis tension. Lateral eye movements produce F7/F8 slow deflections; temporal artery pulsation produces pulse artifact; tongue movement produces slow glossokinetic waves rather than fast muscle activity.

questions.stem: When activity shows clear phase reversal in bipolar but appears equal in all channels in referential, this suggests:
options: Generalized activity of equal amplitude everywhere
A focal discharge with an active reference electrode
Artifact from a loose electrode in the bipolar chain
An amplifier fault affecting the referential channels
questions.explanation: A clear phase reversal in bipolar chains shows a focal discharge; if the referential montage shows it equally in every channel, the reference electrode is picking it up and spreading it. Truly generalized activity would not give a focal reversal, a loose electrode gives a non-physiological artifact, and an amplifier fault would not mimic a field.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 0.1 Hz and HFF 100 Hz. This will:
options: Pass about 0.1-15 Hz, a narrow band
Attenuate nearly all cerebral activity
Change amplitude but not frequency content
Pass about 0.1-100 Hz, a very wide band
questions.explanation: A 0.1 Hz LFF and a 100 Hz HFF pass roughly 0.1-100 Hz, a very wide bandpass that includes slow activity and gamma. A 0.1-15 Hz band would need a 15 Hz HFF; this setting preserves most cerebral activity; and filters change frequency content, not only amplitude.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation with eyes open, photic driving is typically:
options: Usually less prominent
Usually more prominent
Usually unchanged
Seen only in children
questions.explanation: With the eyes open the posterior rhythm is attenuated, so photic driving is usually less prominent (sometimes absent) than with eyes closed. It is not usually more prominent or unchanged, and driving is not limited to children.

questions.stem: Sleep spindles typically have a frequency of:
options: 4-7 Hz
1-3 Hz
questions.explanation: Sleep spindles are 11-15 Hz rhythmic activity. Understanding normal sleep graphoelements and their characteristics is critical for sleep activation and interpretation.

questions.stem: If an electrode shows baseline drift (slow, irregular movement), this may indicate:
options: Normal drowsiness slowing in that region
Focal polymorphic delta from a structural lesion
A high-frequency filter that is set too low
Poor contact, unstable impedance, or sweat
questions.explanation: Slow, irregular drift in a single electrode suggests poor contact, unstable impedance, or sweat. Drowsiness changes are diffuse, not confined to one electrode; focal polymorphic delta has a field over neighbouring electrodes; the HFF setting affects fast activity, not slow drift.

questions.stem: For routine EEG, switching between montages during recording allows:
options: Shortening the recording by skipping activation steps
Improving electrode impedance at the recorded sites
Comparing views to confirm localization and artifact
Raising the signal-to-noise ratio of every channel
questions.explanation: Reviewing the same activity in several montages lets findings be compared, localization be confirmed, and artifact be recognized. Montage changes do not replace activation procedures, do not change electrode impedance (which depends on contact), and do not change the recorded signal-to-noise ratio.

questions.stem: If HFF is set to 20 Hz, beta activity (20-30 Hz) will be:
options: Partly attenuated, more toward 30 Hz
Passed unchanged, as 20 Hz is in band
Boosted in amplitude near the cutoff
Shifted down into the alpha range
questions.explanation: An HFF (low-pass) of 20 Hz reduces activity at the cutoff by about 30% and attenuates progressively more at higher frequencies, so beta at 20-30 Hz is partly attenuated, increasingly toward 30 Hz. It is not passed unchanged, a standard HFF does not boost amplitude, and filters do not shift waves into another frequency band.

questions.stem: Sleep deprivation enhances diagnostic yield by:
options: Preventing sleep during the recording
Promoting sleep and activating discharges
Reducing muscle and movement artifacts
Shortening the time needed for hookup
questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation raises yield by making sleep during the study more likely and by activating epileptiform discharges. It does not prevent sleep, and any effect on artifact or hookup time is incidental rather than the reason it is used.

questions.stem: In the 10-20 system, electrode P3 is located:
options: On the coronal line, 20% of the ear-to-ear distance left of Cz
On the left parasagittal line, midway between C3 and O1
On the left temporal line, midway between T3 and O1
On the midline, 20% of the nasion-inion distance behind Cz
questions.explanation: P3 lies on the left parasagittal line (Fp1-F3-C3-P3-O1), posterior to C3 and midway between C3 and O1. 20% left of Cz on the coronal line is C3, midway between T3 and O1 on the temporal line is T5, and 20% behind Cz on the midline is Pz.

questions.stem: If impedances are balanced (all <5 kΩ) but one electrode pair shows different amplitudes, this suggests:
options: An impedance-related artifact
An amplifier channel fault
A filter mismatch artifact
A true amplitude difference
questions.explanation: With all impedances low and balanced, an impedance artifact is unlikely, so an amplitude difference between channels most likely reflects real cerebral asymmetry. An amplifier fault or a filter mismatch between channels is possible but less likely and would usually be suggested by a calibration abnormality rather than by impedance checks.

questions.stem: If a 100 μV spike is clipping (going off-screen) at sensitivity 5 μV/mm, the technologist should:
options: Raise sensitivity to 3 μV/mm
Raise the low-frequency filter
Lower sensitivity to 10 μV/mm
Lower the high-frequency filter
questions.explanation: Clipping means the display sensitivity is too high for the signal: at 5 μV/mm a 100 μV spike needs 20 mm. Changing to 10 μV/mm (lower sensitivity) halves the deflection and brings it on-screen. Going to 3 μV/mm makes the clipping worse, and filter changes alter frequency content rather than fixing display scaling.

questions.stem: If a digital EEG system samples at 500 Hz, the highest frequency that can be accurately recorded is:
options: 500 Hz
250 Hz
125 Hz
questions.explanation: The Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, so a 500 Hz system can represent activity up to 250 Hz. 500 Hz equals the sampling rate itself, 1000 Hz confuses Nyquist with doubling, and 125 Hz is a quarter of the rate and underestimates what can be recorded.

questions.stem: The ground electrode in an EEG recording serves MAINLY to:
options: Give the amplifiers a common point that aids noise rejection
Act as the reference electrode for referential montages
Carry fault current to earth to prevent patient shock
Lower the impedance of the surrounding scalp electrodes
questions.explanation: The patient ground (isolated common) gives the differential amplifiers a common point, which supports common-mode rejection and reduces interference. It is not the recording reference, and in modern isolated systems it is not a path to earth for fault current; the patient should be connected to only one ground to avoid ground loops. It does not change other electrodes' impedance.

questions.stem: Beta activity may be increased by:
options: Phenytoin and carbamazepine
Hypothyroidism and hypothermia
Benzodiazepines and barbiturates
Hyperventilation and deep sleep
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates are the classic causes of increased (often frontally predominant) beta activity. Phenytoin and carbamazepine tend to produce mild slowing rather than excess beta, hypothyroidism and hypothermia slow the background, and hyperventilation and deep sleep increase slow activity, not beta.

questions.stem: If multiple electrodes show high impedance (>10 kΩ), the technologist should:
options: Continue, as modern amplifiers tolerate high values
Re-prepare each affected electrode before going on
Increase the amplifier gain to restore amplitude
Turn on the notch filter to handle the extra noise
questions.explanation: Several high-impedance electrodes call for systematic re-preparation of each affected site before continuing. High impedance still increases noise and line pickup even with modern amplifiers; increasing gain enlarges noise too; the notch filter only attenuates 60 Hz and does not correct poor contact.

questions.stem: When comparing montages, if activity appears in only one channel in referential but shows phase reversal in bipolar, this suggests:
options: An active reference contaminating the montage
Artifact from a single high-impedance electrode
A widespread discharge with a broad field
A focal discharge that is well localized
questions.explanation: Activity confined to one referential channel shows a restricted field, and a phase reversal at the same electrode in bipolar chains confirms it, indicating a well-localized focal discharge. An active reference would spread the activity across many referential channels, a high-impedance electrode gives a non-physiological artifact, and a broad field would appear in several channels.

questions.stem: A technologist uses LFF 0.5 Hz and HFF 70 Hz. This is appropriate for:
options: Artifact review only
Routine EEG recording
Chin EMG in sleep studies
Recording infraslow (DC) shifts
questions.explanation: LFF 0.5 Hz and HFF 70 Hz are standard settings for routine EEG, passing about 0.5-70 Hz (delta through beta). They are not limited to artifact review; chin EMG uses a much higher LFF (about 10 Hz) to emphasize muscle activity; and a 0.5 Hz LFF attenuates infraslow/DC activity, which needs a much lower LFF or DC recording.

questions.stem: During hyperventilation, a patient becomes markedly lightheaded, unsteady, and says she feels faint. The technologist should:
options: Continue HV and document the symptoms
Shorten HV by 1 minute and document it
Stop HV, let her recover, and document it
Coach faster breathing and document it
questions.explanation: Marked lightheadedness with a feeling of faintness is distress, so HV is stopped, the patient allowed to recover, and the response documented. Continuing or merely shortening HV keeps provoking the symptoms, and faster breathing would worsen hypocapnia.

questions.stem: In neonatal EEG, sleep states are typically classified as:
options: N1, N2, N3, and REM, as in adults
Active, quiet, and indeterminate sleep
Light, deep, and slow-wave sleep
Wake and sleep without further stages
questions.explanation: Neonatal sleep is classified as active sleep (the precursor of REM), quiet sleep (the precursor of NREM), and indeterminate or transitional sleep. Adult N1-N3/REM staging is not applied in the neonatal period, "light, deep, slow-wave" is not a neonatal scheme, and neonatal sleep is subdivided rather than scored as one state.

questions.stem: Eye blink artifact shows positive deflection in Fp1 because:
options: The positive cornea rotates up toward Fp1
The eyelid muscles generate a positive spike
The frontal cortex discharges during a blink
The negative retina rotates up toward Fp1
questions.explanation: During a blink the eyes roll upward (Bell's phenomenon), bringing the positively charged cornea closer to Fp1, which becomes positive. Eyelid muscle activity is small and fast; the deflection is not cerebral; the retina is the negative pole and moves away from Fp1.

questions.stem: For detecting midline activity, using Cz as reference may:
options: Cause contamination if the activity involves Cz
Improve detection by recording close to the source
Have no effect, as the vertex is electrically neutral
Change only the amplitude, not the apparent location
questions.explanation: If midline activity involves Cz, a Cz reference is in the field: it is active and can cancel or invert the activity, giving misleading localization. Proximity to the source does not help a reference, the vertex is not electrically neutral, and contamination alters apparent location and polarity, not just amplitude.

questions.stem: A time constant of 2.0 seconds corresponds to an LFF cutoff of approximately:
options: 2.0 Hz
0.5 Hz
questions.explanation: LFF = 1 / (2π × TC). For TC = 2.0 s, LFF = 1 / (2π × 2.0) ≈ 0.08 Hz; a very long time constant preserves very slow activity. 2.0 Hz just repeats the TC value; 0.5 Hz is 1/TC without the 2π factor; 0.32 Hz corresponds to a 0.5 s time constant.

questions.stem: During photic stimulation, if photic driving is absent at all frequencies, this:
options: Suggests photosensitivity
Suggests a stimulator fault
Suggests bilateral lesions
May be a normal finding
questions.explanation: Some normal people show little or no photic driving, so its absence may be normal. Photosensitivity requires epileptiform discharges; a stimulator fault would be found by checking the lamp, not inferred from the EEG; symmetric absence of driving does not indicate bilateral lesions.

questions.stem: REM sleep is characterized by:
options: Sleep spindles and K-complexes
Low-voltage, mixed-frequency activity, rapid eye movements, muscle atonia, sawtooth waves
Only delta waves
Only alpha activity
questions.explanation: REM sleep shows low-voltage, mixed-frequency activity, rapid eye movements, muscle atonia, and sawtooth waves. Understanding sleep stages is critical for sleep activation.

questions.stem: If electrode cables are creating artifacts during recording, the technologist should:
options: Lower the high-frequency filter for all channels
Decrease the sensitivity until the artifact shrinks
Secure the cables and reposition them if needed
Switch to a montage without the affected leads
questions.explanation: Cable artifact is fixed at the source by securing cables and repositioning them if needed. Lowering the HFF attenuates cerebral activity; decreasing sensitivity only shrinks the artifact; dropping leads loses data.

questions.stem: For detecting temporal lobe activity, the technologist should use:
options: A longitudinal bipolar montage alone
An ipsilateral ear reference alone
Both referential and bipolar montages
A transverse bipolar montage alone
questions.explanation: Temporal activity is assessed with referential montages, which show amplitude, and bipolar montages, which confirm localization through phase reversal. A single bipolar montage can miss end-of-chain maxima, and an ipsilateral ear reference is often active for temporal discharges because the ear lies close to the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: If LFF is set to 3 Hz and HFF is set to 30 Hz, theta activity (4-7 Hz) will be:
options: Markedly attenuated
Increased in amplitude
Shifted into alpha
Largely preserved
questions.explanation: With LFF 3 Hz and HFF 30 Hz the passband is roughly 3-30 Hz, so theta at 4-7 Hz is largely preserved (its slowest part slightly reduced by roll-off near 3 Hz). It is not markedly attenuated or enhanced, and filters do not shift waves into another frequency band.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes factors affecting the hyperventilation response?
options: Age, effort, baseline EEG, and medications
Mainly age; medications have no effect
Mainly effort; age has little effect
Mainly medications; age has no real effect
questions.explanation: The HV response is influenced by age, effort/cooperation, the baseline EEG, medications, and individual variation (blood glucose also matters). Statements that single out one factor and dismiss the others are wrong, because each of these contributes.

questions.stem: During ICU continuous EEG, ictal patterns that evolve in frequency and amplitude suggest:
options: Movement artifact
Interictal activity
Seizure activity
Sleep transients
questions.explanation: Evolution in frequency, amplitude, or field is the hallmark of an ictal pattern, so an evolving rhythmic pattern suggests a seizure. Artifact usually correlates with movement and lacks a cerebral field, interictal discharges are brief and do not evolve, and sleep transients are stereotyped and non-evolving.

questions.stem: A technologist accidentally emails an EEG report to the wrong patient. The report contains protected health information (PHI). What must the technologist do?
options: Ask the recipient to delete it; no report is needed after that
Notify the supervisor, document it, and follow breach protocol
Apologize to both patients by phone and document the call
Delete the sent copy and notify the supervisor only if asked
questions.explanation: Misdirected PHI is a potential breach: notify the supervisor/privacy officer, document it, and follow the facility breach protocol, which may require patient notification without unreasonable delay and within 60 days. Deletion by the recipient, an apology, or reporting only if asked do not satisfy breach procedures.

questions.stem: A patient asks the technologist to interpret their EEG results and explain what the findings mean for their diagnosis. The technologist should:
options: Explain that the neurologist interprets results
Give a brief, general summary of what was seen
Explain the findings if the patient insists
Direct them to reliable online EEG resources
questions.explanation: Technologists record and describe technical observations; interpretation and diagnosis are the interpreting physician's responsibility, so the patient is told the results will come from the neurologist. A brief summary or an explanation on request still conveys an interpretation outside the technologist's scope, and online resources cannot explain this patient's findings.

questions.stem: In a technical report, the technologist should describe epileptiform discharges as:
options: 'Seizure activity' or 'an epileptic seizure pattern'
'Abnormal brain waves' or 'irritable cortex'
'Seizure-like activity' or 'epileptic spikes'
'Epileptiform discharges' or 'spike-and-wave complexes'
questions.explanation: Technical reports use descriptive waveform terms such as 'epileptiform discharges' or 'spike-and-wave complexes', which do not imply a diagnosis. 'Seizure activity' and 'epileptic' terms are clinical/diagnostic labels; 'abnormal brain waves' is too vague; 'irritable cortex' and 'seizure-like activity' are interpretive and imprecise.

questions.stem: During routine equipment check, the technologist notices that calibration signals are consistently about 15% lower than expected across all channels. The technologist should:
options: Take it out of service and use backup equipment
Apply a 15% correction when the study is read
Adjust the sensitivity to offset the difference
Keep using it and recheck at the next service
questions.explanation: A consistent 15% calibration error is well outside the usual ±5% tolerance, so displayed amplitudes are inaccurate; the equipment is tagged out of service, the supervisor is told, and backup equipment is used until it is repaired. Correcting values at reading time or adjusting sensitivity hides rather than fixes the fault, and waiting for the next scheduled service keeps inaccurate equipment in use.

questions.stem: A technologist posts on social media: 'Just finished an interesting EEG case today - patient had some really unusual patterns!' without identifying information. This is:
options: Unacceptable - posting about cases breaches confidentiality
Acceptable, since no identifying details at all were shared
Acceptable if posted from a personal account while off duty
Acceptable if the account is set to private, friends-only
questions.explanation: Discussing patient cases on social media breaches confidentiality and professional boundaries even without identifiers, since date and location context can identify patients. A personal account, off-duty posting, or private settings do not change that.

questions.stem: Before starting an EEG, the technologist notices a frayed power cord on the amplifier. The technologist should:
options: Continue if the amplifier still works normally
Tag it out of service and use backup equipment
Tape the frayed area and continue the study
Continue, keeping the cord away from the bed
questions.explanation: A frayed power cord is an electrical safety hazard, so the equipment is tagged out of service, the supervisor notified and backup equipment used. Normal operation does not make damaged insulation safe, tape is not an approved repair, and keeping the cord away from the bed does not remove the shock or fire risk.

questions.stem: A family member calls and asks for information about a patient's EEG results. The technologist should:
options: Verify the caller is family, then give only general findings
Verify the caller knows the patient's birth date, then share
Verify identity and authorization before releasing any PHI
Refer the call to the physician only if the news is bad
questions.explanation: Before releasing PHI, confirm both identity and authorization (patient consent or legal authority). Being family is not authorization; knowing a birth date confirms nothing about authority; selective referral based on the news is inappropriate, and technologists do not release results.

questions.stem: A technologist documents: 'The EEG shows improvement compared to previous study, suggesting the medication is working.' This documentation is:
options: Appropriate - comparing with prior studies is a tech duty
Inappropriate - it adds a clinical judgment of drug effect
Appropriate if the reading doctor later agrees with it
Appropriate when the improvement is clearly visible
questions.explanation: Technologists describe findings objectively; saying the medication "is working" is a clinical interpretation outside their scope. Noting factual differences from a prior study can be helpful, but judging improvement and drug effect is interpretive; later physician agreement or an obvious change does not make the technologist the one entitled to make that judgment.

questions.stem: A technologist needs to use a cleaning solution for equipment disinfection. The technologist should:
options: Choose the strongest disinfectant available
Review its SDS for use, hazards, and PPE needs
Ask a colleague which product they prefer
Dilute it with water to reduce any hazard
questions.explanation: Before using a chemical, the technologist reviews its Safety Data Sheet (SDS/MSDS) for correct use, hazards, and PPE. The strongest product is not necessarily appropriate, a colleague’s preference is not a hazard assessment, and diluting off-label may make the product ineffective.

questions.stem: During an EEG, a patient has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The technologist should:
options: Insert a bite block between the teeth to protect the tongue
Protect the head, time it, and call for help if over 5 min
Hold the limbs firmly to prevent injury from jerking
Call for help only if it lasts longer than 10 minutes
questions.explanation: During a tonic-clonic seizure the technologist protects the patient from injury, cushions the head, times the seizure, supports the airway, and activates emergency response if it lasts beyond 5 minutes (possible status epilepticus). Nothing is placed in the mouth, limbs are not restrained, and waiting 10 minutes delays treatment.

questions.stem: A technologist overhears colleagues discussing a patient's case in the hallway where others can hear. The technologist should:
options: Join in, since all staff are part of the care team
Let it go if no patients are present in the hallway
Step in only if the details discussed are sensitive
Remind them to move the discussion to a private area
questions.explanation: Patient information should be discussed only in private areas; a brief reminder protects confidentiality. Joining in spreads the disclosure; visitors and other staff can still overhear even without patients present; all PHI is protected, not only sensitive details.

questions.stem: A technologist documents: 'The EEG is consistent with temporal lobe epilepsy.' This documentation is:
options: Inappropriate - it states a diagnosis, not the pattern seen
Appropriate - temporal spikes define this epilepsy type
Appropriate when the spike pattern is a classic one
Appropriate if the patient already carries that diagnosis
questions.explanation: Technologists describe what they see (for example, 'left temporal spikes') and leave diagnostic conclusions such as 'temporal lobe epilepsy' to the interpreting physician. Temporal spikes support but do not by themselves establish a syndrome; a classic pattern or an existing diagnosis still does not make a diagnostic statement part of the technologist's role.

questions.stem: Equipment preventive maintenance should be performed:
options: Whenever a fault or failure is first noticed
Only when the warranty requires a service visit
On the schedule set by manufacturer and facility
Whenever staff have spare time between studies
questions.explanation: Preventive maintenance is done on a regular schedule based on manufacturer recommendations and facility policy, so problems are found before equipment fails. Waiting for a fault is corrective, not preventive, maintenance; tying it to warranty visits or spare time makes it irregular and unreliable.

questions.stem: HIPAA's 'minimum necessary' rule means:
options: Share PHI freely with anyone on the hospital staff
Access and share only the PHI needed for your job duties
Share PHI only with licensed clinical staff members
Withhold PHI unless the patient signs a release form
questions.explanation: The minimum necessary standard limits access, use and disclosure to the least PHI needed for one's job duties. Hospital employment does not create a need; the rule is need-based rather than licensure-based; and it does not require a signed release for treatment, payment, or operations.

questions.stem: Standard precautions for infection control include:
options: Hand hygiene alone for patients without symptoms
PPE only for patients with a known infection
Hand hygiene, PPE as needed, safe equipment care
Gloves and masks only in ICU or isolation rooms
questions.explanation: Standard precautions combine hand hygiene, personal protective equipment selected for the anticipated exposure, and safe handling and cleaning of equipment, and they apply to every patient. Hand hygiene alone is incomplete, and limiting PPE to known infections or particular units misses unrecognized carriers.

questions.stem: A physician asks a technologist to interpret an EEG and provide a diagnosis. The technologist should:
options: Give an interpretation since a doctor requested it
Describe technical observations but defer the diagnosis
Offer a diagnosis only if the pattern is clear-cut
Ask a senior technologist to write the diagnosis
questions.explanation: Technologists provide technical descriptions; interpretation and diagnosis belong to the physician even when a physician asks. A doctor’s request does not expand scope, a clear-cut pattern does not make diagnosis appropriate, and a senior technologist has the same scope limits.

questions.stem: A technologist recognizes a patient from a previous study and mentions details from that study to the patient. This is:
options: Acceptable, because it builds rapport with the patient
Acceptable, provided the earlier findings were normal
Inappropriate unless the patient raises it; keep boundaries
Acceptable, as long as no one else is in the room
questions.explanation: Raising details of a previous study is potentially inappropriate: the patient may not remember it or may not want it discussed, so the technologist keeps professional boundaries and focuses on the current study unless the patient brings it up. Building rapport does not justify volunteering prior findings, normal results are still private health information, and the absence of bystanders does not address the patient's own wishes.

questions.stem: A technologist documents: 'The EEG shows resolution of previous abnormalities, indicating successful treatment.' This documentation is:
options: Appropriate - comparison with prior EEGs is expected
Appropriate if the change from before is clearly obvious
Inappropriate - treatment response is a clinical judgment
Appropriate if the patient's symptoms also improved
questions.explanation: "Successful treatment" is a clinical interpretation outside technologist scope; the technical description should state the current findings objectively.
