Factual comparison with prior studies is fine, but concluding treatment success is not, regardless of how obvious the change is or whether symptoms also improved.

questions.stem: OSHA electrical safety requirements for EEG equipment include:
options: Grounding, cord and plug inspection, careful handling
Requirements that apply only to high-voltage gear
Rules that apply only within hospital settings
Annual inspection by the manufacturer only
questions.explanation: OSHA electrical requirements include proper grounding, inspection of cords and plugs, and safe handling of electrical equipment, which apply to EEG equipment in any setting. They are not limited to high-voltage equipment or to hospitals, and a yearly manufacturer inspection does not replace routine checks.

questions.stem: During an EEG, a patient becomes unresponsive with no pulse. The technologist should:
options: Activate a code and begin CPR if trained to do so
Keep recording first to capture the event on EEG
Check impedances to rule out an artifact first
Call for help if no recovery within one minute
questions.explanation: Pulselessness means cardiac arrest: activate the emergency response (Code Blue) and begin CPR if trained. Recording may continue only if it does not interfere with care, but it is not the priority; checking impedances or waiting a minute delays life-saving treatment.

questions.stem: A technologist leaves a patient's EEG report visible on a computer screen in an unsecured area. This is:
options: A HIPAA violation; unattended screens must be locked
Acceptable if the area is usually staff-only
Acceptable if the results are still unsigned
Acceptable if the screen dims after a few minutes
questions.explanation: PHI must be protected from unauthorized access, so a screen showing a report must be locked or logged out whenever it is left unattended. A usually staff-only area can still be entered by visitors or staff without a need to know, unsigned results are still PHI, and a screen that merely dims leaves the record exposed until it times out.

questions.stem: A technologist documents: 'The EEG pattern is diagnostic of absence epilepsy.' This documentation is:
options: Appropriate - 3 Hz spike-and-wave is pathognomonic for it
Appropriate if the pattern is textbook and fully classic
Appropriate if a typical absence was seen clinically
Inappropriate - it names a syndrome instead of the pattern
questions.explanation: The technologist should describe the pattern (for example, 'generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave') and leave the diagnosis of absence epilepsy to the interpreting physician. Even a classic pattern or an observed clinical absence does not make a syndrome diagnosis part of the technical report, and the pattern is strongly associated with, not by itself diagnostic of, the syndrome.

questions.stem: Equipment calibration checks should be performed:
options: Only after the equipment has been repaired
Once a month during preventive maintenance
Only when recorded amplitudes look abnormal
Routinely, typically at the start of each study
questions.explanation: Calibration is checked routinely according to lab policy, typically daily or at the start (and often end) of each recording, so amplitude and filter accuracy are confirmed for every study. Checking only after repairs, only monthly, or only when amplitudes look wrong would let calibration faults go unnoticed in many recordings.

questions.stem: A technologist discusses a patient's case with a friend who is also a healthcare worker but not involved in the patient's care. This is:
options: Acceptable, as the friend is bound by HIPAA too
Acceptable if the friend agrees to keep it private
Acceptable if the patient's name is left out
A breach; the friend has no role in the patient's care
questions.explanation: PHI may be shared only with people involved in the patient's care (or as otherwise authorized); a healthcare worker outside that care has no need to know, regardless of profession. Being a HIPAA-covered worker does not create a right to access, a promise of secrecy does not authorize disclosure, and leaving out the name does not de-identify a case when other details can identify the patient.

questions.stem: Personal protective equipment (PPE) should be used:
options: When a patient has a confirmed infection
When working in ICU or isolation settings
When the patient or family requests it
Whenever exposure to body fluids is expected
questions.explanation: Under standard precautions, PPE is selected according to the anticipated exposure to blood or body fluids (and per facility protocol), not according to known diagnoses. Waiting for a confirmed infection misses undiagnosed carriers, the care setting does not determine exposure, and patient requests are not the basis for PPE use.

questions.stem: A technologist notices a potential error in a physician's interpretation. The technologist should:
options: Raise it privately with the reader or a supervisor
Correct it openly at the next team conference
Add a note to the chart without discussing it
Leave it, since interpretation is outside your role
questions.explanation: A possible interpretation error is raised privately and respectfully with the interpreting physician or a supervisor, which protects the patient and the working relationship. Public correction is unprofessional, an undiscussed chart note bypasses the reader, and staying silent risks patient harm even though interpretation is not the technologist’s role.

questions.stem: A technologist accesses a patient's EEG records for a study they are not involved in, out of curiosity. This is:
options: Acceptable if access is read-only and not printed
A HIPAA violation; there is no job-related need
Acceptable since staff have system-wide access
Acceptable if the details are not shared further
questions.explanation: Accessing PHI without a job-related need violates HIPAA's minimum-necessary principle and patient privacy, even if nothing is changed or shared. Read-only viewing is still access, having technical system-wide permissions does not create a right to look, and not sharing the details does not undo the unauthorized access.

questions.stem: A technologist documents: 'The EEG findings are consistent with a good prognosis.' This documentation is:
options: Appropriate - a normal background predicts outcome
Inappropriate - prognosis is an interpretive judgment
Appropriate if the findings are clearly favorable
Appropriate if the family has asked about outcome
questions.explanation: Prognosis is a clinical interpretation outside technologist scope; the technical record should contain objective findings only. A reactive, normal background may well be favorable, but stating prognosis is the physician's role; clearly favorable findings or family questions do not change that.

questions.stem: OSHA requires that healthcare workers:
options: Use PPE only for patients with known infections
Follow precautions only in high-risk units
Use standard precautions and appropriate PPE
Wear gloves only when blood is visible
questions.explanation: OSHA requires healthcare workers to follow standard precautions with appropriate PPE for every patient, along with facility safety protocols. Limiting PPE to known infections, to high-risk units, or to visible blood misses exposure to infectious material from patients not yet identified.

questions.stem: During an EEG, a patient has a seizure that lasts 6 minutes without stopping. The technologist should:
options: Keep observing and call if it exceeds 10 minutes
Mark the EEG and wait for it to end on its own
Activate the emergency response immediately
Page the reading neurologist after it stops
questions.explanation: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is treated as status epilepticus, a medical emergency, so emergency response is activated immediately. Waiting for 10 minutes, waiting for it to end, or contacting the reader only afterward all delay treatment.

questions.stem: Lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs, formerly PLEDs) are most commonly associated with:
options: An acute stroke, ischemic or hemorrhagic
A chronic generalized epilepsy syndrome
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy with coma
High-dose sedative or anesthetic medication
questions.explanation: Acute stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) is the most common cause of LPDs (formerly PLEDs); they also occur with herpes simplex encephalitis, tumors, trauma and other acute structural lesions. Chronic generalized epilepsy does not produce lateralized periodic discharges, while toxic-metabolic coma and sedatives cause diffuse rather than lateralized changes.

questions.stem: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are classically associated with which infectious condition?
options: Acute bacterial meningitis
Herpes simplex encephalitis
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
Tuberculous basal meningitis
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs), typically over one or both temporal regions, are the classic EEG association of herpes simplex encephalitis. Meningitis (bacterial or tuberculous) usually causes diffuse slowing, and SSPE produces generalized, not lateralized, periodic complexes at long intervals.

questions.stem: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are characterized by:
options: Bilateral synchronous periodic discharges
Continuous rhythmic delta over one hemisphere
Lateralized discharges at regular intervals
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave in bursts
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are lateralized epileptiform discharges that recur at fairly regular intervals, typically about 0.5-2 Hz. Bilateral synchronous periodic discharges describe GPDs or CJD complexes, continuous rhythmic delta lacks discrete periodic discharges, and 3 Hz spike-and-wave is a generalized absence pattern.

questions.stem: How do LPDs (formerly PLEDs) differ from periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) seen in CJD?
options: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are bilateral; PSWCs are lateralized
LPDs (formerly PLEDs) occur only in sleep; PSWCs when awake
LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are periodic; PSWCs are not periodic
LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are lateralized; PSWCs are bilateral
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are lateralized, reflecting focal cortical dysfunction, while the periodic sharp wave complexes of CJD are bilateral and synchronous. The reversed pairing is wrong, LPDs are not sleep-limited, and both patterns are periodic.

questions.stem: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) may be:
options: Ictal or interictal, depending on clinical context
Ictal in every case, requiring seizure treatment
Interictal in every case, with no seizure risk
A benign finding that needs no clinical follow-up
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) lie on the ictal-interictal continuum: they may be ictal or interictal, so clinical correlation is essential. They are not ictal in every case, they carry a meaningful seizure risk, and as a marker of acute focal cortical dysfunction they are never treated as benign.

questions.stem: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Acute ischemic stroke
Normal sleep in a healthy adult
Herpes simplex encephalitis
Primary or metastatic brain tumor
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are abnormal and indicate acute or subacute focal cortical dysfunction, so they do not occur in normal sleep of a healthy adult. They are well described with acute stroke, herpes simplex encephalitis and brain tumors, as well as trauma and other acute structural lesions.

questions.stem: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) typically occur at what frequency?
options: About 3-4 Hz
About 4-7 Hz
About 0.5-2 Hz
About 8-13 Hz
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) typically recur at about 0.5-2 Hz, i.e. every 0.5-2 seconds, at fairly regular intervals. 3-4 Hz suggests generalized spike-and-wave, 4-7 Hz is the theta range, and 8-13 Hz is the alpha range; none fits the slow periodic repetition of LPDs.

questions.stem: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are:
options: Bilaterally synchronous
Generalized with frontal maximum
Restricted to the occipital leads
Lateralized to one hemisphere
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are lateralized, appearing over one hemisphere or predominantly one side, which indicates focal cortical dysfunction. Bilaterally synchronous or generalized frontally predominant periodic discharges suggest GPDs, triphasic waves or CJD, and LPDs are not restricted to the occipital region.

questions.stem: Besides acute stroke, LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are also commonly seen after:
options: Intracerebral hemorrhage or head trauma
A simple febrile seizure in early childhood
A remote cortical injury stable for years
A routine change in antiseizure dosing
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) reflect acute or subacute focal cortical injury, so besides stroke they follow intracerebral hemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, recent neurosurgery and other acute structural lesions. Simple febrile seizures, long-stable remote injuries and routine dose changes are not typical causes.

questions.stem: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) are often associated with:
options: Excess generalized beta from sedative medication
Focal slowing and suppression over the same region
Prominent sleep spindles over the affected side
A normal, symmetric and reactive background
questions.explanation: LPDs (formerly PLEDs) usually sit on a background with focal slowing and attenuated activity in the affected region, supporting focal cortical dysfunction. Generalized beta reflects medication, spindles are not increased over the injured side, and a fully normal symmetric background is unusual with LPDs.

questions.stem: The precentral gyrus is located in which lobe?
options: Parietal lobe
Temporal lobe
Insular lobe
Frontal lobe
questions.explanation: The precentral gyrus lies just anterior to the central sulcus in the frontal lobe and is the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4). The postcentral gyrus behind the sulcus is in the parietal lobe (somatosensory), and the temporal and insular lobes do not contain the precentral gyrus.

questions.stem: Focal epileptiform discharges over the precentral gyrus (motor cortex) would be best detected by electrodes:
options: C3 and C4
F3 and F4
T3 and T4
P3 and P4
questions.explanation: C3 and C4 overlie the central (rolandic) region, including the precentral motor cortex. F3/F4 overlie frontal cortex anterior to the motor strip, T3/T4 the mid-temporal region, and P3/P4 the parietal region behind the postcentral gyrus.

questions.stem: The most common site for brain tumors in children is:
options: Frontal lobes
Posterior fossa
Temporal lobes
Sellar region
questions.explanation: In children roughly half or more of brain tumors arise in the posterior fossa (cerebellum, brainstem, fourth ventricle), whereas adult tumors are mostly supratentorial. The frontal and temporal lobes are more typical adult sites, and the sellar region (e.g., craniopharyngioma) is a less common pediatric site.

questions.stem: The most common malignant brain tumor in children is:
options: Pilocytic astrocytoma
Ependymoma
Medulloblastoma
Craniopharyngioma
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma, a malignant embryonal tumor of the cerebellum, is classically the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Pilocytic astrocytoma is common but low grade (benign behavior), ependymoma is less frequent, and craniopharyngioma is a benign sellar tumor.

questions.stem: Posterior fossa tumors in children typically:
options: Usually cause focal temporal spikes
Usually cause generalized spike-and-wave
Usually cause periodic lateralized discharges
Usually lack focal epileptiform discharges
questions.explanation: Posterior fossa tumors are far from the cortex, so they usually do not produce focal epileptiform discharges unless there is supratentorial involvement or secondary effects such as obstructive hydrocephalus (which may cause diffuse or rhythmic slowing). Focal temporal spikes, generalized spike-and-wave and lateralized periodic discharges reflect cortical involvement.

questions.stem: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is characterized by:
options: Slowly progressive memory loss over 5-10 years
Isolated motor weakness with preserved cognition
Rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months
Fluctuating confusion with full recovery between
questions.explanation: CJD causes rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months, with myoclonus, cerebellar signs and periodic sharp wave complexes (about 1 Hz) on EEG. A slow course over years suggests Alzheimer disease, isolated weakness spares cognition, and fluctuating confusion with recovery suggests delirium or Lewy body disease.

questions.stem: In Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), myoclonus is:
options: Rare and unrelated to the EEG findings
Limited to the terminal stage of illness
Present mainly during deep sleep stages
Common and often provoked by stimuli
questions.explanation: Myoclonus is common in CJD and is often stimulus-sensitive (sound, touch, light), frequently correlating with the periodic sharp wave complexes. It is not rare or unrelated to the EEG, it appears well before the terminal stage, and it is not a sleep-predominant phenomenon.

questions.stem: In Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), the EEG:
options: May be nonspecific early, with PSWCs appearing later
Shows diagnostic PSWCs from the very first symptom
Remains normal throughout the course of illness
Shows only focal slowing without periodic features
questions.explanation: Early in CJD the EEG may be normal or show nonspecific slowing; periodic sharp wave complexes (about 1 Hz) typically appear as the disease progresses, so serial EEGs help and absence of PSWCs does not exclude CJD. PSWCs are not present from the first symptom, the EEG does not stay normal, and it is not limited to focal slowing.

questions.stem: First-line treatment for infantile spasms (West syndrome) includes:
options: Clonazepam or other benzodiazepines
ACTH, oral steroids, or vigabatrin
Ethosuximide or lamotrigine monotherapy
Phenytoin or carbamazepine monotherapy
questions.explanation: First-line therapy for infantile spasms is ACTH or high-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisolone), and vigabatrin, the preferred choice in tuberous sclerosis; treatment is urgent because delay worsens development. Benzodiazepines are not first line, ethosuximide/lamotrigine target other epilepsies, and phenytoin/carbamazepine can worsen generalized seizures.

questions.stem: Successful treatment of infantile spasms is indicated by:
options: Spasm cessation even if hypsarrhythmia persists
EEG improvement even if spasms continue daily
Spasm cessation plus resolution of hypsarrhythmia
Stable drug levels within the therapeutic range
questions.explanation: Treatment response in infantile spasms requires both clinical cessation of spasms and resolution or marked improvement of hypsarrhythmia on EEG; persistent hypsarrhythmia indicates incomplete response. Clinical or EEG improvement alone is insufficient, and drug levels do not define response.

questions.stem: Vigabatrin, used to treat infantile spasms, requires which monitoring?
options: Serial ECGs to detect QT interval prolongation
Liver function tests to detect hepatotoxicity
Serum sodium levels to detect hyponatremia
Visual field testing for peripheral field loss
questions.explanation: Vigabatrin can cause irreversible peripheral (concentric) visual field constriction, so ophthalmologic monitoring is required. Hepatotoxicity monitoring is associated with valproate, hyponatremia with carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, and QT monitoring is not the characteristic vigabatrin requirement.

questions.stem: The single most effective measure for preventing nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections is:
options: Consistent hand hygiene
Prophylactic antibiotics
Routine contact isolation
Terminal room cleaning
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene (soap and water when visibly soiled, alcohol-based rub before and after patient contact) is the single most effective measure for preventing healthcare-associated infections. Prophylactic antibiotics promote resistance, contact isolation is reserved for specific organisms, and terminal cleaning helps but does not interrupt the main route of transmission via hands.

questions.stem: Effective prevention of nosocomial infections requires:
options: Hand hygiene plus routine antibiotic prophylaxis
Hand hygiene, aseptic technique and early isolation
Environmental cleaning plus universal isolation
Antibiotic prophylaxis plus daily room cleaning
questions.explanation: The foundation of nosocomial infection prevention is hand hygiene, aseptic technique and early isolation of patients with transmissible infections. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis promotes resistant organisms, universal isolation is impractical and not indicated, and room cleaning without hand hygiene and asepsis leaves the main transmission routes open.

questions.stem: Proper sterilization and disinfection of EEG equipment is essential to prevent:
options: Corrosion and wear of the electrode surfaces
Signal drift and electrode polarization
Transmission of pathogens between patients
Skin irritation from residual paste
questions.explanation: Cleaning and disinfecting electrodes and other reusable equipment prevents device-related infections and the transmission of pathogens between patients. Corrosion, polarization and drift relate to electrode maintenance and material, and residual paste is a cleaning issue rather than the reason disinfection is required.

questions.stem: Antimicrobial stewardship in preventing nosocomial infections involves:
options: Using broad-spectrum agents early for all patients
Choosing the most potent antibiotic available
Prescribing antibiotics whenever a patient asks
Right drug, dose and duration only when needed
questions.explanation: Antimicrobial stewardship means avoiding unnecessary antibiotics and using the correct drug, dose and duration, which limits the emergence of multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs). Early broad-spectrum use for everyone, defaulting to the most potent agent, or prescribing on request all increase selective pressure for resistance.

questions.stem: Acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) arise from which cranial nerve?
options: CN VIII (vestibulocochlear)
CN VII (facial)
CN V (trigeminal)
CN IX (glossopharyngeal)
questions.explanation: Vestibular schwannomas arise from Schwann cells of the vestibular division of CN VIII in the internal auditory canal and cerebellopontine angle. Large tumors can compress CN VII and CN V, but those nerves are not the origin; CN IX lies lower and is not the site of origin.

questions.stem: Thrombosis of the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) would most likely cause:
options: Right face/arm weakness, right hemianopia, aphasia
Left face/arm weakness, left hemianopia, left neglect
Left leg weakness, abulia, urinary incontinence
Left hemianopia with intact strength and sensation
questions.explanation: Right MCA occlusion causes contralateral (left) face and arm > leg weakness and sensory loss, left homonymous hemianopia and left hemispatial neglect (non-dominant hemisphere). Right-sided deficits with aphasia fit a left MCA stroke, leg-predominant weakness with abulia fits right ACA, and isolated hemianopia fits right PCA.

questions.stem: Aphasia is most commonly associated with:
options: Right middle cerebral artery stroke
Left posterior cerebral artery stroke
Left middle cerebral artery stroke
Right anterior cerebral artery stroke
questions.explanation: Language areas (Broca and Wernicke) lie in the dominant, usually left, hemisphere within MCA territory, so aphasia is most often due to left MCA stroke. Right MCA stroke usually causes neglect; left PCA stroke causes hemianopia (sometimes alexia); right ACA stroke causes left leg weakness and behavioral change.

questions.stem: Papilledema (bilateral optic disc swelling) is commonly associated with:
options: Inflammation of one optic nerve
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Detachment of the retina
Raised intracranial pressure
questions.explanation: Papilledema is bilateral optic disc swelling due to raised ICP, from causes such as tumor, hydrocephalus, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis or hemorrhage. Optic neuritis is usually unilateral inflammation; glaucoma causes disc cupping rather than swelling; retinal detachment does not swell the optic discs.

questions.stem: Papilledema differs from optic neuritis in that papilledema:
options: Is usually bilateral, with vision preserved early
Is usually unilateral, with pain on eye movement
Is usually unilateral, with early central vision loss
Is usually bilateral, with early painful vision loss
questions.explanation: Papilledema from raised ICP is usually bilateral and vision is typically preserved early, without pain on eye movement. Optic neuritis is usually unilateral, inflammatory, and causes early central vision loss with pain on eye movement; early painful vision loss does not fit papilledema.

questions.stem: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is characterized by:
options: Genetic disorder with hamartomas in multiple organs
Vascular malformation of the face and leptomeninges
Inherited muscle disease with progressive weakness
Acquired skin disorder without brain involvement
questions.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis complex is a genetic multisystem disorder with benign hamartomas (cortical tubers, facial angiofibromas, renal, cardiac and lung lesions), causing seizures often beginning as infantile spasms, and intellectual disability. A facial and leptomeningeal vascular malformation describes Sturge-Weber syndrome; the other options do not fit.

questions.stem: Vigabatrin is especially indicated for infantile spasms associated with:
options: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Tuberous sclerosis complex
Inborn errors of metabolism
Cryptogenic or unknown cause
questions.explanation: Vigabatrin is the first-line choice for infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis complex, where it is particularly effective. For other etiologies, including hypoxic-ischemic injury, metabolic disorders and unknown cause, hormonal therapy (ACTH or prednisolone) is usually preferred.

questions.stem: EEG findings in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) with infantile spasms typically include:
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges
A normal background with no discharges
Hypsarrhythmia with multifocal discharges
Isolated centrotemporal spikes in sleep
questions.explanation: In tuberous sclerosis with infantile spasms the EEG typically shows hypsarrhythmia with multifocal epileptiform discharges, because the cortical tubers act as multiple epileptogenic foci. 3 Hz spike-and-wave is typical of absence epilepsy, a normal background is unexpected, and centrotemporal spikes indicate self-limited rolandic epilepsy.

questions.stem: Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is characterized by:
options: Café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas and optic gliomas
Port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma and focal seizures
Ash-leaf macules, cortical tubers and infantile spasms
Retinal and cerebellar hemangioblastomas with renal cysts
questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder defined by a facial port-wine stain (usually trigeminal V1), an ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma and early-onset focal seizures. Café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas and optic gliomas describe NF1; ash-leaf macules, tubers and infantile spasms describe tuberous sclerosis; hemangioblastomas with renal cysts describe von Hippel-Lindau disease.

questions.stem: EEG findings in Sturge-Weber syndrome typically include:
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave with normal background
Diffuse high-voltage hypsarrhythmia in both hemispheres
Increased amplitude and beta over the affected hemisphere
Slowing, discharges and low voltage over the affected side
questions.explanation: In Sturge-Weber syndrome the leptomeningeal angioma causes cortical ischemia, atrophy and calcification on that side, so the EEG shows ipsilateral focal slowing, focal epileptiform discharges and reduced background amplitude (asymmetry). Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave is typical of absence epilepsy; hypsarrhythmia is the pattern of infantile spasms (classically TSC); increased amplitude and beta suggest a skull defect (breach), whereas SWS typically attenuates the affected side.

questions.stem: Binocular diplopia (present when both eyes open, disappears when one eye closed) is most commonly caused by:
options: A cataract in one eye
Cranial nerve III, IV or VI palsy
Uncorrected astigmatism
Corneal scarring in one eye
questions.explanation: Binocular diplopia resolves when either eye is covered because it comes from eye misalignment: CN III, IV or VI palsies, brainstem lesions, or neuromuscular junction disease such as myasthenia gravis. Cataract, astigmatism and corneal scarring are optical problems that cause monocular diplopia, which persists with the other eye closed.

questions.stem: CN VI (abducens) palsy, causing horizontal diplopia and inability to abduct the eye, is commonly associated with:
options: Posterior communicating aneurysm
Acute demyelinating optic neuritis
Raised intracranial pressure
Idiopathic facial nerve palsy
questions.explanation: The long intracranial course of CN VI makes it vulnerable to stretching by raised ICP, so abducens palsy is a classic false-localizing sign. A PCom aneurysm compresses CN III, optic neuritis affects vision rather than abduction, and Bell (facial) palsy affects CN VII.

questions.stem: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is characterized by:
options: Degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons over time
Antibody attack on neuromuscular junction receptors
Acute peripheral nerve demyelination after an infection
Autoimmune CNS demyelination spread in time and space
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the CNS with lesions disseminated in time and space; common presentations are optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, weakness and internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Motor neuron degeneration is ALS, neuromuscular junction antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, and post-infectious peripheral demyelination is Guillain-Barre syndrome.

questions.stem: In multiple sclerosis (MS), the EEG:
options: Is often normal or shows nonspecific slowing
Usually shows periodic sharp wave complexes
Usually shows generalized spike-and-wave
Usually shows focal temporal spikes
questions.explanation: In MS the EEG is often normal or shows nonspecific focal or diffuse slowing; it is supportive (e.g., to evaluate seizures or encephalopathy) but not diagnostic, as MRI is the key test. Periodic sharp wave complexes suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, generalized spike-and-wave suggests generalized epilepsy, and focal temporal spikes suggest temporal lobe epilepsy.

questions.stem: A scalp-recorded spike or sharp wave is generated by:
options: Synchronous depolarization of cortical pyramidal neurons
Burst firing of thalamic relay neurons projecting to cortex
Action potentials conducted along subcortical white matter
Brainstem reticular activating system neuron discharges
questions.explanation: Spikes and sharp waves arise in the cerebral cortex from synchronous abnormal depolarization of pyramidal neurons (the paroxysmal depolarization shift). Thalamic burst firing drives rhythms such as spindles and spike-wave pacing but does not itself produce the scalp spike; axonal action potentials in white matter are too brief and asynchronous to sum at the scalp; brainstem discharges are too deep to be seen as scalp spikes.

questions.stem: The difference between a spike and a sharp wave is:
options: Amplitude: spikes exceed 100 µV, sharp waves fall below it
Polarity: spikes are surface-negative, sharp waves positive
Duration: under 70 ms for a spike, 70-200 ms for a sharp wave
Field: spikes are focal, sharp waves spread over a hemisphere
questions.explanation: Spikes and sharp waves are separated by duration: a spike lasts under 70 ms (about 20-70 ms) and a sharp wave 70-200 ms. Both share the same cortical origin and mechanism (paroxysmal depolarization shift). Amplitude, polarity (both are usually surface-negative) and field size do not define the distinction.

questions.stem: A left anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stroke would most likely cause:
options: Right face and arm weakness with aphasia
Right leg weakness, abulia, urinary incontinence
Left leg weakness, abulia, urinary incontinence
Right homonymous hemianopia with alexia
questions.explanation: The left ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, so stroke causes contralateral (right) leg-predominant weakness, abulia/apathy, urinary incontinence and sometimes transcortical motor aphasia. Right face/arm weakness with aphasia is left MCA, left-sided leg weakness would come from the right ACA, and right hemianopia with alexia is left PCA.

questions.stem: Which set of deficits is most characteristic of an anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stroke?
options: Face and arm weakness more than leg, with aphasia
Leg-predominant weakness, incontinence, and abulia
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with alexia
Vertigo, ataxia, and crossed facial sensory loss
questions.explanation: The ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area of the motor strip and the medial frontal micturition and motivational regions, so ACA stroke causes leg > arm weakness, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and abulia/apathy. Face-and-arm weakness with aphasia is an MCA pattern; hemianopia with alexia points to the PCA; vertigo, ataxia, and crossed sensory loss are posterior circulation (lateral medullary) signs.

questions.stem: The occipital lobe receives its primary arterial blood supply from:
options: Middle cerebral artery
Anterior cerebral artery
Anterior choroidal artery
Posterior cerebral artery
questions.explanation: The occipital lobe is supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA), a terminal branch of the basilar artery; its calcarine branch supplies primary visual cortex. The MCA supplies the lateral convexity (with some collateral supply to the occipital pole), the ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, and the anterior choroidal artery supplies the internal capsule, optic tract, and medial temporal structures rather than the occipital lobe.

questions.stem: A posterior cerebral artery (PCA) infarct would most likely cause:
options: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia
Contralateral face and arm weakness
Contralateral leg weakness and abulia
Ipsilateral limb ataxia and vertigo
questions.explanation: A PCA infarct involves the occipital (visual) cortex and causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing from MCA collateral supply. Face-and-arm weakness is typical of MCA stroke, leg weakness with abulia of ACA stroke, and ipsilateral limb ataxia with vertigo of cerebellar (posterior inferior or superior cerebellar artery) stroke.

questions.stem: The earliest and most common sign of phenytoin (Dilantin) toxicity is:
options: Broad-based gait ataxia
Horizontal nystagmus
Lethargy and confusion
Dysarthric speech
questions.explanation: Horizontal (gaze-evoked) nystagmus is the earliest and most common sign of phenytoin toxicity, typically appearing above about 20 µg/mL. Gait ataxia and dysarthria usually appear at higher levels (around 30 µg/mL), and lethargy or confusion indicate more severe toxicity (40 µg/mL and above).

questions.stem: Moderate phenytoin (Dilantin) toxicity is characterized by:
options: Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and coarse facies
Isolated gaze-evoked nystagmus with normal gait
Coma, paradoxical seizures and respiratory depression
Ataxia, dysarthria, tremor and incoordination
questions.explanation: Moderate phenytoin toxicity produces cerebellar-type signs: gait ataxia, dysarthria, tremor and limb incoordination. Isolated nystagmus is the earliest/mild stage; coma and paradoxical seizures mark severe toxicity; gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and coarse facies are chronic side effects rather than signs of acute toxicity.

questions.stem: In severe phenytoin (Dilantin) toxicity, the EEG may show:
options: Diffuse slowing of the background
Excess frontocentral beta activity
Periodic lateralized discharges
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave
questions.explanation: Severe phenytoin toxicity depresses the CNS, so the EEG shows diffuse background slowing. Excess beta is the typical effect of benzodiazepines and barbiturates; lateralized periodic discharges point to an acute focal lesion; 3 Hz spike-and-wave is the signature of absence epilepsy.

questions.stem: Chronic phenytoin (Dilantin) toxicity may include:
options: Horizontal nystagmus and gait ataxia at high serum levels
Agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia with marrow failure
Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and coarsened facial features
Weight gain, tremor and hair loss with menstrual change
questions.explanation: Long-term phenytoin therapy causes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and coarsening of facial features, along with peripheral neuropathy, osteomalacia and folate deficiency. Nystagmus and gait ataxia are signs of acute, dose-related phenytoin toxicity rather than chronic effects; agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia are associated with carbamazepine and felbamate; weight gain, tremor and hair loss are typical of valproate.

questions.stem: In a young child with seizures, central precocious puberty is most classically associated with:
options: Craniopharyngioma
Hypothalamic hamartoma
Pituitary prolactinoma
Mesial temporal sclerosis
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic hamartoma is a benign congenital lesion that activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis early, causing central precocious puberty, and it also causes gelastic seizures. Craniopharyngioma and prolactinoma more often cause delayed puberty or hypogonadism; mesial temporal sclerosis causes temporal lobe epilepsy without endocrine change.

questions.stem: Which seizure type is highly characteristic of hypothalamic hamartoma?
options: Epileptic spasms
Myoclonic seizures
Atonic drop attacks
Gelastic seizures
questions.explanation: Gelastic (laughing) seizures are the hallmark of hypothalamic hamartoma; precocious puberty plus gelastic seizures suggests hamartoma until proven otherwise. Epileptic spasms are typical of infantile spasms syndromes such as TSC; myoclonic seizures suggest JME or progressive myoclonic epilepsies; atonic drop attacks suggest Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

questions.stem: The classic clinical presentation of hypothalamic hamartoma includes:
options: Precocious puberty with gelastic seizures
Port-wine stain with focal motor seizures
Ash-leaf macules with infantile spasms
Café-au-lait spots with absence seizures
questions.explanation: The classic presentation of hypothalamic hamartoma is precocious puberty with gelastic (laughing) seizures, often with behavioral problems or developmental delay. A port-wine stain with focal seizures suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome; ash-leaf macules with infantile spasms suggest tuberous sclerosis; café-au-lait spots point to NF1.

questions.stem: In neurophysiology, SDS stands for:
options: Safety Data Sheet
Sharp Waves with Delta Slowing (epileptiform sharp waves superimposed on focal or regional delta slowing)
Surgical Data Sheet
Standard Delta Slowing
questions.explanation: In neurophysiology, SDS stands for Sharp Waves with Delta Slowing - an EEG pattern characterized by epileptiform sharp waves superimposed on focal or regional delta slowing. This combination strongly suggests underlying focal cortical pathology (focal epilepsy, brain tumors, stroke, cortical dysplasia).

questions.stem: Focal sharp waves with associated regional delta slowing on EEG are commonly associated with:
options: A benign variant such as wicket spikes or BETS
Idiopathic generalized epilepsy with absences
Focal cortical pathology such as a tumor or stroke
Diffuse metabolic encephalopathy such as uremia
questions.explanation: Focal sharp waves with associated delta slowing indicate structural or functional cortical abnormality, e.g. focal epilepsy, brain tumor, subacute or chronic stroke, cortical dysplasia or post-traumatic injury. Benign variants lack accompanying focal slowing; idiopathic generalized epilepsy produces generalized discharges on a normal background; metabolic encephalopathy causes diffuse, not focal, slowing.

questions.stem: Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) has an onset:
options: In late childhood, around the onset of puberty
In infancy, with the stain present at birth
In early adulthood, usually after age 20
In mid-childhood, once lesions appear at age 5
questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome presents in infancy: the facial port-wine stain is visible at birth and seizures usually begin in the first year of life, typically focal. Onset in late childhood, adulthood or mid-childhood is not typical, and the skin lesion does not appear later.

questions.stem: The classic presentation of Sturge-Weber syndrome includes:
options: Café-au-lait spots and seizures starting in adolescence
Ash-leaf macules and infantile spasms at 4-8 months
Facial angiofibromas and seizures beginning in adulthood
Port-wine stain at birth and seizures in the first year
questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome classically shows a port-wine stain (nevus flammeus, usually V1) at birth and seizures starting within the first year. Café-au-lait spots suggest NF1; ash-leaf macules with infantile spasms suggest tuberous sclerosis; facial angiofibromas are also a TSC feature and usually appear in childhood.

questions.stem: A tangle of arteries draining directly into veins, with a tendency to bleed, is called a(n):
options: Saccular (berry) aneurysm
Cavernous malformation
Arteriovenous malformation
Developmental venous anomaly
questions.explanation: An arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is an abnormal direct connection between arteries and veins with no intervening capillary bed, so high-pressure arterial flow enters veins and raises the risk of hemorrhage. A saccular aneurysm is a single outpouching of an arterial wall; a cavernous malformation is a low-flow cluster of dilated capillary-like channels without arterial feeders; a developmental venous anomaly is a variant of normal venous drainage with no arterial component.

questions.stem: An arteriovenous malformation (AVM) involving the cortex is most likely to show which EEG finding?
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave complexes
Diffuse beta excess with normal background
Focal slowing or sharp waves over the lesion
Bilateral frontal intermittent rhythmic delta
questions.explanation: A cortical AVM acts as a focal structural lesion, so the EEG may show focal slowing or epileptiform discharges over the involved region; clinically AVMs present with hemorrhage, seizures, headache, or focal deficits. Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave is the pattern of childhood absence epilepsy; diffuse beta excess usually reflects medication effect; frontal intermittent rhythmic delta is a nonspecific, often diffuse or deep-midline finding rather than the signature of a focal cortical lesion.

questions.stem: The third ventricle communicates with the lateral ventricles through the:
options: Foramina of Monro
Cerebral aqueduct
Foramen of Magendie
Foramina of Luschka
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricles drain into the third ventricle through the interventricular foramina (of Monro), one on each side. The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles, while the foramen of Magendie (median) and foramina of Luschka (lateral) let CSF leave the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.

questions.stem: Obstruction at the foramen of Monro (for example, by a colloid cyst) most likely causes:
options: Fourth ventricular dilation with a normal third
Dilation of all four ventricles equally
Enlarged subarachnoid spaces over the convexities
Lateral ventricular dilation, one or both sides
questions.explanation: Blocking the foramen of Monro traps CSF upstream, so one or both lateral ventricles enlarge (unilateral or bilateral obstructive hydrocephalus); common causes are colloid cysts, tumors, and intraventricular hemorrhage. Isolated fourth ventricular dilation (a trapped fourth ventricle) requires obstruction at both the aqueduct and the fourth-ventricle outlets; enlargement of all four ventricles suggests communicating hydrocephalus or fourth-ventricle outlet obstruction; enlarged convexity subarachnoid spaces describe external hydrocephalus or atrophy, not a Monro block.

questions.stem: With larger acoustic neuromas, which cranial nerve is most commonly affected secondarily?
options: CN V (trigeminal)
CN VII (facial nerve) - compression by larger tumors causes facial weakness
CN VI (abducens)
CN IX (glossopharyngeal)
questions.explanation: With larger acoustic neuromas, CN VII (facial nerve) is most commonly affected secondarily, causing facial weakness. CN V (trigeminal) compression may also occur, causing facial numbness. Understanding cranial nerve involvement patterns helps localize tumor size and location.

questions.stem: Acoustic neuromas typically cause:
options: Conductive hearing loss
Progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss (most common presenting symptom)
Bilateral hearing loss
Only tinnitus without hearing loss
questions.explanation: Acoustic neuromas typically cause progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, which is the most common presenting symptom. Other symptoms include tinnitus, vertigo/imbalance, and with larger tumors, facial nerve (CN VII) involvement and trigeminal nerve (CN V) compression.

questions.stem: The cerebellopontine angle (CPA) is a common location for which tumors?
options: Only acoustic neuromas
Acoustic neuromas (most common), meningiomas, epidermoid cysts, and other CPA tumors
Only gliomas
Only metastases
questions.explanation: The cerebellopontine angle (CPA) is a common location for acoustic neuromas (most common CPA tumor), meningiomas, epidermoid cysts, and other CPA tumors. Understanding CPA tumor differentials is important for diagnosis and management.

questions.stem: Bilateral acoustic neuromas are characteristic of:
options: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) - bilateral acoustic neuromas are pathognomonic
Tuberous sclerosis
Sturge-Weber syndrome
questions.explanation: Bilateral acoustic neuromas are characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) and are pathognomonic for this condition. NF2 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the NF2 gene (merlin/schwannomin).

questions.stem: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) typically divides into which main branches?
options: Callosomarginal and pericallosal
Superior and inferior divisions
Calcarine and parieto-occipital
Anterior and posterior choroidal
questions.explanation: Beyond the horizontal M1 segment, the MCA usually bifurcates into superior and inferior divisions (the M2 segments), which continue as opercular (M3) and cortical (M4) branches. Callosomarginal and pericallosal arteries are ACA branches; calcarine and parieto-occipital arteries are PCA branches; the anterior choroidal arises from the internal carotid and the posterior choroidal from the PCA.

questions.stem: The MCA superior division supplies:
options: Lateral and inferior temporal cortex
Medial frontal and parietal cortex
Occipital and medial temporal cortex
Lateral frontal and parietal cortex
questions.explanation: The superior division of the MCA supplies the lateral frontal and parietal lobes, including motor and sensory cortex for the face and arm, which is why MCA strokes weaken the face and arm more than the leg. The temporal lobe is supplied by the inferior division; the medial frontal and parietal cortex (leg area) belongs to the ACA; the occipital and medial temporal cortex belong to the PCA.

questions.stem: In an acute MCA stroke, the EEG most likely shows:
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave over both hemispheres
Focal slowing and attenuation over the affected hemisphere
Increased alpha and faster rhythms on the affected side
Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology
questions.explanation: An acute MCA infarct typically produces focal polymorphic delta slowing and attenuation of background activity over the affected hemisphere; lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs, formerly PLEDs) may appear in the subacute phase. Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave is an absence-epilepsy pattern; ischemic cortex loses rather than gains alpha and fast activity; generalized triphasic periodic discharges suggest a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy rather than a focal infarct.

questions.stem: Complications of large MCA strokes include:
options: Isolated leg weakness that resolves within days
Bilateral visual loss from occipital infarction
Malignant edema with herniation risk and seizures
Pure sensory loss limited to the contralateral face
questions.explanation: Large MCA infarcts can swell massively (malignant MCA infarction), raising intracranial pressure and causing herniation; seizures are another recognized complication. Isolated, rapidly resolving leg weakness fits a small ACA event or TIA; bilateral visual loss requires bilateral PCA (occipital) infarction; pure facial sensory loss is far too limited for a large MCA stroke.

questions.stem: Which cortical sign distinguishes a left (dominant) MCA stroke from a right MCA stroke?
options: Language impairment such as aphasia
Neglect of the left side of space
Contralateral face and arm weakness
Dressing and constructional apraxia
questions.explanation: In most people the left hemisphere is dominant for language, so a left MCA stroke characteristically causes aphasia. Left hemispatial neglect and dressing/constructional apraxia are typical of right (nondominant) MCA stroke; contralateral face and arm weakness occurs with MCA stroke on either side and does not distinguish them.

questions.stem: In papilledema, visual acuity is:
options: Always affected early
Often initially preserved (early stages), but may be affected later with chronic papilledema or optic atrophy
Always normal
Always severely affected
questions.explanation: In papilledema, visual acuity is often initially preserved in early stages, distinguishing it from optic neuritis. However, visual acuity may be affected later with chronic papilledema or optic atrophy. Transient visual obscurations are common early symptoms.

questions.stem: Papilledema can be distinguished from pseudopapilledema (optic disc drusen) by:
options: Only visual acuity
Papilledema shows venous engorgement, hemorrhages, and elevated ICP; pseudopapilledema (drusen) shows buried drusen, no hemorrhages, and normal ICP
Only color vision
Only pupillary response
questions.explanation: Papilledema shows venous engorgement, hemorrhages, and elevated ICP, while pseudopapilledema (optic disc drusen) shows buried drusen, no hemorrhages, and normal ICP. Distinguishing these is critical as papilledema requires urgent treatment of raised ICP.

questions.stem: Before performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with papilledema, it is essential to:
options: Only check blood pressure
Exclude space-occupying lesions by imaging (CT or MRI) - LP can cause herniation if there is mass effect
Only check visual acuity
Only check pupillary response
questions.explanation: Before performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with papilledema, it is essential to exclude space-occupying lesions by imaging (CT or MRI). LP can cause herniation if there is mass effect and raised ICP. This is a critical safety consideration.

questions.stem: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is caused by mutations in:
options: TSC1 or TSC2, encoding hamartin or tuberin
NF1, encoding the protein neurofibromin
GNAQ, a somatic mosaic activating variant
SCN1A, encoding a sodium channel subunit
questions.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis complex is caused by mutations in TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16), causing overactivation of the mTOR pathway; many cases are new mutations. NF1 causes neurofibromatosis type 1; somatic GNAQ variants cause Sturge-Weber syndrome; SCN1A mutations cause Dravet syndrome.

questions.stem: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) in tuberous sclerosis:
options: Commonly spreads through the CSF to the spinal cord
Arises from cortical tubers at the brain surface
Can block the foramen of Monro and cause hydrocephalus
Usually presents first in adulthood after age 40
questions.explanation: SEGA is a slow-growing tumor arising near the foramen of Monro; it can obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus, so TSC patients need monitoring, and treatment may include mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) or surgery. It rarely seeds the CSF, arises from subependymal nodules rather than cortical tubers, and typically appears in the first two decades.

questions.stem: The most common cutaneous feature of tuberous sclerosis is:
options: Facial angiofibromas on the cheeks
Hypomelanotic ash-leaf macules
Shagreen patches on the lower back
Periungual fibromas of the nails
questions.explanation: Hypomelanotic (ash-leaf) macules are the most common skin finding in tuberous sclerosis and often the earliest, best seen with a Wood lamp. Facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches and periungual (Koenen) fibromas are also TSC features but are less common and usually appear later in childhood or adolescence.

questions.stem: Renal angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis:
options: Are always benign and never cause problems
May cause bleeding and require monitoring (risk of hemorrhage, especially if large)
Only occur in children
Only cause hypertension
questions.explanation: Renal angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis may cause bleeding and require monitoring, especially if large. They carry a risk of hemorrhage. Treatment may include mTOR inhibitors or embolization. Regular monitoring is important for TSC patients.

questions.stem: The classic MRI finding in multiple sclerosis is:
options: Only normal imaging
T2/FLAIR hyperintense periventricular plaques (Dawson's fingers) - perpendicular to ventricles, characteristic of MS
Only cortical atrophy
Only brainstem lesions
questions.explanation: The classic MRI finding in multiple sclerosis is T2/FLAIR hyperintense periventricular plaques, often called Dawson's fingers because they appear perpendicular to the ventricles. This pattern is characteristic of MS and helps distinguish it from other demyelinating diseases.

questions.stem: CSF findings in multiple sclerosis typically include:
options: Only normal CSF
Oligoclonal IgG bands and elevated IgG index (supportive but not diagnostic)
Only elevated protein
Only elevated white blood cells
questions.explanation: CSF findings in multiple sclerosis typically include oligoclonal IgG bands and elevated IgG index. These are supportive findings but not diagnostic alone. MRI is the key diagnostic modality for MS. CSF helps support the diagnosis and exclude other conditions.

questions.stem: The most common clinical course of multiple sclerosis is:
options: Primary progressive MS
Relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) - most common, characterized by relapses and remissions
Secondary progressive MS
Progressive-relapsing MS
questions.explanation: The most common clinical course of multiple sclerosis is relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), characterized by relapses (acute attacks) and remissions (recovery). Many patients eventually transition to secondary progressive MS (SPMS) with progressive disability.

questions.stem: Multiple sclerosis must be distinguished from:
options: Only stroke
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMO), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), CNS vasculitis, vitamin B12 deficiency, and other demyelinating conditions
Only brain tumors
Only infections
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis must be distinguished from neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMO), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), CNS vasculitis, vitamin B12 deficiency, sarcoidosis, HIV-related demyelination, and other conditions. NMO is particularly important as it has different treatment.

questions.stem: The classic CT finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome is:
options: Periventricular calcified subependymal nodules
Ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding edema
Enlarged ventricles from aqueductal stenosis
Gyriform 'tram-track' cortical calcifications
questions.explanation: The classic CT finding in Sturge-Weber syndrome is gyriform tram-track calcification following the cortical sulci, which becomes more evident with age; MRI with contrast shows leptomeningeal enhancement. Calcified subependymal nodules are typical of tuberous sclerosis; a ring-enhancing lesion suggests abscess or tumor; aqueductal stenosis causes hydrocephalus unrelated to SWS.

questions.stem: Treatment options for Sturge-Weber syndrome include:
options: Seizure control, low-dose aspirin, surgery if refractory
Everolimus to shrink tumors plus vigabatrin for spasms
Shunting for hydrocephalus plus a ketogenic diet
Immunotherapy with steroids, IVIG and plasma exchange
questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome is managed with aggressive seizure control (often polytherapy), low-dose aspirin in some patients to reduce stroke-like episodes from venous congestion, and epilepsy surgery such as hemispherotomy for refractory cases. Everolimus and vigabatrin are TSC treatments; hydrocephalus shunting is not a standard SWS therapy; immunotherapy is used for autoimmune encephalitis.

questions.stem: A CN III (oculomotor) palsy with a dilated, poorly reactive pupil most strongly suggests:
options: Compression, such as from a PCom aneurysm
Microvascular ischemia from diabetes
Myasthenia gravis affecting the levator
Demyelinating lesion of the MLF in MS
questions.explanation: Pupillomotor fibers run on the outer surface of CN III, so compression (posterior communicating artery aneurysm, uncal herniation) involves the pupil early and needs urgent evaluation. Microvascular ischemia from diabetes or hypertension typically spares the pupil; myasthenia can mimic ptosis and ophthalmoparesis but does not affect the pupil; an MLF lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, not a CN III palsy.

questions.stem: CN IV (trochlear) palsy causes:
options: Horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze
Ptosis with a dilated, fixed pupil
Vertical diplopia, worse looking down
Impaired adduction with nystagmus
questions.explanation: CN IV innervates the superior oblique, which depresses the eye in adduction, so trochlear palsy causes vertical diplopia that worsens when looking down (reading, descending stairs). Horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze suggests CN VI palsy; ptosis with a dilated pupil indicates CN III involvement; impaired adduction with abducting-eye nystagmus is internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

questions.stem: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is caused by a lesion of the:
options: Paramedian pontine reticular formation
Medial longitudinal fasciculus
Oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain
Abducens nerve in the cavernous sinus
questions.explanation: INO results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which links the abducens nucleus to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus; the affected eye cannot adduct and the abducting eye shows nystagmus. It is classic for multiple sclerosis in young adults. A PPRF lesion causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy; an oculomotor nucleus lesion causes CN III palsy with ptosis; an abducens nerve lesion impairs abduction, not adduction.

questions.stem: The mechanism underlying spike and sharp wave generation is:
options: Action potentials propagating along cortical white matter
Synchronous hyperpolarization of thalamic relay cells
Paroxysmal depolarization shift in cortical pyramidal cells
Spreading depolarization of cortical glial cells
questions.explanation: The paroxysmal depolarization shift is a sudden, prolonged, hypersynchronous depolarization of cortical pyramidal neurons followed by a hyperpolarizing after-potential, which correspond to the spike and aftergoing slow wave. White-matter action potentials do not sum at the scalp; thalamic hyperpolarization underlies spindle and burst firing, not focal spikes; glial spreading depolarization relates to migraine aura and injury, not spikes.

questions.stem: Benign sharp transients (e.g., BETS, small sharp spikes) are BEST distinguished from epileptiform spikes by:
options: A higher amplitude than most epileptiform spikes
No aftergoing slow wave and no background disruption
A longer duration than typical epileptiform spikes
Appearing mainly in wakefulness, not drowsiness
questions.explanation: Benign sharp transients such as BETS/small sharp spikes lack an aftergoing slow wave and do not disrupt the background; they are also low in amplitude and very brief. They are lower, not higher, in amplitude and shorter, not longer, than epileptiform spikes, and they occur mainly in drowsiness and light sleep rather than wakefulness.

questions.stem: Bilateral ACA stroke may cause:
options: Cortical blindness with denial of the deficit
Crossed cranial nerve palsy with hemiparesis
Fluent aphasia with poor comprehension
Callosal disconnection, such as alien hand
questions.explanation: The ACAs supply the corpus callosum, so bilateral ACA infarction can cause callosal disconnection syndromes such as alien hand and inability to name objects held in the left hand. Cortical blindness with denial (Anton syndrome) results from bilateral PCA infarction; crossed cranial nerve palsy with hemiparesis localizes to the brainstem; fluent aphasia with poor comprehension is a left inferior-division MCA (Wernicke) syndrome.

questions.stem: Which primitive (frontal release) reflexes are commonly seen in ACA stroke?
options: Moro and tonic neck reflexes
Grasp and snout reflexes
Corneal and gag reflexes
Jaw jerk and Hoffmann sign
questions.explanation: ACA stroke damages the medial frontal lobe, releasing primitive reflexes such as the grasp and snout reflexes. Moro and tonic neck reflexes are infantile reflexes not typically re-emerging with frontal stroke; corneal and gag reflexes are normal brainstem reflexes; a brisk jaw jerk and Hoffmann sign are upper motor neuron signs, not frontal release signs.

questions.stem: PCA stroke may involve the thalamus, causing:
options: Ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor
Contralateral leg weakness and incontinence
Ipsilateral facial weakness and hearing loss
Contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain
questions.explanation: The PCA (via thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate branches) supplies the thalamus, so PCA stroke can cause contralateral sensory loss, thalamic pain syndrome, memory impairment, and altered consciousness, depending on the nuclei involved. Ipsilateral limb ataxia is cerebellar; leg weakness with incontinence is an ACA syndrome; ipsilateral facial weakness with hearing loss suggests an AICA/pontine lesion.

questions.stem: Top of the basilar syndrome involves which territories?
options: Bilateral PCA territories, thalamus, and midbrain
Bilateral ACA territories and the corpus callosum
Both MCA territories and the internal capsules
The lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum
questions.explanation: Occlusion at the top of the basilar artery affects both PCA territories, the thalamus, and the midbrain, producing altered consciousness, visual disturbances, and oculomotor abnormalities. Bilateral ACA territories and the corpus callosum are supplied from the anterior circulation; the MCAs and internal capsules are also anterior circulation; the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum are PICA/vertebral territory.

questions.stem: Phenytoin toxicity risk is increased by:
options: Folate supplements and enzyme-inducing drugs
Hypercalcemia with a high-protein, high-fat diet
Obesity with an increased volume of distribution
Hypoalbuminemia, liver disease or interacting drugs
questions.explanation: Phenytoin is highly protein-bound and hepatically metabolized, so hypoalbuminemia, liver disease and interacting drugs (e.g. valproate displacing phenytoin from albumin) raise free levels and toxicity risk. Folate supplements and enzyme inducers tend to lower phenytoin levels; diet and calcium do not meaningfully raise them; a larger distribution volume lowers rather than raises concentration.

questions.stem: Therapeutic phenytoin levels are typically:
options: 10-20 µg/mL
5-10 µg/mL
20-30 µg/mL
30-40 µg/mL
questions.explanation: The usual therapeutic total phenytoin level is 10-20 µg/mL. Levels of 5-10 are often subtherapeutic; above 20 nystagmus appears, above 30 ataxia, and above 40 lethargy and confusion, so 20-30 and 30-40 are toxic ranges.

questions.stem: Phenytoin differs from carbamazepine in that phenytoin:
options: Only has different dosing
Has non-linear (zero-order) kinetics (small dose increases can cause large level increases), while carbamazepine has linear kinetics
Only has different side effects
Only has different indications
questions.explanation: Phenytoin has non-linear (zero-order) kinetics, meaning small dose increases can cause large level increases, making it prone to toxicity. Carbamazepine has linear kinetics. This is why phenytoin requires careful dose adjustment and monitoring.

questions.stem: Hypothalamic hamartoma is best visualized on:
options: Non-contrast head CT
Cerebral angiography
Thin-slice brain MRI
FDG-PET of the brain
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic hamartoma is best seen on MRI, where thin T1/T2 slices show a well-defined non-enhancing hypothalamic mass. CT may miss small hamartomas; angiography shows vessels, not this lesion; FDG-PET shows metabolism but lacks the anatomic detail needed for diagnosis.

questions.stem: Treatment options for hypothalamic hamartoma include:
options: Antiseizure medication alone, since seizures respond well
Surgical, endoscopic or radiosurgical treatment of the lesion
Vagus nerve stimulation as the sole definitive therapy
Corpus callosotomy to disconnect the two hemispheres
questions.explanation: Gelastic seizures from hypothalamic hamartoma are usually drug-resistant, so treatment targets the lesion: open or endoscopic resection, stereotactic radiosurgery or laser ablation, with medical management of precocious puberty. Medication alone rarely controls these seizures; VNS and callosotomy are palliative and do not address the hamartoma.

questions.stem: In an EEG report, focal sharp waves with associated delta slowing should be described as:
options: Diffuse slowing, consistent with a metabolic encephalopathy
A benign sharp transient of no clinical significance
Electrode artifact that should be rechecked and repeated
Focal sharp waves with regional delta, suggesting a focal lesion
questions.explanation: This should be reported as focal sharp waves with associated delta slowing over the involved region, suggesting underlying focal cortical pathology (epileptogenic cortex with a structural correlate). It is focal rather than diffuse, it is epileptiform rather than benign, and a reproducible field with slowing argues against electrode artifact.

questions.stem: AVMs are commonly graded using:
options: Only size
Spetzler-Martin grading system (size, eloquence of location, venous drainage pattern) - helps determine surgical risk
Only location
Only age
questions.explanation: AVMs are commonly graded using the Spetzler-Martin grading system, which considers size, eloquence of location, and venous drainage pattern. This helps determine surgical risk and treatment approach. Lower grades (I-III) are more amenable to surgery.

questions.stem: Treatment options for AVMs include:
options: Only observation
Surgical resection, endovascular embolization, stereotactic radiosurgery, or combination therapy (depending on size, location, and Spetzler-Martin grade)
Only medical management
Only radiation
questions.explanation: Treatment options for AVMs include surgical resection, endovascular embolization, stereotactic radiosurgery, or combination therapy, depending on size, location, and Spetzler-Martin grade. Treatment decisions require multidisciplinary evaluation.

questions.stem: AVMs differ from cavernous malformations in that AVMs:
options: Only have different imaging
Have high-flow arteriovenous shunting (visible on angiography), while cavernous malformations are low-flow lesions without arteriovenous shunting
Only have different symptoms
Only have different treatment
questions.explanation: AVMs have high-flow arteriovenous shunting (visible on angiography), while cavernous malformations are low-flow lesions without arteriovenous shunting. AVMs are visible on angiography, while cavernous malformations show characteristic popcorn appearance on MRI but are angiographically occult.

questions.stem: The third ventricle communicates with the fourth ventricle through the:
options: Foramina of Monro
Foramen of Magendie
Cerebral aqueduct
Foramina of Luschka
questions.explanation: The third ventricle connects to the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius); aqueductal stenosis causes obstructive hydrocephalus of the lateral and third ventricles. The foramina of Monro connect the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle, and the foramina of Magendie and Luschka drain the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.

questions.stem: The fourth ventricle communicates with the subarachnoid space through the:
options: Foramina of Monro and the cerebral aqueduct
Arachnoid granulations and the dural sinuses
Foramen of Magendie and foramina of Luschka
Cerebral aqueduct and the choroidal fissure
questions.explanation: CSF leaves the fourth ventricle through the median foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka into the subarachnoid space; obstruction here causes obstructive (noncommunicating) hydrocephalus. The foramina of Monro and cerebral aqueduct are upstream connections between ventricles; arachnoid granulations absorb CSF into the dural venous sinuses; the choroidal fissure is where choroid plexus enters the lateral ventricle, not an outflow path.

questions.stem: Obstructive hydrocephalus differs from communicating hydrocephalus in that obstructive:
options: Is caused by a block within the ventricular system
Is caused by impaired CSF absorption at the villi
Is caused by CSF overproduction at the choroid plexus
Is caused by brain atrophy with passive dilation
questions.explanation: Obstructive (noncommunicating) hydrocephalus results from a blockage within the ventricular system, such as aqueductal stenosis or a tumor at the foramen of Monro. Impaired absorption at the arachnoid villi (after subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis) defines communicating hydrocephalus; CSF overproduction (e.g., choroid plexus papilloma) is a rare non-obstructive cause; atrophy with passive ventricular enlargement is hydrocephalus ex vacuo, not true hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: In hydrocephalus, the EEG may show:
options: Diffuse beta excess with a normal background
Increased posterior alpha with no slowing
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave bursts
Diffuse slowing, worse with raised ICP
questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus typically produces diffuse slowing on EEG, which becomes more prominent as intracranial pressure rises; severe cases can show periodic or rhythmic slow patterns. Diffuse beta excess usually reflects medications; increased posterior alpha without slowing would be a normal-looking record; generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave is the signature of absence epilepsy, not raised pressure.

questions.stem: Weber syndrome (midbrain stroke) is characterized by:
options: Contralateral CN III palsy, ipsilateral hemiparesis
Ipsilateral CN III palsy, contralateral hemiparesis
Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral ataxia
Ipsilateral CN XII palsy, contralateral hemiparesis
questions.explanation: Weber syndrome is a ventral midbrain stroke involving the CN III fascicle and the cerebral peduncle, causing ipsilateral oculomotor palsy (ptosis, down-and-out eye) with contralateral hemiparesis because the corticospinal tract has not yet crossed. Reversing the sides is anatomically wrong; ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral ataxia is Claude syndrome (red nucleus); CN XII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis is medial medullary syndrome.

questions.stem: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome classically results from occlusion of the:
options: Anterior spinal artery
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Superior cerebellar artery
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome is classically attributed to posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) occlusion (vertebral artery occlusion is also a frequent cause), producing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, Horner syndrome, ataxia, dysphagia, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss. Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome; AICA occlusion causes a lateral pontine syndrome with facial weakness and hearing loss; superior cerebellar artery occlusion affects the upper cerebellum and dorsolateral pons/midbrain.

questions.stem: Millard-Gubler syndrome (ventral pontine lesion) causes:
options: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
Ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsies with contralateral hemiparesis
Ipsilateral CN XII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
Contralateral CN VI and VII palsies with ipsilateral hemiparesis
questions.explanation: Millard-Gubler syndrome is a ventral pontine lesion involving the CN VI and CN VII fascicles and the corticospinal tract, giving ipsilateral lateral gaze and facial weakness with contralateral hemiparesis. Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis is Weber (midbrain); CN XII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis is medial medullary; reversing the sides misplaces the uncrossed cranial nerve and not-yet-crossed motor fibers.

questions.stem: Vermal (midline) cerebellar lesions cause:
options: Ipsilateral limb dysmetria and tremor
Contralateral limb ataxia and dysmetria
Truncal ataxia and gait instability
Resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity
questions.explanation: The vermis controls midline (axial) structures, so vermal lesions cause truncal ataxia, broad-based unsteady gait, and often nystagmus. Ipsilateral limb dysmetria and tremor come from cerebellar hemisphere lesions; cerebellar signs are ipsilateral, not contralateral; resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity is a basal ganglia (parkinsonian) sign.

questions.stem: Hemispheric cerebellar lesions cause:
options: Ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor
Contralateral limb ataxia and intention tremor
Truncal ataxia with preserved limb coordination
Resting tremor and contralateral rigidity
questions.explanation: Hemispheric cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia; the signs are ipsilateral because cerebellar pathways cross twice. Contralateral signs would be wrong for this reason; truncal ataxia with preserved limbs is the vermal pattern; resting tremor and rigidity are basal ganglia signs.

questions.stem: Parkinson disease results mainly from degeneration of:
options: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra
GABAergic neurons of the caudate nucleus
Cholinergic neurons of the basal forebrain
Glutamatergic neurons of the subthalamic nucleus
questions.explanation: Parkinson disease results from loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, disrupting the basal ganglia motor circuit and causing bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability. Caudate GABAergic neuron loss is characteristic of Huntington disease; basal forebrain cholinergic loss is associated with Alzheimer disease; the subthalamic nucleus becomes overactive in Parkinson disease rather than degenerating.

questions.stem: Huntington disease is characterized by degeneration mainly of:
options: The substantia nigra
The subthalamic nucleus
The caudate nucleus
The cerebellar vermis
questions.explanation: Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant trinucleotide-repeat disorder, causes degeneration of the basal ganglia, especially the caudate nucleus, leading to chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms. Substantia nigra degeneration is the hallmark of Parkinson disease; a subthalamic nucleus lesion causes hemiballismus; vermal degeneration causes truncal ataxia, not chorea.

questions.stem: The ventral posterior (VP) nucleus of the thalamus mainly relays:
options: Visual input to the calcarine cortex
Somatosensory input to the postcentral gyrus
Auditory input to the superior temporal gyrus
Cerebellar input to the precentral gyrus
questions.explanation: The ventral posterior nucleus receives the medial lemniscus (touch, proprioception) and spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature) and relays them to the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus; lesions cause contralateral sensory loss. Visual relay is the lateral geniculate nucleus, auditory relay is the medial geniculate nucleus, and cerebellar output reaches motor cortex through the ventral lateral nucleus.

questions.stem: Thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome) is characterized by:
options: Ipsilateral facial pain after a medullary stroke
Lancinating facial pain from trigeminal compression
Shoulder pain on the weak side after an MCA stroke
Burning contralateral pain after a thalamic stroke
questions.explanation: Dejerine-Roussy (thalamic pain) syndrome is severe, often burning or dysesthetic pain in the contralateral body after a thalamic stroke, especially of the ventral posterior nucleus. Ipsilateral facial pain after medullary stroke occurs in Wallenberg syndrome; lancinating facial pain from vascular compression is trigeminal neuralgia; hemiplegic shoulder pain after MCA stroke is musculoskeletal, not central thalamic pain.

questions.stem: Brodmann area 4 corresponds to:
options: Primary somatosensory cortex
Primary motor cortex
Premotor cortex
Frontal eye field
questions.explanation: Brodmann area 4 is the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, controlling voluntary movement; lesions cause contralateral weakness. Areas 3, 1, and 2 form primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus; area 6 is premotor and supplementary motor cortex; the frontal eye field lies mainly in area 8.

questions.stem: Brodmann area 17 corresponds to:
options: Visual association cortex
Primary auditory cortex
Primary somatosensory cortex
Primary visual cortex
questions.explanation: Brodmann area 17 is the primary visual cortex (V1) along the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe; lesions cause contralateral homonymous field defects. Areas 18 and 19 are visual association cortex; primary auditory cortex is areas 41 and 42 in the temporal lobe; primary somatosensory cortex is areas 3, 1, and 2.

questions.stem: Wernicke area (Brodmann area 22) is located in the:
options: Posterior superior temporal gyrus
Inferior frontal gyrus, pars opercularis
Supramarginal and angular gyri
Anterior middle temporal gyrus
questions.explanation: Wernicke area lies in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere and supports language comprehension; lesions cause fluent aphasia with poor comprehension. The inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis and triangularis) is Broca area; the supramarginal and angular gyri are adjacent parietal regions involved in reading, writing, and repetition; the anterior middle temporal gyrus is not the classic Wernicke location.

questions.stem: Broca area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) is located in the:
options: Posterior superior temporal gyrus
Middle frontal gyrus
Inferior frontal gyrus
Supramarginal gyrus
