questions.explanation: Broca area occupies the inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis and triangularis) of the dominant hemisphere and supports speech production; lesions cause nonfluent aphasia with relatively preserved comprehension. The posterior superior temporal gyrus is Wernicke area; the middle frontal gyrus contains the frontal eye field; the supramarginal gyrus is parietal and linked to conduction aphasia.

questions.stem: Focal aware seizures (formerly simple partial seizures) are characterized by:
options: Retained awareness throughout the seizure
Impaired awareness with oral automatisms
Bilateral onset with brief loss of awareness
Impaired awareness after an initial aura
questions.explanation: Focal aware seizures (formerly simple partial) are defined by preserved awareness: the patient knows the seizure is happening and can respond. Impaired awareness with automatisms or after an aura defines focal impaired awareness seizures; bilateral onset with brief loss of awareness describes absence seizures.

questions.stem: Focal impaired awareness seizures (formerly complex partial seizures) are characterized by:
options: Preserved awareness with a motor or sensory aura
Bilateral onset with 3 Hz spike-and-wave
Impaired awareness, often with automatisms
Generalized stiffening followed by jerking
questions.explanation: Focal impaired awareness seizures (formerly complex partial) involve impaired awareness, so the patient cannot respond appropriately, often with automatisms such as lip smacking or fumbling. Preserved awareness defines focal aware seizures; bilateral onset with 3 Hz spike-and-wave is an absence seizure; stiffening then jerking is a tonic-clonic seizure.

questions.stem: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are characterized by:
options: A clonic phase, then a tonic phase, with preserved awareness
A tonic phase, then a clonic phase, with loss of consciousness
Sudden loss of tone causing a fall, with rapid recovery
Brief staring with eyelid flutter and no postictal state
questions.explanation: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures start with a tonic phase (rigid extension) followed by a clonic phase (rhythmic jerking), with loss of consciousness and postictal confusion. Awareness is not preserved; sudden loss of tone with a fall is an atonic seizure; brief staring with eyelid flutter is an absence seizure.

questions.stem: Status epilepticus is defined as:
options: A seizure over 2 minutes, or two seizures within one day
Any seizure that requires a benzodiazepine for termination
Three or more seizures within 24 hours with full recovery
A seizure over 5 minutes, or seizures without recovery between
questions.explanation: Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or two or more seizures without return to baseline between them; it is an emergency (the older definition used 30 minutes). Two minutes is within typical seizure duration; needing a benzodiazepine does not define status; three seizures in a day with full recovery describes a seizure cluster.

questions.stem: Resting tremor is most characteristic of:
options: Parkinson disease
Essential tremor
Cerebellar disease
Physiological tremor
questions.explanation: Resting tremor, the pill-rolling tremor that improves with action, is most characteristic of Parkinson disease. Essential tremor is a postural/action tremor; cerebellar disease causes intention tremor; physiological tremor is a fine postural tremor enhanced by anxiety, caffeine or fatigue. Tremor recognition helps identify rhythmic movement artifact on EEG.

questions.stem: Chorea is characterized by:
options: Sustained contractions causing twisting postures
Rhythmic, regular oscillation of a limb at rest
Brief, irregular, flowing involuntary movements
Sudden, brief shock-like jerks of a muscle group
questions.explanation: Chorea consists of brief, irregular, involuntary movements that flow from one body part to another; it is classic in Huntington disease and also seen in Sydenham and drug-induced chorea. Sustained twisting contractions are dystonia; rhythmic oscillation at rest is a resting tremor; shock-like jerks are myoclonus.

questions.stem: Dystonia is characterized by:
options: Brief, irregular movements flowing between body parts
Sustained contractions causing twisting or abnormal postures
Rhythmic tremor of the hands during goal-directed action
Wide, flinging movements of a proximal limb on one side
questions.explanation: Dystonia is sustained muscle contraction causing twisting, repetitive movements or abnormal postures; it can be focal (writer's cramp, cervical dystonia), segmental or generalized. Brief flowing movements are chorea; tremor during goal-directed action is intention/action tremor; flinging proximal movements are hemiballismus.

questions.stem: In Alzheimer disease, the EEG typically shows:
options: Periodic sharp wave complexes at about 1 Hz
Excess diffuse beta with a faster posterior rhythm
Focal temporal slowing with a normal background
Diffuse slowing with a slowed posterior rhythm
questions.explanation: Alzheimer disease shows diffuse slowing and slowing or loss of the posterior dominant rhythm, worsening as the disease progresses; early disease may look nearly normal. Periodic sharp wave complexes at about 1 Hz suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease; excess beta reflects medication effect; focal temporal slowing with normal background suggests a focal lesion.

questions.stem: In Parkinson disease, the EEG is typically:
options: Normal early; mild slowing later, often with dementia
Periodic sharp wave complexes from early in the disease
Frequent frontal spikes that correlate with the tremor
Marked diffuse slowing from the time of diagnosis
questions.explanation: In Parkinson disease the EEG is usually normal early; mild diffuse slowing may appear later, especially with Parkinson disease dementia. Periodic sharp wave complexes suggest CJD; the tremor produces rhythmic artifact, not cerebral spikes; marked slowing at diagnosis would suggest another process such as encephalopathy.

questions.stem: Dementia with Lewy bodies is characterized by:
options: Early memory loss with preserved attention and gait
Early disinhibition and apathy with spared memory
Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism
Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and ataxia
questions.explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies features fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behavior disorder; the EEG often shows posterior slowing. Early memory loss with preserved attention and gait suggests Alzheimer disease; disinhibition with spared memory suggests frontotemporal dementia; rapid dementia with myoclonus suggests CJD.

questions.stem: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis most commonly affects:
options: The occipital lobes
The medial temporal lobes
The brainstem and cerebellum
The parasagittal frontal lobes
questions.explanation: HSV encephalitis most commonly affects the temporal lobes, especially the medial temporal and orbitofrontal regions, causing fever, focal seizures, memory impairment and behavior change; EEG may show lateralized periodic discharges or focal temporal slowing, and acyclovir is urgent. Occipital, brainstem/cerebellar and parasagittal frontal involvement are not typical.

questions.stem: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is characterized by:
options: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures with hyponatremia
Ascending weakness, areflexia, raised CSF protein
Subacute dementia, startle myoclonus, periodic complexes
Psychosis, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, dysautonomia
questions.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and autonomic instability, often with an ovarian teratoma; the EEG may show extreme delta brush. Faciobrachial dystonic seizures with hyponatremia suggest LGI1 encephalitis; ascending weakness with areflexia is Guillain-Barre syndrome; dementia with myoclonus and periodic complexes suggests CJD.

questions.stem: Hepatic encephalopathy is characterized on EEG by:
options: Diffuse slowing with triphasic waves
Focal temporal slowing with spikes
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave
Excess diffuse beta with normal PDR
questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy produces diffuse slowing with triphasic waves (classic but not pathognomonic; also seen in uremia and other metabolic states) and may progress to burst suppression when severe. Focal temporal slowing with spikes suggests focal epilepsy or a lesion; 3 Hz spike-and-wave suggests absence epilepsy; excess beta suggests a sedative drug effect.

questions.stem: Severe hypoglycemia on EEG may show:
options: Excess beta activity with a faster posterior rhythm
Periodic sharp wave complexes at about 1 Hz
Diffuse slowing that may progress to seizures
Isolated focal spikes with a normal background
questions.explanation: Severe hypoglycemia causes diffuse slowing, may provoke epileptiform discharges or seizures, and if prolonged can progress to an isoelectric record; it must be corrected urgently. Excess beta is a sedative drug effect; 1 Hz periodic sharp wave complexes suggest CJD; isolated focal spikes on a normal background suggest focal epilepsy.

questions.stem: Temporal lobe seizures (focal impaired awareness) are often associated with:
options: Hypermotor thrashing with very rapid recovery
Déjà vu aura, lip smacking and postictal confusion
Elementary visual hallucinations and eye deviation
Brief staring with no aura and no postictal state
questions.explanation: Temporal lobe focal impaired awareness seizures typically have an aura (déjà vu, fear, epigastric rising), oral or manual automatisms and postictal confusion; EEG shows temporal spikes or sharp waves, often maximal at T1/T2 or sphenoidal electrodes. Hypermotor seizures with rapid recovery suggest frontal lobe; visual hallucinations with eye deviation suggest occipital lobe; staring without aura or postictal state suggests absence.

questions.stem: Frontal lobe seizures are often characterized by:
options: Déjà vu aura, lip smacking and prolonged confusion
Elementary visual hallucinations and eye deviation
Brief staring with 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG
Brief nocturnal hypermotor seizures with rapid recovery
questions.explanation: Frontal lobe seizures are often brief, frequent and nocturnal with hypermotor behavior (thrashing, bicycling), vocalizations and rapid postictal recovery; the scalp EEG may show frontal spikes or be normal when the focus is deep. Déjà vu with lip smacking suggests temporal lobe; visual hallucinations suggest occipital lobe; staring with 3 Hz spike-and-wave is an absence seizure.

questions.stem: Typical absence seizures are characterized on EEG by:
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave with abrupt onset and offset
Generalized 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave on photic stimulation
Generalized 1.5-2.5 Hz slow spike-and-wave, gradual onset
Focal centrotemporal spikes activated by drowsiness and sleep
questions.explanation: Typical absence seizures show generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave with abrupt onset and offset, often provoked by hyperventilation, with brief staring and no postictal confusion. 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave with photosensitivity suggests JME; 1.5-2.5 Hz slow spike-and-wave suggests atypical absence in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome; centrotemporal spikes suggest self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes.

questions.stem: Alpha coma pattern on EEG is characterized by:
options: Posterior alpha rhythm that attenuates with eye opening
Sleep spindles and vertex waves in a comatose patient
Diffuse alpha-range activity that does not react to stimuli
Frontal alpha that increases with painful stimulation
questions.explanation: Alpha coma is widespread, often frontally prominent 8-13 Hz activity that is non-reactive to eye opening or stimulation; it follows diffuse anoxic injury (typically frontally prominent), brainstem (pontomesencephalic) lesions (often posterior), or drug/sedative intoxication; prognosis is usually poor except in drug-induced cases, which are often reversible. A reactive posterior alpha is the normal rhythm; spindles and vertex waves in coma define spindle coma; reactivity to pain argues against alpha coma.

questions.stem: Spindle coma pattern on EEG is characterized by:
options: Non-reactive diffuse alpha activity in a comatose patient
Sleep-like spindles and vertex waves in a comatose patient
Alternating bursts and flat periods in a comatose patient
Continuous diffuse beta in a sedated comatose patient
questions.explanation: Spindle coma shows sleep-like spindles (often with vertex waves and K complexes) in a comatose patient, indicating relatively preserved brainstem and thalamocortical function and generally a better prognosis than alpha coma, depending on cause. Non-reactive alpha is alpha coma; alternating bursts and suppression is burst suppression; diffuse beta suggests sedative drug effect.

questions.stem: Burst suppression pattern on EEG indicates:
options: A normal quiet-sleep pattern in a healthy term neonate
A focal structural lesion confined to one hemisphere
A benign drowsiness variant seen in healthy adults
Severe diffuse brain dysfunction or deep anesthesia
questions.explanation: Burst suppression, alternating bursts of activity with periods of suppression, indicates severe diffuse cerebral dysfunction, e.g. after anoxia or drug overdose, or deep anesthesia; prognosis depends on the cause and is poor after anoxia but the pattern is reversible when drug-induced. The normal term-neonate quiet-sleep pattern is trace alternant; the pattern is diffuse, not focal; it is not a benign variant.

questions.stem: In term neonates, the normal EEG background during quiet sleep shows:
options: Trace alternant pattern
Trace discontinu pattern
Burst-suppression pattern
Low-voltage irregular pattern
questions.explanation: In term neonates, normal quiet sleep shows trace alternant: high-amplitude bursts alternating with lower-amplitude (not suppressed) periods. Trace discontinu is the normal pattern of preterm infants; burst suppression indicates severe encephalopathy; low-voltage irregular activity characterizes active (REM) sleep.

questions.stem: The posterior dominant rhythm (PDR) frequency in children:
options: Matches the adult 8-13 Hz range from early infancy
Decreases with age as the brain matures and myelinates
Increases with age, reaching about 8 Hz by age 3
Stays near 4 Hz until puberty, then jumps to alpha
questions.explanation: The posterior dominant rhythm speeds up with maturation: about 3-4 Hz at 3-4 months, 5-6 Hz at 1 year, about 8 Hz by age 3, and adult 8-13 Hz by adolescence; this is normal maturation and must be considered in pediatric EEG. It does not start in the adult range, does not slow with age, and rises gradually rather than jumping at puberty.

questions.stem: Hyperventilation is most effective in activating:
options: Temporal lobe seizures
Typical absence seizures
Frontal lobe seizures
Myoclonic seizures in JME
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation is the most effective activation for typical absence seizures with 3 Hz spike-and-wave. It lowers PaCO2, causing cerebral vasoconstriction and reduced cerebral blood flow; diffuse slowing (build-up) is a normal response. Focal temporal or frontal seizures are activated far less reliably, and myoclonic seizures in JME are better provoked by photic stimulation and sleep deprivation.

questions.stem: Photic stimulation is MOST likely to activate which finding in a photosensitive patient?
options: Focal temporal spikes with an epigastric aura
Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta
Generalized photoparoxysmal spike-and-wave
Rhythmic midtemporal theta bursts
questions.explanation: Intermittent photic stimulation can provoke a photoparoxysmal response (generalized spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave) in photosensitive epilepsies such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and some absence epilepsies, which is why it is a standard activation procedure. Temporal spikes with an aura reflect focal temporal lobe epilepsy, which is not typically photosensitive; FIRDA is a nonspecific encephalopathic pattern; rhythmic midtemporal theta is a drowsiness variant, not a photic response.

questions.stem: Sleep activation is most effective for:
options: Only absence seizures
Focal epileptiform discharges (especially temporal lobe spikes) and some generalized epilepsies - sleep increases epileptiform activity
Only generalized seizures
Only myoclonic seizures
questions.explanation: Sleep activation is most effective for focal epileptiform discharges, especially temporal lobe spikes, and some generalized epilepsies. Sleep increases epileptiform activity. NREM sleep (especially stage 2) is most effective. Sleep deprivation before EEG increases yield.

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam, diazepam) on EEG typically cause:
options: Increased frontal beta activity
A faster posterior dominant rhythm
Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta
Periodic lateralized discharges
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines (and barbiturates) characteristically increase beta activity, roughly 18-25 Hz, often most prominent frontally. They do not speed the posterior dominant rhythm (sedation tends to slow it), FIRDA reflects encephalopathy or deep midline dysfunction, and periodic lateralized discharges point to an acute focal lesion rather than a drug effect. Recognizing medication beta avoids misreading it as abnormal fast activity.

questions.stem: Some antiepileptic drugs (e.g., phenobarbital) may cause:
options: Periodic generalized sharp waves
A faster posterior alpha rhythm
Prominent occipital lambda waves
Excess generalized beta activity
questions.explanation: Barbiturate antiseizure drugs such as phenobarbital increase beta activity, similar to benzodiazepines, so the technologist should note current medications when fast activity is seen. Periodic generalized sharp waves suggest conditions such as CJD or anoxia, sedating drugs do not speed the posterior alpha rhythm, and lambda waves are a normal eyes-open visual scanning phenomenon unrelated to medication.

questions.stem: Ictal EEG patterns are characterized by:
options: Isolated spikes that recur at a fixed interval
Rhythmic discharges evolving in frequency and field
Brief sharp waves each followed by a slow wave
A steady rhythm that stays unchanged in frequency
questions.explanation: Ictal patterns are rhythmic discharges that evolve, changing in frequency, amplitude, or spatial distribution over the course of the seizure. Isolated spikes at a fixed interval and single sharp-and-slow-wave complexes are interictal; a steady unchanging rhythm lacks evolution, which is the key feature separating seizures from interictal or non-ictal rhythmic activity.

questions.stem: Interictal epileptiform discharges (spikes/sharp waves) are:
options: Brief, non-evolving discharges seen between seizures
Rhythmic discharges that evolve over several seconds
Brief discharges recorded only during seizures
Sustained rhythmic activity with clinical change
questions.explanation: Interictal epileptiform discharges (spikes and sharp waves) are brief, non-evolving transients that occur between seizures; they indicate epileptogenic potential but are not seizures themselves. Evolving rhythmic discharges and sustained rhythmic activity with clinical change describe ictal patterns, and IEDs are by definition recorded between, not only during, seizures.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child with tonic seizures in sleep and atypical absences has a slow background with diffuse polymorphic delta and 1.5-2.5 Hz slow spike-and-wave on EEG. This is MOST consistent with:
options: Childhood absence epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic)
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS)
questions.explanation: LGS typically begins between 18 months and 8 years; tonic seizures are required, with at least one other type such as atypical absence, atonic, myoclonic or GTC seizures. The EEG shows a slow, disorganized background with diffuse polymorphic delta, slow spike-and-wave at 1.5-2.5 Hz, GPFA in sleep, and cognitive impairment. Childhood absence epilepsy shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave on a normal background at an older age; JME begins in adolescence with 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave; SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy) shows centrotemporal spikes on a normal background.

questions.stem: The characteristic interictal EEG pattern in Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) includes:
options: 3 Hz spike-and-wave on a normal background
Centrotemporal spikes activated by drowsiness
Slow spike-and-wave, diffuse delta, sleep GPFA
Hypsarrhythmia with electrodecremental spasms
questions.explanation: The interictal EEG in LGS shows slow spike-and-wave at 1.5-2.5 Hz (slower than the 3 Hz of absence epilepsy), diffuse polymorphic delta reflecting diffuse cortical dysfunction, and generalized paroxysmal fast activity during sleep. 3 Hz spike-and-wave on a normal background is childhood absence epilepsy; centrotemporal spikes are SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy); hypsarrhythmia is the pattern of infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (formerly West syndrome) that may precede LGS.

questions.stem: Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) is characterized by:
options: Typical absence seizures with normal cognition
Tonic, atonic, atypical absence and other types
Nocturnal focal motor seizures of the face
Myoclonic jerks on awakening in adolescence
questions.explanation: LGS is defined by multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic drop attacks, atypical absence, myoclonic and GTC seizures), forming a triad with slow spike-and-wave and cognitive impairment. Typical absences with normal cognition describe childhood absence epilepsy, nocturnal facial focal seizures describe SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy), and morning myoclonic jerks in adolescence describe JME.

questions.stem: Dravet syndrome in a 2-year-old may show:
options: Hypsarrhythmia with clusters of epileptic spasms
Centrotemporal spikes activated by drowsiness
Generalized spike-wave, slowing, photosensitivity
Classic 3 Hz spike-and-wave on a normal background
questions.explanation: Dravet syndrome begins in the first year with prolonged febrile and afebrile seizures; by age 2 the EEG often shows background slowing, generalized spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave, and photosensitivity, with myoclonic seizures and developmental delay emerging. Hypsarrhythmia with spasms is infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (formerly West syndrome), centrotemporal spikes are SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy), and 3 Hz spike-and-wave on a normal background is childhood absence epilepsy.

questions.stem: Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (formerly Doose syndrome / myoclonic-astatic epilepsy) may present with:
options: Myoclonic-atonic drops, generalized spike-wave
Epileptic spasms with a hypsarrhythmic EEG
Focal seizures with centrotemporal spikes
Typical absences with 3 Hz spike-and-wave
questions.explanation: Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (formerly Doose syndrome) presents in early childhood with myoclonic jerks followed by atonic drops, often with GTC seizures, and generalized 2-6 Hz spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave, often with a 4-7 Hz parietal theta rhythm; prognosis is variable, with some children remitting and others evolving toward LGS. Spasms with hypsarrhythmia are infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (formerly West syndrome), centrotemporal spikes are SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy), and typical absences with 3 Hz spike-and-wave are childhood absence epilepsy.

questions.stem: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (formerly West syndrome) may evolve to:
options: Childhood absence epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic)
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS)
questions.explanation: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (formerly West syndrome; spasms with hypsarrhythmia) frequently evolves into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, with hypsarrhythmia giving way to slow spike-and-wave and diffuse polymorphic delta as tonic and other seizures develop; both belong to the epileptic encephalopathy spectrum. Childhood absence epilepsy, JME and SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy) are self-limited or genetic generalized syndromes with normal backgrounds and are not typical outcomes of infantile spasms.

questions.stem: Diffuse polymorphic delta activity in children with GTC seizures indicates:
options: A benign maturational variant of early childhood
Diffuse cortical dysfunction, as in encephalopathy
A focal structural lesion confined to one lobe
Drowsiness-related slowing of no significance
questions.explanation: Diffuse polymorphic delta in a child with GTC seizures indicates diffuse cortical dysfunction, such as a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (e.g., LGS) or severe brain injury, and needs clinical correlation. It is not a benign maturational variant; a focal lesion produces focal, not diffuse, polymorphic delta; and drowsiness slowing is monomorphic and reactive rather than persistent polymorphic delta in wakefulness.

questions.stem: Generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) during sleep is highly characteristic of:
options: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS)
Childhood absence epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic)
questions.explanation: Generalized paroxysmal fast activity (about 10-20 Hz bursts) during sleep, often accompanying tonic seizures, is a hallmark of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and, with slow spike-and-wave and diffuse polymorphic delta, helps distinguish it from other syndromes; sleep recording is therefore important. Childhood absence epilepsy shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave, JME shows 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave, and SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy) shows centrotemporal spikes.

questions.stem: Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) is associated with:
options: Normal development with remission by puberty
An isolated motor deficit with normal cognition
Language regression with otherwise normal IQ
Cognitive impairment and developmental delay
questions.explanation: Cognitive impairment and developmental delay are part of the LGS triad (multiple seizure types, slow spike-and-wave, cognitive impairment), and the prognosis is generally poor. Normal development with remission describes self-limited syndromes such as SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy); an isolated motor deficit is not characteristic; acquired language regression with preserved nonverbal ability suggests Landau-Kleffner syndrome.

questions.stem: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) can be distinguished from epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (EMAtS, formerly Doose syndrome) by:
options: Only LGS shows generalized spike-and-wave
Only EMAtS shows a diffuse slow background
Course: LGS persists, while EMAtS may remit
LGS begins later, usually after age 10
questions.explanation: The clearest difference is the clinical course: LGS is chronic and persistent with cognitive impairment, whereas epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (formerly Doose syndrome) may remit by about age 5-10 years and has a better prognosis. Both can show generalized spike-and-wave, both can have a slowed background and GTC seizures, and LGS typically begins at 1-8 years, not after age 10.

questions.stem: Other conditions that may present with diffuse polymorphic delta activity and GTC seizures in 2-year-olds include:
options: SeLECTS or self-limited occipital epilepsy
Severe brain injury or metabolic encephalopathy
Childhood absence epilepsy with normal cognition
Self-limited focal epilepsy of later childhood
questions.explanation: Besides LGS, diffuse polymorphic delta with GTC seizures in a 2-year-old can result from severe brain injury, metabolic encephalopathy, post-encephalitic epilepsy, or other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, all of which cause diffuse cortical dysfunction. SeLECTS (formerly benign rolandic epilepsy) and self-limited occipital epilepsies, childhood absence epilepsy and other self-limited focal epilepsies have a normal background and begin later in childhood.

questions.stem: Which arterial territory is MOST commonly affected by ischemic stroke?
options: Anterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Vertebrobasilar system
Middle cerebral artery
questions.explanation: The MCA territory is the most common site of ischemic stroke; the MCA is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery and supplies the lateral frontal, parietal and temporal lobes. ACA strokes are uncommon, and PCA and vertebrobasilar strokes together account for a smaller share (posterior circulation is about 20% of strokes).

questions.stem: A left middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke affecting the anterior division would most likely cause:
options: Non-fluent aphasia with good comprehension
Fluent aphasia with poor comprehension
Non-fluent aphasia with poor comprehension
Fluent aphasia with impaired repetition only
questions.explanation: The anterior (superior) division of the left MCA supplies the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area), producing Broca aphasia: non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension. Fluent speech with poor comprehension is Wernicke aphasia (posterior division); non-fluent speech with poor comprehension is global aphasia (whole MCA); impaired repetition alone is conduction aphasia.

questions.stem: A right middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke would most likely cause:
options: Non-fluent aphasia
Left hemispatial neglect
Right homonymous hemianopia
Isolated right leg weakness
questions.explanation: The right hemisphere is non-dominant in most people, so a right MCA stroke characteristically causes left hemispatial neglect along with left face and arm weakness. Aphasia points to the dominant (left) hemisphere; a right hemianopia and right leg weakness would come from left-sided lesions (left PCA and left ACA).

questions.stem: The EEG finding most characteristic of a middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke is:
options: Midline frontal and central region slowing
Occipital region slowing on one side only
Lateral frontal, temporal and parietal slowing
Bilateral frontal rhythmic delta bursts
questions.explanation: The MCA supplies the lateral convexity, so focal slowing appears over lateral frontal, temporal and parietal electrodes (e.g., F3/F7, T3/T5, P3 on the left). Midline frontal/central slowing (Fz, Cz) fits ACA territory, occipital slowing fits PCA territory, and frontal intermittent rhythmic delta is a nonspecific pattern of diffuse or deep dysfunction rather than a cortical MCA lesion.

questions.stem: Internal carotid artery (ICA) occlusion can cause:
options: Isolated contralateral hemianopia
Brainstem signs with vertigo and ataxia
Isolated ipsilateral third nerve palsy
Combined ACA and MCA territory deficits
questions.explanation: Both the ACA and MCA arise from the internal carotid, so ICA occlusion can produce combined ACA and MCA deficits with a large territorial infarct; ophthalmic artery ischemia can cause amaurosis fugax. Isolated hemianopia suggests PCA stroke, brainstem signs suggest vertebrobasilar disease, and an isolated third nerve palsy suggests a PCom aneurysm.

questions.stem: The hallmark sign of posterior cerebral artery (PCA) stroke is:
options: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia
Contralateral face and arm weakness
Contralateral leg-predominant weakness
Non-fluent aphasia with good comprehension
questions.explanation: The PCA supplies the occipital (visual) cortex, so its hallmark is a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing. Face and arm weakness is typical of MCA stroke, leg-predominant weakness of ACA stroke, and non-fluent aphasia of a dominant anterior MCA stroke.

questions.stem: Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) stroke would most likely cause which EEG finding:
options: Midline frontal slowing with a normal posterior rhythm
Occipital slowing with a reduced posterior rhythm
Temporal slowing with a normal posterior rhythm
Diffuse suppression of all background activity
questions.explanation: A PCA stroke damages the occipital cortex, so slowing appears over the occipital electrodes (O1/O2) with loss or reduction of the posterior dominant rhythm on the affected side. Midline frontal slowing suggests ACA territory, isolated temporal slowing with a normal PDR suggests a lateral MCA-territory lesion, and diffuse suppression reflects severe global injury rather than a single PCA infarct.

questions.stem: Basilar artery stroke is characterized by:
options: Left neglect with face and arm weakness
Fluent aphasia with poor comprehension
Diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo and ataxia
Leg weakness with abulia and incontinence
questions.explanation: The basilar artery supplies the pons, midbrain and cerebellum, so occlusion produces brainstem signs: diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo, ataxia and reduced consciousness; severe pontine infarction can cause locked-in syndrome. Left neglect with face/arm weakness is right MCA, fluent aphasia is left posterior MCA, and leg weakness with abulia is ACA.

questions.stem: A patient with a basilar artery stroke has a depressed level of consciousness. Which EEG finding is MOST expected?
options: Focal slowing over one temporal region
Focal slowing over one occipital region
Lateralized periodic discharges on one side
Diffuse slowing with reduced reactivity
questions.explanation: Basilar strokes that impair the brainstem arousal systems produce diffuse slowing with reduced reactivity (a brainstem lesion may instead give an alpha-coma pattern, which is often posterior-predominant and partly reactive). Focal temporal or occipital slowing and lateralized periodic discharges point to a hemispheric cortical lesion. Note that a pure ventral pontine (locked-in) lesion that spares arousal can leave the EEG near normal.

questions.stem: Locked-in syndrome is caused by:
options: Basilar artery occlusion
Bilateral ACA occlusion
Bilateral PCA occlusion
Large left MCA occlusion
questions.explanation: Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral ventral pontine infarction, usually from basilar artery occlusion: quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements. Bilateral ACA infarction causes abulia or akinetic mutism, bilateral PCA infarction causes cortical blindness, and a large left MCA stroke causes right hemiplegia with global aphasia.

questions.stem: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is caused by:
options: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Superior cerebellar artery
Anterior spinal artery
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome results from occlusion of the PICA or the parent vertebral artery: vertigo, nystagmus, dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ataxia. AICA occlusion causes lateral pontine syndrome, SCA occlusion mainly cerebellar ataxia, and anterior spinal artery occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome.

questions.stem: Berry aneurysms most commonly occur at:
options: Distal cortical branches of the MCA
Small deep lenticulostriate arteries
Branch points of the circle of Willis
Cervical segment of the vertebral artery
questions.explanation: Saccular (berry) aneurysms form at arterial branch points around the circle of Willis, most often the ACom, PCom and MCA bifurcation; rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage. Distal cortical aneurysms suggest infectious (mycotic) aneurysms, lenticulostriate microaneurysms relate to hypertensive hemorrhage, and the cervical vertebral artery is more prone to dissection.

questions.stem: A posterior communicating artery (PCom) aneurysm would most likely cause:
options: Sixth nerve palsy with horizontal diplopia
Facial nerve palsy with loss of taste
Trigeminal sensory loss over the face
Third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil
questions.explanation: A PCom aneurysm compresses the oculomotor nerve (CN III): dilated pupil, ptosis, and a "down and out" eye from unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique. A sixth nerve palsy is a classic false-localizing sign of raised ICP; facial and trigeminal deficits arise from lesions of CN VII and CN V, not PCom compression.

questions.stem: An anterior communicating artery (ACom) aneurysm would most likely cause:
options: Frontal behavioral and personality change
Third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia
Hoarseness with difficulty swallowing
questions.explanation: ACom aneurysms (especially after rupture) affect the medial frontal lobes, causing behavioral and personality change, abulia and memory problems. A third nerve palsy suggests a PCom aneurysm, homonymous hemianopia suggests PCA territory, and hoarseness with dysphagia suggests lateral medullary (PICA) involvement.

questions.stem: The Circle of Willis provides:
options: Venous drainage from deep cerebral structures
Collateral flow between carotid and basilar systems
The main route for CSF absorption into blood
The sole arterial supply to the brainstem
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis is an arterial ring linking the anterior (carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulations, so collateral flow can maintain perfusion if one vessel is occluded. Deep venous drainage is through the internal cerebral veins and vein of Galen, CSF is absorbed through arachnoid granulations, and the brainstem is supplied mainly by vertebral and basilar branches.

questions.stem: Watershed infarcts occur at:
options: The core of a single major arterial territory
Territories of small deep penetrating arteries
Border zones between major arterial territories
Regions drained by the dural venous sinuses
questions.explanation: Watershed infarcts occur in border zones between ACA, MCA and PCA territories, typically with systemic hypotension or severe ICA stenosis, and may give bilateral parasagittal slowing on EEG. Infarcts in the core of one territory are embolic or thrombotic territorial strokes, small penetrating-artery infarcts are lacunes, and venous infarcts follow sinus thrombosis.

questions.stem: Acute ischemic stroke on EEG typically shows:
options: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges
Bilateral frontal intermittent rhythmic delta
A normal background with no focal change
Focal polymorphic delta over the affected area
questions.explanation: Acute cortical ischemia produces focal polymorphic (arrhythmic) delta slowing, often with loss of faster activity, over the affected territory. Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave is typical of absence epilepsy, FIRDA is a nonspecific sign of diffuse or deep dysfunction, and EEG changes appear within minutes of cortical ischemia, so a normal record is not expected in a cortical stroke.

questions.stem: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) from aneurysm rupture would most likely cause:
options: Diffuse slowing, sometimes with lateralized periodic discharges
Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges with normal background
Normal background with isolated benign vertex sharp transients
Focal excess beta activity limited to the frontal midline region
questions.explanation: Aneurysmal SAH spreads blood over the cortical surface and raises ICP, producing diffuse slowing; focal cortical irritation can add lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs, formerly PLEDs), and EEG can also detect vasospasm-related focal slowing. Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave is an absence epilepsy pattern, vertex sharp transients are normal sleep features, and isolated midline beta does not reflect SAH.

questions.stem: A large middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke would most likely cause:
options: Gaze deviation away from the side of the lesion
Gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion
Vertical gaze palsy with eyelid retraction
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia on one side
questions.explanation: A large MCA stroke damages the frontal eye field, so the intact opposite field drives the eyes toward the side of the lesion ("looks at the lesion"). Gaze away from the lesion suggests a seizure focus or a pontine lesion; vertical gaze palsy with lid retraction is a dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) sign; INO comes from medial longitudinal fasciculus lesions.

questions.stem: The key difference between anterior and posterior circulation strokes is:
options: Anterior: vision and balance; posterior: limbs and language
Anterior: vision and alertness; posterior: limbs and balance
Anterior: limbs and language; posterior: vision, balance, alertness
Anterior: language and alertness; posterior: limbs and vision
questions.explanation: Anterior circulation (ICA, ACA, MCA) strokes typically affect movement, sensation and language; posterior circulation (vertebral, basilar, PCA) strokes affect vision, balance, eye movements and consciousness. The other options mix up or reverse these associations.
